name: Kansas Reflector
title: Former Kansas employee sues Republican legislators who wanted her fired over Charlie Kirk post
text:
Kansas Senate President Ty Masterson speaks ahead of President Donald Trump's rally Oct. 19, 2026, at Heartland Credit Union Arena in Park City. Masterson called for former state employee Katie Allen to be fired last year over a comment she made when Charlie Kirk was killed. (Photo by Sherman Smith/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — A former state employee sued Kansas Senate President Ty Masterson and two other Republican legislators for demanding she be fired over a comment she posted to Facebook when Charlie Kirk was killed in September 2025.
Katie Allen, who was a research analyst at the Kansas State Department of Education, was fired five days later,  after Masterson, Sen. Brad Starnes and Rep. Megan Steele directed the public to contact then-education commissioner Randy Watson and demand she lose her job. Her lawsuit, filed Wednesday in federal court, accuses them of violating her First Amendment right to free speech.
The lawsuit says Watson believed he had no choice but to fire her after receiving thousands of emails from angry Kansans. She previously sued the state agency and Watson for wrongful termination, and a jury trial is scheduled for March 2.
Masterson also posted Allen’s personal cellphone number on his official Kansas Senate President Facebook page and urged people to call her, according to the lawsuit. She received death threats, including an email titled “resign or die,” in which the writer promised to “blow your f*****g brains out if you don’t resign.” Masterson later deleted his post.
The lawsuit says “Masterson acted with evil motive and intent or with reckless or callous indifference to Allen’s First Amendment rights.”
Allen is represented by Overland Park attorneys Mark Dugan and Heather Schlozman. Campaign finance reports show Dugan has donated $400 to Democrat Cindy Holscher’s campaign for governor.
“Two weeks before an election, a lawyer who donates to Cindy Holscher filed a lawsuit to try to help her campaign. That tells you what this is,” said Garrett Henson, a spokesman for Masterson’s campaign. “It doesn’t change what Ty believes: no one should be celebrating political violence. That’s something Kansans of every party agree on.”
Holscher’s campaign declined to comment.
Kirk, the conservative activist described in the lawsuit as “a polarizing public figure,” was shot and killed Sept. 10, 2025, while speaking at Utah Valley University.
While walking to her car after work that day, the lawsuit says, Allen saw a Facebook post about one of Kirk’s quotes on gun violence.
“I think it’s worth to have a cost of, unfortunately, some gun deaths every single year so that we can have the Second Amendment to protect our other God-given rights,” Kirk said in 2023, as reported by Media Matters.
Allen commented on the Facebook post: “Well deserved.”
The lawsuit says she thought better of the commented by the time she reached her car and deleted it. Later that night, she posted an apology, saying she made the comment in “an emotional moment,” and then “quickly realized I didn’t intend the meaning of the two words I wrote.”
“That is not who I am or what I believe — which is why I deleted that comment so fast,” she wrote. “Like many of you, I am deeply concerned about the violence and discontent happening in America today and will continue to advocate for common sense laws that keep our kids (and) community safe. When I make a mistake, I own it and promise to do better.”
The next day, Masterson and wrote on his Facebook, X and Instagram accounts that Watson needed to immediately remove her form his position. He and Starnes also issued a press release that day calling for her to be fired.
On Sept. 12, Masterson posted a “call to action” on Facebook, urging people to call Watson and demand she be fired. He also listed Allen’s personal cellphone number and encouraged people to call her directly.
Masterson has since removed his Sept. 11 and Sept. 12 Facebook posts, the lawsuit says.
After Watson fired her on Sept. 15, Masterson took credit for the firing and called for her to resign from her position on the Manhattan-Ogden school board, where she still serves.
Starnes, who is in the middle of a four-year Senate term, and Steele, who is running unopposed for her House seat, represent districts that include the Manhattan-Ogden schools.
Starnes posted his press release on his Facebook page and reposted Masterson’s posts. Starnes also sent email messages from his Senate account to Watson and a Kansas State Board of Education member asking for Allen to be fired.
Steele posted on her Facebook page to “strongly urge” Watson to fire Allen and asked her followers: “Take a stand. Demand she resign.” Steele also wrote to each member of the State Board of Education identifying herself as a House member. The lawsuit said she called Allen’s comment “disgusting and inexcusable” and said she “has no place working for the State of Kansas or any place near our children’s education.”
“I strongly urge you to immediately demand Allen resign or be fired,” she wrote.
Board member Cathy Hopkins responded and said she was speaking with Watson about the matter.
Watson called Allen on Sept. 15 and asked her to resign. She declined and proposed a 30-day suspension, the lawsuit says. Watson fired her instead.

name: Daily Montanan
title: Democrat Sam Forstag outraises Republican Aaron Flint in western US House district
text:
Voters enter a polling location at the Lewis and Clark County Library on Nov. 5, 2024. (Photo by Blair Miller, Daily Montanan)As the 2026 election cycle nears its close, campaign spending continues to heat up in Montana’s competitive races.
Campaign finance filings through Oct. 14 show Democrat Sam Forstag with a lead in both total fundraising and cash on hand over Republican Aaron Flint in a tight race for Montana’s western Congressional district.
Forstag has raised $4.3 million and had $726,000 on hand, while Flint has raised $2.8 million and has about $408,000 on hand, according to the most recent reports with the Federal Election Commission.
In the last quarter alone, Forstag received more than $2 million, while Flint took in about $1.2 million.
Earlier this month, three political analyses moved the race toward Forstag, including two that rate it a “toss up.”
But Flint has been the beneficiary of high-level visits by President Donald Trump, House Speaker Mike Johnson and, next week, Vice President JD Vance. Flint noted the Vance visit on a social media post.
In the U.S. Senate race, independent candidate Seth Bodnar has raised slightly under $5 million, while Republican Kurt Alme, favored to win by analysts, has raised a bit more than $3 million. Alani Bankhead, the Democratic U.S. Senate candidate, has raised less than $200,000 per federal election filings and Libertarian candidate Kyle Austin has self-funded to the tune of $250,000.
In the eastern U.S. House district, incumbent Republican Rep. Troy Downing has raised about $2.1 million. Democrat Brian Miller has raised about $30,000.
Montana’s congressional delegation has been all Republican since Democratic U.S. Sen. Jon Tester lost re-election in 2024.
Flint and Forstag’s campaigns did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Election Day is Nov. 3.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Candidates for Iowa governor discuss their top priorities: cancer, cost of living
text:
Republican Zach Lahn and Democratic state Auditor Rob Sand are competing in the Nov. 3, 2026 election to become Iowa's next governor. (Candidate photos by Zach Sommers for Iowa Capital Dispatch, Iowa Capitol photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)In the race for Iowa governor, Democrat Rob Sand and Republican Zach Lahn agree addressing high cancer rates and making life more affordable for Iowans are their top priorities if elected Nov. 3, 2026 — but the candidates shared different opinions on how to tackle these problems.
For the first time since 2006, Iowa has an open gubernatorial race as Republican Gov. Kim Reynolds announced she would not seek reelection. Sand, the state auditor and only Democrat to currently hold statewide elected office in Iowa, quickly emerged as the frontrunner to become the Democratic nominee and exited the primary unopposed. Lahn, a self-described entrepreneur and farmer, faced a more contentious journey to the general election ballot. He emerged as the GOP gubernatorial nominee from a five-man primary, which included U.S. Rep. Randy Feenstra, who was endorsed by President Donald Trump.
Iowa Capital Dispatch sat down with the two candidates to speak about why they joined the race and what they hope to accomplish if elected.
 Why run?



Sand said his road to running for governor began when he served as the state’s “chief public corruption prosecutor” as assistant attorney general, and then ran and won his seat as state auditor in 2018. He said during his time in office, he put together a senior leadership team that included an independent and Republican, and said his office worked together, across party divisions to uncover “a record amount of misspent money across the state of Iowa in my first term.”
“And then the Legislature came back to town and made it harder for us to find misspent tax money,” Sand said. “So, that to me was a clarifying moment. You know, I’ve been working against corruption for years and then it turned out that the Legislature went and passed the biggest pro-corruption bill in Iowa history to try to stop us from doing our jobs.”
Sand has long been critical of Senate File 478, a law signed by Reynolds in June 2023. The measure prevents the auditor from going to court for subpoena enforcement against state agencies, departments, boards, commissions and statewide elected officials. The law instead directs these disputes to a board of arbitration made up of two members appointed by the parties involved, and a third member appointed by the governor. It also limits the state auditor’s ability to access personal information when performing investigations.
When this law passed, Sand said it mean two things for him — the first being that there “wasn’t much point in running for a third term as state auditor, because I can get told that I’m not allowed to do my job.”
“The other piece of it was, it really clarified for me just how bad things had gotten in the Capitol building,” Sand said. “If they are at a moment where we are at the bottom for economic growth, we’re at the top for cancer growth, our education system is now in the bottom half, we have a water quality crisis, we have a cancer crisis — and their definition of a problem they have to address is making sure the state auditor can’t find misspent money, then I think we need a new direction.”



Lahn said he had “no intention” to run for Iowa governor, but decided to enter the race because he believed many of Iowans’ top concerns were not being addressed by those currently in office.
“I saw long-term issues that our state’s been facing for many years that hadn’t been addressed,” Lahn said. “And I often say, that’s both parties that have been in power as some of these long-term trends have gone the wrong way. You know, we’ve we’re losing our kids faster than 46 other states. We’ve lost 10,000 family farms (in) the past 20 years. Our public education system went from number one when I was in elementary to number 27. And we have the fastest rate of new cancer in the country. … They’re long-term issues, so they’re going to take long-term efforts. But I wanted do give those issues of voice, and that’s why I got in.”
Lahn has not previously held elected office, though he has experience in politics working for Americans for Prosperity, a conservative political advocacy group affiliated with the founders of Koch Industries, and working for a state senator in Colorado. After working for Americans for Prosperity, he moved to Witchita, Kansas, and launched Wonder, a private pre-kindergarten through 12th-grade school, in 2018 on the campus of Wichita State University. The businessman said his experience in the private sector would help inform his approach to the Iowa governorship.
“The way I look at it, from a business standpoint, … I always look at, ‘what are the key metrics I want to be tracking?'” Lahn said. “The lagging indicator to me is, are Iowa’s kids staying or going? … If you look at this, kids aren’t going to want to stay or come back if they have a higher chance of getting cancer, if the public education system’s in the bottom half, if the rural communities are being hollowed out. So, I think it takes a full, different look at how we’re addressing this.”
 Top issues
Lahn said keeping Iowa’s youth in the state is a top priority for his campaign — and said addressing concerns like rising cancer rates, improving the state’s education system and incentivizing people living and working in rural communities are ways to keep young families in Iowa. He said his policies focus on an “Iowa First” approach — prioritizing population retention for the state.
He proposed incentive programs for children graduating from Iowa high schools to encourage them to stay in the state, such as eliminating the income tax “for a set amount of years that would go into an account that they could use on a down payment on a home.”
“If you look at the math on this, let’s say, even if it was $50,000 (in lost revenue through income taxes) … every kid (that) we lose, that leaves our state is about $400,000 in lost tax revenue to the state over their lifetime,” Lahn said. “And that’s aside from the cultural piece of tight-knit families, good communities, good rural areas, all of these things. The state’s also losing tax revenue, and I see that as a way that we can, you know, take some of that, pay it forward so to speak, as a down payment.”
He also said he would focus Iowa’s medical research and agricultural institutions on “local problems instead of global problems,” such as addressing high cancer rates and water quality problems in the state. Additionally, he said he would support other measures, like tying public university funding to the percentage of Iowans going to these educational institutions, as ways to prioritize Iowans.
Lahn said he was “looking at the problems we’re facing from that standpoint of ‘Iowa first,’ and how can we direct the economy and the governor of the state to make life better for the people who live in the state.”
“On the other end of this, you have groups that are, you know, kind of categorized as special interests, lobbyists, corporate giants which have gotten far too much for a very long time from the government both from the state and federal level,” Lahn said. “And so those are a bit of the things that I am fighting against as well to say that incentives that we have should go to the people. And if they’re going to business, they need to go to Iowa’s home grown businesses.”
Sand said over the course of his campaign, three major issues have stood out.
“We’ve got high costs, we’ve got high cancer and we’ve got high corruption,” Sand said. “We need to address all three of those.”
Sand said his campaign has released specific plans on how to address these three subjects. His campaign has released policy platforms that include proposals on how to tackle these issues. His affordability plan includes proposals to end the privatization of Medicaid, provide universal free school lunches and his cancer proposal includes a call to invest in radon testing and water quality monitors, and he supports higher penalties for people convicted of stealing taxpayer funds. But Sand said these problems facing Iowans stem from a larger problem with how politicians currently approach the two-party political system.
“We are centered on ending the special legal privileges of the Democratic and Republican parties, because we’re going to have high costs and high corruption and high cancer rates — or other serious problems — as long as politicians don’t have to solve our problems,” Sand said. “And right now they don’t. You don’t have to solve problems in order to get reelected, and that’s bad. It should be that whether or not you succeed is dependent upon whether or not you’ve actually delivered for people. But instead we have a system that really functions to help incumbent politicians get re-elected, and that’s not good for us.”

name: Kansas Reflector
title: U.S. labor secretary praises Kansas manufacturing industry in visit to Topeka business
text:
From left, U.S. Rep. Derek Schmidt, U.S. Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling and U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall visit Haas Metal Engineering's main hub on Oct. 23, 2026, in Topeka as part of the secretary's tour across the northeastern part of the state. (Photo by Anna Kaminski/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — U.S. Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling lauded U.S. job growth and Kansas’ manufacturing industry during a series of visits Friday, assuaging criticisms against the Trump administration for burdensome tariffs.
He appeared Friday afternoon alongside U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall and U.S. Rep. Derek Schmidt at Haas Metal Engineering in Topeka. It was the secretary’s last stop on a three-part tour along the Interstate 70 corridor, visiting Kansas City Kansas Community College in Olathe and the University of Kansas Research Innovation Park in Lawrence. He hosted discussions on each of the stops to talk about how to connect students to the workforce.
Sonderling described the current state of the manufacturing industry as undergoing a “renaissance,” as Marshall did during a debate Wednesday. He touted workforce investments, job growth in the private sector and increased demand for manufacturing products. 
“My visit in Kansas today has really been seeing that the national policies that we’re working on, the three of us are working on together, along with President Trump, are really paying off here, and it’s ultimately benefiting local workers here in Kansas,” Sonderling said. “We’re going to give them a workforce and an education system to meet these jobs that are being created.”
U.S. Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling, left, and U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kansas, on Oct. 23, 2026, visit Haas Metal Engineering’s main hub in Topeka, Kansas, as part of Sonderling’s series of visits across the northeastern part of the state. (Photo by Anna Kaminski/Kansas Reflector)
Some manufacturers have a less rosy view of the economy as tariffs have hiked up costs associated with steel and aluminum imports, gas is a dollar more in Kansas than it was a year ago and the average price of a gallon of diesel has doubled in the past year.
Schmidt, who is running for reelection in the 2nd District against Democrat Don Coover, said building more refining capacity in the U.S. is critical to controlling the cost of fuel long-term.
“Because when we build it here, when we manufacture it here, we control our destiny,” Schmidt said. “And we’ve seen what happens when you allow your competitors to have leverage over your supply chains.”
Marshall, who is running for reelection against Democrat Adam Hamilton, said he was tired of aluminum and steel being imported from China and Canada on a “free ride.”
“We want that aluminum steel to be made here as well, and we’re going to make it with clean energy and with fair labor,” he said.
Haas Metal Engineering fabricates structural steel, shipping to job sites across the U.S. It has contributed to the construction of McConnell Air Force Base in Wichita, the U.S. Air Force Academy in Colorado and the Immaculata Church in St. Marys, Kansas.
The company has more than 780 employees, and Jon Haas, president of Haas Metal Engineering, attributes most of the troubles facing the manufacturing industry to supply and demand.
Jon Haas, president of Haas Metal Engineering, speaks to reporters on Oct. 23, 2026, outside his business in Topeka, following a visit from the U.S. labor secretary. (Photo by Anna Kaminski/Kansas Reflector)
He buys mostly American steel, so tariffs haven’t had an outsized impact on his business, he said.
“Supply and demand is what really governs the price of our raw materials,” Haas said. “With the economy the way it is right now with construction, that’s driving the prices.”
He said the construction economy is “booming like we’ve never seen before.”
He said he has a multiyear backlog. He said the company consistently has government contracts, calling it “a big part of what we do.” The company helps build hospitals, schools and wastewater treatment plants, and Haas said data centers have provided a steady flow of work. 
Sonderling, Schmidt and Marshall conducted a roundtable with Haas and other business owners from the area, which was closed to the press. Beforehand, Sonderling took a tour of the company’s hub.
Haas on Monday will host Vice President JD Vance near the same location of the secretary’s Friday visit. He said it was a “great honor” to be chosen by the White House. 
Haas, an engineer who started the company from his garage in the ‘90s, said he will be supporting Schmidt and Marshall on Election Day.

name: The Texas Tribune
title: Trump administration can hold immigrants in ICE custody without bond, court rules
text: The entrance to the Bluebonnet Detention Center in Anson on Aug. 22, 2026. The privately run immigration detention center is operated by Management & Training Corporation, under contract with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Immigrants in ICE detention have no due process rights under US Constitution, federal appeals court says
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Bobbi-Jeanne Misick is an investigative reporter at Verite News, and Mukta Joshi is an investigative reporter at Mississippi Today. They are spending a year as New York Times Local Investigations fellows covering immigration and other issues. They can be reached at bobbi.misick@nytimes.com and mukta.joshi@nytimes.com. 
NEW ORLEANS — Immigrants who enter the United States without appointments with immigration officials can be detained indefinitely and are not entitled to bond hearings, regardless of how long they have lived in the country, the 5th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals ruled Friday.
The 10-7 decision was issued in the case of three immigrant fathers in Texas who were detained without bond. It applies to immigrants who have already entered the U.S., as well as those who will enter in the future, and it has far-reaching implications for the more than 20,000 people held indefinitely in detention centers in Texas, Louisiana and Mississippi – the states in the appeals court district. 
Rebecca Cassler, an attorney at the American Immigration Council, who represented the three men, said the ruling is “an affront to the U.S. Constitution.”
“The principle at stake here is simple: if the government wants to detain someone, it has to explain why depriving them of their liberty is necessary. And anyone who is detained has the right to ask a judge for review of that detention,” Cassler said. “Instead, this ruling allows the government to lock people up when detention plainly serves no purpose, and without any way to challenge it.” 
Texas, Louisiana and Mississippi hold more than 40% of all ICE detainees by average daily population, making the 5th Circuit the largest jurisdiction for people challenging their confinement as unconstitutional. So far, it continues to be one of only two circuits to have upheld the Trump administration’s mandatory detention policy.
The Supreme Court has agreed to take up a similar case from the 8th Circuit Court of Appeals, which will allow for precedent to be set regarding bond eligibility and indefinite detention for immigrants in removal proceedings. That case is expected to go before the justices early next year.
The 5th Circuit reversed an earlier decision by a panel of three of its own judges, which had granted  bond to immigrants in detention after 90 days. The new ruling says people in ICE detention have no constitutional right to due process.
In the majority opinion issued Friday, Judge Cory Todd Wilson wrote that immigrants who have been in the U.S. a long time are still “applicants for admission” and therefore are subject to mandatory detention without bond.
The seven judges who dissented agreed that constitutional rights, including the right to liberty, are available to all people present in the United States. Judge Leslie H. Southwick wrote in dissent, “statutory admission status does not decide when aliens gain due process rights. The Constitution, after all, is supreme, with statutes’ needing to conform to its dictates, not the Constitution to statutes.” 
James Percival, general counsel for the Department of Homeland Security, praised the majority’s ruling.
“Big win in the Fifth Circuit on mandatory detention for illegal aliens, a principle codified in 1996 legislation but ignored by the deep state for decades,” Percival said Friday.
The three-judge panel had ruled in July that the Trump administration’s policy of denying certain due process rights to immigrants who entered the United States without formal appointments with immigration officials, no matter how long they had resided in the country, was unconstitutional. The panel ruled that the government must hold bond hearings for immigrants arrested within the U.S. within 90 days of their detention. 
However, 10 days later, and with no official prompting from the federal government, the entire court decided to re-consider the case. The announcement of the hearing paused the relief that the panel of judges had granted to the three men. The 5th Circuit is generally regarded as one of the most conservative in the nation.
In 2025, constitutional petitions by immigrants pleading to be released began inundating federal courts across the country, after the Trump administration stopped a long practice of providing bond hearings to those who had lived in the U.S. for years. To date, more than 80,000 such petitions have been filed nationally. About a quarter of these have been filed within the 5th Circuit.
Federal district courts in Texas, Louisiana and Mississippi will continue to have the power to grant habeas corpus petitions on a discretionary basis,  but Friday’s ruling “would foreclose nearly all of those petitions from being granted on constitutional grounds,” Cassler said. 
Until the Trump administration ramped up its immigration crackdown in 2025, federal courts for decades had distinguished between people arrested at the U.S. border and those who had built lives in the country. The latter would automatically receive bond hearings, which would allow an immigration judge to decide whether the person was dangerous or posed a flight risk.
Then Trump’s second presidential term began and ICE detention populations exploded. In August, ICE boasted that it had broken its own record of the number of people it had arrested, as populations inside detention facilities across the South swell, triggering complaints of crowding. Andrei Zykov, a detainee at the Adams County Correctional Center in Mississippi, said Thursday that the facility designed to hold 2,200 people has been holding more than 2,600 for weeks, based on the number of meals kitchen workers were asked to prepare. 
The 5th Circuit’s latest decision has effectively sealed the path for hundreds of them who hoped to be released while immigration judges decided whether they could remain in the U.S.  
Attorneys for American Immigration Council and the National Immigration Project, who represent the three men, argue that the case, as well as the issue of habeas corpus, is about personal liberty, a constitutional right that they say is granted to all people within the United States. 
The government continues to argue that immigrants who entered the country without those formal appointments, which is called entering without inspection, are not entitled to certain constitutional rights no matter how long they have lived in the U.S., because their very presence in the country is unlawful. 
Illegally entering the U.S. is, in most cases, a misdemeanor. Cassler said the government is trying to rob immigrant detainees of  rights that are guaranteed even to violent criminals. 
“When people murder someone and they’re put on trial for it, the government’s interests are at their strongest,” Cassler said. “They want to protect the community. They want to make sure that that person doesn’t go kill someone else. And even in those cases, that person has very robust rights to due process with regard to their pretrial custody. Violating the law doesn’t take away your constitutional rights.”
Robert Stewart of Verite News contributed reporting.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Trump comes to Fort Myers to fire up the GOP base
text:
Screenshot of President Donald Trump speaking in Fort Myers on October 23, 2026.With some polls showing the races for governor and U.S. Senate relatively close in the Sunshine State 11 days before Election Day, President Donald Trump held a rally Friday afternoon in Fort Myers.
His mission was to inspire Florida Republicans — who maintain a more than 1.5 million voter registration advantage over Democrats — to get to the polls to vote for the GOP up and down the ticket, but particularly for Byron Donalds for governor and Ashley Moody for Senate.
He did so for a few minutes at both the beginning and the end of his 90-minute address, with the main body of the speech focused on his own accomplishments in the White House, as well a lot of other stream-of-consciousness commentary.
That same day, Florida Democratic gubernatorial candidate David Jolly and Angie Nixon, running for U.S. Senate, rallied at the Florida A&M University campus in Tallahassee.
Trump called Jolly, a former Republican congressman, a “radical left candidate.”
“I never told Byron this, but I knew Jolly as a Republican,” the president said. “And he was thrown out of the party like a dog. We threw him the hell out. He was terrible. He didn’t represent anything that we stood for. He was in the party and didn’t represent. He was also a bad guy. The guy had no heart. No soul. Everybody hated this guy so much … a very disloyal person.”
Jolly acknowledged in 2018 when he left the GOP that he found it impossible to be “never-Trump” and remain a Republican. He didn’t become a Democrat until last year.
As Vice President JD Vance did in his appearance in Lakeland earlier this month, Trump emphasized Jacksonville state Rep. Angie Nixon’s membership in the Democratic Socialists of America.
“This is the free state of Florida, where people come to escape communists and not to elect them,” he said. “The Sunshine State is not going to send a Marxist maniac to the Senate.” He later referred to Nixon as “a lunatic.”
Trump has always been popular in Florida, winning the state by 1 point in 2016, 3 points in 2020 (when he lost the general election to Joe Biden), and 13 points in 2024. And although his poll numbers are historically bad nationally at the moment (a CNN/SSRS survey recently found his approval rating at a record-low 32%), an NBC6/Telemundo poll showed the president’s approval at 48% in Florida, with his disapproval rating also at 48%.
The president did get into some foreign policy in his speech.
He hinted that the U.S. may attack Iran again soon, adding, “If they’re smart, they’ll just say, ‘Let’s get down to business.’ But I doubt they’ll do that.” He added that ships returning from the Middle East could stop over in Cuba on their way back from Iran.
In addition to Donalds and Moody, U.S. Sen. Rick Scott, Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier, Agriculture Commissioner Wilton Simpson, U.S. Rep. Greg Steube, and Republican National Committee chair Joe Gruters all addressed the crowd at Alico Arena at Florida Gulf Coast University.
‘Communist’
Trump took a few breaks during this appearance, allowing Donalds, Moody, and Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. to speak. RFK Jr. used his time on stage to announce the Trump administration’s “America First Seafood Strategy,” which included a rollout of a new, voluntary “U.S. Caught Seafood” label.
In her speech before Trump appeared, Moody called Nixon a “communist.”
“Do you think that this is a time to keep calm and carry on? We must win this battle. The state of Florida is under attack. Listen to me: We have to make the slogans, ‘Don’t tread on me’ and ‘Don’t mess with Texas’ look PG. You know what we need to say? ‘Don’t F with Florida,’” she said with a grin. “You got that?”
One Florida Republican who did not speak at the rally was Ron DeSantis. The governor did greet the president when he landed at Southwest Florida International Airport in Fort Myers earlier in the day.
Florida Democratic Party chair Nikki Fried derided the president’s visit. She said the fact that Trump was visiting a county he won by nearly 30 points just two years ago implies that one of two things was happening.
“Either they’re having trouble turning out their base, including in Lee County, and have to have daddy come home and rev up the base; or two, they went to Lee County to do less harm to the rest of the Republican ticket,” she told reporters Thursday.

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Republican candidate Michael Alfonso supports voucher style system for healthcare
text:
Republican candidate Michael Alfonso has said he would support a voucher style system for healthcare (Alfonso headshot courtesy of campaign)Republican candidate Michael Alfonso has said he would support a voucher style system for healthcare, including Medicare, in the U.S., according to a Milwaukee Journal Sentinel report Friday.
Alfonso, the son-in-law of Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, is running against former Democratic state lawmaker Fred Clark to represent Wisconsin’s 7th Congressional District. The district, which encompasses a large swath of northern Wisconsin, is currently represented by Republican U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany, who is running for governor.
Alfonso was at a campaign event in River Falls when he was asked about school choice programs that direct public money to cover private school tuition for some students  in Wisconsin, and whether a similar approach might be applied to healthcare. 
Alfons said that the concept is his “entire approach” to healthcare, adding that the current system is a “nightmare.”
“If you look at it like school choice, instead of giving the money to the system or to the marketplace, give it to the people and they can choose their coverage,” Alfonso said.
According to KFF, the policy, also known as a premium support system, would provide a payment to Medicare beneficiaries to help them purchase a health insurance plan, either a private plan, Medicare Advantage plan or traditional Medicare. 
The approach has been supported by representatives in Congress before including former House Speaker and Wisconsin U.S. Rep. Paul Ryan. In 2012, analysts said the approach could leave beneficiaries with higher costs, less coverage or both.
The Medicare Rights Center, a national nonprofit, recently wrote about the issue saying that “under this type of system there would be no standard benefit package and no guarantee that the coverage a person buys with their voucher would cover essential health services.” Medicare beneficiaries currently receive a guaranteed standard of health coverage. 
“As much as I want to get the government out, you can’t do it overnight,” Alfonso said. “The first step is giving the money to you, and you can pick your coverage. If you want a high deductible and save some money, great. If you want a low deductible because you’re someone that’s going to meet that deductible real quick, then awesome. I don’t think the government knows what’s best for you. I think you know what’s best for you.”

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Madison Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway announced she is dropping reelection bid
text:
Madison Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway is ending her bid for reelection. Rhodes-Conway speaking at an SEIU event in 2021. (Erik Gunn | Wisconsin Examiner)Madison Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway announced Friday that she will not run for a third term in office, canceling her reelection bid citing threats to herself, city council members, staff and her family
Rhodes-Conway had initially announced her reelection campaign in July 2026. She was first elected in 2019 and won reelection in 2023 by an 11-point margin. In her statement, she said that she was “confident that voters would judge my record favorably and grant me another term,” but that the “price of serving has become too high.” 
“This was not an easy decision, but it is the right decision for me and my family, our personal safety, mental health and wellbeing,” Rhodes-Conway said. 
Over the summer, Rhodes-Conway and the city faced significant criticism following the killing of 38-year-old Corey Ruiz at the hands of a Madison police officer. A protest encampment on the east side of Madison, near the site of the shooting, was eventually cleared by the city, triggering more controversy. 
This week, the interim independent police monitor who had been investigating the Ruiz shooting was fired in a 14-6 vote by the city’s common council. Local activists, who testified against the firing, protested the council’s vote and shouted “shame” as council members were escorted out of the building by police.
Aeiramique Glass, the independent monitor, had drawn criticism for getting into an altercation with police officers while they worked to clear the protest encampment at the site of the Corey Ruiz shooting. A dispute also emerged within city government over her authority to subpoena materials related to the incident from the police department and the Wisconsin Department of Justice. 
Rhodes-Conway did not directly mention the issue in her statement. 
“Madison has long been home to impassioned and spirited debate. But it is not hyperbole to say local democracy is at risk, not just from MAGA and right-wing extremists in the federal and state governments, but from a toxic political culture that is transcending partisanship and ideology,” Rhodes-Conway said. 
Rhodes-Conway said she wants people to take a “hard look at our local political ecosystem” during the remainder of her term. She said over her time in office she has seen “the balance has shifted from productive discussion to increasingly vitriolic, personal attacks from people who seem not to care about actually understanding and debating an issue.”
“How can any leader govern responsibly when personal attacks and baseless conspiracies carry more weight than facts? How can any mayor be effective when a difference of opinion is cast as unforgivable betrayal that justifies threats of violence?” Rhodes-Conway said. “When I ran for mayor, I expected to make sacrifices – but I did not expect the level of threats to myself, Council members, my staff, and my family. I did not expect our civic discourse to deteriorate so severely. And I did not expect the levels of implicit and explicit sexism to which I have been subjected to from the very beginning of my first campaign.”
Dane County Executive Melissa Agard thanked Rhodes-Conway for her service and said in a statement that she was troubled by the role threats and harassment played in Rhodes-Conway’s decision.
“No one who steps forward to serve their community should have to fear for their safety or the safety of their loved ones. We must do better to ensure that public service remains something people can pursue without intimidation,” Agard said. 
The mayor’s departure creates an open race for the leader of Wisconsin’s capital city. Eight candidates had already announced they would challenge Rhodes-Conway. They include One City Schools founder Kaleem Caire, former Madison Common Council President Syed Abbas, Brian Benford, April Kigeya, Marcus Robert Johnson, Natalia Hacerola and Larry Williams. 
“We need leaders who are more interested in making the government function well than in performing for social media,” Rhodes-Conway said in the statement announcing her departure.  “We need leaders who want to continuously improve, but won’t let the perfect be the enemy of the good. We need leaders who are able to listen to and balance a wide range of voices. Above all, we need leaders who put the needs of Madison before their popularity or political futures, and we need to elect leaders who understand the job they are running for.”
Rhodes-Conway said she is proud that during her time in office she has been able to steer the city though the COVID-19 pandemic, dealt with lawmakers who wanted to take “away our funding and powers,” helped build new housing and invest in new infrastructure as well as launch the city’s new bus rapid transit system.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: Some Measure 1 backers see it as a roadblock to potential abortion rights initiatives in ND
text:
Voters mark their ballots during the first day of early voting at the Bismarck Event Center on Oct. 22, 2026. Some supporters of Measure 1 see it as a way to thwart a future potential abortion rights initiative in North Dakota.
(Photo by Jack Dura/North Dakota Monitor)Some supporters of a ballot measure to require at least 60% voter support to change North Dakota’s constitution say the move would help block a potential abortion rights initiative in the future.
Opponents say the measure would make it harder to pass any constitutional amendment, giving more power to a minority of voters.
[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: The info you need to cast your ballot.]
North Dakota Right to Life and figures such as North Dakota’s Catholic bishops are among those urging “yes” votes on Measure 1. State Sen. Janne Myrdal, an anti-abortion leader in the Legislature, said she expects the Washington, D.C.-based Fairness Project or another out-of-state group will support a ballot initiative to add abortion rights to North Dakota’s constitution in 2028.
“That is their stated intention, and that’s been their intention all along, is from what we’re seeing now,” said Myrdal, R-Edinburg. 
The Fairness Project has spent more than $1.6 million to defeat Measure 1, according to online campaign finance filings as of Friday.
The organization did not immediately respond to North Dakota Monitor emails for comment. Measure 1 supporters have cited statements on the organization’s website, such as: “We’re running progressive policies in red states — and we’re winning.” Its website lists a Virginia reproductive rights measure among its campaigns.
North Dakota has a near-total ban on abortion.
60% threshold for changing North Dakota’s constitution debated as a protection or a barrier

In the group’s 2023-2024 Impact Report, the Fairness Project describes defeating North Dakota’s Measure 2 in 2024 — a measure Myrdal introduced that would have added several requirements amounting to a higher bar to amend the state constitution, such as a single-subject requirement, more ballot initiative petition signatures and approval in two elections.
The report said: “We won with 57% of the vote, keeping North Dakota on the map for a future abortion ballot measure, minimum wage, paid sick leave, and more.”
The report also describes a constitutional initiative for abortion rights as “an option” for six states in 2026, including North Dakota. Such a measure did not emerge this year.
“We are not slowing down on our mission to protect reproductive rights in state constitutions by passing ballot measures wherever we can,” the nearly 2-year-old report said.
The 2023 Legislature banned the performance of an abortion as a felony crime. The only exceptions are in cases of rape or incest in the first six weeks, and to protect the life or health of the mother.
A lawsuit by North Dakota’s only abortion provider, since moved from Fargo to nearby Moorhead, Minnesota, ended last year when the state Supreme Court upheld the abortion ban. Though three of the five justices found the law to be unconstitutional, North Dakota requires four of the five justices to do so, a high bar rare among states.
Myrdal cited Prairie Action North Dakota Executive Director Amy Jacobson as an opponent to Measure 1. The Fairness Project’s report quotes Jacobson “as a state-based partner.” 
Jacobson is a sponsor of Measure 2 to provide free school meals to K-12 students. She called the messaging about an abortion rights initiative “a fear tactic” that Myrdal and others are “using to try to motivate their base with a disingenuous message.” 
“My only response would be that there’s nothing to indicate that that is happening, and that it is clearly an intentional tactic that they’re using to strike fear into their voters, and they’re not being honest,” Jacobson said.
Sponsor, opponent debate need for North Dakota ballot measure to change constitution

Jacobson, also a member of a coalition that opposes Measure 1, said during an event this week that it would make any constitutional ballot measure difficult to pass. Another member of the coalition, the American Cancer Society Cancer Action Network, wants to preserve constitutional ballot measures for possible public health issues, citing a recent South Dakota vote related to expanding Medicaid. 
North Dakota Right to Life and Catholic Bishops John Folda of Fargo and David Kagan of Bismarck have urged voters to support Measure 1, citing other states where abortion rights amendments have passed with less than 60% of the vote, including neighboring Montana. They also referenced a 2024 Florida abortion rights measure that received 57% support but didn’t go into that state’s constitution because of a 60% requirement.
“A 60 percent threshold would provide an additional safeguard against constitutional changes that could undermine North Dakota’s commitment to protecting unborn children,” the bishops wrote in a social media post Friday.
Republican Gov. Kelly Armstrong blasted the Fairness Project in a recent ad by StrongND, a group aligned with him.
“A radical, liberal special-interest group is pouring millions into North Dakota. Their goal? Running progressive policies in red states. Those are their words, not mine,” Armstrong said in the ad, which features the logos of Measure 1 endorsers such as North Dakota Right to Life.
“What we will see out of the Fairness Project in future elections is whatever their liberal donors want to run. I don’t know what that is,” Armstrong said in an interview with the Monitor.
The organization is not spending money in this election cycle to sit out the next one, he said.
“They’re not doing this out of the goodness of their heart. So whatever that is, I don’t think that will be something that Republicans in North Dakota support,” the governor said.
He said he is concerned about constitutionally mandated spending in future ballot initiatives. The governor acknowledged that all future constitutional amendments, even ones proposed by the Legislature, would need to reach 60% voter support to pass. 
“That’s a good thing. Changing the constitution should be harder no matter who is proposing the change. It should take broad support from North Dakotans,” Armstrong said.
StrongND has spent more than $1.5 million to support Measure 1, according to online campaign finance filings as of Friday.
Advocates make case against measure to raise constitutional amendment threshold

Measure 1 supporters have said North Dakota’s constitution should not be easy to change and needs a higher bar than a simple majority to do so. House Speaker Robin Weisz, R-Hurdsfield, sponsored the measure as a resolution in the Legislature last year. Blocking abortion rights was not his motivation to introduce the measure, he said.
“My main reason for doing it is that I believe our constitution is extremely important and needs to be protected and it should just be hard to change, no matter what the issue is,” Weisz said.
Opponents say the 60% threshold would trample on their rights and make it harder to enact change when the Legislature does not act as constituents wish.
The vast majority of constitutional amendments in recent years have passed with more than 60% support, including ones creating the Legacy Fund, crime victim rights, gubernatorial and legislative term limits and a congressional age limit.
Measure 1 needs a simple majority to pass.
Reach North Dakota Monitor reporter Jack Dura at jdura@northdakotamonitor.com.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Come together: Jolly and Nixon stump on FAMU campus as election draws near
text:
Student organizers at Florida A&M University protested the university police department's cooperation with federal immigration efforts during Friday Oct. 23, 2026, homecoming festivities. Top-of-ticket candidates David Jolly and Angie Nixon appeared before a rally on campus later in the day. (Photo by Jay Waagmeester/Florida Phoenix)The two Democrats at the top of the Florida party’s statewide ticket came together Friday on the campus of Florida A&M University — one of the few times they have campaigned in tandem since winning their nominations.
Both Democratic gubernatorial candidate David Jolly, a former Republican, and Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Angie Nixon, who embraces Democratic Socialist principles, stood on a stage on FAMU’s campus with famed film producer Will Packer, an alumnus who riled up the crowd by saying the university is “under attack right now because of the forces in politics.”
He referred to FAMU President Marva Johnson, whose presidency has alarmed a considerable bloc of alumni because of her political ties to Gov. Ron DeSantis.
As the Democrats gathered briefly on the stage in Tallahassee, President Donald Trump was in Fort Myers, where he led a campaign rally for Republican gubernatorial nominee Byron Donalds and Ashley Moody, running for election to the Senate in her own right, having been appointed by DeSantis.
Friday marked Jolly’s sixth visit to FAMU in as many months, his most recent at a student government-sponsored event. He told the crowd he wants to return FAMU to its golden era of civil rights advocacy. To that end, he repeated his commitment to deliver $2 billion in enhanced funding to the university, money former students have alleged in a lawsuit the state owes the university.
In Lakeland visit, JD Vance says Angie Nixon ‘doesn’t belong in America’

Nixon, who followed Jolly onstage, started her remarks with her usual, “Can I get a Duuu-val?” — the chant borrowed from her hometown NFL team, the Jacksonville Jaguars. She reminded the crowd of Vice President JD Vance’s comments that she “doesn’t belong in America,” and hammered away at her opponent, Moody, and her involvement as Florida attorney general in the Hope Florida controversy.
“Ashely Moody can call me whatever she wants. JD Vance can say whatever he wants about me. Donald Trump can say whatever they want. But come Nov. 3, they will be calling me senator. Let’s go. Let’s go,” she told the crowd.
Muted anti-ICE march
Before Nixon and Jolly took the stage, on the other side of campus FAMU student organizers marched to call upon the university to revoke its 287(g) agreement with the federal government, deputizing campus police officers to assist in federal immigration enforcement. 
The protest, which drew about eight students, came well more than a year after Florida universities’ police departments made national headlines for signing the agreements. 
Led by FAMU Students for a Democratic Society, the gathering began alongside a bustling stretch of food vendors celebrating FAMU homecoming. Participants chanted, “No hate, no fear, immigrants are welcome here.”
Jayla Jones, a fourth year political science student, flagged Johnson’s appointment as president as a sticking point. “Our campus culture has shifted a lot,” she said.
“Our protest is surrounding the 287(g) agreement, and we do understand that to get it off we do need a different governor than Ron DeSantis and the Republican Party that allows for the 287(g) agreement to be in Florida and to also be on FAMU’s campus,” Jones said. 
“Especially with recent attacks on voting rights, I feel like this has made our campus more urgent to vote,” Jones said. “FAMU is definitely down with going to the polls.”
Early voting
As of 8:05 a.m. Friday, about half of vote-by-mail ballots requested from county supervisors of elections had been returned — more than 1.21 million — while more than 1.25 million remained outstanding. Of those returned, 522,621 were from registered Democrats, 437,393 from registered Republicans, and 229,440 from no-party-affiliation voters. 
At the same time, 763,595 people had voted at an early voting location, with 333,394 registered Republicans and 282,005 registered Democrats. Nearly 130,000 no-party-affiliation voters had cast early ballots. 
The Leon County supervisor of elections office operates 10 early voting sites across the county, including one at FAMU with three voting machines. According to the Leon County elections office, 50 people had voted as of 2:30 p.m. Friday.
FAMU alum Achaia Jackson said he tried to early-vote Friday but he wasn’t registered in Leon County. The opportunity to vote Florida’s first Black governor or first Black senator, he said, didn’t distinguish this election from past years’.
“For me, it’s just like do your job and do what’s in favor of the people, essentially, and not abuse the power. That’s my thing, really. It doesn’t matter about anyone’s race,” he said.
Jackson wasn’t well-versed on either Jolly’s or Donald’s politics, he said. He did know about Nixon, though, as he follows her on social media.
“Angie Nixon is amazing. I’ve seen her all over social media and she’s really in favor of doing the right thing. (She’s) in favor of people, especially with student debt. As a graduate right now, I’m still in debt and it would be great to have, you know, a lot of my fees waived and paid off.”

name: Source New Mexico
title: Gov. Lujan Grisham calls for 2027 to be the ‘year of New Mexico senior citizens’
text:
New Mexico Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham addresses attendees at the New Mexico Aging & Long-Term Services Department Conference on Aging Oct. 20, 2026, in Glorieta. (Leah Romero for Source NM)New Mexico Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham called for the upcoming 2027 legislative session to be the “year of New Mexico senior citizens” as the state is projected to have one of the largest populations of seniors 65 or older by 2030.
Lujan Grisham spoke to attendees of the state’s 48th annual Conference on Aging this week in Glorieta where approximately 1,000 New Mexico seniors, caregivers, professional careworkers and others gathered for informational sessions, panels and activities held over two days. This was the final aging conference before Lujan Grisham’s second and final term ends.
“You’re the reason this state works,” Lujan Grisham said on Tuesday, the first day of the conference. “It’s all of the retirees, it’s the grandparents raising grandchildren, it’s the families and generations of commitments that make this state who she is, and will determine what kind of future she has.”
Lujan Grisham praised the Legislature for supporting funding for universal childcare, early education, free access to college and decreasing childhood poverty rates during her administration, but said the populations needing the most support now are adults with disabilities, veterans and retirees. 
“Those are game changers for New Mexico’s future, but we can’t measure our future with those numbers and successes that I just rattled off if we aren’t taking care of the families who are still left behind by lack of federal support and funding, by inflation that is crippling everyone,” Lujan Grisham said. “This is not unique, I wish it was, and it’s cyclical. It’s happened before.”
She pointed to more direct transportation benefits, including the use of Uber, to make sure older adults can go to medical appointments; raising healthy food standards across the state, particularly as food costs have increased; and expanding and improving senior centers as a hub for services. Lujan Grisham added that she will be living in Albuquerque after her term ends and will commit to working with an area senior center to help make improvements. 
“Let’s rebuild something that New Mexico, for a long time, was known as one of the leaders in the country, because we can do that again, and we can do it in a way that supports our sovereign nations, our rural communities, our homebound elders and their families, and we can also create more working opportunities for people who desire that for their future,” Lujan Grisham said. 
Aging and Long Term Services Department Secretary Emily Kaltenbach told Source NM that insufficient caregiving capacity and social isolation are major issues facing the state currently. 
“We have older adults who live in rural areas without the natural supports because younger generations are moving to find economic stability elsewhere, leaving a lot of older adults in rural areas, and that social isolation really makes me nervous,” Kaltenbach said. “We’d like to support programs that address it early.”
According to the New Mexico Department of Finance and Administration, ALTSD’s Fiscal Year 2028 general fund request is $97 million, which is 25% higher than the previous year, and more than $120 million counting federal and other funding. The budget includes requests to add staffing within the Adult Protective Services Division and to make the Kiki Saavedra Dignity Fund, used to address “high-priority” services such as transportation and food insecurity, a permanent endowment. Kaltenbach is expected to present the department’s budget request to the Legislative Finance Committee in the next few weeks.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Commentary: Alaska’s ingenuity is a national asset
text:
Neal Brown preparing for the launch of a Taurus-Tomahawk sounding rocket, used for the “Bubble Machine I” barium-release experiment launched from Poker Flat in March 1981 in Fairbanks, Alaska. (Photo courtesy of Kristopher Brown)For a time growing up, I called a rocket range home.
My late father, Neal Brown, directed Poker Flat Research Range outside Fairbanks for 18 years. To the scientists who traveled there, it was a place to send instruments into the northern lights. To me, it was part of childhood: familiar people doing remarkable things in a place where winter demanded as much ingenuity as the science itself.
Helping recently bring his memoir to publication with Fairbanks writer Sue Mitchell has deepened my appreciation of what those people accomplished. “Northern Lights and Rocket Flights: My Years at Poker Flat Research Range,” has also reinforced my belief that scientific research is essential to Alaska’s future and to the nation’s strength.
Alaskans grow up understanding something that maps of the Lower 48 can obscure: Our state occupies a consequential place in the world. We face Russia across the Bering Strait and connect the United States to the Arctic and North Pacific. Our location makes Alaska central to national defense and Arctic affairs. It gives us an understanding of changes that carry consequences far beyond our borders.
But geography alone does not create strength. People, knowledge and institutions turn location into capability.    

Neal Brown and his son Kristopher in Fairbanks, Alaska, in front of a sign for the “Neal Brown” entrance road of Poker Flat Research Range in June 1986. (Photo courtesy of Kristopher Brown)
 

My father’s book captures how that happens. At Poker Flat, scientific ambition met the practical resourcefulness Alaska demands. Studying the upper atmosphere required sophisticated instruments and careful calculations. Getting those instruments off the ground required launchers, heated shelters, reliable equipment and people who could solve unexpected problems in extraordinary cold.
A mechanic’s experience or a technician’s judgment could be as essential to a successful mission as the scientist’s research plan. People built things, adapted equipment and learned from each launch. An elegant idea still had to work outside in an Alaska winter.
That combination feels familiar to anyone who grew up here. Alaskans value someone who can look at an unfamiliar problem and figure out what to do next. At Poker Flat, that ability helped build a research institution with international importance.
It also took persistence far from the launch pad.
My father traveled to Washington, D.C., and worked with Senators Ted Stevens and Frank Murkowski to help secure funding for Poker Flat. Explaining why research outside Fairbanks mattered to the country was part of keeping the range operating. Those relationships helped connect Alaska’s capabilities with federal support.    

Neal Brown on the phone is his office at Poker Flat in Fairbanks, Alaska, on May 1976. (Photo courtesy of Kristopher Brown)
 

His trips reflected a practical truth: ingenuity needs investment. A skilled crew cannot maintain a research facility on enthusiasm alone. Instruments, buildings, training and safety require sustained funding. So does the patient work between discoveries.
That continuity matters strategically as well as scientifically. A nation’s ability to operate in the Arctic depends partly on understanding its environment and sustaining people who know how to work there. Alaska’s research institutions help develop both that knowledge and that expertise.
Poker Flat offers a concrete example. Research into the aurora and upper atmosphere can improve our understanding of space weather, including conditions that affect satellite navigation. Understanding the environment above Alaska has practical implications for technologies on which civilian communities and military operations depend.
Across the state, research into permafrost, oceans, earthquakes and other natural systems also informs decisions about infrastructure, transportation and community safety. Alaska is a place where knowledge with national importance is generated.
The benefits begin at home. Research supports skilled employment, brings visiting teams into local businesses and gives young Alaskans opportunities to become scientists, engineers and technicians. A child watching a rocket launch can discover that ambitious work happens here, with Alaskans helping lead it.
I live in New York now, but Fairbanks is my hometown, and my pride in Alaska has never faded. Working on my father’s book reminded me how much I owe to a childhood surrounded by curious, capable people willing to attempt something difficult.
When I think about Alaska’s future, I think about those people. They understood the possibilities of their location and built the tools to explore them. Alaska’s importance to the nation rests partly on where it is. Its enduring strength comes from what its people can imagine, build and discover there.

name: VTDigger
title: Vermont commits $15.3M to expand heating assistance amid high fuel prices
text:
A Dead River Company fuel truck on a snowy Main Street in downtown Brattleboro, Vermont. Photo by Artaxerxes/Wikimedia Commons

Theo Wells-Spackman is a Report for America corps member who reports for VTDigger.
Vermont officials approved a $15.3 million state funding package to expand home heating aid programs on Friday.
The state administers lump-sum seasonal fuel assistance benefits for financially qualifying households and also directs funds to a program that provides aid in crises when eligible people run out of fuel later in the heating season. 
The new state money approved Friday will increase the amount of seasonal aid that Vermont can provide this year for households heating with oil and kerosene, which have skyrocketed in price. More than half of the roughly 15,000 financially qualifying households across Vermont that received help from the program last year rely on those two fuel types, officials said.
The package will also double the “crisis fuel” program’s capacity, allowing an extra 2,400 households to be able to receive payments to avoid a heating emergency this winter.
Residential heating oil prices have risen by about 76% since last fall, with kerosene prices soaring by 61% over the same period, officials estimated. A number of state and federal officeholders in Vermont have expressed increasing concern in recent weeks about their constituents’ ability to keep warm this winter in a state that depends heavily on oil for heating.
Vermont’s Emergency Board, which includes Republican Gov. Phil Scott and the four Democratic lawmakers who chair committees that oversee state finances, unanimously passed the proposal Friday.
In the past, seasonal heating benefits have generally covered about 45% of recipients’ anticipated fuel needs, drawing primarily on funds from the federal Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program, which is set to send Vermont nearly $23 million this year. The newly bolstered state program can likely cover about 62% of fuel needs this year for Vermonters using oil or kerosene, according to Miranda Gray, who leads the Economic Services Division of the Department for Children and Families.
About 38% of fuel assistance recipients in Vermont use home heating oil, and 14% use kerosene, according to her department, with others relying on alternatives like propane, wood or natural gas.
Vermont has taken similar steps to bolster heating assistance in response to fuel prices before, including in 2023, but a spokesperson for the Department for Children and Families could not immediately find records of a state contribution this significant in the past. 
The current cost pressures are essentially “unique,” according to Sen. Andrew Perchlik, D/P-Washington, who chairs the Senate Appropriations Committee and sits on the emergency board. His goal while helping negotiate the proposal, he said, was to keep low-income Vermonters’ winter fuel costs essentially in line with last year.
Time was running out to make such an adjustment to the program, Perchlik added, given that Vermont generally dispenses lump-sum fuel assistance benefits in November.
Scott likewise underlined the measure’s importance in the emergency board meeting, saying it would “give some comfort to those who we need to protect across Vermont.”
He added that the sharp increase in fuel prices “could have been avoided, but hasn’t been,” appearing to refer to the Trump administration’s decisions with respect to the Iran war. 
House Ways and Means Committee Chair Emilie Kornheiser, D-Brattleboro, agreed, adding that other cost pressures — like food — are weighing on her constituents simultaneously.
“So many of us don’t have any extra wiggle room at all in our budgets,” she said, saying protecting Vermonters’ access to bare necessities is “the basic minimum that a government can do.”
It’s a message that Travis Poulin, community action network director at the Champlain Valley Office of Economic Opportunity, is hearing more often as temperatures begin to drop.
“Any additional funds that can help prevent a family from running out of home heating fuel, from having their pipes burst, is money well spent,” he said in an interview Thursday in advance of the board’s meeting. 
Fuel prices will inevitably put a strain on households across the state, affecting vulnerable families and older Vermonters the most, Poulin said.
“It’s going to be a difficult winter,” he said.
The funds for Friday’s proposal will be drawn from a pot of money that lawmakers set aside last year as a cushion to shore up state agencies affected by federal funding cuts. Friday marked the second time the emergency board has drawn from those reserves, after it approved a state-funded stopgap for food assistance payments during the federal government shutdown a year ago.
Vermont’s congressional delegation has also sounded the alarm over heating assistance in recent weeks, with Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., calling for a broad expansion of federal LIHEAP funding. 
If more federal funding does become available, unused money from Friday’s proposal could be returned to the state’s reserves, Gray said.
Some state legislators are cautious about expecting such a windfall.
“I’m not going to hold my breath,” said Perchlik.

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: First influenza-related death of 2026-27 season reported in Idaho
text:
An influenza vaccine is pictured at the Ellis R. Shipp Public Health Center in West Valley City on Thursday, Sept. 17, 2026. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)The Idaho Department of Health and Welfare said an Owyhee County man has died after influenza-related illness — the first flu death of the season in the state.
The man was older than 65, but an exact age was not given in a press release issued by the department.
Public health officials said in the release that while a flu season’s timing and length vary, emergency department and urgent care visits relating to influenza have been higher during the last two weeks than they were during this same time last year.
Idaho has averaged about 60 reported influenza-related deaths annually for the last five flu seasons, with most reported deaths among people over 50, according to Health and Welfare officials.
“The Department of Health and Welfare is reminding residents that flu can be very serious,” said Idaho Deputy State Epidemiologist Dr. Kathryn Turner. “Influenza activity is on the rise in Idaho and across the country, with the highest nationwide activity currently being seen in Western states.”
Annual flu shots can reduce the risk of serious illness, hospitalization and death from flu, Turner said in the press release, and she encouraged Idahoans to consult their healthcare professional or pharmacist for information and recommendations about the annual influenza vaccine.
According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, this year’s vaccines are designed to protect against three different influenza viruses expected to circulate during the flu season.
“Regular hand washing, covering coughs, and staying home when sick are also excellent ways Idahoans can reduce the spread of flu,” the press release said.
Turner encouraged Idahoans at higher risk for serious flu-related complications to take extra precautions. Those at higher risk include people with chronic health conditions, pregnant women, young children and anyone 65 or older.
Symptoms of the flu include fever, cough, sore throat, runny nose, body aches, headache, chills and fatigue. Although most people who get the flu recover after a few days, some can have serious complications that can lead to hospitalization or death, the press release said.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: SpaceX to lease UL Lafayette property on Pecan Island before buying it
text:
One of SpaceX’s Falcon Heavy side boosters that launched NASA’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope from Launch Complex 39A at the agency’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida on Sunday, Aug. 30, 2026, returns to land at Landing Zone 2 at nearby Cape Canaveral Space Force Station. (Photo courtesy of NASA)The University of Louisiana System Board of Supervisors has approved a lease agreement that would allow SpaceX to access ULLafayette-owned property at minimal cost ahead of an anticipated purchase. 
The deal involves 5 acres of university property that was once the site of Pecan Island High School. The school closed after damage from Hurricane Rita in 2005. UL-Lafayette obtained the property through a donation last year and has leased the property to an affiliated nonprofit for $1 per year. The organization would then sublease the property to SpaceX in exchange for improvements to the property and buildings on it. 
The promised improvements are detailed in an attachment to the sublease agreement the UL System did not include when it provided the contract to board members ahead of Thursday’s meeting. The Illuminator asked for the attachment and was directed to file a public records request, which the system has not responded to yet.  
The lease comes as SpaceX moves forward with a $100 billion launch facility on Pecan Island, in Vermilion Parish, called Starbase Louisiana.
SpaceX is being offered low-cost rent as UL Lafayette faces ongoing budget issues that have led to staff layoffs and other austerity measures, including faculty being prevented from using promised funds and traveling to present their research. 
The campus chapter of the American Association of University Professors called out system leaders on its Facebook page this week ahead of the meeting. 
“How does [the lease] fit with goals for raising revenues and closing the budget gap?” the post reads. 
The lease includes a provision that could result in some level of compensation for the university. If the improvements are delayed, SpaceX would have to pay a fair-market rental rate for the property. 
The Vermilion Parish assessor’s website lists the value of the parcel for tax year 2027 at more than $340,000, or roughly $72,000 per acre. The undeveloped property just to the west is valued at $152 per acre.
The lease allows Space X to use the property for: 

business and administrative offices
engineering, scientific and research activity
residential lodging, dormitory and housing for personnel, contractors and guests
dining and recreational facilities
training and workforce-development uses
warehousing, staging, laydown and storage
parking, maintenance and fueling of vehicles and equipment
fabrication, assembly, testing and light industrial operations
communications, antenna, satellite and information-technology facilities
standby and emergency power generation and associated fuel storage
security and access-control facilities
construction, installation, operation, maintenance, repair, replacement, demolition and removal of any of the above 

“This structure of the transaction and ultimately the sale is consistent with the board procedures for lease and our sales,” Chris Herring, the UL System’s vice president for facilities, capital planning and development, told the board. “University stands to receive either fair market value in rents if the project is delayed or the proceeds from the sale once conducted later next year.” 
The lease will “facilitate the development of Starbase Louisiana and support the educational, research, workforce development and public-service missions of” the university, according to the document. 
Details on the sale were not included in the documents.

name: Washington State Standard
title: More than 700,000 WA state voters have cast ballots
text:
Washington Secretary of State Steve Hobbs speaks about the importance of returning ballots early alongside U.S. Sen. Maria Cantwell, right, and leaders from the Seattle King County NAACP and the League of Women Voters of Snohomish County on Wednesday, Sept. 2, 2026, in Seattle. (Photo by Jake Goldstein-Street/Washington State Standard)Washington state voters are getting the message: Don’t wait to turn in your ballots.
As of Friday afternoon, 705,231 ballots had been returned with 66.4% arriving via drop boxes, a sign early voters are heeding repeated warnings from state and local officials to steer clear of the U.S Postal Service to ensure their ballots are counted.
Voters are turning in their ballots fastest in Jefferson County in western Washington, which had 32.8% of ballots already in hand. Five other counties — San Juan, Asotin, Thurston, Lincoln and Skagit — topped 20% on Friday.
By sheer volume, the state’s three most populous counties — King, Snohomish and Pierce —   accounted for 47% of those mailed in or put in a drop box.
Overall, 13.7% of the state’s 5.15 million registered voters had turned in a ballot. At this stage four years ago, 13.9% of voters had done so.
Secretary of State Steve Hobbs said this week that he’s not expecting final turnout for the Nov. 3 election to eclipse the 64.6% mark for 2022. 
“I hope it’s higher,” he said, but some voters only engage when there is a competitive high-profile statewide contest, like for a U.S. Senate seat. There isn’t this time, but there was four years ago when Democratic U.S. Sen. Patty Murray defeated Republican Tiffany Smiley.
Hobbs is pleased drop boxes are the first choice of most early voters. Since August, election officials have sounded the alarm over the Postal Service not postmarking mail-in ballots on the day they’re received due to reduced service and faraway processing centers. 
Those who mail their ballots back are being told to do so at least a week before Election Day. And next week, Hobbs said, they should go to their local post office and ask a clerk to postmark it on the spot.
More than 20,000 ballots were not counted in the August primary because of a late postmark. In rural counties, the percentage of rejected ballots this year was much higher than the 2024 primary.
Meanwhile, in the current election, 4,229 ballots have been challenged thus far. Of those 2,026 had a signature on the return envelope that did not match on the voter’s registration form, and 1,374 weren’t signed. Those who voted with those ballots will be given a chance to cure the problem and have them counted.
‘Throwing monkey wrenches at us’
With voting underway, Hobbs said election officers continue to deal with a maelstrom of challenges and threats from a federal government that’s tried to exert more authority over elections.
Unlike past cycles, he said the federal government has not shared as much real-time information on potential security threats and bad actors. On Wednesday, Hobbs said he expected to receive a classified briefing “soon” and that Washington is part of a separate multistate task force monitoring for potential bad actors.
In the summer, the U.S. Department of Justice threatened Washington state election officials with criminal prosecution if they fail to prevent noncitizens from voting in this year’s federal elections. In recent weeks, more than 60 subpoenas for records of individual voters have been received from federal authorities.
Hobbs said the office is reviewing the subpoenas to ensure that the responses comply with applicable state and federal laws.
“We take our responsibility to protect voter information seriously and will only respond to requests that follow due process,” he said. “However, we see what’s happening in California and don’t want Washingtonians to be harassed.”
The Trump administration has sued California to prevent the counting of thousands of ballots that it alleges were cast by noncitizens. Washington Attorney General Nick Brown has filed a legal brief opposing the federal government’s demand.  
Hobbs also anticipates federal election observers will be present in some counties, such as in southwest Washington where the hotly contested race for the 3rd Congressional District is taking place.
This week the Trump administration informed King County leaders that federal monitors will be sent there though it’s unclear what role they’ll play. Critics fear they’ll try to interfere with elections, but the U.S. Department of Justice maintains their efforts are routine.
This year’s situation is more difficult than elections two and four years ago, Hobbs said, because of the constant “push and pull” with the Trump administration.
Hobbs and Brown put together a guide to help election officials navigate the terrain.
“The federal government is not really there at the same time they’re throwing monkey wrenches at us,” he said.
This story was updated at 3 p.m. with new ballot return figures.
