name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Department of Justice brings additional noncitizen voting charges ahead of 2026 election
text:
The Department of Justice has charged nine more Pennsylvania residents with voting as a noncitizen. (Photo by Seth Tupper/South Dakota Searchlight)Votebeat is a nonprofit news organization reporting on voting access and election administration across the U.S. Sign up for Votebeat Pennsylvania’s free newsletter here.
The Department of Justice has charged nine more Pennsylvania residents with voting as a noncitizen, according to a Friday press release.
The charges, which have not yet been proved, come amid the Trump administration’s nationwide crackdown on election crimes ahead of the 2026 midterms.
There is no evidence the cases are related or that voter fraud is happening on a widespread or coordinated scale.
 Who was charged?

Artur Kopacz, 50, of Philadelphia, Inna Henry, 52, of Harrisburg, were both charged with two counts of voting by an alien in the 2022 and 2024 general elections.
Osmal Loy, 70, of Fountain Hill, Yehuda Peer, 30, of Merion Station, Alfredo Santiesteban, 73, of Philadelphia, Joyce Donovan, 38, of Selinsgrove, Nina Nyawara, 21, of Selinsgrove, and Joyce Pitts, 80, of Effort, were all charged with with one count of voting by an alien in the 2024 election.
Nourten Kuruju, 64, of Luzerne, was charged with one count of voting by an alien in the 2022 general election.
Kopacz, Loy, Peer, Donovan, Henry, Nyawara, Pitts, and Kuruju are all lawful permanent residents of the U.S., according to the department. The immigration status of Santiesteban was not listed.
Chuck Peruto, Kopacz’s attorney, said Kopacz passed the citizenship test twice, but failed to include a certified copy of his criminal extract showing he had no criminal record, and voted while waiting to become a citizen because he believed he was eligible.
“He’s been here since he was 17 and is now 50, happily married to an American citizen,” Peruto said in an email.
Attorneys for Donovan, Henry, Kuruju, Nyawara, and Pitts did not immediately return an email seeking comment.
Attorneys for Loy, Peer, Santiesteban could not be located, and no one responded to emails sent to addresses associated with Loy and Santiesteban.
 What is the context?

The charges announced Monday bring the total number of individuals charged with noncitizen-voting-related crimes in Pennsylvania to 20 since September.
Election officials contend that while voter fraud, including noncitizen voting, does occasionally happen, it is exceedingly rare.
A Votebeat and Spotlight PA analysis of election crimes since mid-2015 found just 176 allegedly fraudulent ballots have been cast out of more than 67 million votes cast in that period, even if these latest charges — which haven’t yet been proved — are included. If the nine individuals charged Friday are found to have illegally voted, their votes would represent 0.00009% of all votes cast in those elections.
The Trump administration has claimed that there are thousands of potential noncitizens on Pennsylvania’s voter rolls. In July, the Department of Homeland Security claimed it had identified 250,000 potential noncitizens registered to vote in four states, including 14,576 in Pennsylvania. As of today, DHS has not yet shared the list of potential noncitizen voters with Pennsylvania officials nor has the state spoken to DHS since a Sept. 8 email in which the Department laid out its methodology for finding the potential noncitizen voters.
Carter Walker is a reporter for Votebeat in partnership with Spotlight PA. Contact Carter at cwalker@votebeat.org.
Votebeat is a nonprofit news organization covering local election integrity and voting access. Sign up for their newsletters here.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: USC touts financial strength as construction debt climbs to $1.7B
text:
The University of South Carolina Health Sciences Campus is seen under construction in the Bull Street District in Columbia, S.C. on Monday, Jan. 19, 2026. (Travis Bell/STATEHOUSE CAROLINA)COLUMBIA — The University of South Carolina’s debt load will more than double over the next four years as it embarks on a massive construction spree, which includes a revamp of the student center, new dormitories and football stadium upgrades.
Debt taken on to build those projects is expected to peak at $1.7 billion in 2030, chief accountant Mandy Kibler told the university system’s governing board Friday. In that year, the school expects to make $140 million in principal and interest payments on that debt, compared to the $60 million in annual payments it’s making now.
USC leaders tout buildout, enrollment growth amid broader higher ed headwinds

In all, this takes up about 80% of the school’s operating revenue, Kibler said.
But Kibler tried to put trustees at ease about the increase, saying the university spent years preparing for this moment.
“While this is a substantial increase — and I can see on all of your faces as you actually see this visually — it is why we have been really planning very intentionally, looking ahead over the last six to seven years, so that we can ensure that we have full repayment,” she said.
One project the university won’t have to finance is its proposed $350 million neurological hospital with one-time funding in the last state budget. The school plans to break ground on the hospital sometime next year.
Kibler reiterated that the school has the confidence of Wall Street ratings agencies.
“We really have a very strong university,” she said. “In the last two ratings calls that I’ve had, they have been very surprised at how strong we are and what our balance looks like.”
In particular, she said, the agencies were impressed by the number of students applying annually to attend the state’s largest university system: 69,000 applicants to the main Columbia campus this fall.
Total enrollment reached nearly 42,000 in Columbia and more than 61,000 across the system’s eight campuses statewide.
In the last school year, the university brought in $2.1 billion in revenues, compared to the $1.9 billion it paid out in operating expenses, Kibler said.

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Jackson changes course after initially saying he would skip second Trump rally this month
text:
Rick Jackson, the Republican nominee for Georgia governor, speaks at a Donald Trump rally near Marietta, Georgia. Ross Williams/Georgia RecorderRepublican candidate for governor Rick Jackson will join President Donald Trump at a second rally this month after all. 
Jackson’s campaign said on Monday that he would skip Trump’s upcoming Saturday rally in middle Georgia, opting instead to act as “a force multiplier” at an event with Gov. Brian Kemp in suburban Atlanta as the race, which polling averages indicate is a virtual tie, enters the final stretch.
By Friday afternoon, the campaign changed course, saying that Jackson will now do both as Republicans try to boost turnout.
“We can confirm that after working out the logistics, Rick will now be able to attend both his rally with Gov. Kemp in Cherokee and the president’s rally in Perry,” said Jackson’s spokesperson Garrison Douglas.

Rick Jackson, the GOP nominee for governor, speaks alongside President Donald Trump at a rally in Dalton on Friday, Oct. 16, 2026. Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder
Since Jackson won the GOP nomination in June, the Republican who once said he would be “Trump with a Southern tone” has sought to align himself more with Republican Gov. Brian Kemp. But about one week ago, Jackson joined Trump on stage at a rally in Dalton after also taking part in a tele-rally with the president the previous Sunday. Now, Jackson will campaign with Kemp Saturday afternoon and then join Trump in Perry in the evening for another push to turn out his supporters for the midterms. The rally was first announced for Macon but will now take place at the Guardian Centers in Perry. 
Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms’ campaign pounced at the opportunity to tie Jackson to Trump, which has been a focus of her campaign as Trump’s approval rating sits at 33% in Georgia, the lowest since his second term began, according to a Civiqs poll. And a new poll from the Atlanta Journal-Constitution also shows that 55% of likely Georgia voters disapprove of Trump’s job performance.
“Slick Rick Jackson proved again today that he will always come running every time Donald Trump calls for him,” said Bottoms’ campaign spokesperson TaNisha Cameron. “Georgia voters know all that they need to know: Rick Jackson will always put Donald Trump first, and Georgians last.”
The Democratic Party of Georgia piled on, with party spokesperson Jake Strickland saying in a statement that “when it comes to Trump, Slick Rick Jackson is like a moth to a flame.”
“The fact that Jackson is spending precious time campaigning with the president on three different occasions in just the last few weeks tells you that he will never, ever stand up to Donald Trump – and will bend the knee no matter how much it hurts the people of Georgia,” Strickland said.

title: Water rate hike request, Medicaid changes: CT politics news
text:
Tong opposes Connecticut Water rate hike
Attorney General William Tong asked state regulators on Thursday to block a proposed $25 million rate increase for Connecticut Water customers, saying his office identified roughly $19 million in unjustified costs in the application.
Tong’s filing with the Public Utilities Regulatory Authority also seeks to cut the company’s requested return on equity from 10% to 8.3%. PURA has yet to render a decision on the application.
Connecticut Water estimates the increase, if approved, will raise customer bills by an average of $15.54 a month. The company said the increase is being driven by approximately $145 million worth of investments in water infrastructure.
— John Moritz, Energy & Environment Reporter
Blumenthal concerned about Trump’s posture toward Russia
U.S. Sen. Richard Blumenthal is raising alarm bells about the Trump administration’s recent actions regarding Russia — whether that’s been the easing of sanctions or the diesel deal despite the Connecticut Democrats’ legislation — and what that ultimately means for Ukraine.
“The desire basically is to bleed Ukraine, strong-arm them, into submission and it’s part of a pattern that appears very conscious and purposeful,” Blumenthal said on CNN.
Through one of his committees, Blumenthal opened an inquiry Thursday into SpaceX’s Starlink and Starshield technologies to get answers about why Ukraine’s military access to it was downgraded.
— Lisa Hagen, Federal Policy Reporter
A focus on women’s health
President Donald Trump on Monday signed an executive order meant to “strengthen research, prevention, diagnosis, treatment and care for women and girls through every stage of life.” The order establishes a Women’s Health Division within the National Institutes of Health and creates a White House Women’s Health Task Force.
The executive order mentioned several diseases, including osteoporosis, endometriosis, menopause and fibroids, but did not specifically mention reproductive healthcare.
Monday’s executive order also revoked previous executive actions carried out by former President Joe Biden to advance women’s health research and create a dedicated White House Initiative on Women’s Health Research.
— Katy Golvala, Health Reporter
CT delegation warns of Medicaid changes
Members of Connecticut’s federal delegation held events this week criticizing the Trump administration for policy changes that they say will restrict people’s access to affordable healthcare.
U.S. Sens. Richard Blumenthal and Chris Murphy appeared in Hartford on Monday and Congresswoman Rosa DeLauro joined advocates in New Haven on Thursday.
Both events highlighted pending changes to Medicaid eligibility going into effect on Jan. 1 that state officials estimate could put over 100,000 Connecticut residents at risk of losing coverage if they fail to comply with new work requirements.

name: VTDigger
title: Patricia Foulkes
text:
Born: 01/30/1944
St. Louis, MO
Died: 09/23/2026
Burlington, VT
Details of service: 
Patricia’s friends and family will hold a celebration of her life on November 8th at 3 p.m. at the Unitarian Church of Montpelier with a reception to follow.

Patricia “Pat” Foulkes of Montpelier passed away unexpectedly on September 23, 2026, at the age of 82.
Born in St. Louis to Carl and Margaret Leupold, she moved at age eight to Jacksonville, Florida where she grew up alongside her two brothers. She graduated from Florida Presbyterian College (now Eckerd College) in 1965 and soon drove west to Sonoma County, California where she settled and raised her daughter. Pat earned her master’s degree in special education from San Francisco State University and spent her career teaching for Sonoma County as well as for Santa Rosa Junior College.
Pat had a creative and adventurous spirit. She loved travel of any kind, from flying in her father’s Cessna to driving coast to coast in her Scamp trailer with her beloved dog Jackson, making friends all along the way. In later years, she took up kayaking and spent happy hours on Vermont’s lakes and ponds with her daughter and close friends. From her childhood in Florida through her last summer in Vermont, Pat loved being in the water, floating, swimming and laughing with her grandchildren. She walked the woods of Hubbard Park often, usually with a rescue dog at her side, and had a special love for the beech trees that hold their curled leaves through the winter. Pat was a lifelong ceramist with a focus on Raku pottery as well as a painter, bringing color and imagination to every part of her life.
Above all, Pat delighted in her family in whom she found a deep well of happiness and love that both surprised and completed her. She treasured the smallest moments with those she loved: building extravagant creations with Legos, weekly painting dates, cooking breakfasts and walks through the woods. You could always hear her strong “woohoo” from the sports sideline.
Pat was devoted to her community and lifted up her friends in countless ways. She was strong and vibrant until the very end and she will be deeply missed by all who knew her.
She is survived by her daughter Sian Foulkes and Sian’s partner, Eyrich Stauffer; her beloved grandchildren Kathryn and Calvin; her brothers John and Stephen Leupold; her nieces and nephews Grady Leupold, Ashley Juiliani and Nick Leupold; and the many friends she loved, supported and leaned on in both California and Vermont.
Patricia’s friends and family will hold a celebration of her life on November 8th at 3 p.m. at the Unitarian Church of Montpelier with a reception to follow. In lieu of flowers, please consider a gift in her name to the Central Vermont Humane Society or Hubbard Park in Montpelier.
Arrangements are in the care of Guare & Sons Funeral Home. To share online condolences, please visit www.guareandsons.com.

name: Washington State Standard
title: DOJ sending election monitors to WA’s King County
text:
An election worker in Thurston County processes ballots on Oct. 30, 2025, in Tumwater, Washington. (Photo by Jake Goldstein-Street/Washington State Standard)It’s unclear what role federal election monitors will play or how many there will be in King County on Election Day.
The U.S. Department of Justice informed King County Elections Director Julie Wise this week that the administration is sending election monitors for the Nov. 3 midterms. 
“As the Civil Rights Division has done in the past, our monitors only observe,” the Justice Department’s Anelise Powers wrote in an email to Wise. “They do not intrude or interfere in any way in the voting process.”
Unlike other states with polling places, Washington has long voted by mail, a system that has faced allegations and legal threats from President Donald Trump. Voting commenced last week ahead of the Nov. 3 election. Voters can vote in person at their county election center, but almost all ballots are returned via drop box or the mail. 
The monitors will look for compliance with federal voting rights and disability access laws. The Trump administration has also used voting laws, including the National Voter Registration Act and Help America Vote Act, as legal backing in its push for the state’s sensitive voter data, one of several flashpoints between the state and federal government over elections this year. A judge tossed the Justice Department’s lawsuit seeking this data.
Trump has repeatedly espoused claims of rampant fraud, and critics fear the monitors could use those false allegations to interfere in elections, which are run by states.
The Department of Justice described the actions it’ll take in Washington’s most populous county and elsewhere as “routine election monitoring the department has done for decades.”
“All monitors must meet the same legal and ethical requirements, including that they not interfere with the voting process,” spokesperson Kiersten Pels said in an email Friday. “Every monitor has the same role: observe for potential violations of federal law and report concerns to the Department, which the Department will review after Election Day and act where appropriate.”
But Halei Watkins, spokesperson for King County Elections, said in her seven-plus years there, the county has “never been sent a monitor from the Department of Justice.”
Secretary of State Steve Hobbs’s office said the Department of Justice has sent elections observers to Washington in the past. 
“We’re unaware of any issues stemming from their presence,” spokesperson Stefanie Randolph said in an email.
All observers — private citizens, or those affiliated with political parties and government agencies — have to abide by state law, she said.
“They may not touch ballots, voting equipment, tabulation machines or interfere with voting,” Randolph added. “County auditors have the authority to remove anyone who does not follow these rules from the premises.”
Washington is one of at least 10 states where it’s been reported that a county received a similar notification. Oregon’s Multnomah County, which covers Portland, is another. Pels said the Justice Department will have monitors in every state.

SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 
Monitors were also deployed during this year’s primary elections, with few reported issues. In Wyoming, however, Republican Gov. Mark Gordon was concerned the monitors were “aggressive” and “irregular.” Justice Department officials contested Gordon’s characterization.
Harmeet Dhillon, head of the federal agency’s Civil Rights Division, said last month that Department of Justice planned to send 1,000 monitors nationwide, which she called the “largest monitoring effort” ever.
In 2022, the department under then-President Joe Biden sent monitors to 64 locales in 24 states for those midterms, but none to Washington.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: The Competition Problem
text:
ELECTION 2026 | EDITION 1
The Competition Problem

Welcome to CommonWealth Beacon‘s Election 2026 newsletter run.
The most generous thing we can say about electoral competitiveness in Massachusetts is that it’s gotten marginally better since the last cycle — from a starting point of rock bottom. 
All 200 state legislative seats are on the ballot in November. As has become the standard, most of those have already been decided, either because the primary was the only contested election or, more commonly, because nobody felt like challenging the incumbent. 
Only 44 of those legislative contests will feature both a Democrat and a Republican on the ballot. That’s a little better than two years ago, when only 40 districts had candidates from both major parties. Representing just 20 percent of the total seats up for grabs, the rate was the lowest in the country. 

For a state that prides itself on punching above its weight politically, very little politicking actually happens locally, at least when it comes to Beacon Hill. (There’s more competition for statewide offices, where Republicans are challenging every office but auditor, and for federal offices, where the GOP has a candidate in six of 10 races.)
Ballotpedia, the nonprofit online political encyclopedia, tracks data on state legislative elections — assessing how often seats open up, how often incumbents face primary challenges, and how often voters get to pick between a Republican and a Democrat. In each of the past five cycles, Massachusetts has come in dead last in the “competitiveness index” Ballotpedia calculates based on those findings. 
Much of the stagnation comes from Republicans, who are already outnumbered in the Legislature more than five to one, running candidates in less than 30 percent of districts. And few sitting Democrats draw primary challenges. 
When it comes to the most powerful figures in the House and Senate, difficult election seasons are especially rare. House Speaker Ron Mariano, unopposed this year, has faced an opponent two times in the past decade. Senate President Karen Spilka hasn’t been involved in a contested election since 2013, when she finished fifth in a crowded Democratic primary for an open congressional seat. 
There is a clear relationship between legislative party domination and competition: Generally, fewer races are contested in states with one-party rule, and states where legislative control changes hands have more candidates willing to challenge incumbents. In Michigan, for example, where Democrats have a two-member margin in the Senate and Republicans have a six-member margin in the House, there was only a single uncontested seat two years ago.  

It hasn’t always been like this in Massachusetts. For decades, most legislative races in the state were contested; in the early 1970s, the competition rate surpassed 80 percent. But the trend has tilted steadily downward for decades as Democrats have assembled a seemingly impregnable supermajority.
So where is a voter with opinions to express and no alternative to the incumbent supposed to turn? The answer, at least this time around, is all the way down-ballot.  
Nine statewide ballot questions will go before voters, tying the record last set in 1994 for the most in a single year. Several take aim at or are directly inspired by the Legislature. Proponents of one measure seeking to place all candidates on a single primary ballot regardless of party are even pitching their idea as a way to give voters more options. 
To some, like former Rep. Jay Kaufman, there’s an inextricable link between the volume of ballot questions and the lack of options in the House and Senate. 
“Uncontested elections and the rise of citizen initiatives are two sides of the same coin, evidence of democracy in decline,” Kaufman wrote in an opinion piece for CommonWealth this summer. 
Voters will have plenty of choices to make this fall. They just won’t have much say over their reps and senators.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Drake University students say civility comes from open-minded conversations
text:
Drake University students, from left,  Josie Thompson, Gabrielle Brooks, Jack Harrington and Sebastian Meyers speak on a panel about political civility on Oct. 23, 2026. (Photo by Brooklyn Draisey/Iowa Capital Dispatch)College Republican and Democratic party leaders at Drake University said Friday they want to see people bring an open mind and an interest in learning to the political conversations they participate in, both before and after ballots are cast in the upcoming elections.
Drake University hosted a teach-in event Oct. 23, with faculty and expert discussions and panels for students to share their thoughts on political civility and their reasons for voting and encouraging others to do the same.
Members of Drake College Republicans and Drake Democrats told panel moderator and Robert D. and Billie Ray Center Executive Director Scott Raecker that national politics and the rhetoric shared in advertisements on social media do impact their lives on campus. They said in order to create a more civil political climate, people need to approach conversations not with the feeling that they’re right and the other person is wrong but with the hope to gain a better understanding of the other’s thoughts and reasonings for their belief.
“Go in with the open mindset that I don’t know exactly how I should feel about this. I want to get more information from this person, and then I can do some self-reflecting and then have my own opinion about that matter,” said Drake sophomore and Drake College Republicans Political Director Sebastian Meyers. “You know, I think that goes hand in hand with respect.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Meyers, joined by Drake College Republicans President Josie Thompson, Drake Democrats President Gabrielle Brooks and Drake Democrats Political Director Jack Harrington, said the university itself and its proximity to the Statehouse have allowed students to become politically involved and active.
Civility means curiosity, not certainty of who is right
Civility, to these students, means being able to share opinions without the fear of ostracization and have conversations where disagreements are approached with respect. Brooks said that too often these days political conversations either don’t happen at all to avoid tension or end up in verbal “fisticuffs.”
Brooks brought up a recent conversation she and Meyers had on campus about vaccine mandates — an issue she is in favor of, but he is against. Meyers said he didn’t go into the discussion with the idea that he would change Brooks’s mind, but to learn.
“Neither one of us, I think, entered the space thinking or wanting to change the other person’s mind,” Brooks said. “It was more about coming to an understanding, and I think that if I can speak for you, Sebastian, that we ended the conversation with a greater understanding of the other person and where they were coming from within that specific issue.”
Building a connection beyond political discussions is also important in bringing civility to them, the panelists said. The two student organizations work together on programming and events, including efforts that brought back an early voting location to campus this year, which Thompson said has allowed the students to learn more about each other as people and find common ground.
From constant political advertisements to social media giving constant access to political happenings and strife, the students said national politics and rhetoric have come to campus and despite Drake’s good example of civility, Thompson said there could be more done.
Social media allows people to start political debates without having any real interaction with the people on the other side of the screen, the panelists said, and that dehumanization grows even more when posts can be made anonymously.
Thompson brought up the example of social media posts relating to the anniversary of Charlie Kirk’s killing, saying that one “sexually explicit” post about Kirk and Drake College Republicans got 400 upvotes, or the equivalent of 10% of Drake’s student population.
While Harrington proposed getting social media out of politics entirely, Brooks said that as the only person of color on the panel, she believes that social media can provide an important space for disenfranchised people to get their opinions heard. In order to create a “culture of decorum” online, she said that culture first needs to be developed off-line.
Keeping an open mind beyond the election cycle
The lack of civility surrounding politics is something Harrington said he believes comes from the top down, meaning that interactions in national politics trickle down to how political discussions go between peers.
“I can’t really stand either party at the moment, but I think we need to find a way … I think, to cool down the rhetoric up top. We need to find a way to cool that off and find a way to moderate ourselves up there,” Harrington said.
Thompson agreed, saying she didn’t believe so much vitriol would have been posted about Kirk and the student organization if similar things hadn’t happened on a national scale through social media. She said the approach should be “bottom-up” rather than top-down, with students having conversations about politics like this panel and making their own voices heard, rather than letting national political officials and those who comment on politics speak for them.
When asked by Raecker what advice they’d provide for people to be better “bridge builders” and generate more civility leading up to the election, each student voiced the same point in different words — remember the people you’re talking to are human, and don’t start a conversation with your mind already closed to it. As Brooks put it, one side shouldn’t “boogeyman-ify the other side.”
Thompson reminded the group and audience that the respect and open-mindedness needs to last beyond Election Day and into its aftermath. People also need to keep in mind that they may be role models without realizing it, she said, like for faculty and their students or senior students and the freshmen wanting to emulate them.
“There’s always a lot of harsh feelings, especially on college campuses after elections happen, and I think if we’re at least open-minded, like leading up to it, even if we know we can’t change each other’s minds, we have to listen to each other so we can build respect for each other,” Thompson said. “So by the time the election’s over, we’re all not … personally angry at each other. Maybe we can be angry about what happened, but we have to build that respect.”

name: VTDigger
title: Return of the ‘Mountain Brigade’ from training Ukrainian troops
text:
Vermont National Guard soldiers wait for the start of a deployment ceremony at the Ethan Allen Firing Range in Jericho on Friday, May 29, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
The Vermont National Guard’s 86th Infantry Brigade will soon touch down on Green Mountain soil as its deployment to train Ukrainian soldiers in Germany comes to an end.
As the National Guard returns home, active U.S. Army units are taking over the training.
“They have done a very valuable mission in their training responsibilities, and I believe that they have learned a lot as well as having been valuable instructors for the region,” said Joseph Brooks, spokesperson for the Vermont National Guard.
The 86th Infantry Brigade, also known as the “Mountain Brigade” for its specialized training in mountain warfare, was sent to Germany in February. The deployment of just over 150 members came immediately before the four-year anniversary of the Russian invasion of Ukraine.
Now the unit is undergoing a standard Army return process to prepare for the journey home. The process typically takes around two weeks, Brooks said. 
The U.S. military recently transitioned two European missions that the National Guard operated for over a decade to active-duty U.S. Army units, according to a report from the National Guard Association of the United States. 
The Vermont National Guard was in charge of the Joint Multinational Training Group-Ukraine. The mission originated in 2015 in Yavoriv, Ukraine, before moving operations to Grafenwoehr, Germany.
The handover to an active Army unit “marks a shift toward supporting training requirements for our Ukrainian partners on a more permanent and sustainable basis,” said Col. Michael Weisman, a senior Army spokesperson, according to the report.
The mission, as with other collaborative missions, has further strengthened the U.S. military’s relationship with European military forces, Brooks said.
“We speak a common language when we go and work with other partner militaries,” Brooks said. “And we form fast friendships all the time because we share knowledge, and that makes us all stronger.”
As part of the return process outlined by the U.S. Army, unit members will travel to a deployment station for administrative processing as well as counseling and briefings before they come home, Brooks said.
Brooks did not disclose the location of the deployment station, saying the military typically waits until the unit arrives before releasing the information for security purposes.

READ MORE

As soon as the process is completed and the flights are booked, Brooks said, the Vermont National Guard will alert the families of the return date and organize a homecoming ceremony.
The brigade’s return comes after members of the Vermont Air National Guard arrived home in September from an eight-month deployment in the Caribbean and Middle East.
“As with any deployment, I’m sure that everybody is very much looking forward to coming home and seeing their families,” Brooks said. “A lot of change happens in the time of deployment for a soldier’s life.”
A sense of accomplishment will come with the joy of seeing their loved ones again, Brooks said.
“Without a doubt, they are, as I’ve seen from a lot of reports, very proud of the work that they did,” he said.

name: WyoFile
title: Kemmerer coal mine set to close in 2029, spurring Wyoming’s soda ash industry to seek new fuel source
text:
After years of speculation and rumor, the Kemmerer coal mine in southwest Wyoming is set to close at the end of 2029, officials say.
At least that’s the plan for now.
“It’s a dynamic business, you know,” Kemmerer Operations President and Mine Manager Don Crank told WyoFile. “Things do change from year to year, and we’re hoping to figure a few things out to go further. But that’s kind of what we’re planning right now.”
There are no plans for layoffs for now, Crank added. About 153 miners work there, according to federal data. About two-thirds are organized under the United Mine Workers of America, Local 1307, which has been active at the mine for more than 100 years.
Now that the adjacent Naughton power plant has stopped buying coal from the Kemmerer coal mine, nearby trona and soda ash producers lament the eventual demise of the primary fuel source they use to fire boilers and, in some cases, to generate a portion of their electricity.
The Kemmerer coal mine (left) and Naughton power plant, pictured Jan. 19, 2022. (Dustin Bleizeffer/WyoFile)
Talk of the mine’s potential closure has swirled in the tiny neighboring southwest Wyoming towns of Kemmerer and Diamondville since 2018, when its former owner Westmoreland Coal Company filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy. Though the mine has continued to operate under new owners — from Westmoreland to PhenixFIN and now ECC Capital Corporation — the future has felt tenuous because of changes with its biggest client.
Naughton’s majority owner PacifiCorp, which operates as Rocky Mountain Power in Wyoming, began converting coal-burning units at the power plant to natural gas in 2020, and completed the switch in December 2025. Kemmerer mine has seen its annual production slip from 4.2 million tons in 2017 to 2.4 million in 2024 and 1.5 million in 2025, according to federal data.
Trona industry impact
Among its remaining clients are a handful of trona mines that convert the mineral into soda ash — the primary ingredient for glass and dozens of manufacturing and household products. Many rely on daily truckloads of Kemmerer coal to heat boilers in the trona-to-soda ash process, and some also use the coal to generate a portion of electricity used onsite.
Contemplating the loss of Kemmerer coal — along with spiking rates for utility-supplied electricity and plans to expand trona and soda ash operations — some within the industry have considered contracting for third-party power from new natural gas-fired generation or renting modular nuclear microreactors. 
As for a new source to fire boilers, WE Soda plans to turn to natural gas.
The Wyoming Energy Authority earlier this month recommended a $13 million grant to help the company build a “natural gas supply connection” to its operations. In its pitch for the grant, WE Soda noted, “The project will help maintain the competitiveness of Wyoming-produced soda ash by providing a cost-effective and reliable thermal energy source for current operations in time to replace the economical local coal which will be depleted by the end 2027.”
Crank declined to discuss the mine’s contracts.
Meantime, the Wyoming Energy Authority has been exploring options for how the state might help the trona and soda ash industry prepare for the mine’s eventual closure. The industry, after all, produces more than half of Wyoming’s global commodity exports at about $1.3 billion annually. It employs some 2,500 workers in the southwest corner of the state.
Among five soda ash processing plants in southwest Wyoming, two consume a combined 1 million tons of coal annually, according to the agency’s commissioned Wyoming Coal Study published in February. “The coal supply for these industrial plants is threatened by the announced plans to close the Kemmerer mine, and the state should support the extension of the Kemmerer mine or the development of a replacement local coal supply,” the report stated.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: National groups power spending against higher bar for constitutional amendments
text:
Mailed campaign materials from L-No, a South Dakota ballot question committee formed to opposed a measure that would require 60% voter approval to change the state constitution. (John Hult/South Dakota Searchlight)https://southdakotasearchlight.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Amendment-L-campaign-finance-web.wav
 Listen to an audio version of this story produced by reporter Meghan O’Brien. Broadcasters: See below for a downloadable version with a host intro script.
Groups opposing a higher bar for approving state constitutional amendments have so far outspent supporters of the ballot question by nearly $2 million, according to campaign finance reports filed this week.
L-No, a state-level ballot question committee formed to defeat the proposal, has raised over $2.2 million — primarily from a Washington, D.C.-based nonprofit called The Fairness Project — and spent $1.7 million. The Fairness Project has independently spent an additional $260,000 against the ballot question.
Meanwhile, the Save our South Dakota Constitution committee has raised about $93,000, including a last-minute infusion from a federal political action committee connected to U.S. Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-South Dakota, and spent about $11,000.
Fundraising and spending will continue through Election Day, and there are no limits on contributions to ballot question committees.

 Hear pro and con voices on Amendment L in an episode of the Searchlight Report podcast.

The fight is over Amendment L, one of four statewide questions on South Dakotans’ Nov. 3 general election ballot. It deals with the process for gaining voter approval for state constitutional amendments.
Lawmakers can place amendments on the ballot, and so can citizens if they collect enough petition signatures from registered South Dakota voters. Amendments currently need a simple majority from voters to pass, but Amendment L would change the threshold for future amendments to 60%.
Supporters of Amendment L say it will protect the constitution from policies that don’t belong in it, and preserve fundamental elements like the structure and function of government.
Opponents allege Amendment L — which was placed on the ballot by the Republican-dominated Legislature — is an attempt by Republican lawmakers to block voters from adopting policies like Medicaid expansion, which voters put in the constitution four years ago, or abortion rights, which petitioners have unsuccessfully attempted to place in the constitution.
“The stakes are high,” said Rep. John Hughes, R-Sioux Falls, a member of the Save our South Dakota Constitution committee and the sponsor of the legislative resolution that put Amendment L on the ballot.
National, state contributors back L-No
The Fairness Project contributed nearly $1.7 million to the L-No committee, and the organization has also spent $260,000 independently, raising its total effort against Amendment L to nearly $2 million.
The nonprofit, which does not disclose its donors, has spent millions of dollars to support ballot measures that protect abortion rights across the country, including Florida, Missouri, Montana and Nebraska. The group has also backed other initiatives, including Paid Sick Leave for Nebraskans and Protect Majority Rule, a Missouri group that opposed raising the bar for passing statewide ballot initiatives.
[Voter Guide: 2026 general election Voter Guide: The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
The group has helped more than 40 ballot measures succeed, according to an emailed statement provided to Searchlight by Executive Director Hannah Ledford.
“Those wins have improved the lives of more than 23 million people,” Ledford said. “Our work is rooted in a simple principle: Power belongs with the people, and when politicians fail them, they can take matters into their own hands.”
Other major contributors to L-No include the National Education Association, which pitched in $500,000, and the South Dakota Education Association, with a $100,000 contribution.
Approving Amendment L would invite more “big money” into South Dakota campaigns, said Ryan Rolfs, executive director of the South Dakota Education Association, in a written statement to Searchlight. A higher bar for constitutional amendments, he said, “leaves only the best-funded interests able to clear it.”
“This isn’t about any one issue,” Rolfs said. “It’s a permanent change to the rules for every future decision, including those that affect our schools.”
Similar attempts to raise the threshold for voter approval of ballot questions have been rejected by voters in past elections. In 2018, voters defeated Constitutional Amendment X, which would have raised the approval requirement for constitutional amendments to 55%. Constitutional Amendment C failed in 2022. That measure would have required 60% voter support for ballot questions that increase taxes or fees or require the state to spend $10 million or more in a measure’s first five years of implementation.
“The people of South Dakota don’t want this, and that’s been very, very apparent,” said John Fiksdal, who works with L-No.
The American Cancer Society Cancer Action Network has independently spent about $11,500 on advertising against Amendment L. A spokesperson for the organization said it wants to help preserve the ability of citizens to pass constitutional amendments such as expanded Medicaid coverage, which passed with 56% of the vote in 2022.
Thune-affiliated committee helps pro-Amendment L group
Save our South Dakota Constitution, the committee organized to support Amendment L, has received about $53,000 from individuals and groups in the state, according to campaign filings.
The rest of the committee’s income is from Heartland Values PAC, according to a Wednesday filing by the ballot committee, listing a $40,000 contribution. The PAC is affiliated with Thune.


For broadcasters

Produced 1 minute, 19 second audio story with host intro script.



The largest personal contribution is $25,000 from Kathy Sullivan, whose address is listed as a Sioux Falls post office box. A nearly $11,000 donation came from Jerald Berg, a Sioux Falls resident. Searchlight was not able to reach either of them for comment.
Other contributions include $5,000 from South Dakota Right to Life PAC.
Rhonda Milstead, who runs the ballot question committee, said Washington, D.C., donors to Amendment L’s opponents “don’t belong in South Dakota.” She said the state’s current simple majority requirement is too easy to clear for campaigns with enough funding.
“But 60%, whether it’s good or bad for either side, 60% means that it has to be more people that get involved in it,” Milstead said. “If you are passionate, if it’s the right thing to do, you darn well better get 60%. And if you can’t get 60%, you don’t belong in the game.”



Spending on other amendments
South Dakotans are deciding on three other proposed amendments to the state’s constitution. Amendment I would repeal the Medicaid expansion mandate if federal funding for it declines. The federal government currently covers 90% of the program costs, and South Dakota pays for the remaining 10% of the program.
A ballot question committee called No on I is opposing the amendment and said it filed a campaign finance report, but the Secretary of State’s Office had not made the committee’s report public as of Friday morning, four days after the filing deadline.
The American Cancer Society Action Network has independently spent about $32,600 against Amendment I.
No ballot question committees have surfaced to fund support or opposition to the two other questions, and no communication expenditures have been filed.
Amendment J asks South Dakotans to add language to the constitution specifying people who are not U.S. citizens are “disqualified from voting.” The state constitution already affirms the right of U.S. citizens to vote.
A fourth question, Amendment K, asks voters to allow the state Investment Council to manage a trust fund consisting of unclaimed property proceeds. No organized opposition to that amendment has surfaced.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: ‘Cause for celebration’: SC opens 7th state forest
text:
Conservationists stand under a tree at the dedication of Pocotaligo Station State Forest in Yemassee, S.C., on Friday, Oct. 23, 2026. (Photo courtesy of SC Forestry Commission)COLUMBIA — The state’s seventh publicly owned forest opened for visitors Friday amid a boom in state-owned public lands.
Pocotaligo Station State Forest, which spans parts of Beaufort, Jasper and Hampton counties, is the second new state forest to open this year. Before Old Beech Hill State Forest’s dedication in June, the last new state forest to open was Wee Tee State Forest in 2004.
The state parks department has also experienced a major uptick in properties, with three new parks opened in the past two years.
Pocotaligo Station State Forest has sections in Beaufort, Jasper and Hampton counties and opened Friday, Oct. 23, 2026. (Courtesy of SC Forestry Commission)
Foresters can still harvest timber from state forests, with the state Forestry Commission’s permission.
State ownership is meant to ensure the wood is harvested responsibly and sustainably, allowing the forest to stay standing for future generations, according to the commission.
It uses revenues from timber and land leases to manage the forests and pay employees’ salaries. A quarter of all earnings goes to public schools in the counties where the forests are located.
“The creation of a new state forest is cause for celebration,” said State Forester Scott Phillips in a statement. “We look forward to managing these lands for recreation, education and sustainable forestry, ensuring they continue to thrive and delight for generations to come.”
Running along Interstate 95 and major train lines, the property was considered to be at high risk of development, especially for factories and other industrial purposes, according to the Forestry Commission.
With major thoroughfares nearby, the land also “includes one of the area’s most visible remaining green spaces,” conservation nonprofit Open Space Institute said in a news release.
But development could pollute the water on the property, which runs off into nearby nature preserves.
Because of that, conservationists considered the land key in protecting the Ashepoo-Combahee-Edisto Basin, the 300,000-acre undeveloped watershed more commonly known as the ACE Basin, and Port Royal Sound, according to Open Space Institute, which bought the land before selling it to the state.
“By keeping the property wild and undeveloped, the land will continue meeting critical purposes: filtering and recharging water as it flows into local waterbodies and absorbing excess floodwaters, thereby protecting downstream communities from some of the devastating impacts of extreme weather,” the forest’s website reads.
The property has historical value as well.
The Yemassee Tribe, sometimes spelled Yamasee, lived in that area in the late 1500s, according to the Open Space Institute. Historians believe members of the tribe may have attacked British settlers on or near the new state forest’s land amid growing frustrations over the loss of their land and broken promises in fur trading.
That attack led to the Yemassee War in 1715, which ultimately drove many Native Americans out of South Carolina and down to Florida and Georgia.
The property also has ruins from British-built Fort Balfour, a Loyalist camp captured by Patriots in 1781 during the Revolutionary War.
“This is another major milestone for conservation in the Lowcountry,” Nate Berry, chief land protection officer for the Open Space Institute, in a statement. “With rapid development, we have to be strategic about protecting land.”
Although hiking and biking are allowed on the property, hunting is not yet permitted. The Forestry Commission is in the process of allowing hunters, with the goal of opening for the 2027-28 hunting season, according to the agency.

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Colorado must approve federal election observers in Adams County, state law says
text:
People cast general election ballots at the Adams County Human Services Center on Nov. 5, 2024. (Photo by Andrew Fraieli for Colorado Newsline)Colorado election officials are treating the U.S. Department of Justice’s plan to send election monitors to Adams County for the upcoming midterm elections as a request that requires approval, rather than a mandate, according to correspondence between state and federal officials.
The DOJ’s Civil Rights Division first notified Adams County Clerk Josh Zygielbaum on Tuesday that it intends to send monitors on Election Day, Nov. 3. Colorado Deputy of Secretary of State Andrew Kline then sent a letter to the DOJ on Thursday, pointing to state laws that require certain people, such as the DOJ monitors, to be appointed as official observers before they can go into non-public election spaces.
“Colorado is not subject to any relevant court orders or settlement agreements, and none of the statutes cited in your email provide the Department of Justice with authority to observe election activities in non-public spaces,” reads Kline’s letter to DOJ Attorney Jake Bachand, which the secretary of state’s office provided to Newsline Friday.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Kline then asked for information about each proposed observer, including the time and location they intend to monitor.
The Denver suburbs of northern Adams County make up the more Democratic-leaning half of Colorado’s 8th Congressional District, a toss-up district that has had extremely close results in the two elections since its creation in 2021. The race between incumbent Republican Rep. Gabe Evans and Democrat Manny Rutinel will be key in determining which party gains control of Congress.
Weld County, which includes the district’s more heavily Republican half, did not receive a similar notice, officials there told The Colorado Sun. The DOJ mistakenly sent another notice to the conservative-leaning Douglas County on Wednesday, but backtracked Thursday afternoon.
DOJ spokesperson Kiersten Pels wrote in an email that Adams County was chosen because is covered by Section 203 of the Voting Rights Act for language assistance. Jurisdictions covered by that section have at least a 5% share of voters who don’t speak English.
In a Thursday Facebook post, Zygielbaum wrote that his office is coordinating with the secretary of state’s office about the plan.
“Regardless of the DOJ’s presence, our election procedures and commitment to the voters of Adams County remain unchanged,” he wrote. “Our priority is to ensure every eligible voter can confidently cast their ballot, and every valid vote is counted through a secure, transparent, and accessible election process.”
DOJ this week began notifying the counties it wants to observe on Election Day, including jurisdictions in Oklahoma, Indiana, Utah and Michigan. Election monitors from the department are not atypical, and their job is to check for compliance with federal voting rights laws like the Voting Rights Act, the National Voter Registration Act and the Voting Accessibility for Elderly and Handicapped Act. There were monitors in 64 counties across the country for the 2022 midterm election, though none went to Colorado. Observers do not wear uniforms, talk to voters or intervene in the voting process.
Last month, the head of the Civil Rights Division, Harmeet Dhillon told a conservative news show that she intends to send 1,000 monitors out for the midterms, the “biggest DOJ election observer effort in history.” But President Donald Trump’s attempts to assert federal control over the election process, including eroding trust in mail-in voting and seeking sensitive state voter roll data, make the notice of DOJ election observers worrisome to some state leaders.
“When outsiders try to interfere, it’s because they know our collective power can change the direction of our state and our country,” Meghan Carrier, the executive director of the nonprofit Together Colorado said in a statement. “Voters hold the real power. We urge everyone to vote today, track your ballot, and encourage your neighbors to do the same. We won’t back down to intimidation.”
On Friday, the Democrats in Colorado’s congressional delegation sent a letter to Dillon asking whether the division plans to send any other monitors, whether DOJ communicated with the White House or the Department of Homeland Security about the plan and why the division is planning to send criminal division prosecutors, rather than civil staff, as monitors.
“There is nothing routine or conventional about the DOJ’s approach to its election monitoring program this year,” they wrote.
“This type of coordinated, bad-faith conduct subverts Congress’ and the states’ constitutional authority to regulate elections. The United States Department of Justice owes Coloradans answers about why federal officials are attempting to monitor our elections, and who those officials are.”
Secretary of State Jena Griswold, a Democrat, did not have a comment about the election monitoring plan as of Friday afternoon.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Kentucky Court of Appeals hears latest arguments in Kinship Care dispute
text:
The Kentucky Court of Appeals in Frankfort, Kentucky, on Oct. 23, 2026. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Sarah Ladd)FRANKFORT — Kentucky’s auditor has asked the Court of Appeals to send her lawsuit against the Beshear administration back to Franklin Circuit Court so she can iron out the kinship care dispute that’s kept them in court for more than a year. 
In October 2024, Auditor Allison Ball, launched an inquiry into the financial viability of a 2024 law that aimed to give much-needed relief to kinship care families, which the Beshear administration said it couldn’t implement without specific funding from the General Assembly. (It has since started implementing the law after receiving funding during the 2026 legislative session). 
Alleging that the administration did not cooperate with that inquiry, she sued and asked the Franklin Circuit Court to rule that the administration must implement the law. 
Ball argued on behalf of her own office before the three-judge panel that met inside the Judge Sara Walter Combs Courtroom Friday afternoon. 
The judges on the panel were Allison Jones, who was appointed to the bench by former Gov. Steve Beshear in 2013 and Lisa Jones and Susan Cetrulo, who were both appointed to the bench by Gov. Andy Beshear. 
Ball said her office, which is constitutionally tasked with auditing state agencies and county governments, is “at risk of becoming an empty shell” if she cannot have confidence that she will receive documentation she requests in the course of audits. 
Wesley Duke, the general counsel for the Cabinet for Health and Family Services, said the cabinet did indeed work with the auditor in the inquiry process. 
“There were …  particularly two responses I don’t think the auditor’s office liked, but we did not decline to respond,” Duke said. “We did not refuse to respond, and there’s nothing that was ever presented in the record of the case that shows that the cabinet ever indicated they would even do so.”  
Travis Mayo, general counsel for Gov. Andy Beshear, said the governor should have never been named in the lawsuit because the investigation wasn’t about him. The auditor said she named him because the cabinet based their actions on his interpretation of state law. 
“This case has really never been about the implementation of Senate Bill 151 or the auditor’s investigatory authority as to the governor,” Mayo said. “Instead, it’s always been about bringing the governor into a lawsuit to gain media attention based on facts that weren’t justiciable and simply never existed.” 
Ball addressed that in her rebuttal: “There can be the impression that we’ve been trigger happy, that we’ve jumped the gun,” she said. But, she said, she would prefer mediation in this case. 
“I’m really not interested in being in the courtroom,” she said. “I don’t want that to become a regular practice of what I have to do in order to be able to do my job as an auditor.” 
The background 
The Kentucky legislature approved and Beshear signed Senate Bill 151 in 2024 to provide financial relief to grandparents and others raising children who otherwise would be in state care by making it easier for the family members to qualify for foster care payments.
Beshear’s administration contended that without specific funding — at one point, an estimated $20 million — it couldn’t implement the law. The General Assembly pushed back, saying he had the responsibility to implement it. 
For the next two years the legislature, auditor’s office and Beshear’s administration debated over who is responsible for funding and where the money should come from. 
In Beshear’s budget request for 2026, he asked the legislature to appropriate $14.6 million in each fiscal year — nearly $30 million over the biennium — to fund the law. 
When the Senate initially added funds for SB 151 implementation, Beshear said “If they provide us $5 million, we’ll provide $5 million to those families.” 
By the end of the 2026 session, lawmakers upped the funding, giving Beshear $6 million each year — $12 million total — to fund SB 151. 
In a pre-hearing briefing, Ball’s office argued, among other things, that the governor finds money for his priorities — lawyers pointed to the Pre-K for all pilot program, for example — and therefore could do the same for kinship care families. 
Beshear’s administration, on the other hand, argued that the General Assembly’s appropriation of funding for the law in 2026 “moots the auditor’s appeal, her investigation or ‘examination,’ and her entire case, warranting dismissal.” 
Ball’s office wants a guarantee that kinship care families won’t stop getting payments after that money — $12 million for two years — runs out. 
“Once the Governor and CHFS, in their minds, believe the money for executing SB 151 runs out, they will stop executing SB 151, and there will, again, be an entire population of kinship caregivers and kinship care children that they will preclude from receiving the benefits of SB 151,” the auditor’s office wrote in a supplemental brief ahead of the Friday arguments. 
Duke, the cabinet’s attorney, called that reasoning “purely speculative” in court Friday. 
“We feel this issue is moot as it relates to 151,” he said. “We are implementing today. We have our budget appropriation.”  
The judges will deliberate and try to rule within 40 days.

name: VTDigger
title: At vigil, memories of two who died while unhoused and a call for change
text:
Community members form a large circle during a candlelight vigil at Trinity United Methodist Church in Montpelier on Oct. 16. Photo by Tracy Brannstrom/The Bridge

This story by Tracy Brannstrom was first published in The Bridge on Oct. 20, 2026. 
MONTPELIER — Two people who died this fall while experiencing homelessness were remembered at a candlelight vigil Oct. 16 at Trinity United Methodist Church in Montpelier.
The deaths of Faith Deuso and Jeff Santamore have reverberated through Montpelier’s unhoused community, with people involved in local efforts to support unhoused residents describing widespread grief and concern among those who knew them.
The Rev. Jay Voorhees of Trinity United Methodist Church opened and facilitated the vigil, and the church’s chorus sang. About 80 people formed a circle for the candle lighting, passing the flame from one person to the next, following reflections from attendees about the lives of those being remembered.
Deuso was remembered as passionate. “A firecracker,” one person said. Another called her “my street daughter.”
People spoke of Santamore’s sharp wit — one person compared his humor to that of comedian George Carlin — as well as his humility, trustworthiness and striking blue eyes.
Sarah Munro remembered Santamore for his intelligence and curiosity. He was a father figure to her daughter’s children, she said, and he and her daughter lived in Munro’s home for a time before becoming unhoused again. “He had a million books in my basement,” Munro recalled. She said he often shared books on philosophy and religion with her, choosing titles that reflected her interests.
“He was a beautiful soul,” Munro said.
Some alluded to the difficulties both Deuso and Santamore had endured.
David Swett, who lives outside in downtown Montpelier, recalled seeing Santamore struggle in the period before his death. “You try to get behind him and everything that’s bringing him down, and it’s just, it’s sad. He gave up. He gave up the things he loved, and he isolated. We’ve all seen it before,” he said. 
“The whole community cared about (Deuso) and knew she was having a hard time,” Seth Collins told The Bridge over a dinner of pizza and chocolate cake served to attendees at the end of the evening. 
The gathering was animated, with laughter and tears throughout. At one point, several people in the audience broke into a spontaneous rendition of “Iris” by the Goo Goo Dolls.
Cindy Gauthier, kitchen coordinator at Another Way, urged people to show greater care for one another.

Bob Emmons of Montpelier shares memories at the vigil about those who were lost. Photo by Tracy Brannstrom/The Bridge

“As a community we just have to come around, all of us, and just care for each other more. Something’s missing,” she said. “Reach out to folks you know and explain that we’re all human beings and we all deserve dignity.”
Voorhees closed by reflecting on the lasting impact Deuso and Santamore had on those who knew them. “Each one of us that knew them has been changed by them. We carry them with us throughout the rest of our lives. Whether we want to or not, they have changed us and made us different people,” he said.
He urged that those gathered honor their memories by questioning the conditions that leave people experiencing homelessness vulnerable to premature death.
“Because we live in a place where it is — how do I say this? — a scandal, that people have to die on the streets. It is an absolute scandal,” Voorhees said. “My hope is that you will go forth from this place tonight and begin asking the question, why? Why did this have to happen and what can we do to change it?”

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Ethics complaint filed over Van Orden’s use of AI
text:
U.S. Rep. Derrick Van Orden and Rebecca Cooke met Oct. 20, 2026 for a debate in the race for Wisconsin's 3rd Congressional District. (Photo by Henry Redman/Wisconsin Examiner)A complaint has been filed with the Wisconsin Ethics Commission against U.S. Rep. Derrick Van Orden over his use of artificial intelligence to generate images of his Democratic opponent Rebecca Cooke that were posted to his and his campaign’s online accounts. 
Ahead of the Oct. 20 debate between the two candidates, a Van Orden campaign account posted an advertisement for the event that included what Cooke’s campaign says is a computer generated deepfake image of her. 
Van Orden has spent much of the campaign cycle posting AI photos and videos to social media. Late last month, Cooke’s campaign sent a cease and desist letter to Van Orden seeking to stop him from posting fake material about Cooke, including a video in which she is made to look as if she’s saying she’s running to “take advantage of as much corruption as possible, and give every illegal immigrant free healthcare.”
After the debate advertisement was posted, Eau Claire resident Cassandra Butzler filed a complaint against Van Orden with the state ethics commission, alleging he has broken a 2024 law which requires that any political ad that contains AI must be clearly labeled as such. So far, Van Orden’s posts have not been subject to the law because they don’t qualify as advertisements. 
“Derrick Van Orden continues to spend his time posting AI-generated deepfakes instead of offering real solutions for the working families of our district,” Cooke said in a media release. “He has now gone so far as to violate Wisconsin’s ethics rules, but voters won’t be fooled, Van Orden has never put his constituents first, and he never will.”
Van Orden has previously dismissed the complaints about his AI use as a stunt. Grace Kim, his spokesperson, similarly told the Milwaukee Journal-Sentinel that the ethics complaint is a “cheap publicity stunt.”

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Oklahoma AG opinion prevents extra vote on Jewish charter school
text:
Attorney General Gentner Drummond listens to the State of the State Address on Feb. 2. Drummond issued a binding opinion Thursday that blocked a Friday vote on a Jewish charter school. (Photo by Kyle Phillips/For Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY — An attorney general opinion has blocked the Statewide Charter School Board from taking an uncommon extra vote on a Jewish charter school.
Attorney General Gentner Drummond issued the legally binding opinion Thursday, stating a third vote on the school’s charter application would be illegal. He said state law allows the board to vote no more than twice on whether to approve a new online charter school.
The board had scheduled a special meeting Friday to reconsider Ben Gamla Jewish Charter School, which is seeking to become the first taxpayer-funded religious school in the nation. In light of Drummond’s opinion, though, the board opted not to vote on the school’s application to open.
The Statewide Charter School Board meets Friday at the state Capitol in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)
A representative of Ben Gamla’s founding group did not immediately return a request for comment Friday afternoon.
The board had rejected Ben Gamla in March because the school pledged to teach the Jewish faith along with secular class subjects. Oklahoma law and a 2024 state Supreme Court decision require charter schools to be non-religious.
However, an Oklahoma City federal court judge decided in September a charter school cannot be denied solely because of its religious character. 
The board voted Friday to appeal the federal ruling to the Tenth Circuit Court of Appeals in hopes of clearing up the conflicting judicial decisions.
“I think this is a question that begs to be answered of where do we stand,” board Chairperson Brian Shellem said after the meeting. “Should we be allowed to discriminate against those with a religious character? I would say what we want is just those who can competently carry out the mission of educating.”
Statewide Charter School Board chairperson Brian Shellem attends a board meeting May 12, 2025, at the Oklahoma History Center in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)
The board supported Ben Gamla’s case in court, so the decision to appeal its desired ruling is “strange, to say the least,” a spokesperson for the Attorney General’s Office said.
“We are not aware of another instance in which a state board has asked a federal court for an injunction, gotten it, and then voted to appeal its own victory,” spokesperson Carrie Burkhart said. “We will monitor any filings, but the Attorney General will not approve the expenditure of a single state dollar on an appeal the Board has no standing to bring.”
The September federal court ruling prompted the board to vote again Oct. 12 on the school’s application, but Ben Gamla still failed to pass. Only four members voted in favor of it, falling short of the five votes required for the nine-seat board to give final approval.
Friday’s meeting agenda signaled another attempt to reconsider, but to do so would be unlawful, the attorney general said.
Drummond issued the opinion after Rep. Ellen Pogemiller, D-Oklahoma City, and Rep. Ronny Johns, R-Ada, requested his input on whether an additional vote would be legal following the Oct. 12 rejection.
Oklahoma law establishes a “closed, two-step application process” for proposed online charter schools, and the board cannot add a third step, Drummond wrote in his opinion.
“It authorizes no third vote, rehearing, reconsideration, or rescission,” the opinion states.
Ben Gamla’s leading founder, former U.S. Rep. Peter Deutsch, urged the board to approve both the school and the court appeal. Without both approvals, Ben Gamla would be forced to withdraw its application, he wrote in a Tuesday letter to the board, which Oklahoma Voice obtained.
“No other Oklahoma charter school is forced to endure these types of existential risks,” Deutsch wrote. “And based on my experience, I’m confident that a Board decision here to leave the (state Supreme Court) decision intact would dissuade other potential religious charter schools from opening in Oklahoma.”
