name: Source New Mexico
title: ‘A terrible crisis’: San Juan County officials describe widespread flooding impacts
text:
Ongoing flooding in San Juan County has damaged an estimated 1,500 homes, according to a National Weather Service database, and required the rescues of dozens of people. (Photo courtesy San Juan County Office of Emergency Management)
San Juan County officials on Friday described widespread damage due to recent flooding along the San Juan and Animas rivers, with one county official saying the region faces a “terrible crisis” until the floodwaters recede. 
Heavy rains in the headwaters of the rivers in southern Colorado swelled both rivers and caused them to jump their banks as they flowed south into Farmington and elsewhere in northwest New Mexico. Much of northwest New Mexico, including the Four Corners area and the eastern edge of the Navajo Nation, have seen floods, but the area between Farmington and Bloomfield appears to be the hardest hit as of Friday.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
According to a National Weather Service database, floods in that area have damaged approximately 1,500 homes and prompted crews to conduct swiftwater rescues of at least 60 people since Thursday afternoon. 
The NWS database cites figures from the San Juan County Sheriff’s Office. Sheriff’s office spokesperson Devin Neeley told Source NM on Friday that the actual number of rescues and damaged homes could be higher.
Several people needed to be rescued from the rooftops of their homes, tribal, local and state officials said during a news conference Friday. 
In addition to the rescues and home damage, floodwaters breached the Bloomfield wastewater treatment center, turning all of the San Juan River into a “haz-mat situation” zone, Neeley said Friday during the conference. 
“There is raw sewage in the river, and there is nothing that we can do to mitigate that at this point,” Neely said. “So stay out of the water.”
San Juan County Commission Chair Sam Gonzales said Friday the county is seeking both state and federal disaster declarations that would unlock additional resources to help the communities affected. 
“San Juan County is in grave danger right now,” he said. “We ask you folks to — don’t panic. We are in a crisis. We are doing the best we possibly can.”
San Juan County Commission Chair Sam Gonzales speaks at a news conference Oct. 23, 2026, regarding the ongoing flooding in San Juan County, which has damaged an estimated 1,500 homes. (Screenshot of San Juan County Office of Emergency Management news conference)
Officials said Friday that no one had died due to the flooding. 
Danielle Silva, a spokesperson for the state Department of Homeland Security and Emergency Management, said the state has activated an Emergency Operations Center that is prepared to provide any additional resources, and it has sent additional swiftwater rescue teams to the area. 
Silva noted that the New Mexico governor’s office issued a disaster declaration in late September due to ongoing flooding across the state, so San Juan County has access to some of approximately $3.75 million the governor authorized for flooding response. 
“I’m sure things will update, we’ve got more rain coming, but right now [we’re] just focused on the response piece,” Silva said.
Leah March, a spokesperson for Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham, told Source NM in an email Friday that the state has “deployed every available resource to San Juan County” amid the flooding emergency, including helicopters for rooftop rescues and boats. 
“The state will support San Juan County through every stage of this recovery,” she said.
Randall Hergert, an NWS meteorologist, told Source NM on Friday that heavy rain and river flooding across the San Juan Basin remains the “biggest concern” Friday and Saturday.
New Mexico governor’s office releases up to $3.75M in emergency response to flooding

The service has issued multiple flood watches and warnings in the San Juan Basin that are in effect through the weekend, and Hergert noted that additional runoff could come from southern Colorado and pose additional concerns even if the rain stops in San Juan County. 
Herbert noted that areas of Sandoval and Rio Arriba counties also saw between two and three inches of rain since Thursday, prompting their own flooding. The service’s forecast predicts additional rain in both counties through Saturday. 
Much of New Mexico could face extreme weather, Herbert said, including hail, severe wind gusts and even a tornado somewhere in the state’s central mountain chain on Friday. 
But, by Sunday, forecasters predict the winds and rain will calm, Herbert said. 
“We have to get through today. We have to get through tomorrow,” he said. “And then we do have drying conditions into next week.”

name: VTDigger
title: Magical thinking won’t fix Vermont’s problems
text:
This commentary is by Matt Swenson, the founder of Omnidex Solutions, an independent research and strategic analysis company. He lives in Vermont.
Vermont’s future depends on whether ordinary people can build a decent life here. That means work that pays the bills, a healthy workplace and communities where starting a business or raising a family feels possible.
Too much of our politics runs on magical thinking. Pass another program, raise another tax, give another reassuring speech and the problem will somehow solve itself. Wish hard enough, and the rent becomes affordable. It’s comforting. It just doesn’t work.
Start with wages. Before writing this, I spent time on Indeed.com and other job sites looking at what Vermont employers actually pay. One emergency medical transport job advertised roughly $18 to $27 an hour. The Massachusetts Institute of Technology estimates a single Vermont adult with no children needs $24.92 an hour, working full time, to cover basic costs. The people we count on in emergencies can earn less than it takes to support one person.
As I argued in a previous commentary for VTDigger, affordability belongs at the center of the housing debate. An available apartment doesn’t mean much when the paycheck can’t cover the rent.
At today’s costs, Vermont should set a long-term path toward $30 to $40 an hour, phased in and measured honestly for its effects on jobs and prices. Bring down housing costs, taxes and other necessities, and a paycheck goes further. Reduce what businesses pay to operate, and employers have room to pay more. Both sides of that equation matter.
Hours matter as much as the rate. Full time should mean four eight-hour days as a baseline. Anyone who wants more hours should be free to work them, but no one should have to work themselves into the ground just to survive. At 32 hours a week, $30 to $40 an hour comes to $49,920 to $66,560 a year before taxes. Around-the-clock workplaces will need careful planning, but the goal should be clear.
A healthy workplace is more than an hourly rate. Predictable schedules, adequate staffing, safe equipment, reasonable breaks and respectful management decide whether a job is sustainable. Workers should be able to raise concerns without fear of retaliation, and that includes seasonal and international employees. Good employers benefit when experienced people want to stay.
Lower business taxes and fees can help pay for better wages and conditions. But relief meant for workers should produce measurable gains in pay and benefits. Broader tax cuts require honest spending choices, including a hard look at administrative costs and publicly funded organizations.
For years, Vermont has tried to be San Francisco: high costs, big ambitions and a growing list of programs paid for by asking the wealthy to chip in a bit more. But Vermont doesn’t have San Francisco’s economy, and taxing the rich only stretches so far before the money runs out.

READ MORE

Sen. Bernie Sanders belongs in that conversation. He’s run on helping working people for longer than many Vermont workers have been alive. Yet over decades in Congress, only a handful of the hundreds of bills he’s introduced have become law, and two of those were to rename Vermont post offices. Wages here still don’t match the cost of living. I don’t think Vermont is feeling the Bern.
Rural Vermont deserves more attention too. Plans built around compact neighborhoods and frequent transit can’t simply be applied everywhere. A repair shop, general store, farm or small manufacturer can anchor a town’s future. These businesses need reliable infrastructure, practical permitting and access to workers. And border towns competing with New Hampshire’s lack of a sales tax deserve a serious proposal for targeted relief.
Homelessness demands the same practical approach. Vermont’s 2025 count recorded slightly fewer homeless people overall but substantially more people without shelter. Treatment capacity has to be part of the answer. The state still tracks adults waiting for psychiatric inpatient placement, and the 27 new residential substance-use beds in Vergennes are a real improvement. But announced capacity means little without the staff to run it and somewhere appropriate for patients to go afterward.
Public safety belongs in that discussion. Homelessness doesn’t make anyone dangerous, and people without homes need protection themselves. But threats and violence require a response regardless of housing status. Leaving someone in repeated crisis on the street serves no one. Secure treatment, when it’s necessary, must include due process and regular review.
This is where my own outlook comes in. I call it post-human techno-fundamentalism. The future is already here, and living in the past won’t change that. Vermont should welcome AI businesses, advanced manufacturing and employers offering paid training. Hiring should recognize demonstrated ability, including that of neurodivergent adults and people who learned outside conventional paths.
I’d go farther. Vermont could be one of the first states to let AI help run parts of government: analyzing budgets, tracking whether programs work and clearing permitting backlogs, with due process and a right to appeal. Doing that carefully means keeping our power grid, water and food supply from being one hack away from failure. And as AI agents grow more capable, the question of their rights, even whether they could one day hold office, is coming. Vermont should lead that conversation, not inherit someone else’s answer.
Better wages, lower costs, effective care and technological progress belong in the same conversation. Magical thinking won’t fix these problems. Sustained work and honest choices will.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Judge weighing whether Election Commission must take up complaints before Election Day
text:
Lincoln Party secretary of state candidate Greg Ballard speaks with reporters outside a Marion County courtroom on Friday, Oct. 23, 2026. (Photo by Tom Davies/Indiana Capital Chronicle)An attorney for the state argued Friday that the Indiana Election Commission has no obligation to consider campaign misconduct allegations ahead of Election Day.
A judge said she would rule Monday on a motion filed by Lincoln Party secretary of state candidate Greg Ballard seeking an order forcing the commission to convene a public meeting to take up campaign finance complaints against Republican Max Engling and Democrat Beau Bayh.
Ballard’s lawyer said during Friday’s hearing on the lawsuit filed last week against the commission that it “has completely abdicated its statutory duty to enforce campaign finance law” by not meeting about those complaints.
Deputy Attorney General Marie Queen, however, maintained that state law does not set a time frame for the commission to review campaign finance complaints.
“This is ultimately an attempt by a political candidate to use the commission to influence voters before Election Day and that is an entirely and wholly inappropriate use of the process,” Queen told Marion County Superior Court Judge Jennifer Harrison.
Complaints awaiting commission review
The most prominent of the pending complaints was filed in July alleging that Engling’s campaign improperly accepted $60,000 from Hoosier Leadership for America, a dark money political group associated with Republican U.S. Sen. Jim Banks.
Engling’s campaign has reported it refunded the money a week before the complaint was filed by Knox County Clerk David Shelton, who finished second to Engling in seeking the Republican nomination during June’s state party convention.
Other pending complaints allege:

That Engling’s campaign finance filings didn’t identify who paid for a hospitality suite the night before the GOP state convention.
That Bayh attended several hosted events where he was a featured speaker but reported no in-kind donations from the host groups.
That Bayh attended several events sponsored by county Democratic parties but reported no in-kind donations from those groups.

State law gives Election Commission Chair Beth Boyce, who is also the Johnson County Republican chair, authority over calling meetings of the panel. 
The commission — made up of two Republicans and two Democrats — is next scheduled to meet on Nov. 20, which is 17 days after Election Day.
Ballard attorney Michelle Harter argued Friday that the commission’s inaction was depriving voters of information about the actions of the secretary of state candidates.
“He’s not asking for a specific outcome or to control the manner in which the commission performs its duties, but they have to meet prior to the election and decide if investigation into those campaign finance violations is warranted,” Harter said. “Otherwise they are not executing their duties in a meaningful manner.”
Ballard, the former Republican mayor of Indianapolis, said after the hearing that he saw little value in the commission possibly considering the complaints on Nov. 20, saying “they’ll just gloss over it.”
“There’s an unfairness to all this about two parties staying in power, and they’re writing laws to stay in power, and they’re having policies to stay in power, and to not let anybody else get into the voting system,” Ballard told reporters.
Shelton brushes off Republican criticism
Shelton, who is also the Knox County Republican chair, faces animosity from some Republicans over recent actions that include filing a legal brief in support of Ballard’s lawsuit.
Knox County Clerk David Shelton speaks with reporters outside a Marion County courtroom on Friday, Oct. 23, 2026. (Photo by Tom Davies/Indiana Capital Chronicle)
Bayh also announced this week that Shelton had agreed to assist with an independent audit of spending by current Republican Secretary of State Diego Morales if Bayh wins the election.
Shelton attended Friday’s court hearing and said afterward that he wasn’t involved with either the Bayh or Ballard campaign and considered himself “a one-man watchdog looking after the taxpayers of Indiana, just trying to give them as much information as possible.”
Some Republicans consider Shelton’s actions disloyal, such as Vanderburgh County GOP Chair Kyhle Moers posting on social media that Shelton should be removed as a county chair and “blocked from further association with the party.”
“Shelton clearly has an axe to grind, because as a typical politician (even though he tells you he isn’t) he feels like he was OWED the Secretary of State seat and because that didn’t happen 2 state conventions in a row he’s willing to stoop so low as to align himself with 2 candidates that would have otherwise been opponents,” Moers posted this week.
Shelton, who received nearly 40% of the Republican convention vote for secretary of state, said he had not talked with Engling since the June party convention. 
When asked by the Capital Chronicle whether he was supporting Engling’s election, Shelton responded: “I’m supporting my local candidates in Knox County. We have a lot of contested races there in Knox County, a lot of candidates, but I have not had any contact or communication with the Max Engling campaign at all.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Tax records show big gap between Lamont’s income and Fazio’s
text:
Gov. Ned Lamont’s adjusted gross income averaged more than $16.2 million between 2025 and 2021, while GOP challenger Ryan Fazio averaged $109,634 over the past three years, according to tax records released Friday by their respective campaigns.
Lamont, who has declined his $150,000 governor’s salary throughout his eight years in office, made nearly 90% of his earnings, an average of $14.1 million per year, through capital gains. The remainder involves a combination of dividends, interest and social security payments.
Both campaigns allowed reporters to inspect select documents from their federal income tax returns on Friday. Lamont’s records covered the last four tax years while Fazio’s involved the last three.
The governor also shared a summary sheet that disclosed state income taxes paid and charitable contributions made.
“Releasing the governor’s tax returns, as he did in 2018 and 2022, is about continuing to be transparent with Connecticut, as he has always been, and it is something he believes all candidates should do,” Rob Blanchard, senior adviser to Lamont’s campaign, said Friday.
Lamont’s adjusted gross income ranged from $35.2 million in 2024 to slightly less than $6.1 million in 2022. Over the four-year period his records covered, he paid yearly averages of almost $3.9 million in federal taxes and more than $1.1 million to Connecticut.
Lamont reported charitable contributions averaging $481,750 per year between 2025 and 2022. According to his campaign, recipients included: GLAAD (formerly known as the Gay & Lesbian Alliance Against Defamation); the University of Connecticut; Yale University; Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Foundation; Girls with Impact; 4-CT; and Filling in the Blanks, a nonprofit dedicated to fighting childhood hunger.
The governor opted out of public financing and has largely self-funded his campaign, as he did in his two successful runs for governor in 2018 and 2022 and in his loss in the 2010 Democratic gubernatorial primary. 
As of Aug. 31, Lamont had contributed $10.2 million to his campaign. But much of his attention during the summer was focused on defeating Rep. Josh Elliott of Hamden in an Aug. 11 primary for the Democratic gubernatorial nomination.
And twice in September, Lamont contributed $2.6 million to his campaign.
Fazio, who is using public financing, reported incomes of $134,601 in 2023 and $143,319 in 2024. That reflected his earnings as a business analyst for Capital Services and as a state senator from Greenwich. He took time off from business consulting in 2025 to begin his campaign for governor and reported earnings of $50,984.
Fazio paid an average of $12,693 in federal income taxes between 2025 and 2023. He didn’t disclose information on state taxes paid or on charitable contributions.
The GOP nominee, who received his $18 million Citizens’ Election Program grant on July 15, spent $9.6 million of those funds between July 1 and Sept. 30.
State Capitol Bureau Chief Mark Pazniokas contributed to this story.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Housing expert: Affordability crisis, declining immigration are slowing demand for housing
text:
A Habitat for Humanity Home in Durham. (Photo: Greg Childress/NC Newsline)Housing demand across the country is slowing due to an affordability crisis that makes it difficult for people with moderate-to-low incomes to buy a home or pay high rents, said Alexander Hermann, a senior research associate at the Harvard Joint Center for Housing Studies.
High housing costs, high home prices, high rents and rising interest rates are all part of the problem, Hermann said. Other key factors include a decline in the immigrant population and a “tepid and difficult job market for a lot of potential housing consumers,” he said.
Alexander Hermann (Photo: Harvard University Joint Center for Housing Studies)
At the same time, student loan debt repayments have restarted for a lot of young people. 
“These factors all prevent new households from forming, and cause more young adults to double up and live with parents,” Hermann said. 
Hermann’s remarks came Thursday at the N.C. Affordable Housing Conference in Raleigh. Nearly 1,400 people signed up for the two-day event, which ended today. The annual conference is presented by North Carolina Housing Finance Agency, the North Carolina Housing Coalition and Centrant Community Capital. 
Hermann said the nation is struggling through one of the most expensive housing markets in years. In 2020, when the market was booming, monthly payments on median-priced homes were under $2,300, he said.
“As interest rates rose, you saw payments on median-priced homes rise up to $3,000 pretty quickly in 2022, and it peaked at just under $3,400 as recently as last year,” Hermann said.
Nearly 1,400 people attended the NC Affordable Housing Conference in Raleigh. (Photo: Greg Childress/NC Newsline)
Citing data from “The State of the Nation’s Housing,” the center’s flagship annual report, Hermann said home prices in Charlotte and Raleigh have risen even more rapidly in recent years than in the U.S. overall.
The  problem is hitting young adults and people of color hardest, Hermann said. The strongest growth in homeownership was among those groups in 2021-2023, but he said that progress has been reversed.
According the National Association of REALTORS®, the median age of first-time homebuyers is now about 40 years old. A growing number of young adults report needing money from their parents to buy a home, Hermann said. 
Rentals
The rental market is impacted by many of the same problems as the for-sale market, Hermann said. Slower immigration, a weaker labor market, rising interest rates and inflation all have impacted the rental market. 
Growth in rents has remained flat since 2023, but they’re still 33% higher than they were in 2019, the year before the pandemic, Hermann said.
In North Carolina, rents in five of the six markets tracked by Realpage remained flat or declined, Hermann said. Only Wilmington saw rents increase, and that was by 4.5%, he said. 
Stagnant rent and an increase in rental construction should have improved affordability, even amid rising operating costs, but that hasn’t happened, Hermann said.
Housing took bigger bite out of household budgets in 2025, new report shows

“In fact, renter unaffordability in some ways is at record levels, and certainly hasn’t come down at all from peak unaffordability just a couple of years ago,” Hermann said.
 A record high number of 22.7 million renter households – about half, Hermann said – were cost-burdened by their rents in 2024, he said. That means they spent more than 30% of their incomes on rent and utilities. The 22.7 million households is a 2.3 million increase since 2019.
“About 26% are severely burdened, meaning they spend more than half their income on housing,” Hermann said. 
In North Carolina, 730,000 renter households are cost-burdened, which is an increase of 100,000 since before the pandemic and almost double the number since 2001, Hermann said. Of those, 380,000 households are severely cost-burdened. 
Looking ahead, Hermann said projections for the next 10 to 20 years suggest growth in the number of American households will be “significantly lower than what the nation has experienced recently and historically.”
“That’s due largely to the aging of the population, but also declining fertility rates,” Hermann said. “Further, future household growth will be even lower if immigration levels remain modest, and there’s a lot of potential bad that comes with that.”
Scott Farmer (Photo courtesy N.C. Housing Finance Agency)
The good news about the slowing demand for housing is that it will take time for efforts to boost the nation’s housing supply to work. The slowdown should give the market time to right itself.
“That’s still going to require more housing, but ideally the equilibrium in the future is one that’s more affordable for households at every income level, but also has a diversity of housing types, and it exists in a wide range of communities where people want to live,” Hermann said.
Scott Farmer, executive director of NCHFA, said despite the challenges in the housing market, he’s optimistic that affordable housing is now a major topic of discussion among national, state and local leaders.
Samuel Gunter, executive director of the N.C. Housing Coalition, agreed that the attention is encouraging.
“That is a promising sign that more people are willing to get creative, because the affordability challenges have crept so far up the income ladder that no one is untouched by it, no matter how wealthy you are,” Gunter said. “You’ve got kids, you’ve got in-laws, you’ve got grandkids who are struggling to get into a home.”

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico House Speaker Martínez won’t fill vacant seat on Epstein ‘Truth Commission’
text:
New Mexico House Speaker Javier Martínez announced on Oct. 23, 2026, that he won’t appoint a new member to the state Legislature’s Epstein “Truth Commission” after Rep. Andrea Reeb (R-Clovis) resigned and created a vacancy. (Danielle Prokop/Source NM)New Mexico Speaker of the House Javier Martínez (D-Albuquerque) will not fill a vacant seat on the investigatory subcommittee dedicated to investigating the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein’s time in New Mexico.
Former Rep. Andrea Reeb (R-Clovis) resigned from her job as a state lawmaker, and from the bipartisan subcommittee known as the “Truth Commission,” earlier in October after a judge ruled that her role as a lawmaker conflicted with her work as a special prosecutor in the involuntary manslaughter case against actor Alec Baldwin.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The Legislature established the committee in this year’s lawmaking session and charged it with producing two investigative reports — one over the summer and one by the end of the year.
In a statement Friday, Camille Ward, a spokesperson for Martínez, noted the end-of-year deadline and said its remaining work does not require any changes to its existing membership.
“As the Commission works with legal counsel to conclude the investigation and finalize their report, there are no remaining votes to be taken and therefore there is no need for further changes to the Commission’s membership in these final weeks,” she said. “We fully expect the Commission to fulfill their promise to the people of New Mexico and survivors of Jeffrey Epstein’s horrific abuse by delivering a final report to the public in December that meaningfully addresses the unanswered questions about what happened at Zorro Ranch.”
As the deadline for the commission’s final investigative report approaches, it is left with just three members; Reps. Andrea Romero (D-Santa Fe), Marianna Anaya (D-Albuquerque) and William “Bill” Hall (R-Aztec).
When commissioners unveiled their first report in August, they acknowledged that it did little to tread new ground regarding Epstein and his crimes, but said that it condensed what’s known about his time in the state into a single document.
Infighting quickly characterized the commission as its Republican members accused Romero and Anaya of omitting references to Deb Haaland, the former U.S. Interior secretary and current Democratic nominee for New Mexico governor. Ahead of the June primary election, campaign ads accused Haaland of flying on an Epstein-owned jet in 2014, when she was running on former state Attorney General Gary King’s gubernatorial ticket as a candidate for lieutenant governor. However, publicly available documents show that the plane did not belong to Epstein and that King had requested Epstein’s help in chartering a flight.
Republican leaders subsequently called on Romero, the commission’s chair, to resign, alleging that she inappropriately worked for the local district attorney’s office while serving as a state lawmaker. Romero resigned from her job with the First Judicial District Attorney’s Office but continued to serve as commission chair.
Reeb’s resignation sparked a volley of criticism between Democratic and Republican state House leaders, with New Mexico House Democrats saying Reeb and House Republicans should apologize to Romero, noting Reeb did not acknowledge her own potential conflict of interest when Romero resigned.
In response, House Republican Leader Gail Armstrong (R-Magdalena) issued a lengthy statement in which she rejected Martínez’s call for an apology and said he should issue an apology “to every New Mexican and to the victims this commission was supposed to serve.”
A spokesperson for New Mexico’s House Republicans did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Martínez’s decision not to replace Reeb.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: ICE agents arrested U.S. citizen at gunpoint in Charlotte, NC immigration advocates say
text:
A masked ICE agent knocks on the window of an observer's car in Minneapolis, Minn., Jan. 12, 2026. (Photo: Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)Immigration advocates are demanding answers after a U.S. citizen said he was arrested at gunpoint by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement on his way to work in Charlotte earlier this week.
Atilio Portillo, a resident of east Charlotte who owns a small construction business, told reporters during a press conference Friday that ICE agents stopped him as he was on his way to work early Wednesday morning with his brother and nephew.
The agents blocked his work truck with unmarked vehicles, broke its windows, and pointed guns at the passengers, according to Portillo. He said his requests for a warrant or explanation of the stop were denied.
Bystander video compiled by the advocacy group Siembra NC shows a man in an ICE uniform holding a a handgun while breaking Portillo’s driver’s side window. It also shows Portillo yelling, “I am a U.S. citizen” while agents put him in handcuffs.


“They never told me who they were looking for, and after a long period of argument back and forth, they broke both windows,” Portillo told reporters in Spanish. “They pointed a gun at me, and they threw my phone away. They violently removed me from my vehicle, and they arrested me for 30 minutes while they checked my status.”
Originally from El Salvador, Portillo said he has been living in the U.S. since 1988 and became a naturalized citizen in 2013. His whole family is in the U.S.
Portillo said the agents kept him in handcuffs near the vehicle, despite him repeatedly telling them he was a U.S. citizen. He said he always keeps his passport with him, but at the moment, he didn’t remember it was there.
“They took my wallet out of my pants, and then they saw I had my license there, so I’m assuming that’s the document that they used for verifying my identity and my citizenship,” Portillo said in Spanish.
Agents also handcuffed Portillo’s nephew, he said, who is a U.S. citizen as well. Both men were released after about 30 minutes, but ICE agents took Portillo’s brother into custody, where he is currently detained in Georgia.
Portillo declined to offer further information about his brother, but told reporters he’s exploring legal action against ICE.
“They abused my rights. They treated me with violence,” Portillo said in Spanish. “I have not slept for two nights because I am so worried… I have this fear that they might come to my house in the middle of the night with made-up charges after this experience.”
North Carolina state Rep. Jordan Lopez, a Democrat from Mecklenburg County, said it’s “ridiculous” that ICE agents are operating in this manner.
Analysis: Trump deportations near 1M, but few are criminals

“We’ve got to do what we can to make it stop,” Lopez said. “It’s a good reminder that there are elections going on right now. There is an extraordinarily powerful check that we as people can put on this administration that has seemed hell-bent on targeting folks and violating rights of citizens.”
Siembra NC legal defense manager Andreina Malki said this isn’t an isolated event. Four U.S. citizens and a visa holder filed a class action lawsuit in U.S. District Court for the Western District of North Carolina in February, claiming Department of Homeland Security agents detained people without warrants, NC Newsline previously reported.
And Malki said it could become a more frequent problem. Earlier this year, state lawmakers overrode Gov. Josh Stein’s veto of Senate Bill 153, the “North Carolina Border Protection Act.” The measure requires local and state law enforcement agencies to work with ICE.
“How many more cases like Atilio’s are we going to have?” she asked.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Court upholds Kentucky’s ban on child sex dolls after constitutional challenge
text:
Attorney General Russell Coleman, along with representatives from the Kentucky Multidisciplinary Commission on Child Sexual Abuse, released an updated protocol on how to handle child sexual abuse in the state. April 22, 2026.  (Kentucky Lantern photo by Sarah Ladd)A Union County judge has rejected a man’s constitutional challenge of Kentucky’s ban on child sex dolls. 
Kenneth Moore, 50, was charged in August 2025, according to court records, with a total of 16 counts of possession or viewing matter portraying a sexual performance by a minor, promoting a sexual performance by a minor less than 16 years of age and one count of trafficking a child sex doll — all felonies. 
In February, he asked the Union Circuit Court to declare House Bill 207, the ban passed by the General Assembly in 2024, unconstitutional and dismiss the charges against him related to that law. He argued at that time that his child sex doll was “homemade, essentially papier-mached out of different materials with the head of some sort of doll attached” and that “at no point was any child abused.” 
KY man challenges constitutionality of child sex doll ban. AG pushes back.

Kentucky Attorney General Russell Coleman defended the law, saying child sex dolls were not a form of protected speech. 
According to Judge Daniel M. Heady’s October order rejecting Moore’s claims, items examined in Moore’s case included:  

Two or more purported child sex dolls, torsos, or parts thereof, as said evidence appears to be a combination of doll heads and homemade sex dolls or body parts, including at least one head or doll with extremely childlike in appearance head and facial features.
10 nude or sexually explicit photographs containing a combination of a nude/sexually explicit body with a child’s face, so that each photograph is a morphed image of what appears to be a real child’s face on a nude/sexually explicit body. 
Approximately five sexually explicit computer-generated videos containing subjects that appear to be the combination of an adult (or what appears to be an adult) nude/sexually explicit body with a child’s face, so that each video appears to be a morphed sexually explicit video with an actor/actress possessing what appears to be a real child’s face on a nude body. 

“Moore argues that a possession of a child sex doll is a protected act of expression and entitled to First Amendment protections,” Heady’s ruling said. “This Court disagrees as possession of child sex dolls are not a form of protected speech or expression. Defendant acknowledges that a child sex doll or at least the purported child sex dolls items that he possessed were masturbatory tools, intended for use in conduct and not implicating speech, establishing that a child sex doll is a sexual device used for non-expressive conduct and not entitled to First Amendment protection.” 
When Moore first brought the challenge, his petition argued that “there is nothing to indicate what differentiates features of a minor from those with features of an adult,” an idea Heady rejected emphatically. 
Heady wrote: “The Defendant’s contention that ‘there is nothing to indicate the head, or rest of the body resemble a minor’ is completely without merit, and a borderline sanctionable offense as a misrepresentation of fact to the tribunal, as one of the dolls (or doll heads at least) is clearly that of a minor (or made to resemble a minor) and this Judge is of the strong opinion that any and every ordinary citizen of Union County, Kentucky would agree.” 
Rep. Stephanie Dietz, R-Edgewood, who sponsored the ban of child sex dolls, said in a Friday statement that “we will not tolerate” sexual exploitation of minors. 
“Our goal with HB 207 was to give law enforcement every possible tool to investigate and successfully prosecute cases involving the sexual abuse of children,” she said.  
Moore is scheduled to be sentenced on Jan. 11, according to court records. 
“Parenting in this ever-changing digital landscape can feel like whack-a-mole at a breakneck pace,” Coleman said in a statement. “We have a duty as parents and elected leaders to constantly be learning and adapting to combat the threat from predators. I am so grateful to Representative Stephanie Dietz and Senator Chris McDaniel who led the unanimous passage of this law through the General Assembly. Our kids are safer because of it.”

name: Daily Montanan
title: Public Service Commission to take up NorthWestern, Black Hills merger
text:
Electricity pylons (Photo by Getty Images). The Montana Public Service Commission is scheduled to take up the $15.4 billion merger proposal by NorthWestern Energy and Black Hills Corp. on Tuesday.
PSC legal and regulatory staff recommend approval of the merger.
NorthWestern Energy, the largest public utility in Montana, has argued the merger will not harm Montana customers, and some of the parties in the case are in support of the deal following their own settlement agreements with the utilities.
PSC staff recommend approval based on those agreements, including one with the Montana Consumer Counsel, which advocates on behalf of customers.
Released on Friday, a PSC staff memo said the merger will not harm customers.
“The concerns of all intervenors — with the exception of 350 Montana and Montana Farmers Union — were addressed” in the settlements, the staff memo said.
For example, the Laborers International Union of North America Local 1686 requests approval of the merger given the utilities agreed to take steps to support union workers.
Those steps include a “new commitment” giving preference to contractors hiring workers in or near their own communities, Local 1686 said in a filing.
But 350 Montana and Montana Farmers Union describe the merger as “a shell game” that will place financial risks on Montanans. 350 Montana has a mission to reduce atmospheric carbon dioxide.
The two parties urge the PSC to reject the merger — or set conditions that protect Montanans, especially from the potential costs of data centers.
The PSC is a five-member body, currently all Republican, that regulates monopoly utilities in Montana.
“In the end, this is not about love. This is about money,” wrote lawyer Monica Tranel on behalf of 350 Montana and the farmers union. “Enforceable conditions are the necessary prenuptial here.”
The Public Service Commission is scheduled to consider the merger at its 1:30 p.m. meeting Tuesday, Oct. 27. The meetings are available by video on the PSC website.
Nov. 12 is the deadline for a final decision.
Montana is the last state that needs to approve the merger, according to the South Dakota Searchlight. Regulators in South Dakota, where Black Hills is based, approved the deal in June.
The new company, to be named Bright Horizon Energy, would operate in Montana, South Dakota, Arkansas, Colorado, Iowa, Kansas, Nebraska and Wyoming.
This story will be updated.

name: Delaware
title: From Sea Witch to 5Ks, Delaware has a full weekend ahead
text:
Beyond Halloween, Delaware’s Oct. 23-25 weekend features live music, comic books, fall festivals, history, cycling, charity races and family adventures across all three counties.
WILMINGTON, Del. — Halloween may dominate the calendar, but Delaware residents looking for something different this weekend have plenty of options.
From the streets of Rehoboth Beach to historic New Castle, the Delaware State Fairgrounds and the farms of Kent County, communities are celebrating the final full weekend of October with festivals, performances, outdoor activities and family entertainment.
Runners and walkers also have several opportunities to support local causes, including breast cancer awareness, education and community organizations.
Here are Delaware LIVE’s top picks for Oct. 23-25.
Sea Witch brings three days of fun to Rehoboth Beach
One of Delaware’s biggest fall traditions returns this weekend as the 36th annual Sea Witch Festival fills downtown Rehoboth Beach with parades, live entertainment, shopping and family activities.
Running Friday through Sunday, the festival draws visitors from across the Mid-Atlantic for a combination of Halloween celebrations and traditional beach-town festivities.
The centerpiece is Saturday’s costume parade, beginning at 11 a.m. along Rehoboth Avenue. Elaborate costumes, decorated floats, community organizations and families are expected to fill the downtown streets.
Beyond the costumes, visitors can enjoy artisan vendors, live entertainment, seasonal shopping and local restaurants.
The festival also includes Sunday’s Sea Witch 5K Classic and one-mile Fright Walk, giving visitors an opportunity to participate in the celebration.
When: Friday through Sunday, Oct. 23-25
Where: Downtown Rehoboth Beach
Learn more: Rehoboth Beach-Dewey Beach Chamber of Commerce
Blue Hen Comic Con brings pop culture to Harrington
Comic books, anime, gaming, cosplay and pop culture take center stage Saturday and Sunday as Blue Hen Comic Con returns to the Delaware State Fairgrounds in Harrington.
The two-day convention brings together comic creators, artists, vendors, celebrity guests and fans for a celebration of entertainment and creativity.
Activities include cosplay competitions, Artist Alley, interactive gaming, panels and workshops.
Families with teenagers, comic enthusiasts and anyone interested in movies, superheroes or gaming will find an alternative to the traditional fall festival.
When: Saturday, 10 a.m.-6 p.m.; Sunday, 10 a.m.-4 p.m.
Where: Delaware State Fairgrounds, Harrington
Admission: $15 Saturday, $13 Sunday or $21 for the weekend.
William Penn Day celebrates Delaware’s beginnings
History takes center stage Saturday in Old New Castle as the New Castle Court House Museum commemorates the arrival of William Penn in 1682.
William Penn Day offers a glimpse into Delaware’s colonial history through educational presentations, historical interpretation and live music.
The day begins with a presentation by the Iron Hill Science Center about the Indigenous people and natural environment encountered by early European settlers.
At 2 p.m., musicians from the Suzuki Academy of the Delaware Music School will perform Baroque music reflecting the colonial era.
Visitors also can explore the museum and historic streets of Old New Castle.
When: Saturday, 10 a.m.-4 p.m.
Where: New Castle Court House Museum, New Castle
Learn more: Delaware Historical and Cultural Affairs
Acclaimed pianist opens Coastal Concerts season
Music lovers can spend Saturday afternoon in Lewes as internationally acclaimed pianist Awadagin Pratt opens the Coastal Concerts 2026-27 season.
Pratt has performed at Carnegie Hall, the Kennedy Center and Lincoln Center and with major orchestras across the United States.
His program, “America 250,” features works by American composers Florence Price, George Walker, Nathaniel Dett and Julius Eastman.
The concert offers a cultural alternative to the weekend’s crowded festivals and an opportunity to experience internationally recognized musical talent in coastal Delaware.
When: Saturday, 2 p.m.
Where: Bethel Fellowship Hall, 129 W. Fourth St., Lewes
Learn more: Coastal Concerts
Fifer Orchards offers classic fall family fun
Families looking for a traditional fall outing can visit Fifer Orchards near Wyoming, where Fall Fest continues Saturday.
The farm offers pumpkin and apple picking, a five-acre corn maze, outdoor attractions and seasonal favorites such as apple cider, cider doughnuts, kettle corn and ice cream.
This year’s attractions include an interactive Minion Maze and expanded children’s play area.
Fall Fest runs from 10 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., with visitors asked to leave by 5 p.m. Admission is $18 online or $24 at the gate for ages 3 and older.
When: Saturday, 10 a.m.-4:30 p.m.
Where: Fifer Orchards, Wyoming
Learn more: Fifer Orchards
Broad Creek Bash combines cycling and community
Cyclists will take to the roads of western Sussex County Saturday for the second annual Broad Creek Bash in Laurel.
Organized by the Western Sussex Chamber of Commerce, the event offers 25-, 50- and 65-mile routes through scenic countryside, historic communities, and waterways.
Riders will pass through a region known for its rural landscapes, historic sites and outdoor recreation opportunities.
An after-party at Janosik Park will feature live music and food trucks, giving friends and supporters a chance to join the celebration even if they are not cycling.
Online ride registration has closed, but visitors can still check with organizers about the community festivities.
When: Saturday, with cycling beginning at 7:30 a.m.
Where: Laurel, with activities at Janosik Park
Learn more: Western Sussex Chamber of Commerce
Runners and walkers take to Delaware streets for weekend 5Ks
Delaware runners and walkers have several opportunities to get active this weekend, with races supporting breast cancer awareness, education and other community causes.
On Saturday, Wilmington Friends School hosts the 30th annual Smith McMillan 5K, beginning at 8:30 a.m. The event benefits a financial aid endowment honoring two former students. A free children’s dash begins at 8:10 a.m.
Other Saturday events include the Boo & Brew 5K and Eternal Rest 5K Run/Walk in Wilmington and the Boo-K It! 5K in Odessa.
Sunday brings two notable races.
The 10th annual Deer Park Goes Pink 5K begins at 9 a.m. at Deer Park Tavern, 108 W. Main St. in Newark. The event supports the Delaware Breast Cancer Coalition and includes a one-mile fun walk and post-race celebration. Organizers say all race proceeds benefit the coalition.
At the beaches, the Sea Witch 5K Classic begins at 9 a.m. Sunday at Grove Park in Rehoboth Beach. The event also includes a one-mile Fright Walk, providing another way to participate in the festival.
Whether running for a personal best, walking with family or supporting a cause, the weekend’s races offer an opportunity to combine fitness and community involvement.
When: Saturday and Sunday, Oct. 24-25
Where: Wilmington, Odessa, Newark and Rehoboth Beach
Learn more: RunSignup or individual race organizers’ websites.
Seaford celebrates the harvest season
Downtown Seaford will host its Fall Harvest Festival Saturday, offering an afternoon of food, shopping, vendors and community activities.
Organized by the Downtown Seaford Association, the festival brings residents and visitors to High Street to enjoy the autumn season while supporting local merchants and small businesses.
The family-friendly event is a good choice for people interested in a traditional small-town celebration rather than a Halloween attraction.
When: Saturday, 10 a.m.-4 p.m.
Where: High Street, downtown Seaford
Learn more: Downtown Seaford Association
Explore the stars at Delaware Museum of Nature and Science
Families can travel through the universe without leaving Wilmington this weekend.
The Delaware Museum of Nature and Science will offer Star Lab programs Saturday and Sunday, allowing visitors to explore the night sky inside an inflatable, 360-degree planetarium.
This weekend’s presentations focus on myths, constellations and star lore from cultures around the world.
Programs are scheduled at 10:30 a.m., 11:30 a.m. and 1:30 p.m. An additional ticket is required beyond regular museum admission.
For adults seeking something more adventurous, the museum also hosts Museum of the Macabre Saturday evening from 6 to 9 p.m., combining science and natural history with a Halloween atmosphere.
When: Saturday and Sunday for Star Lab; Saturday, 6-9 p.m., for Museum of the Macabre
Where: Delaware Museum of Nature and Science, Wilmington
Learn more: Delaware Museum of Nature and Science
Outdoor walks offer a change of pace
Not every weekend adventure requires tickets or a scheduled event.
Delaware’s state parks, nature preserves and public trails offer opportunities to enjoy the cooler weather and changing fall colors.
Brandywine Creek State Park in northern Delaware offers wooded trails and views along the creek. In Kent County, Killens Pond State Park provides lakeside walks and wooded paths.
Farther south, Trap Pond State Park near Laurel offers trails around one of Delaware’s best-known natural areas, with its distinctive bald cypress trees.
Visitors also can explore the Wilmington Riverfront, where walking paths follow the Christina River and connect to restaurants, parks and other attractions.
Delaware LIVE’s best bets for the weekend
Whether looking for a full-day festival, live music, a community race or a quiet afternoon, Delaware has something happening in every corner of the state.

Biggest festival: Sea Witch Festival, Rehoboth Beach
Best for pop culture fans: Blue Hen Comic Con, Harrington
Best for history lovers: William Penn Day, New Castle
Best for music: Awadagin Pratt, Lewes
Best for families: Fifer Orchards Fall Fest, Wyoming
Best for community involvement: Deer Park Goes Pink 5K, Newark
Best for science lovers: Star Lab, Wilmington
Best for outdoor adventure: Broad Creek Bash, Laurel
Best small-town festival: Seaford Fall Harvest Festival

With Halloween celebrations sharing the calendar with concerts, community races, harvest festivals, history and outdoor recreation, this weekend offers a reminder that Delaware’s fall season has something for just about everyone.
TO GO: Delaware weekend roundup
When: Friday through Sunday, Oct. 23-25, 2026
Where: Locations throughout New Castle, Kent and Sussex counties
Highlights: Sea Witch Festival, Blue Hen Comic Con, William Penn Day, Coastal Concerts, Fifer Orchards Fall Fest, Broad Creek Bash, community 5Ks, Seaford Fall Harvest Festival and Delaware Museum of Nature and Science programs.
Admission: Varies by event. Some activities are free; others require tickets or advance registration.
Planning tip: Sea Witch visitors should expect traffic congestion and parking restrictions in downtown Rehoboth Beach. The Saturday costume parade begins at 11 a.m.
More information: Visit individual event websites for schedules, tickets, parking information and last-minute changes.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: BP, Louisiana leaders agree on Deepwater Horizon settlement payout to ‘resolve’ coastal lawsuits
text:
Fireboats pour water on the flames of the Deepwater Horizon drilling structure on April 21, 2010, in the Gulf of Mexico. Eleven crew members on the rig died in the offshore drilling disaster that coated the Gulf Coast with oil from the resulting underwater leak. (U.S. Coast Guard photo)Louisiana has agreed to a lump-sum payment for the remainder of what BP owes from the Deepwater Horizon disaster settlement. It will also bring to an end the remaining lawsuits that parishes have brought against the company for related coastal damages, according to a news release BP issued Friday.
More than $6 billion was directed to Louisiana in the settlement for the 2010 offshore oil rig explosion that killed 11 workers and leaked 168 million gallons of crude oil, sullying a large swath of the Gulf Coast. All but $373 million has been paid to the state, with payments scheduled over the next seven years. 
BP said Louisiana will take a single $350 million payout, and the remaining lawsuits against the company will be “resolved,” according to the news release.
Paul Takahashi, a BP spokesman, said in response to emailed questions that terms of BP’s coastal litigation agreement are confidential, and that it “resolves all outstanding coastal zone lawsuits and similar claims against BP by the parishes and State of Louisiana.”
The Deepwater Horizon settlement deal announced Friday represents a “resetting the relationship between BP and Louisiana so both can focus on the future,” the company’s news release said.
Statements from the Gov. Jeff Landry and Attorney General Liz Murrill were included in the BP news release. Neither of their offices responded immediately to questions seeking more details on the agreement. Both have traveled to Paris for the New Orleans Saints game Sunday.
“We have tackled legacy lawsuits, which many said was impossible,” Landry’s quote reads, in part. “We have now disposed of claims and settled with all but one of the major defendants in these coastal cases. This sends a signal to job creators all over America that Louisiana welcomes jobs and economic growth while responsibly dealing with the issues of the past.” 
“Louisiana has been a leader in defending, building and protecting energy security nationally and internationally,” Murrill said. “I’m grateful to join Governor Landry and BP America as we build a stable energy supply. Resolving issues of the past paves our way to a brighter future working relationship.”
The agreement with BP is separate from the settlements Landry has previously brokered to end so-called legacy lawsuits parishes have brought against Shell, ExxonMobil, ConocoPhillips, Hillcorp and Freeport-McMoRan for decades of marsh and wetlands damage from energy exploration.
The lone active major case involves Chevron in Plaquemines Parish, which a state court awarded $745 million in damages in March 2025. Chevron has asked the U.S. 5th Circuit Court of Appeals to move the case to federal court, where the company anticipates a more favorable ruling.
This is a developing story.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Scott Colom says he’ll delete AI-generated Cindy Hyde-Smith ad after AG Fitch threatens legal action
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Republican Attorney General Lynn Fitch said Friday that Scott Colom, the Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate, likely violated state law with a digital ad that featured an artificial intelligence-generated depiction of Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith running away from reporters. 
Colom told Mississippi Today he would delete the post because he didn’t want Fitch to launch litigation with taxpayer money. That came after Fitch sent Colom a complaint letter demanding that he remove that ad from his social media accounts. If he did not, the complaint said, the attorney general’s office could file an injunction against him. 
“As violations of this election integrity law can carry criminal penalties, Attorney General Fitch has also asked Scott Colom and his campaign to preserve all records related to this matter so as not to obstruct justice,” the statement reads. 
In a statement, Colom said that Hyde-Smith is “clearly desperate” and that she and her allies are “once again trying to weaponize the justice system to distract from the real issues, which is that she has sold out our farmers, sold out our small businesses, and sold out our families.” 

“Clearly this was parody, maybe too close to home because she knows she does love to hide from her own constituents and reporters,” Colom said. 
Fitch’s threat is the latest salvo between Colom’s campaign and the state GOP in a race that has generated national attention and millions of dollars from national party interests leading up to the Nov. 3 election. National pundits are saying the Mississippi race, initially taken for granted by Republicans, is in play.
The complaint follows a letter that Mississippi GOP Chairman Mike Hurst sent to Fitch asking her to launch an investigation and criticizing the Colom campaign for not labeling the content as AI-generated.   
After a rally with former Vice President Kamala Harris on Thursday, before Fitch had acceded to Hurst’s request to investigate the matter, Colom said Republicans were mounting a coordinated attack to distract from his campaign’s increasing momentum. He pointed out that the ad has been up for weeks, yet Hurst and Fitch were first opining on the matter 11 days before the election. 
“They understand that I’m a threat. Mike Hurst does this all the time. Every time somebody gets competitive, they try to weaponize the justice system to intimidate their opponents,” Colom said. “I thought they weren’t snowflakes. You’re telling me they can’t take a joke?” 
If Fitch does pursue legal action, it would be a rare instance of her office enforcing campaign laws. 
During the 2023 statewide election cycle, Lt. Gov. Delbert Hosemann claimed for months that his Republican primary challenger, state Sen. Chris McDaniel, violated campaign finance laws by accepting more than the state’s legal limit from corporations. 
Several Mississippi Republicans agreed that it was a clear-cut example of a campaign-finance law violation, but Fitch later declined to pursue any action against the campaign or the leaders of a political action committee involved in the donations. 
Her reluctance to investigate or prosecute alleged campaign finance violations prompted other state leaders to call for reform and more enforcement. Most of those attempts have failed in the Legislature.
Hurst and Fitch issued similar statements about a Democrat close to a competitive election. Fitch shortly before last year’s elections said she was investigating former state Rep. Sonya Williams Barnes, the Democratic nominee for mayor of Gulfport, over allegations that residents had received meal vouchers in exchange for voting. No charges were filed against Williams Barnes.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: RNC chair looks to squash Nebraska’s independent experiment
text:
Republican Sen. Joe Gruters, of Sarasota and Manatee counties in Florida. (Photo by Jackie Llanos/Florida Phoenix)OMAHA — Republican National Committee Chair Joe Gruters sipped a vanilla latte at Rally Coffee Co. in a state where he hadn’t expected to spend time at the beginning of the midterm cycle. 
“But I love Nebraska,” Gruters quickly told the Examiner Wednesday. “I’m glad I’m here … we don’t always get to come to Nebraska because you guys aren’t usually competitive, but this cycle you are, and so hopefully we won’t have to come back here again in two years.”
Gruters — despite the political environment — said he believes Republicans still have a path to maintain control of both the U.S. House and Senate because the GOP has the fundraising advantage and candidates who he thinks can win. Meanwhile, the independent Dan Osborn campaign and Nebraska Democrats see the visits as a sign that Republicans are concerned about holding the traditionally red state. 
Gruters said Republicans’ secret weapon is President Donald Trump. 
“(Trump) has been able to turn out low-propensity voters three times. That’s why when he’s at these rallies, he says, ‘I’m on the ballot,’” said Gruters, who became chair of the RNC last year. “He is, because if somehow the left wins, either the House or the Senate, they’re going to investigate, obstruct, impeach.”
Nebraska Sen. Pete Ricketts speaks in North Platte on Oct. 22, 2026. (Juan Salinas II/Nebraska Examiner)
In the last month before Election Day Nov. 3, Trump, Senate Majority Leader John Thune and now Vice President JD Vance have visited Nebraska to campaign for incumbent Republican Sen. Pete Ricketts. 
Gruters said the GOP can lean on Ricketts’ reputation as  a “conservative fighter” with “robust knowledge of the policy issues” to win the race
The former governor is in a bitter race against registered nonpartisan Osborn as both have engaged in heavy mudslinging.  Gruters said the recent events aim to energize the GOP base.
“What we have to do is we’re going all over the country, including states that we wouldn’t normally go to, because it’s all about turnout,” Gruters said. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Nebraska Democratic Party chair Jane Kleeb, who is the Democratic National Committee’s vice chair, said in a statement that Gruters’ visit to Nebraska is “very telling that things are very bad for local Republicans.”
“We will not take our foot off the gas no matter what the RNC plans,” Kleeb said. “Our coalition of supporters has been on the ground and talking to voters from Alliance to Plattsmouth. Democrats across Nebraska are mobilizing this upcoming weekend to knock 10,000 doors in a day to ensure voter turnout translates into victories for our Democratic and independent candidates up and down the ballot.” 
Dan Osborn speaks at Red Cloud Community Center on Oct. 1, 2026. (Juan Salinas II/Nebraska Examiner)
Kleeb said ensuring victory for those candidates is necessary to stop “local MAGA candidates like Pete Ricketts, Mike Flood, and Adrian Smith from rubber-stamping all of Trump’s hurtful and disastrous policies.”
The Nebraska Senate race set a trend for other red states with independent candidates. Osborn is one of a handful of nonpartisan candidates who have been painted as Democrats by their opponents.
The Osborn campaign released a statement about GOP leaders’ recent visits to Nebraska, saying that if only “Ricketts brought this much attention to Nebraska before his job was in jeopardy, he wouldn’t have to spend millions on a reelection campaign.”
“We have a busy schedule finishing the 93-county tour, but would happily make time for either Leader Thune or Vice President Vance if they wanted to meet,” said Xavier Royer, an Osborn spokesperson.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Central Iowa couple sues over years-long delays in immigration cases
text:
(Photo by simpson33 via iStock / Getty Images Plus)
A Carlisle couple is suing the federal government over delays in processing the immigration papers for people married to American citizens.
Jordan Sarae Pastrana Bates and her husband, Olman Javie Pastrana Linarez, are suing U.S. Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin, U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche and U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services in U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Iowa.
The couple, who married in March 2026 and have a child together, alleges that Bates, a U.S. citizen by birth, filed a Petition for Alien Relative, also known as an I-130 application form, with CIS in May 2026 on behalf of her husband, who is a citizen of Honduras.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
That application seeks to establish a valid family relationship that would represent the first step in Linarez’s family-based immigration process. Typically, after CIS approves the application, the beneficiary can either apply for an immigrant visa or an adjustment of their residency status.
The lawsuit alleges CIS now takes an average of 80 months, or six and half years, to process I-130 applications, placing the applicants at risk of being deported from the United States.
According to the lawsuit, federal data shows the length of time the federal government takes to process such applications has increased by 420% over the past year, and by 635% in the past five years.
“This is not a marginal delay or a temporary fluctuation,” the couple’s attorney, Jessica Donels, has told the court. “It reflects a systemic failure to process applications in a timely manner.”
The lawsuit seeks a court order that will compel CIS and the other defendants to “perform their duties” as required by law.
The U.S. Department of Justice has yet to file a response to the lawsuit.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Pa. Supreme Court denies request to intervene in questioned capital punishment cases
text:
A judge's gavel in a courtroom. ((Stock photo by Greenleaf123/Getty Images)Pennsylvania’s highest court on Friday declined to intervene in the cases of two men charged with capital murder after defenders raised alarms about the district attorney’s prolific pursuit of the death penalty in Washington County.
The Atlantic Center for Capital Representation filed a petition in July 2025 asking the state Supreme Court to restrict Washington County District Attorney Jason Walsh’s use of the death penalty. The court’s two-page order didn’t explain the decision.
It alleges Walsh had pursued the death penalty without evidence supporting capital punishment and outlined a pattern in which Walsh’s office has allegedly held other defendants for trial with the intent to seek the death penalty without establishing facts to support it.
One of the men, Joshua George, was found not guilty of killing his 6-month-old son by a Washington County jury last October.
Frances Harvey, executive director of the Atlantic Center for Capital Representation, said the group is deeply disappointed by the court’s decision not to address what she described as an “obvious problem.”
“But that doesn’t change the fact that Jason Walsh has overreached in the most serious decision-making any district attorney has, which is to seek another person’s execution,” Harvey said. “What’s happening in Washington County is a disgrace to our justice system, and we will continue to call out this sort of misconduct when we see it.”    
Walsh did not respond to a voicemail left at his office.
The petition asked the court to exercise its power to intervene in any case to order the Washington County District Attorney’s Office to be precluded from seeking death sentences without the approval of a judge from another county. 
It requested the court to bar the office from seeking the death penalty against George and Jordan Clarke. The men were charged separately in the deaths of their infant children. Clarke remains held without bail awaiting trial.
The Atlantic Center’s petition asked the Supreme Court to appoint a special master to supervise the district attorney’s office and require the district attorney to consult with the Pennsylvania Attorney General’s capital unit regarding decisions to seek death.
It also asked that a judge from another county be assigned to review every capital case in Washington County since 2021. Walsh filed notices of his intent to pursue sentences of death in 11 out of 18 homicide cases his office has prosecuted since he took office in 2021, according to the petition.
“This is a systemic and ongoing problem that is harming people,” Harvey said. “The acquittal of Joshua George last year and the dismissal of charges against Jah Sutton are perfect examples of how people have lost years of their lives in county jail because of Jason Walsh’s reckless pursuit of the death penalty. That kind of misconduct deserves a systems-level response, not mere individual reviews.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Sutton was one of three people charged with capital murder in the killing of a Donora convenience store clerk in 2021. A state appellate court in August upheld a Washington County judge’s decision dismissing the charges against Sutton after finding there was no prima facie evidence linking her to the shooting.
“Jason Walsh is the kind of problematic prosecutor who exemplifies why capital punishment is broken and irredeemable in Pennsylvania,” Harvey said.
Under Pennsylvania law, the death penalty may be applied only when the killing at issue was intentional and there is at least one aggravating factor.
Aggravating factors can include when the victim is a police officer or other first responder, murder for hire, torture, killing in the commission of another felony and more than a dozen other circumstances. 
In the case of Clarke, the petition alleges, Walsh filed homicide charges and notice of aggravating factors to pursue the death penalty before the manner of his two-month-old son’s death had been determined. It also claims Walsh attempted to improperly influence the death investigation.
In an affidavit in support of the petition, Washington County Coroner Timothy Warco accused Walsh of fraudulently obtaining a court order directing Warco’s office to take jurisdiction over the death of Clarke’s son after an autopsy was performed in Allegheny County.
When two-month-old Sawyer Clarke died in 2022, Walsh was actively campaigning for his first election as district attorney, having been appointed to his post a year earlier. His primary platform was harsh punishment for people who kill infants and children, Warco’s affidavit said. 
Although Sawyer died at Children’s Hospital of Pittsburgh in Allegheny County, an assistant district attorney told Warco that Walsh wanted the Washington County Coroner’s Office to perform the autopsy, according to the filing.
According to Warco’s affidavit, Walsh obtained a court order from President Judge John DiSalle listing the child’s place of death as Peters Township, Washington County, in order to give Warco’s office jurisdiction over the death. 
The Atlantic Center contends the district attorney’s pursuit of a death sentence is not supported by the evidence produced at a preliminary hearing.

name: Maine Morning Star
title: DOJ sending election observers to polls in Portland, Lewiston
text:
Voters and election officials at the Lewiston Armory on Election Day, Nov. 4, 2025. (Photo by Jim Neuger/ Maine Morning Star)The U.S. Department of Justice is sending election monitors to polls in Portland and Lewiston to oversee the Nov. 3 elections, the Maine Secretary of State’s office confirmed. 
The Department of Justice has in recent years sent observers to other states on a smaller scale, usually in response to a civil rights violation. But this comes amid several efforts by the Trump administration to assert authority over the election and following an attempt to force Maine, among other states, to hand over voter information.
Secretary of State Shenna Bellows said she doesn’t expect the observers will have any impact on election processes.
“Any monitors are subject to the same laws and rules as any other observer at the poll,” Bellows told Maine Morning Star. “That means they can observe what’s taking place, but they may not interact with voters, handle ballots or equipment, or disrupt voting in any way.” 
“We will monitor the monitors very carefully to ensure that they don’t cross any lines,” Bellows added.
This is the first time since Bellows became secretary of state in 2021 that federal election observers have been dispatched to Maine, which is among several states that were notified this week of the federal presence on Election Day.
The DOJ in August announced plans to send 1,000 election monitors to midterm election polling places nationwide, as first reported by Bloomberg. That’s significantly more than the 289 observers sent out for the 2022 midterm elections, and the 714 involved in the 2024 presidential election, CBS News reported.
Bellows said the DOJ observers will be among many other Election Day monitors, including those dispatched by the parties and nonpartisan groups including the League of Women Voters and ACLU.
They will dress in business casual clothing and won’t be allowed to use any DOJ identifiers. They also aren’t allowed to talk to voters inside polling places or to carry firearms.
The goal, according to letters sent by the DOJ, is to monitor for compliance with federal voting rights laws, including people with disabilities’ access to the ballot box, among other civil rights assurances. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Portland and Lewiston are Maine’s two most populous cities and are home to the state’s largest share of immigrants. In the weeks leading up to the election, President Donald Trump has launched an aggressive campaign against noncitizen voting, including attempts to purge voter rolls and send sensitive personal information to the Department of Homeland Security with the aim of flagging potential noncitizen voters.
Last year, the DOJ sued Maine after Bellows twice rejected requests from the Trump administration for Maine’s full, unredacted voter rolls — among other information. In May, a federal judge dismissed the administration’s lawsuit, following similar legal setbacks in other states.
Bellows said her office “will do everything in our power to ensure a positive voting experience for every citizen.” She added, “voter intimidation or interference is a crime, and we will hold the DOJ monitors to the same standards and expectations as anyone else who’s at the voting point on Election Day.”
She also pointed out that anyone who is concerned can cast a ballot at their municipal clerk’s office anytime during business hours before the end of early voting on Oct. 29.
There have already been reports of voter harassment in Lewiston. This week, an employee of the Maine Wire filmed members of the immigrant community at the city clerk’s office. 
“We’ve been in close communication with the city clerk, and we understand the city of Lewiston has taken some measures to enforce order at the voting place,” Bellows said, noting the city has put up notices warning that filming or photography (outside of selfies) is prohibited at polling locations. “No one should be harassed or filmed without their consent by anyone, whether that person is purporting to be a member of the media, or there for partisan political purposes.”
The rightwing outlet alleged those seeking interpretation assistance were in some way violating voting rules. But Bellows said her office has not received a credible report that an interpreter is engaged in illegal electioneering.
