name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: Commentary: Finding unexpected common ground with my immigrant neighbors
text:
Players in the inaugural Common Ground Cup, held in June 2026, pose for a photo outside Mitchell Road Presbyterian Church. (Photo by Aaron Johnson/Courtesy of World Relief Upstate SC)This summer, I gathered some friends from church, and we participated in the Common Ground Cup, a soccer tournament hosted by World Relief.
The goal was to raise funds, bring awareness, and foster connections with local refugees and residents in Greenville.
The unique twist? Our tournament team included seven refugees.
As the day neared, I felt anxious.
I’m not the best soccer player, and as team captain, I carried extra communication responsibilities — I feared the language barrier might make it hard to engage with the refugees.
I worried I couldn’t show them I cared or welcome them as I would a neighbor who spoke my language. I wanted them to feel accepted and connected, and to enjoy playing soccer with us.
I hoped Jesus’ love would shine through me. Though welcoming strangers is something we are called to do as Christians, I was uncertain about how it would feel to welcome those I believed I had little in common with.
Ah, hence the name of the tournament: The Common Ground Cup.
As things got underway, it didn’t take long for me to see that I was totally overthinking what God was asking me to do. He wanted me to trust Him, and trust that the Holy Spirit would do the work that I couldn’t do. He wanted me to faithfully show up, smile, laugh, be kind, be curious, and encourage.
It wasn’t about what I could or couldn’t say to my teammates. It was about being a vessel of Christ’s love.
A passion for soccer gave us common ground, and God gave us opportunities for small, meaningful interactions. God shared His love through me that day, and He also shared His love for me through my new teammates, as they smiled, laughed, showed interest, and encouraged me.
Looking back on how quickly my fear melted away, I’ve been thinking about what has fueled so much of it in the first place.
With the amount of political rhetoric around immigration and resettlement, I can become paralyzed and feel helpless about having meaningful conversations or getting involved at all.
I can start to see gray as black and white, and I can see polarized sides where there should be community.
Loving your neighbor through a soccer tournament doesn’t make a viral headline, but as Christians, sharing the love of Jesus with strangers and neighbors alike should be the big story.
We give our fears over to God, and we jump in.
I feel strongly that, as believers, we have to ask for courage and compassion that come from Jesus Himself and seek to obey His commands to “do good, be rich in good deeds, and be generous and willing to share” (1 Timothy 6:17-19).
I believe He is calling us to move toward people in our community so that they may experience the love of Jesus.
He is calling us beyond the media narratives and asking us to walk boldly in our own neighborhoods, lift our heads, look one another in the eyes, and love as He does.
Maybe you have a neighbor you should invite over for dinner or set up a play date for your kids. Maybe through smiling and waving to your neighbor, you will start to get to know them and learn of a need they have that you can fill in a practical way — helping them with groceries, understanding school papers for their children, or navigating doctor’s visits or appointments at the Department of Motor Vehicles.
I don’t believe we should be reckless where caution is truly warranted, and there is certainly a great need for meaningful policy changes.
However, I have a new fear: that our rhetoric would stifle our ability and willingness to be the hands and feet of Jesus to our neighbors living around us.
So, I ask you the questions I have started asking myself: Am I willing to go where Jesus leads, even if it makes me uncomfortable or costs me something? Am I willing to lay down my desires and place the needs of someone else above my own? Am I willing to extend a hand to my neighbor and go out of my way to make someone feel seen, heard, and cared for?
On that summer day, as my new friends and I leaned into the messiness of cross-cultural friendship — and the chaos of a soccer tournament — I gained as much or more than I brought to the table.
I came to bless but was blessed in return.
I hope that others will join me in the joyful unexpectedness that comes when we step out of our comfort zone and seek out friendship with someone whose story and life experiences are so totally different from our own.
Who will you meet today?

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Haskell Indian Nations University and EPA expand collaboration to support student careers
text:
The entrance to Haskell Indian Nations University at Lawrence in April 2024. (Photo by Max McCoy/Kansas Reflector)LAWRENCE — For Haskell Indian Nations University students, a renewed partnership with the Environmental Protection Agency is expected to open the door to internships, research opportunities and future careers serving tribal communities.
The university is expanding its relationship with the EPA after the two organizations signed a five-year memorandum of understanding in September, continuing a partnership that has been in place since 1999. 
“The partnership is intended to foster ongoing knowledge exchange, create meaningful learning and internship opportunities, and advance shared environmental priorities in a way that benefits Haskell students, EPA, and tribal communities,” said Jim Macy, a regional EPA administrator. 
More than 90 Haskell students have participated in the previous EPA-Haskell mentor program, and seven students later interned with the EPA, which Macy said provides students with valuable insight into how tribes collaborate with the EPA.
“They can take that knowledge back to support their respective tribes,” Macy said. “The partnership inspires students to follow their passions and consider turning those passions into meaningful careers they truly enjoy, creating a path for long-term success in environmental leadership and tribal service.”
The agreement outlines collaboration focused on student opportunities, environmental research and tribal engagement. The agreement was created to address barriers to opportunities that Haskell students have faced in the past. 
The updated agreement says there will be more hands-on learning, internship opportunities and professional connections to address these barriers, according to an EPA press release. The agreement replaces a previous memorandum signed in October 2022 and continues a partnership that EPA and Haskell officials say has lasted more than 25 years.
Haskell president Alex Red Corn said the partnership will benefit students of all majors. 
“Any opportunities for our students to get their foot in the door with internships and job opportunities can help make job transitions into federal positions or other industries much easier,” Red Corn said. “Our students come from across the country, and each student will have opportunities to explore connections to their home tribal communities.”
Red Corn said the EPA plans to host guest lectures and attend career fairs, which he said could reach thousands of students in the next few years. He said the ongoing partnership will create job opportunities in tribal communities across the country. 
“Haskell is always looking for ways to collaborate with the tribal nations it serves,” Red Corn said. “Access to EPA mentorship and internship opportunities, along with hands-on learning across all our programs, will strengthen tribal capacity for environmental and health initiatives when our students graduate and begin their careers across Indian Country.”

name: Delaware
title: Dr. Joe’s Arminio’s Oct. 28 event offers Delaware voters a different perspective on lowering costs, reviving growth
text:
Republican challenger proposes sweeping debt relief and economic reforms, while Democratic incumbent Sarah McBride emphasizes targeted assistance for working families. No debates, forums, or town meetings between the candidates have been announced.
WILMINGTON — Delaware voters looking for answers to rising living costs will have an opportunity Wednesday, Oct. 28, to hear a different approach to economic growth as Republican congressional candidate Dr. Joe Arminio presents his proposals just days before the Nov. 3 general election.  As of Friday afternoon,  the McBride Campaign has no similar public event on her calendar.
Arminio, who is challenging Democratic U.S. Rep. Sarah McBride for Delaware’s only seat in the House of Representatives, argues that reducing America’s enormous debt burden is essential to restoring economic growth and making life more affordable.
McBride, seeking a second term, has made affordability a central campaign priority, emphasizing lower housing, health care, child care and energy costs, along with tax relief for working families.
Both candidates recognize the financial pressures facing Delaware households. Their differences lie largely in how they believe Washington should respond.
Arminio proposes a different economic direction
Arminio, a Wilmington native and political scientist with a doctorate from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, has built his campaign around what he calls the American Prosperity Plan.
He argues that excessive personal, business and government debt has weakened the economy, leaving families with less money to spend and businesses with fewer opportunities to grow.
His proposals include:

Debt relief: A proposed “debt jubilee” providing $92,400 per adult to reduce private debt, with government-backed bonds compensating creditors.
Monetary reform: Changes to the federal monetary system, including government-created currency intended to reduce dependence on borrowing.
Infrastructure investment: Establishing a federal infrastructure bank to finance transportation improvements, public infrastructure and affordable housing.
Economic growth: Pursuing policies he believes could restore the stronger growth rates associated with the 1950s.

Arminio contends that reducing debt would free household income, encourage business investment and expand economic opportunities.
His campaign message, “Relieve Debts, Stop the Wars,” also connects economic prosperity to reduced American involvement in overseas conflicts, which he argues contribute to government borrowing, instability and inflation.
The proposals depart significantly from conventional economic policy. Important questions remain about how the debt relief would be financed, its effects on taxpayers and financial institutions, and whether the changes could produce the growth Arminio predicts without increasing inflation.
Some of Arminio’s economic assertions also differ substantially from official federal statistics. He contends that the United States has experienced little or no meaningful inflation-adjusted economic growth since 2008, although Bureau of Economic Analysis data show substantial real economic growth during that period.
McBride emphasizes targeted relief for families
McBride has approached affordability through legislation intended to reduce specific household expenses while expanding economic opportunities.
She has co-sponsored the American Affordability Act, which includes provisions intended to increase affordable housing, provide tax assistance for first-time homebuyers and renters, reduce health care and child care expenses, and lower energy costs.
McBride has also supported expanded paid family and medical leave, more affordable child care and greater access to home-based services for seniors and people with disabilities.
Her campaign argues that reducing these expenses would allow working families to keep more of their earnings while helping more people enter or remain in the workforce.
McBride has criticized federal tariffs, arguing that they increase prices for consumers and businesses.
Her approach relies primarily on targeted federal programs, tax incentives and investments rather than the broad restructuring of the financial system proposed by Arminio.
Those policies also raise questions about federal spending, financing and how quickly Delaware households might experience meaningful relief.
Two approaches to a shared concern
For Delaware residents facing high electricity bills, expensive housing, grocery costs and growing financial obligations, the candidates offer contrasting economic strategies.
McBride emphasizes reducing specific household expenses, expanding access to essential services and using federal legislation to provide relief.
Arminio argues that reducing debt and changing the nation’s financial structure would create stronger, sustained economic growth, ultimately benefiting families and businesses.
Neither approach guarantees immediate results, and both would require congressional support to become law.
The candidates also differ in their foreign-policy priorities. Arminio has made opposition to continued overseas military conflicts a central campaign theme. McBride has also called for ending prolonged conflicts and has criticized the Trump administration’s handling of foreign affairs, although the candidates differ on American policy toward Israel and Iran.
Few opportunities to compare the candidates directly
While both campaigns have published their priorities and participated in public campaign activities, opportunities for voters to hear the candidates directly compare and defend their proposals have been limited.
Arminio issued a public challenge Oct. 5 for a Lincoln-Douglas-style debate with McBride, proposing an extended discussion in which both candidates could explain their positions and respond to each other’s arguments.
The candidates previously appeared at a Sept. 17 forum hosted by the Jewish Federation of Delaware. Arminio was removed from that event after misgendering McBride.
McBride also participated in an extended candidate interview with Delaware Public Media, discussing her priorities and record in Congress.
As of Oct. 23, Delaware LIVE could not identify an additional publicly announced debate or comparable candidate forum involving McBride scheduled before the Nov. 3 election.
That does not mean voters have lacked opportunities to hear from the incumbent. McBride has campaigned throughout Delaware, participated in interviews and outlined her positions through public statements and her campaign website.
However, a forum allowing both candidates to respond directly to the same questions would offer voters an additional way to compare their economic proposals.
Oct. 28 offers a chance to hear another perspective
Arminio’s Oct. 28 campaign event comes during Delaware’s early voting period, less than a week before voters decide who will represent the state in Congress.
The event offers an opportunity to examine proposals that have received less attention than traditional debates over taxes, federal spending and government programs.
It also raises practical questions: Would broad debt relief help younger families purchase homes? Could changes in monetary policy strengthen small businesses? How would Arminio’s proposals affect inflation and federal finances? And how do those ideas compare with McBride’s plans to reduce household expenses?
For Delaware voters, the congressional race presents competing ideas about how government can help families afford everyday life while encouraging economic growth.
Although Arminio’s campaign event is not a substitute for a debate between both candidates, it offers voters another opportunity to hear an alternative perspective, examine its potential benefits and risks, and make a more informed choice before Election Day.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: West Virginia Attorney General McCuskey issues subpoenas on environmental groups
text:
West Virginia Attorney General JB McCuskey, shown speaking in a legislative interim meeting, has subpoenaed at least six environmental groups. (Photo by Perry Bennett/West Virginia Legislative Photography)The West Virginia Attorney General’s Office subpoenaed at least six environmental groups, asking for records regarding climate change, in a move at least one advocated called a “fishing expedition intended to stifle our collective voice.” 
The subpoenas, sent out in September, asked for internal documents regarding public statements made about West Virginia coal mines, gas wells and other energy sources and their contributions to climate change. The attorney general is also asking for materials used to solicit donations and any dealings with alternative energy producers and advocates. 
The legal maneuvering is part of an investigation into “alleged unfair or deceptive acts or practices and other possible violations of the West Virginia Consumer Credit and Protection Act,” according to a copy of the subpoena. 
The rash of subpoenas came to light Thursday after the West Virginia Rivers Coalition and 350.Org, an organization that advocates for renewable energy, filed suit in federal court to block them. 
“The Attorney General’s demands here also retaliate against WV Rivers and 350.org for speech, association, and petitioning that the First Amendment protects, and they are unreasonable demands under the Fourth Amendment, issued in investigations that the Attorney General has no authority to conduct,” lawyers for the organizations argued in their motion filed in the United States District Court of Southern West Virginia. 
That law covers a wide range of business practices and empowers the attorney general to address unsavory practices like predatory lending, a contractor taking a deposit and never doing the work and bait-and-switch marketing. 
Attorney General JB McCuskey, a Republican, enjoyed support from the fossil fuel industry during his 2024 run for office. Since taking office, he has supported efforts to rollback federal greenhouse gas emissions rules, opposed the United State’s participation in international climate talks, and advocated for keeping gas pipelines open. 
McCuskey’s office did not reply to a request for comment. 
The federal lawsuit mentions, but does not name, at least four other organizations that had received subpoenas. 
Jennie Smith, the executive director of the West Virginia Rivers Coalition, said in a statement issued Thursday that the attorney general’s investigation has led to a chilling effect for her organization’s work in promoting clean waterways. 
“Under this sham investigation, we may not be able to protect the identities of anyone who has worked in coalition with us. With that truth in mind, we have slowed public rollout of projects and awards to protect smaller groups and individuals from being targeted,” Smith said. 
U.S. District Court Judge Joseph R. Goodwin has set a hearing for a temporary restraining order on Oct. 29 in Charleston at 1 p.m.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: US DOJ opens investigation into gun permitting in Middletown, Waterbury
text:
The U.S. Department of Justice announced this week that it has opened an investigation into firearm permitting process in two Connecticut cities.
The DOJ’s Civil Rights Division announced via a press release that it is investigating Waterbury and Middletown over the two municipalities “policies and practices” for issuing firearm permits.
In certified letters sent to the mayors and police chiefs in the two cities, the DOJ explained that it intends to investigate whether local authorities are “unnecessarily” delaying or denying gun permits.
It unclear from the release why the DOJ is singling out Waterbury and Middletown or whether this is part of a larger push by the Civil Rights Division to investigate local firearm permitting in other parts of the country. 
The investigation into firearm permitting in Connecticut comes at a time when the Trump administration is busy changing some of the traditional missions of the DOJ’s civil rights division. 
That office, which was created in 1956 amid the Civil Rights Movement, historically handled cases involving things like voting rights, housing discrimination, police misconduct and the civil rights of prisoners. 
The press release from the DOJ said the investigation into Waterbury and Middletown is focused on upholding people’s 2nd Amendment rights. 
“All law-abiding Americans have a constitutional right to bear arms for self‑defense,” said Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon, the head of the DOJ’s Civil Rights Division. “This right is not a luxury reserved for a privileged few, but a fundamental liberty for all, including the residents of Middletown and Waterbury, Connecticut.”
The Connecticut Mirror contacted local officials in Waterbury and Middletown for this story, as well as the Connecticut Attorney General’s office, which has defended the state’s gun control laws in court in recent years. 
Through a spokesperson, Attorney General William Tong said his office would defer to local officials for comment.
A spokesperson for Middletown’s Democratic Mayor Gene Nocera did not immediately respond to a phone call. 
Waterbury’s Democratic Mayor Paul Pernerewski issued a statement saying his city would be cooperate with the DOJ investigation.
“Mayor Pernerewski is aware of the U.S. Department of Justice’s investigation and has received notification of the matter,” the statement read. “The city takes its responsibilities seriously and expects to fully cooperate with the Department of Justice throughout the investigation. As this is an ongoing matter, we will have no further comment at this time.”
Connecticut has some of the strictest firearm permitting laws in the country, and those laws were tightened after the mass shooting at Sandy Hook Elementary in 2012.
In order to obtain a pistol permit in Connecticut, applicants must first apply for a local pistol permit, which can be obtained from a town or city police department. Only after that step can people apply for a state pistol permit. 
It’s not immediately clear how many firearm permit applications Waterbury or Middletown have handled in recent years, or whether their processing times vary significantly from other municipalities in Connecticut. 
In the letters sent to officials in Waterbury and Middletown, DOJ officials wrote that they had “not reached any conclusions about the subject matter of this investigation.”
“We will notify you upon completion of our investigation. If we conclude that there is no pattern or practice of violating federal constitutional or statutory rights… , we will notify you and close the investigation,” the letters said.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Fisheries, rising costs and schools dominate Southwestern Alaska House debate
text:
Vessels in the commercial crab fishing fleet out of Dutch Harbor, Alaska, prepare for the 2020 king crab season in mid-October. (U.S. Coast Guard photo by Petty Officer 2nd Class Holly Hugunin)Four candidates are vying for an open seat to represent the Southwestern Alaska House District 37, one of the state’s largest rural districts where fisheries, skyrocketing costs of living, transportation and schools are top of mind this election season.     

Alaska House District 37 spans from the Aleutian Islands to Bristol Bay to the middle Kuskokwim region. (Screenshot of Alaska Division of Elections map)
 

The district includes communities from the middle Kuskokwim region including Aniak and Sleetmute in the north, southeast across Bristol Bay and Lake Clark regions to Cook Inlet, and south across the Alaska Peninsula, the Aleutian Islands and Pribilof Islands. 
The four candidates are Republican Brenda Wilson of King Cove, Democrat Evelynn Trefon of Newhalen, independent Mark Smith of Aleknagik and independent Cade Woods of Dillingham. 
Rep. Bryce Edgmon, a Dillingham independent and House Speaker, has represented the region since 2007 and declined to run for re-election this year to make a bid for the Senate seat representing the region. 
In the primary, Wilson got 22.6% of the vote, Trefon received 19.8%, Smith received 17.5%, and Woods finished sixth with 9.2% of the vote. Voter turnout was 25.1% with 2,468 ballots counted. 
The race could have implications for the balance of power in the Alaska House. The multi-partisan majority coalition holds 21 seats, compared to the Republican-led minority with 19 seats. Each House District represents approximately 18,335 residents, and representatives serve two-year terms. 
Three of the four candidates appeared Wednesday in an online candidate forum called the Aleutian Debates, a non-partisan citizen-led initiative broadcasted online and on KSPD Radio. The questions were compiled by residents across the Aleutians region. 
“Too often, candidates pass through our region quickly or not at all. So we wanted to bring the conversation here to you, to the people living with the issues every day,” said Amy Mack of Sand Point, who works for the local tribe and KSPD radio. She and co-hosted the debate with Carter Uttecht, a small business owner from King Cove.     

Brenda Wilson is running to represent House District 37 in the 2026 election. (Photo courtesy of Brenda Wilson)
Evelynn Trefon is running to represent House District 37 in the 2026 election. (Division of Elections photo)
Mark Smith is running to represent House District 37 in the 2026 election. (Photo courtesy of Mark Smith)
Cade Woods is running to represent House District 37 in the 2026 election. (Division of Elections photo)
 

Wilson, Trefon and Smith participated in the Zoom forum and expressed their commitment to representing the rural communities of the district, which are only accessible by boat and plane. 
Wilson is a long-time resident of King Cove, where she raised her family, and where she most recently worked as the behavioral health director for Eastern Aleutian Tribes. She serves on the Aleutians East Borough School Board and the Aleutians East Borough Assembly, and has served on the local city council and tribal council. 
“So I have a lot of experience in working with monies. I’ve gone to Juneau many, many times,” she said. “To make sure that our communities had what they needed, not just King Cove. So it’s been a lot of work to make sure that we have the resources we need.” 
Trefon is of Yup’ik heritage and lives in Newhalen, a community near Lake Iliamna, with her family. She has worked as a secretary for the Lake and Peninsula School District for the last twelve years, and previously served on the local city council and electric cooperative board.
“I’m tired of arguing with our school district over funding. I want to see what can be done at the state level, so that’s why I signed up to run this year. I was the first one to sign up on April 26th,” she said. 
Smith lives in his home-town of Aleknagik, on the west side Bristol Bay, and has commercially fished and managed fuel companies delivering to communities across Southwestern Alaska. He’s also served on his local city council and as mayor. 
“I have had the privilege of serving most of District 37 from the pilot house of a tug, and delivered fuel along the coast and up the tributary rivers, the Kuskokwim and the Bristol Bay rivers. So, really, I’ve spent my life being part of those communities,” he said. 
Woods could not attend the Wednesday forum, according to organizers. He lives in Dillingham and works as a fuel terminals manager and serves as chair of the Dillingham Planning Commission. 
All four candidates are running for the Alaska State Legislature for the first time. 
Fisheries and economic development
All three candidates expressed support for the district’s wide variety of fisheries. Dutch Harbor is the nation’s No. 1 fishing port by volume, and Bristol Bay sees the largest sockeye salmon returns in the world, but smaller fisheries like in the Chignik, Yukon and Kuskokwim rivers have seen dramatic declines in recent years. 
Moderators asked how candidates would represent all fishing user groups, particularly as the southern Aleutian Area M fishery, which they said is often blamed for declining runs in Western Alaska. 
Wilson said she would support all user groups fairly regardless of gear type. Trefon said she would prioritize support for subsistence fishing above others, and said she thinks the Alaska Department of Fish and Game is underfunded and understaffed, contributing to management issues. Smith said he would work to ensure the Board of Fisheries is making management decisions based on science not politics. He also noted the need for timely data to help address declining salmon runs in Western Alaska. 
All three candidates said they support the trawl fishing fleet in state waters. Trawl bycatch – the accidental harvest of nontargeted species — has become a hot-button issue this election season. But all three candidates said they oppose any state bans because trawl fishing is a major economic driver in the region. Smith noted improving management data could help reduce bycatch numbers, and he begged the audience to seek news and information about trawling beyond social media. 
“Trawling is part of vital Alaska fisheries, and it helps both the Aleutians and the Bering Sea,” Smith said. “It also helps make the processing of other smaller stocks possible, where otherwise there’d be a difficulty in keeping year-round processing.”
The three candidates were asked about processor closures and unpaid fishermen. Processing plants receive fish harvests from fishing fleets and have seen a wide variety of turnover and closures in recent years. In 2024, the owner of a major King Cove plant that was backed by state-funding, Peter Pan Seafoods, went bankrupt. Peter Pan Seafoods shut the plant and failed to pay fishermen and boat owners millions they were owed, as reported by ProPublica. 
All three candidates said they supported increased accountability and oversight of processors, and wanted to see processors pay fishermen what they’re owed. Smith floated the idea of a payment bond system to ensure fishermen get paid. 
Trefon said she wanted to see the new plant owner paying those existing debts, like back taxes. Wilson said she would support legislation to make sure processors can’t walk away from local debts, though bankruptcy is regulated by federal laws. 
“If a processor fails to meet its obligation, the state should have the authority to impose penalties, restrict future operations and require restitution. Accountability must mean something,” Wilson said. 
Rising costs and rural subsidy programs
Rural Alaska communities are seeing skyrocketing fuel costs this year, driven by the U.S. war in Iran, which is pushing up the cost of groceries, heating fuel and travel. The state’s Power Cost Equalization program helps rural communities subsidize high energy costs, but not all communities qualify — including King Cove, which lost eligibility after switching to hydropower in 2017.
All three candidates said rural energy costs are a concern, and said they would support state investment in infrastructure to help utilities connect regionally and lower costs.
[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
Wilson said she would support changing the formula for power cost equalization eligibility to be “renewable-friendly” to incentivize communities switching from diesel to renewable forms of energy. 
“I support legislation that allows communities to qualify for PCE based on needs and location,” she said. “Coal-based extreme electricity costs threaten services all over the region.”
All three candidates expressed support for building a controversial road to connect King Cove and Cold Bay, which would run through the Izembek National Wildlife Refuge and is currently being litigated in federal court. The candidates said they see it as essential for medical evacuations, transportation and the economic future of the two communities.
Another area of agreement between candidates was supporting state ferry service and affordable air travel throughout the region. Air travel across the district is at an all-time high, moderators said, and asked how the candidates would address affordable and reliable air service. 
Wilson said she would work with Alaska’s federal delegation, the state and commercial airlines to invest in a central air service to the region and ongoing runway maintenance. Smith said he would also support investments in infrastructure, and expressed hope the U.S. military’s promise to invest $115 million in Adak would benefit the larger region.
Trefon said she would work to protect Essential Air Service, a federal subsidy program for passenger transit, mail, medical evacuations and groceries, as well as advocate for investments in infrastructure. 
“We do need to make it more affordable and reliable by investing in our transportation systems,” she said. “And we need to make sure the federal government is doing their part to make sure that the instrument landing systems are up and running continuously, not just sometimes.”   
Education
All three candidates said they support increasing state funding for education by boosting the base student allocation, the core of the state’s funding formula. 
[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
In House District 37, many schools are facing declining enrollment, moderators said, which puts them at risk for closure if they fall under the state-funding threshold of 10 students.
Trefon said she would work to protect rural schools and prevent any change to that rule. “Urban legislators have often suggested raising that number to 20. If that were to happen, that would close a tremendous amount of schools through rural Alaska,” she said.
Wilson said she would work to stabilize schools through housing incentives for teachers, local teacher training and dual credit and distance learning opportunities, “ensuring rural students receive the same opportunities as every other child in Alaska,” she said.
Smith emphasized the need for diversifying state revenue to address deferred school maintenance. He also said he supports reviving the defined benefit pension system for teachers, which he said could reduce turnover and help stabilize small schools.  
All three candidates said they support reliable state funding for preschool programs statewide. 
Size of the Permanent Fund dividend
While the amount and cost of the annual Alaska Permanent Fund dividend can be a highly partisan topic, all the candidates agreed they support a dividend that is balanced with the state budget. 
Trefon said she would support boosting new state revenues by implementing what she called a high-earners’ income tax, “which would tax the people making $120,000 or more annually and individually, and I think that that would generate a lot of revenue for the state of Alaska,” she said. 
“Until we get more revenue into the state of Alaska, then I don’t think that we are able to pay a full statutory permanent fund dividend. But I would like to,” she said. 
Smith said he supports diversifying state revenues, particularly income from natural resources, to counteract state funding fluctuating with the price of oil. “We’d all like to pay a full dividend, but it’s just not realistic until we address the budget issues,” he said.
Wilson said she supports a dividend that is fair but also protects the long-term health of the state budget. “The PFD is important, but so is a balanced budget,” she said. “A balanced approach helps rural Alaska most.”
Campaign fundraising 
According to campaign finance reports filed one month ahead of the general election with the Alaska Public Offices Commission, Smith is leading in fundraising efforts with more than $43,600 raised. He also contributed more than $17,000 to his own campaign, plus a $5,000 loan.  
Trefon has raised more than $21,000, with over $4,200 in non-monetary donations to her own campaign, such as airline miles and supplies. Wilson has raised more than $4,500, with $500 from the Alaska Republican Party and over $3,500 in non-monetary contributions to her own campaign. Woods has raised roughly $650, with $450 in self-funding.
Early voting has begun across Alaska and will continue until the polls close at 8 p.m. on Nov. 3.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Federal monitors to observe elections in three Oklahoma counties
text:
Voters mark their ballots in the Crown Heights Christian Church on June 16, 2026 in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Courtney Bell/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY – Three Oklahoma counties will have an extra set of eyes when voters go to the polls Nov. 3.
The U.S. Department of Justice notified the Oklahoma State Election Board this month that it will be sending monitors to Tulsa, Oklahoma and Muskogee counties.
The agency will be monitoring compliance with federal voting rights laws, including the Voting Rights Act, the National Voter Registration Act and the Voting Accessibility for Elderly and Handicapped Act. 
They also check for compliance with the Americans with Disabilities Act.
Tulsa and Oklahoma counties are the state’s two most populous counties with a combined population of 1.5 million, according to the U.S. Census Bureau. Just under 67,000 residents live in Muskogee County. The federal agency did not indicate why the three counties were selected.
“As the Civil Rights Division has done in the past, our monitors only observe,” wrote Jake T. Bachand, an attorney with the agency, in an email to the three counties that was provided to Oklahoma Voice. 
“They do not intrude or interfere in any way,” Bachand wrote.
Monitors will follow state law, not enter any polling place, and not intrude on the voting process, said State Election Board Secretary Paul Ziriax.
Paul Ziriax, election board secretary, speaks about candidate filing during a media briefing on Tuesday, April 2, 2024. (Photo by Janelle Stecklein/Oklahoma Voice)
They will carry identification, but not outwardly identify themselves, he said.
Monitors may seek to interview voters after they leave the polling place, but participation is voluntary, Ziriax said.
“Based on my conversation with Department of Justice officials, I expect the monitoring process to fully comply with the requirements and limitations of state law,” Ziriax said. “I see no cause for alarmism regarding this matter.”
U.S. Department of Justice monitors have notified other states that they will be observing, according to NPR. Those states include Colorado, Michigan, Utah, Florida, Minnesota, Texas and Washington.
According to the agency’s website, it sent monitors to several states during the primary election, including Minnesota, Massachusetts, New Hampshire, Florida, Wyoming, South Carolina and Rhode Island.
Oklahoma election officials said federal monitors were in the state in 2016 or 2018 to monitor an election in Texas County, a county of about 20,000 people in the state’s Panhandle.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Utahns should watch out for deer on the roads as nights grow longer, DWR says
text:
A buck tempts fate in Millard County’s Oak City in 2022. (Courtesy of the Utah Division of Wildlife Resources)Talk about bad timing. 
Starting Nov. 1, Utah roads will get darker earlier when daylight saving time ends. State wildlife managers say deer will also be on the move, migrating to lower elevations in search of food. 
They’re urging drivers to keep their eyes peeled, turn on their high beams when possible and look for the faraway shine of an animal’s eye to avoid hitting big game animals. The risk is highest in November, said Makeda Hanson, coordinator for the state’s wildlife migration initiative. 
It’s also mating season for deer and the time of their annual migration. So the animals tend to cross more roads, with male deer roving much more to find a mate, Hanson said in a prepared statement. 
“It also doesn’t help that the daylight hours are shorter during this time of year, creating lower visibility for drivers,” Hanson said. 
Early mornings and evenings are typical commuting hours for deer, too, the division said. Its managers are urging drivers to stay alert, take note of wildlife crossing signs, scan the whole road and put away distractions like phones. 
While drivers should slow down if they see a deer or smaller animals, they should not swerve and should not approach an injured animal. 
Hanson’s team at the Division of Wildlife Resources tracks and studies migration patterns of fish and wildlife, using GPS trackers and transmitters. They’re also encouraging Utahns to use an app to report roadkill to the state, saying the data helps identify where to place wildlife crossing structures. 
As of Oct. 8, more than 3,700 animals were hit by cars this year and removed from Utah roads, the division said. That’s out of roughly 19,400 since 2022. To help limit those collisions, more than 60 wildlife crossings have gone up across the state, in addition to fencing, the agency said in a news release.

name: Delaware
title: Del-One donates $3,300 to help Dover Little League rebuild after tornado
text:
Pictured L-R: from Dover Little League: Baseball Director Videll Slade, City Liaison Director Ed Coker, President Bill Kinsey, Concessions Director Mary Pritchett, Equipment Director Ralph Pann, & Del-One’s President & CEO Dan McCarthy
Credit union’s contribution will support repairs at Schutte Park after August storm damaged fields, fencing, lights and dugouts
DOVER, Del. — Dover Little League’s effort to recover from tornado damage received a boost from Del-One Federal Credit Union, which donated $3,300 to help restore the organization’s fields at Schutte Park.
The contribution, made in partnership with Visa as part of a community reinvestment initiative, comes after an EF-1 tornado swept through Dover in late August with winds exceeding 100 mph.
The storm caused significant damage to the Little League complex, including fencing, light poles, scoreboards and dugout roofs.
For Dover Little League, the damage affected more than a collection of baseball fields. The complex has served generations of area children, coaches, volunteers and families.
“The devastation caused by the tornado was felt across the entire community, and we know how much this Little League field means to local families,” Del-One President and CEO Dan McCarthy said. “We are proud to help restore a place where children can play, grow and make memories.”
McCarthy said the donation reflects the credit union’s emphasis on supporting the communities it serves.
“Community is built on neighbors helping neighbors, and we are honored to be part of that effort,” he said.
Dover Little League officials receiving the donation included President Bill Kinsey, Baseball Director Videll Slade, City Liaison Director Ed Coker, Concessions Director Mary Pritchett and Equipment Director Ralph Pann.
Del-One Federal Credit Union has more than $984 million in assets and more than 106,000 members, with full-service branches throughout Delaware.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Trump administration sues to block Alaska’s US Senate election result if Peltola wins
text:
The Alaska general election ballot showing all four candidates is seen on Monday, Oct. 19, 2026, the first day of early voting. (James Brooks photo/Alaska Beacon)This article is developing and will be updated.
The U.S. Department of Justice filed suit against the Alaska Division of Elections late Thursday, seeking to block the division from certifying the result of the state’s U.S. Senate election if the Democratic challenger, Mary Peltola, wins.
Peltola is the leading opponent to incumbent Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan, and polls show her with a small lead over Sullivan, but the race also includes two other candidates — Republicans Gerald Heikes of Palmer and Dan J. Sullivan of Petersburg.
In the complaint, the Department of Justice claims that Dan J. Sullivan’s candidacy is “frivolous,” and was intended solely to confuse voters and benefit Peltola. 
Until there is an investigation to determine the extent of that confusion, the Department of Justice argues, Alaska should not be permitted to certify the result of the ongoing Senate election.
Legal experts immediately dismissed the federal argument as bunk. 
Under the U.S. Constitution, states have authority over their own elections. The federal claim is based on the preamble to the National Voter Registration Act, which states in part that the law is intended “to protect the integrity of the electoral process.”
[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
In an immediate analysis posted online, Notre Dame Law School election law professor Derek Muller said, “the legal argument is one of the worst ones I’ve ever seen.”
In addition to being poorly argued, it was poorly written, he said, noting that one paragraph is missing a verb that would ask the court to take action.
Libby Bakalar is a former Alaska state elections attorney who frequently speaks against the Trump administration. On social media Friday morning, she said the federal argument “is laughably bad, almost to the point of sanctionably frivolous. Watching MAGA on the ropes like this in court up here is a sad and scary sight.”
Reached by email Friday morning, Dan J. Sullivan declined immediate comment, saying the lawsuit came as a surprise and he was still analyzing it. 
The Beacon contacted the Division of Elections and Lt. Gov. Nancy Dahlstrom early Friday morning but has not yet received a response.
In numerous prior interviews, Dan J. Sullivan has said that his candidacy was motivated by dissatisfaction with Sen. Sullivan, and that he is not linked to the Democratic Party or Peltola’s campaign.
Democratic officials have said the same thing.
But that hasn’t stopped President Donald Trump and Sen. Sullivan — as well as other Republicans — from accusing both Peltola and Petersburg Sullivan of fraud.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Marine life dramatically declined in Gulf of Mexico in years after BP oil spill, study finds
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
WASHINGTON — In a deep, dark part of the Gulf of Mexico, the number of marine animals plummeted by about 60% in the years following the 2010 Deepwater Horizon explosion, a new study found.
In a crucial part of the Gulf between the light surface and the darkest depths, where the BP-operated well failed and dumped 134 million gallons of oil, the number of fish found dropped by 63.5% from the year after the spill to 2015. Crustaceans, including shrimp and krill, a key food for whales, went down 62%, and larger animals like squid and octopuses fell 59.7%, according to a study published Monday in the journal PNAS.
And those populations haven’t come close to recovering, the study found.
A large plume of smoke rises from BP’s Deepwater Horizon offshore oil rig in the Gulf of Mexico on April 21, 2010.  Credit: AP Photo/Gerald Herbert
Researchers focused on the ocean’s “twilight zone,” a vast area above the seafloor, where much of the surface marine life, including dolphins and whales, feast on creatures. Yet little is known about this gigantic ecosystem, and this region of the Gulf had not been studied before the 2010 spill, said study lead author Tracey Sutton, a biological oceanographer at Nova Southeastern University.
A 2011 post-spill exploration cited in the research, which used six sets of nets at different depths and acoustic sonar, gave scientists a good sense of how much sea life was in the area between the surface and 5,000 feet deep. They returned to the same place with the same equipment three-and-a-half years later and found sea life was between one-third and one-quarter of what it was in 2011.
“We saw this big decline,” Sutton said. “The question was then why? So we looked at all of the natural variables we thought could account for it, namely temperature, oxygen supply and food. None of those vary with the decline. The event that did was the oil spill. So we think that’s the most likely cause of the decline.”
Researchers kept on sampling since 2015 and the low populations remained, with a slight rise in 2022 and 2023 that did not prove statistically significant or lasting, Sutton said.
Documenting the decline
Sutton’s team documented the population declines with three different lines of evidence: what they caught in the nets, what their acoustic sonar found and genetic studies showing the species losing genetic diversity because of inbreeding.
A lot of marine life died instantly after the explosion, which killed 11 workers, and from nearly five months of leaking oil and gas. Those pollutants got stored in the eggs of survivors and subsequent generations of critters got more compromised and weaker, Sutton said.
BP spokesperson Paul Takahashi said the accident “forever changed” the company: “We have made many changes intended to help prevent an event like this from ever happening again.”
Both the oil and the dispersants used to clean the spill hurt fish, but in different ways, said study co-author Isabel Romero, a chemical oceanographer at the University of South Carolina. Oil is more toxic and an overall threat, but the dispersant breaks the oil into smaller droplets, increasing the exposure of animals that live in the deeper water column, she said.
Dispersants caused many problems, and new studies show that in future accidents, it would be better to avoid those chemicals and instead add agents that increase oil-munching microbes, said former National Science Foundation Director Rita Colwell, a University of Maryland environmental microbiologist who headed a 10-year, $500 million BP-funded program to study spill effects.
Sutton said his team couldn’t prove an exact causal link to the BP oil spill, but by eliminating the other possibilities and looking at the timing, it’s logically clear that the spill caused the problem.
The krill population dropped 72%. Lanternfish — odd fish with blue-green lights embedded over their bodies — are a third of what they used to be, Sutton said. The stunning but scary dragonfish — with sharp teeth, light organs and a lure attached to its head — also had big losses, he said.
“These are foundational species,” Sutton said. “They’re the things most things eat. So it’s no wonder that we had wholesale changes across the community.”
The inner ocean is more unknown than outer space
Scientists learned much about this unexplored area of the Gulf.
“One of our biggest findings from the whole thing is how connected the whole oceanic Gulf is from top to bottom because the animals move up and down,” Sutton said. “There are predators at the top that dive deep. Lots of things that are deep that come up at night. So the system is one very large pulsing system, rather than just a layered system like people might have thought beforehand.”
Outside scientists were especially bothered by where the spill damaged.
“We know more about space in some ways than we do about the inner ocean. Because we can’t see these regions, there is a tendency to assume everything is fine, but here we have a clear result showing that something went very wrong,” Scripps Institution of Oceanography marine scientist Kaitlin Frasier said in an email.
Frasier, who wasn’t part of the study released Monday, published a post-spill study in 2024 looking at Gulf of Mexico whales and dolphins, finding population drops as high as 83%.
“It’s shocking how a single failure in a drilling rig can have this vast and sustained impact over thousands of square kilometers, with little visible recovery over 13 years after the spill,” said Dalhousie University marine scientist Boris Worm, who wasn’t part of the study. “It is important that we see this, because for the longest time these consequences were completely out of sight and out of mind.”
Worm and Colwell said this damage should be kept in mind as the world talks about deep-sea mining and increased oil drilling in deep waters.

title: Trump’s DOJ sues over Alaska Senate race, expanding preelection legal fights
text: The U.S. Department of Justice is stepping up its legal campaign over the midterm elections, suing Alaska over its U.S. Senate election and appealing a lawsuit against suspected noncitizen voters in California.Election law experts have cast doubt on the strength of the cases, criticizing them as performative.The Justice Department sued Alaska election officials late Thursday in a preemptive attempt to stop the state from certifying the results of its Senate election if, under the state’s ranked-choice voting method, the Republican incumbent loses by a smaller margin than the votes earned by another candidate of the same name. Separately, the Justice Department appealed to the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals a lawsuit seeking to prevent California election officials from counting the ballots of approximately 20,000 voters it says are likely noncitizens unless they can prove their citizenship. The DOJ had demanded a district court decision by Thursday.Collectively, the Justice Department’s actions signal an expanding legal effort to assert authority over voting as Election Day approaches. President Donald Trump faces political peril in the midterms, with Democrats all but certain to launch investigations into his administration if they retake the House or Senate.The Trump administration’s past attempts to influence how states run elections largely failed, with the U.S. Supreme Court blocking proposed restrictions on mail ballots and federal judges dismissing DOJ lawsuits to obtain states’ sensitive voter data. But in the waning days before the midterm elections, federal officials are again ramping up election-related activity.Another Dan Sullivan suitThe Alaska lawsuit came hours after U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche refused to rule out efforts to block states from certifying their elections. Speaking to reporters after an unrelated event in Virginia, Blanche said it wasn’t the DOJ’s intention to “improperly interfere” with election certifications even as he left room for his department to act.“I mean, is there any scenario? Yes, of course there’s scenarios that we could all come up with, hypothetically, you know, some doomsday scenario, for example, right?” Blanche said.The Alaska Division of Elections and the Justice Department didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment.In the Alaska Senate race, Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan and his supporters have cast Dan J. Sullivan, also a Republican, as a spoiler in a competitive race against Democrat Mary Peltola. State officials initially kept Dan J. Sullivan off the August primary ballot but the Alaska Supreme Court overturned the decision. He finished third, with 2.5% of the vote, qualifying for the four-way general election.Trump had previewed a possible lawsuit earlier in the week. On Truth Social, the president on Wednesday called the Senate race in Alaska “totally confusing” and slammed Dan J. Sullivan’s presence.“We are looking at powerful legal options to remove the fraudulent Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. from the Ballot, and holding the Democrats accountable for their Election Interference, in the pursuit of Justice and Fairness,” Trump wrote.Experts skepticalEarly expert reaction to the Justice Department’s complaint has been sharply critical. The complaint cites the preamble of the National Voter Registration Act, which says one of its purposes is “to protect the integrity of the electoral process.” Writing in Election Law Blog, Derek Muller, a professor of law at the University of Notre Dame focused on elections, called the legal argument “one of the worst ones I’ve ever seen.”“Some, in a panic, might react that the Department is trying to deny certification of an election in a state. Of course that’s what the Department is trying to do. But the legal claim is so absurdly thin, there’s essentially no likelihood of success,” Muller wrote.California noncitizen case appealedIn California, Assistant U.S. Attorney Julie Hamill filed a notice of appeal in the Justice Department’s lawsuit over alleged noncitizen voters just three days after the the DOJ requested a temporary restraining order to halt ballot counting for individuals on the list of 20,000. Hamill wrote that the DOJ was interpreting U.S. District Court Judge David Carter’s silence as a denial of its request. Carter, an appointee of President Bill Clinton, had only taken on the case a day earlier and had set a hearing for Oct. 27. Earlier this year, he became the first federal judge in the country to rule against the Justice Department’s lawsuits attempting to force states to turn over sensitive voter data.On Friday, the Justice Department filed a new motion asking Carter to block the ballot counting and requested a ruling by noon Pacific time. In that filing, Hamill wrote that “every minute” of ballot processing that occurs without setting aside ballots of suspected noncitizens dilutes the votes of U.S. citizens.Case ‘exceedingly weak,’ critics sayCritics of the Justice Department’s actions argue the time crunch is largely of its own making. David Becker, executive director of the nonpartisan Center for Election Innovation & Research, noted during a press call Thursday that the DOJ didn’t file its lawsuit until more than a week after California began mailing ballots — and then several more days to seek a temporary restraining order.“I think this case is exceedingly weak,” said Becker, who worked as a senior trial attorney in the Justice Department’s Voting Section during the Clinton and George W. Bush administrations.Attorneys for California Secretary of State Shirley Weber, a Democrat, and Los Angeles Registrar-Recorder/County Clerk Dean Logan have both asked Carter to dismiss the lawsuit. Logan’s legal team on Wednesday wrote that Los Angeles County hasn’t changed how it conducts elections. What’s changed, they wrote, was the federal government’s posture.“Weeks before Election Day, the United States asks this Court to intrude on the administration of an election,” Logan’s lawyers wrote.

name: Delaware
title: Wilmington office market rebounds as vacancy falls to 20-year low
text:
Caption: A new report from commercial real estate firm Newmark shows the Wilmington area’s office vacancy rate fell to 15.9% during the third quarter of 2026, its lowest level in two decades. Image created on 10/23 using AI.
Newmark report shows stronger leasing, business expansion, and renewed investor confidence, signaling a potential turning point after years of uncertainty.
WILMINGTON — After six difficult years for Delaware’s office market, commercial real estate professionals are seeing something they have been waiting for: measurable signs of recovery.
A new report from commercial real estate firm Newmark shows the Wilmington area’s office vacancy rate fell to 15.9% during the third quarter of 2026, its lowest level in two decades.
The improvement reflects businesses occupying more office space, stronger leasing activity and growing demand from expanding companies. Investors are also beginning to return to a market that has struggled since the COVID-19 pandemic.
“For six years, when someone asked, ‘How is the office market in Delaware?’ I said ‘challenging,'” said Wills Elliman, senior managing director at Newmark. “I meant terrible but didn’t want to say it out loud. That’s changing, and we saw it this quarter.”
Businesses are keeping and expanding their space
According to Newmark’s third-quarter Delaware Office Market Overview, businesses occupied a net additional 139,842 square feet during the quarter.
That brought net absorption for the first nine months of 2026 to 208,458 square feet, already exceeding the full-year totals recorded in every year since 2012.
Net absorption measures the change in occupied office space. Positive absorption means businesses are collectively occupying more space than they are vacating.
Wilmington’s overall vacancy rate declined from 16.8% in the second quarter to 15.9% in the third quarter, well below the market’s 20-year average of 18%.
Leasing activity also improved, with nearly 195,000 square feet leased during the quarter.
Elliman said the improvement reflects an important shift in how businesses are making decisions about their offices.
“Tenants took less space when they moved or renewed. Now, more are keeping their space or expanding. We’re seeing that especially with law firms.”
Among the largest transactions was Morris, Nichols, Arsht & Tunnell’s renewal of an 82,549-square-foot lease at 1201 N. Market St.
Financial technology company Fiserv also signed a lease at 800 Delaware Ave., while Gordon, Fournaris & Mammarella leased 9,540 square feet along Lancaster Pike.
Those transactions demonstrate the continuing importance of Delaware’s legal, financial and professional services industries to Wilmington’s commercial real estate market.
Growing businesses offer reason for optimism
Perhaps the most encouraging finding involves companies currently searching for office space.
Newmark identified approximately 603,000 square feet of active tenant demand in the Wilmington market.
Nearly 370,000 square feet of that demand comes from businesses seeking to expand or enter the market.
That distinction is important. Companies renewing existing leases help maintain occupancy, but expanding businesses and new employers can create opportunities for additional jobs and economic activity.
The broader regional economy is also supporting demand.
Unemployment across the Philadelphia-Camden-Wilmington metropolitan area stood at 3.8% in August, compared with the national rate of 4.1%.
Employment in office-oriented industries remains approximately 4% above pre-pandemic levels.
Investors are returning to the office market
Beyond improving occupancy, Elliman sees another encouraging development: Investors are purchasing office properties again.
“Investors are buying office buildings again. Good buildings in good locations are trading at prices that make sense,” Elliman said. “Add renewed confidence in Wilmington’s business climate, and there’s reason to feel better about the office market than we have in years.”
The return of buyers is significant because office buildings have faced uncertainty over tenant demand, operating expenses and property values since the pandemic.
Elliman said Newmark is involved in another transaction that could further demonstrate improving investor confidence.
“We just put a large office building under contract, and we’ll have more to say about it in our Q4 2026 review,” he said. “It’s the kind of building tenants will love, at a price that makes sense for the buyer. That deal is one more reason to have confidence in this market.”
The property and terms of the pending transaction have not been disclosed.
While Elliman’s observations suggest renewed investment activity, Newmark’s quarterly report focuses primarily on leasing, occupancy and asking rents rather than broader commercial property sales trends.
Downtown is improving, but challenges remain
The recovery is not occurring evenly across Wilmington’s office market.
Downtown Wilmington recorded particularly strong activity during the third quarter, with positive net absorption of 148,681 square feet.
However, downtown’s vacancy rate remains at 18.2%, higher than the overall market average.
Other Wilmington-area office markets present a mixed picture.

Wilmington South experienced negative absorption during the quarter, meaning more space was vacated than occupied.
Older buildings also face competition from newer properties offering modern layouts, amenities and updated technology.
Office buildings constructed since 2000 have a vacancy rate of 14.4%, compared with 15.9% across the overall market.
Still, Newmark reports that the gap between newer buildings and older properties has narrowed, suggesting demand is improving beyond just the newest office towers.
Limited construction is helping the market
One significant factor behind Wilmington’s improving vacancy rate is the absence of new office construction.
Newmark reports that no office buildings are currently under construction in the Wilmington market.
The most recent major delivery was the 100,000-square-foot Avenue North office building completed in 2024, which is now 88% leased.
With few new buildings entering the market, businesses looking for office space are increasingly choosing from existing properties.
Another factor is the conversion of older commercial properties to residential or other uses.
Such conversions can reduce excess office inventory while bringing additional residents into business districts, potentially supporting restaurants, retail businesses and other downtown services.
However, declining vacancy does not automatically mean every building is becoming more financially successful. Removing vacant buildings from the office inventory can improve marketwide statistics even without equivalent growth in occupied space.
In Wilmington’s case, the report identifies both positive net absorption and constrained supply as contributors to the improvement.
Office rents remain relatively stable
Despite stronger demand, office rents have not increased dramatically.
Average asking rents reached $26.14 per square foot during the third quarter, up 1% from the previous quarter but down 3.3% compared with a year earlier.
Newmark attributes much of the annual decline to Wilmington University’s purchase of a large vacant building at 3 Beaver Valley Road in 2025, which removed higher-priced space from the available inventory.
That change affected the marketwide average rather than necessarily reflecting widespread rent reductions.
For businesses considering expansion or relocation, relatively stable rents and a substantial selection of available properties could present opportunities.
For property owners, the challenge remains attracting tenants while managing operating costs, property improvements and financing.
A potential turning point for Wilmington
The latest report offers reasons for optimism after several years in which remote work and changing workplace habits raised questions about the future of traditional office districts.
Vacancy is declining, office employment has stabilized and businesses are actively searching for additional space.
Perhaps more importantly, according to Elliman, tenants and investors appear increasingly willing to make longer-term commitments to Wilmington office properties.
Still, the market has nearly 3 million square feet listed as available, including space occupied by existing tenants but being marketed for lease.
That leaves significant room for improvement.
The long-term question is whether Wilmington can build on its advantages as a center for banking, law, financial services and other professional industries while continuing to attract new businesses.
The next phase of recovery may depend not only on filling traditional office buildings but also on creating an environment where employers, residents, restaurants and retail businesses can grow together.
For now, Newmark’s findings and Elliman’s observations point in the same direction: After years of difficult conditions, Wilmington’s office market is showing renewed momentum.
Whether that momentum becomes sustained growth will depend on continued tenant expansion, successful property investments and the strength of Delaware’s business climate
