name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico utility regulators advance investigation into PNM electricity billing complaints
text:
The New Mexico Public Regulation Commission on Oct. 22, 2026, took a step toward investigating complaints that PNM estimated some customers’ energy use this summer, resulting in excessively high bills. (Photo by Danielle Prokop for Source NM)New Mexico utility regulators on Thursday advanced an investigation into complaints that the state’s largest electric provider excessively overcharged some residents this summer.
Staffers for the New Mexico Public Regulation Commission in early October recommended the commission open an investigation after residents reported that PNM was estimating residential bills in the Alamogordo and Ruidoso areas rather than obtaining readings from meters, largely due to a worker shortage. When the commission held a town hall meeting in Alamogordo in September, some residents complained that their monthly bills had skyrocketed from the usual $150 or $200 to as much as $1,700, according to the PRC staffers’ filing.
At a Thursday meeting in Las Cruces, the PRC’s three members voted on a draft order authorizing an investigation into the matter. However, rather than voting to approve or deny an investigation, commissioners unanimously voted to edit the order’s language to give investigators clearer guidance on the scope of their probe.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
In particular, commissioners agreed that the order authorizing the probe should direct investigators to focus on Alamogordo and Ruidoso, but not preclude them from examining whether overbillings occurred elsewhere across the state.
They also directed Commissioner Greg Nibert to edit the order to specify that investigators should share the results of meter tests they conduct with PRC commissioners.
“I’m hopeful that the issue is not widespread, but I want the investigation to proceed to determine if it is,” Nibert said at Thursday’s meeting.
When the PRC’s Public Interest Advocacy team in early October urged the commission to open an investigation, a PNM spokesperson told Source NM that company officials “welcome the opportunity to provide the New Mexico Public Regulation Commission with information about what occurred, how customers were affected and the actions PNM has taken in response.”
In September, New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez wrote a letter to Don Tarry, the CEO of PNM and its parent company, informing him that residents had complained to the New Mexico Department of Justice about exceedingly high bills.
Torrez’s letter included copies of those complaints, including one from an Otero County married couple who wrote that they received a bill for more than $1,000 this summer.
“Though we completely understand staffing issues, an electric bill of over $1,000, when we have not had one over $200 in the last year, is absurd,” they wrote, adding that PNM did not read their meter in July.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Follow the money: Who’s bankrolling Missouri’s final election push?
text:
Boone County voters cast ballots Friday in Columbia during the state's "no-excuse absentee" early voting period. County Clerk Brianna Lennon said her office has averaged about 1,000 voters per day since early voting began on Tuesday. (Rudi Keller/Missouri Independent)Missouri Democrats confidently predict voter discontent will deliver victories in tight legislative races, but campaign finance reports show Republicans well provisioned for defense.
And Republicans are using that financial advantage to shape how voters see their candidates.
On Thursday, the House Republican Campaign Committee transferred $1.5 million to two political action committees that attack Democrats while promoting Republican candidates as independent-minded lawmakers willing to challenge their own party’s leadership.
It’s one example of how campaign money is being used not just to win elections, but to influence the messages voters hear in the final days before Nov. 3.
Reports for the third quarter were due last week for all candidate, ballot measure and special interest political action committees raising, spending or donating money to influence the election. Final pre-election federal reports were due Thursday; state candidates face a Monday deadline for their final reports.
Tracking by The Independent shows almost $60 million has been raised since the start of 2025 for Nov. 3 ballot measure campaigns. In candidate races, $24.9 million has been collected by nominees in the eight congressional districts — almost 90% by incumbents seeking re-election.
In the General Assembly, there are 17 state Senate races. The nominees and political action committees affiliated with their campaigns have raised $17 million. 
In the Missouri House, where all 163 districts are on the ballot, there are 34 seats with no major party contest and another 90 that are almost certain to remain with the incumbent party. In 39 districts rated by The Independent as less than safe for the incumbent party, candidates and affiliated PACs have raised $5.2 million.
In the only statewide race, for auditor, incumbent Republican Scott Fitzpatrick is seeking his second term. He raised $536,286 since the start of 2025, had $484,097 on hand on Sept. 30 and spent only $7,553 since the primary on his re-election campaign.
A political action committee backing Fitzpatrick, Missourians for a Responsible Budget, has raised slightly more than his campaign and had about $30,000 more on hand on Sept. 30. The only broadcast ads in the race found by The Independent’s tracking are $63,000 by Fitzpatrick’s PAC in Springfield.
Quentin Wilson, the Democratic nominee, has raised just under $125,000, spent $10,506 since the primary and had $40,200 on hand on Sept. 30.
The Independent has been tracking the spending, the donors behind it and the government actions they pursue. Often, ads paid for by one interest group are entirely focused on unrelated issues to defeat candidates who would oppose their goals.
That happened in the August primary, when J&J Ventures of Effingham, Illinois, spent almost $100,000 through a PAC it established, Legio XIII, in the 16th District state Senate race. The ads did not mention that the targeted candidate would oppose legalizing video lottery terminals, which are central to J&J Ventures’ business.
With the election less than two weeks away and early votes being cast, this article will update readers on where big donations are coming from, where the money is being spent and how it is being used to deliver campaign messages.
Tori Schafer, an ACLU attorney and candidate for the Missouri House, speaks at a Stop the Ban campaign canvassing kick-off event on Aug. 29 in St. Louis County. (Photo by Anna Spoerre/Missouri Independent)
 Ballot measures

In the November 2024 election, the top ballot measure campaigns combined to spend nearly $100 million. The committees working on this year’s ballot measures are unlikely to match that amount.
Through Thursday, they had combined to collect $59.6 million, including money spent on signature campaigns and legal battles before the ballot was finalized.
The most expensive ballot measure campaign is over Amendment 3, which would ban most abortions as well as enshrine a ban on gender-affirming medical care for minors in the state constitution. Opponents organized as Stop the Ban have raised almost $26 million and purchased $7.25 million of the $13.6 million in ballot measure broadcast advertising tracked by The Independent.
Supporters have split their efforts between two committees. Gov. Mike Kehoe is tied to the effort of Her Health, Her Future, a committee with First Lady Claudia Kehoe as treasurer. Two other leading Republicans, former Attorney General Andrew Bailey and U.S. Sen. Josh Hawley, have established a second committee, Yes on Amendment 3, to promote the ban.
Her Health, Her Future has reported $6 million in contributions and paid for $1.2 million in broadcast ads. Yes on Amendment 3 has raised $1 million and spent $517,000 on broadcast ads.
The other two ballot measures with major campaigns have not faced significant opposition spending.
Respect Mo Voters reported raising $1.5 million for its campaign to put Amendment 6 on the ballot and another $400,000 since Sept. 30. The committee is focusing fall spending on get-out-the-vote efforts while a second committee, Yes on Amendment 6, has raised $5.5 million, almost exclusively from unions. 
Yes on Amendment 6 has spent $3.2 million on broadcast ads.
MO Protect PAC, working against Amendment 6, has reported raising $40,000 during the fall campaign.
People Not Politicians, the committee that put Proposition A on the ballot, has no active opposition committee. After fighting for a year to get a vote on the gerrymandered redistricting plan passed in 2025, and after Republicans spent $3.1 million to obstruct the petition drive, Republicans have mounted no effort to persuade voters the map should stand.
People Not Politicians has raised nearly $11 million since it was formed, including $2.9 million in large donations since Sept. 30, and purchased $1.4 million in broadcast ads.
Republican 6th District nominee Chris Stigall speaks during a primary campaign stop at Koch’s General Store in Macon. Stigall has not campaigned extensively since winning the primary in the district considered safe for the GOP. (Annelise Hanshaw/Missouri Independent)
 Congress

The best evidence that Republicans are increasingly worried about the result in Missouri’s 2nd District may be the $628,000 spent this week by the Congressional Leadership Fund on television ads in the St. Louis market.
In the race between incumbent Republican U.S. Rep. Ann Wagner and Democratic challenger Fred Wellman, Wagner has the advantage of both name recognition and accumulated cash. The Independent’s ad tracking shows Wagner has spent $1.4 million on broadcast ads compared to $357,00 for Wellman.
In recent days, Wellman has been promoting polls showing him even with or slightly ahead of Wagner in the district that has been held by Republicans since 1992.
Missouri’s other seven districts are considered safe for the incumbent party, with Republicans holding five of the seats and Democrats two. Nominees of incumbent parties have raised almost 90% of the funds for this year’s congressional elections.
State Rep. Keri Ingle and House Speaker Jon Patterson are running in the Missouri Senate’s 8th District. The race is one of two eyed statewide for its potential to turn a historically Republican seat blue. (Photos provided by candidates’ campaigns)
 State Senate

More money has been spent on broadcast ads in Missouri’s three competitive state Senate races than in all eight congressional races.. 
The most expensive race is the 8th District in suburban Jackson County, a GOP seat being sought by Republican House Speaker Jon Patterson and Democratic state Rep. Keri Ingle. More than $2.2 million has been spent on broadcast ads.
Patterson has raised $800,000 for his campaign and $1.5 million for Missouri Alliance PAC. Ingle has raised $512,000 for her campaign and $316,000 for KERI PAC. 
Patterson has spent $552,000 on broadcast ads while Ingle has spent $316,000. 
Missouri Alliance has spent $609,000 on broadcast ads while the Senate Democratic Campaign Committee has purchased $818,000 worth of ads to back Ingle’s campaign.
In Springfield, the spending isn’t just from candidates, their PACs and party committees. 
Legio XIII PAC, set up by slot machine vendor J&J Ventures as it pursues video lottery legalization, has purchased $65,000 worth of radio ads opposing the 30th District Democratic nominee, state Rep. Betsy Fogle. The company has given the PAC $575,000 since Sept. 30.
Fogle and state Rep. Melanie Stinnett are contesting a seat that hasn’t elected a Democrat in 80 years.
Fogle and Stinnett’s full reports show almost identical fundraising numbers – about $1.4 million each between their campaign committees and PACs — but Fogle’s Forward PAC has taken in $220,000 in large donations since Sept. 30 while Stinnett’s Heart of SGF PAC has received $15,000.
The unexpectedly competitive state Senate race this cycle is the 34th District, in northwest Missouri. Republicans have purchased almost $325,000 in broadcast ads to defend the seat that covers Platte and a portion of Buchanan County. 
 Missouri House

There are 16 districts targeted by one or both of the two major parties in the St. Louis, Kansas City and Springfield regions. Republicans are defending 14 of the targeted districts while Democrats held the other two after the 2024 election.
Republicans won 111 seats in 2024. Democrats want to win at least 55 for the first time since 2010, when they lost 17 seats.
The candidates in those races have raised $892,000 since the primary, 58% of all money raised in the 39 districts rated less than safe for the incumbent party by The Independent. Candidates in those districts reported $1.6 million on hand for the final month of the campaign, more than half the total for all 39 districts.
Tracey Steele, right, speaks with Sonya Mosier while campaigning Oct. 10 in the Thousand Oaks neighborhood for the 12th District Missouri House in southern Platte County. (Rudi Keller/Missouri Independent)
Democratic candidates, in general, lagged behind their Republican opponents in fundraising during the period and had about half as much cash on hand as their Republican opponents — $582,000 compared to $1 million.
Of the 10 districts that could go to either party but are not targeted in this year’s cycle, mainly because of strong incumbents, seven are held by Democrats and three are in Republican hands. In those districts, Democratic nominees have an edge in total fundraising but Republicans held more cash on Sept. 30.
Another 13 districts that are not rated safe have a strong lean toward one party and include one Democratic district and 12 GOP-held seats.
The backstop for Republicans in Missouri House races is the political action committee dedicated to maintaining their majority. The House Republican Campaign Committee accumulated $3 million from incumbents and lobbying interests as of Sept. 30. The committee has reported $661,000 in donations greater than $5,000 since that date.
Its counterpart, the House Democratic Action Fund, had $348,000 in the bank on Sept. 30 and has not reported a single large donation since.
The money will fuel the final push to election day. Mailboxes will fill with flyers urging action on issues and candidates while the airwaves and online platforms overflow with video and text messages.
And in areas where the Republican name is tarnished, Republicans are making sure it isn’t on those mailbox ads. On Thursday, the House Republican Campaign Committee donated $750,000 each to Missourians for Justice and Citizens for Better Government, PACs set up this year with the same treasurer as the HRCC deputy treasurer.
The PACs attack Democrats and promote Republican candidates as mavericks who question GOP leadership.
 Missouri Independent 100

The 100 PACs identified by The Missouri Independent as the most active donors and spenders representing interest groups made contributions to other committees their largest expense in the third quarter of the year.
While the PACs took in $4.8 million, they spent $1.1 million and contributed $5.7 million to other committees.
The PACs collectively have raised $46.3 million since the start of 2025, spent $11.1 million and contributed $29 million. On Sept. 30, they were holding $17.5 million.
Gambling interests, through PACs in the Missouri Independent 100 and direct company contributions, were the leading donors early in the election cycle, providing $1 out of every $8 raised by legislative candidates through the end of March.
Since then, the total from gambling interests has increased from $4.7 million to almost $8 million.
The goal for J&J Ventures, which has donated almost $3 million to Missouri candidates and PACs, is to legalize video lottery terminals as unlicensed slot machine games are driven out of retail locations. Opposition comes from casinos, which have donated $1.6 million both directly and through the Missouri Gaming Association PAC.
The Missouri State Medical Association, which donated $1.5 million split between two new PACs, has spent about $250,000, mainly to support Republicans in the two most competitive state Senate races.
A PAC helping Democrats at the grassroots level, Will of the People Coalition, has raised almost $3 million this year.
 Big donors

Three of the five largest sources of campaign cash in Missouri this year are donors to the Stop the Ban committee opposing Amendment 3. They are The Fairness Project, which has contributed $8 million, the ACLU and the ACLU Foundation, which has given $2.8 million and Lynn Schusterman of Oklahoma, who gave $3 million. 
The other two donors are mainly helping Republican candidates and causes. 
St. Louis businessman Michael Rayner, who is part of the family that owns Cargill, has contributed $3.1 million to MCR PAC, which in turn donates to candidates and other PACs.
Rex Sinquefield, the GOP’s most prolific donor of the past 20 years, has given $2.3 million, much of it under his own name and some to PACs that then donate to other committees.
Sinquefield, who has ardently pushed for eliminating the state income tax, has contributed almost $79 million since he began political giving in 2006.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: CT homicides are down; domestic violence killings are not
text:
Homicides have declined in Connecticut for years, but domestic and family violence killings have held steady and now account for about one-third of the state’s homicides.
In the first half of 2026, there were 38 confirmed homicides, excluding negligent manslaughter. But 14 of the 38 homicides, or 37%, were the result of domestic or family violence.
Across the state, violent crimes against people such as assault and homicide are down 11.8% in the first half of 2026 compared the first half of last year, part of a broader six-year trend that extreme domestic violence cases do not seem to follow.
“We are seeing a faster escalation to violence or lethality within the family or intimate partner dynamics statewide,” Meghan Scanlon, the president and CEO of the Connecticut Coalition Against Domestic Violence, said.
As crime in the state continues to fall, extreme domestic and family violence cases are either holding steady or increasing slightly. This trend is particularly prevalent when looking at homicides; in 2021, 18% of homicides were domestic or family violence related compared to 33% last year.
While the most extreme domestic violence cases do not follow the broader trend of violent crime in the state, the frequency of all reported domestic and family violence crime has decreased since 2014. Extreme cases involving stalking, strangulation, homicide, risk of injury, kidnapping and sexual assault make up a small percentage of all reported domestic and family violence in the state.
These trends are not unique to Connecticut, according to Scanlon.
California, like Connecticut, is seeing fewer domestic violence reports. However, the reported cases are more severe, according to an analysis by the Public Policy Institute of California.
Scanlon also said people are staying longer at the shelters, people are coming in with more trauma, and more children are victims of physical violence themselves.
The organization, which is made up of 18 sites across the state that provide domestic violence services, has seen a steady number of people seeking help. However, there is  not always have room at their safe houses for those in need — especially as average stays continue to get longer.
“It does make it quite hard to ensure that when people are reaching out to our system that they feel like they’re getting all the services that they feel like they need,” Scanlon said. “Unfortunately, sometimes we just don’t have the space, so we have to be honest with them about that.”
The state is facing severe funding gaps, Scanlon said. Federal funding shrank in both the first and second Trump administrations, and there is very little supplemental funding available.
“At this point, every state is really advocating for funds to stabilize services,” Scanlon said.
And at the state level, Scanlon said, the organization will also be advocating for funding stabilization this legislative session.
“I think when it comes to the positions that are embedded within the court system, we really are asking the state to step up and fund the family violence victim advocates,” Scanlon said.
If you are facing domestic or family violence, please call or text 888-774-2900 for the Domestic Violence Support Hotline, or chat www.ctsafeconnect.org. In an emergency, call or text 911.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Ballot rejections soared in rural counties after USPS reduced mail service
authors: Ken B. Morales, Jen Fifield, Misty Harris
text:
Jacque Laird sorts ballot envelops at Direct Mail Enterprises in Spokane, Washington Friday October 9th, 2026.   
(Photo by Rajah Bose for ProPublica)This story was first published by ProPublica. 
In early August, election workers north of Spokane, Washington, went across the street to the post office to check for late mail-in ballots. It was three days after the primary and they were expecting no more than a few dozen.
Instead, their mailbox was brimming with envelopes — more than 500 of them, each a vote that wouldn’t count. The sight was “jarring,” said Auditor Lori Larsen, a Republican who oversees voting in Stevens County.
Across the region, other election officials were getting similar jolts. In the 11 predominately rural counties in eastern Washington, nearly 2,000 ballots came in late, compared to about 600 in 2022, the previous midterm primary.
In recent weeks, concerns about mail-in voting disruptions have focused almost entirely on President Donald Trump’s now-shelved plan to sharply restrict who can vote by mail.
But a ProPublica data analysis shows that delays resulting from the U.S. Postal Service’s cost-cutting measures have endangered the validity of ballots cast in rural areas, not only in Washington, but across the country.
Over the past three years, as mail volume continued to plummet and annual deficits ballooned, the Postal Service started consolidating the processing of first-class mail at larger regional plants instead of at smaller hubs closer to local post offices. Then, in a little-noted switch that mostly took effect after the 2024 election, the agency cut the frequency of mail pickups in half at many post offices 50 miles or more from these processing plants, from twice daily to once.
The changes often added a day or more to delivery time and, most importantly for ballots, pushed back postmarking, which doesn’t happen until mail reaches the regional centers.
In this year’s primary, the effects of the cuts were clearest in five states that make detailed data on mail-in ballots available: Washington, California, Ohio, North Carolina and Oregon. All have or recently had grace periods allowing ballots to count if they come in after Election Day as long as they’re postmarked by the deadline.
In these states, the number of ballots rejected for arriving late soared in counties affected by the service changes compared to 2022, ProPublica’s analysis showed.
Rejection rates in counties where services were cut doubled or tripled from what they were four years ago, dwarfing any increases in counties where postal pickups remained as they were, our analysis showed. In urban Spokane, for example, the number of ballots rejected for being late actually dropped this year.
Across the five states, the delays have had the most substantial effect in areas that voted for Trump in 2024, ProPublica’s analysis shows. In Washington, Secretary of State Steve Hobbs, a Democrat, said he sees the service changes directed by Republican appointees leading the Postal Service as a way to undermine mail-in voting.
“I don’t think they realized how much it was going to affect their voter base,” he said, adding that Washington has “a lot of rural Republican voters.”
The chart shows the four states where data on all returned absentee ballots was available. Data from North Carolina and Washington tracked absentee ballots returned by mail. Data from California and Ohio tracked absentee ballots returned by any method, including drop boxes. Sources: California secretary of state, North Carolina State Board of Elections, Ohio secretary of state, Washington secretary of state. (Chart by Ken B. Morales/ProPublica)
Postal Service leaders say such delays are less likely in the Nov. 3 general election because of “extraordinary measures” the agency puts into place for these votes, when there’s typically far more turnout. They have circulated a memo to the nation’s more than 30,000 post offices saying that for the 10 days before the election, managers should separate completed ballots from other first-class mail and deliver those intended for local election offices the day they come in.
At an Oct. 15 news conference, Postal Service leaders emphasized the agency’s longstanding recommendation that voters mail ballots back at least a week before their states’ deadlines, while defending the agency’s ability to fast-track ballots through the system.
“We work to identify and address issues quickly,” said Amber McReynolds, chair of the Postal Service board of governors, “so ballots can continue to move swiftly from election offices to voters and from voters back to election offices.”
Election consultants, researchers and former Postal Service officials told ProPublica that the guidance for the upcoming vote gave more detailed directions on how to expedite ballots. They said they hoped the agency’s special measures would limit delays, but some said mistakes were likely.
“I don’t think we can say with any kind of conviction that there will be no ballots rejected,” said Tammy Patrick, chief programs officer of the National Association of Election Officials. “It isn’t a question of ‘if,’ but a question of ‘how many.’”
A pilot program instituting the delivery changes in 18 regions before the 2024 election ran into problems. An audit by the Postal Service’s inspector general found that agency staff in these areas sometimes didn’t handle ballots correctly, mainly because instructions weren’t clearly communicated. (A Postal Service spokesperson said “learnings from the pilot” have been applied as the program has expanded.)
After this year’s primary, reports by media outlets noted that mail-in ballot rejection rates were higher than in the past, but ProPublica’s analysis shows these increases were directly connected to Postal Service changes. Research published in September by the Brookings Institution also found this connection, projecting that if the pattern held in the general election, tens of thousands of mail-in ballots could be rejected.
At least seven closely contested congressional districts — including Washington’s 3rd, California’s 22nd and North Carolina’s 11th — are in areas that were affected by service changes in the primary, ProPublica found.
Elena Patel, who conducted the Brookings analysis, said service changes may still imperil mail-in votes in the general election.
“I think there remain risks to ballots,” she said, adding that the Postal Service’s plan for the general election “depends on flawless execution.”

Mail-in voting has become more popular over the last decade, with many states broadening access to it during the COVID-19 pandemic.
Nearly 1 in 3 Americans voted this way in 2022 and 2024. Trump himself frequently votes by mail, and in recent weeks has started to encourage his supporters to do so as well, though he has claimed without evidence that the process is rife with fraud.
The Postal Service has mostly ensured the timely delivery of hundreds of millions of ballots, even as mail volume overall has dropped 50% from its high in 2006.
When Louis DeJoy was appointed postmaster general in spring 2020, he inherited an $81 billion operating deficit and rapidly took steps such as eliminating overtime to reduce costs, under pressure from Trump and others in his administration. (DeJoy did not respond to questions from ProPublica.)
The NAACP sued that August, alleging the measures could affect mail-in votes in that year’s general election. Courts ordered DeJoy to reverse some of the cuts and the Postal Service agreed to implement special procedures to ensure ballots weren’t delayed. The Postal Service has continued following those procedures since.
Still, DeJoy went forward with a 10-year restructuring plan designed to save the agency billions. It ended evening pickups from some post offices, often in rural areas. Trucks serving these places travel long distances and at times were mostly empty. This part of the plan — called regional transportation optimization, or RTO — was projected to eventually save the Postal Service $4 billion a year.
The agency announced the national rollout of the RTO plan in 2024, but DeJoy agreed to pause it leading up to that year’s November election, leaving only about 4,000 ZIP codes in the pilot project affected by the service changes.
ProPublica analysis of Postal Regulatory Commission filings. (Graph by Ken B. Morales/ProPublica)
In January 2025, the Postal Regulatory Commission, which oversees the Postal Service, warned that moving forward with the plan would be disruptive to rural communities and might not save as much money as expected. The Postal Service rolled out the reductions anyway, extending the changes to almost 20,000 ZIP codes to date. Officials said they expect the system to be fully implemented within two years.
This January, the agency put out a statement saying the transportation cuts would mean it took longer for mail, including ballots, to be postmarked and delivered. But the Postal Service didn’t specify which voters would be affected by the slowdowns and which wouldn’t.
ProPublica analysis of Postal Regulatory Commission filings. (Graphic by Chris Alcantara/ProPublica)
Though the delay from RTO is often only a day, mail can be delayed longer if it’s deposited in a mailbox after the daily pickup time, or just before Sunday or a holiday.
A Postal Service spokesperson said the agency told election officials that RTO would change schedules and reemphasized the need for voters to get their ballots in the mail at least a week ahead of time. Election officials in Washington said the Postal Service wasn’t direct enough about the fact that the changes would lead to delays in delivering and postmarking ballots.
“What they said was, ‘We are going to change the way we do postmarks,’” said Hobbs, Washington’s secretary of state. “That was it.”
Patel, the Brookings analyst and a former Postal Regulatory Commission employee, said that more direct communication to voters could have helped change their behavior. “That’s the part that I think has not been super transparent about the whole process,” she said.

Many of the areas that saw a spike in late ballots were in Western states, which were the earliest and most enthusiastic adopters of expanded mail-in voting.
In 2004, Washington became the second state to start conducting all-mail elections, in which every eligible voter automatically receives a mail-in ballot. Most residents vote by putting their ballots in drop boxes. Still, in 2024, about 33% put them in the mail.
In the 30 mostly rural Washington counties most affected by RTO, the percentage of ballots postmarked late more than tripled compared to the 2022 primary, ProPublica found.
In Garfield County, in southeastern Washington, 19 ballots — nearly 1 in 10 cast — had late postmarks this year. In 2022, only a single ballot was postmarked late. In Pend Oreille County, in northeast Washington along the Idaho panhandle, 6% of ballots were rejected for arriving late, compared to 1% in the 2022 primary.
“It was pretty awful telling people we couldn’t count their votes,” said Marianne Nichols, Pend Oreille’s longtime auditor. “They were quite upset because they felt like, ‘Why? This was in the mailbox on election day, the post office picked it up and had it.’ They felt like it should have counted.”
In Stevens County, the percentage of ballots rejected for having a late postmark jumped to 8%, from 1% in 2022.
Steve Hutkins, a retired professor who analyzes the effect of Postal Service changes on Savethepostoffice.com, also found that places in Washington with RTO had more ballot rejections during local elections earlier this year for school board and other measures. The patterns “set off the alarm bells,” he said.
Stuart Holmes, the state’s director of elections, said he reached out to Postal Service officials to find out what had happened, but got few answers and no specifics on delays related to RTO, which were a “total surprise,” he said.
Election officials in California and Oregon also reported thousands more ballots rejected for arriving late during their primaries. Counties affected by RTO, including Kern County, California, had substantially higher rates of ballots rejected for mail-related reasons, ProPublica found.
Kern County’s assistant registrar of voters, Laura Cantu, said election officials are urging rural voters to use drop boxes to cast their ballots in the general election.
The expansion of RTO had a similar effect in North Carolina and Ohio, where the rates of late ballots were about twice as high in counties affected by the restructuring as rates in counties that weren’t. Since 2022, these states have also eliminated grace periods in which ballots postmarked by Election Day could count even if they arrived later. Voters unused to the tighter deadlines also could have contributed to an increase in late ballots.
ProPublica didn’t find any association between RTO and higher rates of late ballots in Wisconsin, even though clerks reported delays involving mail-in ballots cast in its state election, held this spring. (Other Postal Service changes may have contributed to the delays.)
Wisconsin’s data does not distinguish ballots sent by mail from those cast in drop boxes or in person, making it impossible to definitively measure rejection rates just for ballots returned by mail. Election researchers said Wisconsin’s deadline for mail ballots, which must come into election offices by 8 p.m. on Election Day, also probably had an effect.
“If you know that you don’t have a grace period, it probably affects voter behavior,” said Patel, the Brookings researcher.
Jacque Laird sorts ballot envelops at Direct Mail Enterprises in Spokane, Washington Friday October 9th, 2026.  (Photo by Rajah Bose for ProPublica)
Recent Postal Service audits have found that RTO-related changes had saved the agency about $2.8 billion by the end of fiscal year 2025 — less money than expected — and are slowing down all first-class mail, not just ballots. Residents of rural areas are waiting longer for everything from prescriptions to bills, a report published in September by the Postal Service’s inspector general said.
A Postal Service spokesperson still defended the plan, both for financial reasons and to adjust to the changing marketplace. “These savings are both significant and necessary,” he said.
In the lead-up to Nov. 3, the agency’s plan is to route ballots meant for local election offices to a nearby postal facility or directly to their destination. They shouldn’t go to regional plants, which the Postal Service says should minimize delays.
Larsen, the Stevens County auditor, is encouraging Washington voters to deposit their ballots in drop boxes rather than relying on the mail. Since the primary, she’s increased the number of red, white and blue drop boxes that sit outside government buildings from seven to 12. Near each box, there’s a large sign encouraging people to take selfies when they vote and send the photos to Larsen.
In prior years, Larsen said, she avoided telling voters how or when to vote, concerned they might regret choices they made if critical information later emerged about the candidates. That’s no longer uppermost in her mind.
“Now we are more concerned that we get your ballot,” she said.



How We Reported This Story
To quantify the effects of logistical changes at some U.S. post offices on mail-in ballot rejection rates, we compiled a list of affected ZIP codes and compared them with ballot-rejection tallies we obtained from nine states.
Not every state tracked ballots the same way. Only Washington, North Carolina and Oregon tracked rejection rates with enough detail to distinguish ballots received in the mail from those received by some other means, like a ballot drop box. In these states, our analysis found a direct relationship between counties where the U.S. Postal Service’s logistics changes were implemented and increased rejection rates for ballots sent by mail and received late during the 2026 primaries. A ballot was considered late if it arrived at an elections office later than is allowed or was postmarked after the deadline.
In California and Ohio, states with less detailed data, we were able to connect these logistical changes with increased rejection rates generally, which experts said were likely tied to the changes at the Postal Service. In California, data was missing for four counties in the 2022 primary data, affecting 2% of registered voters. We could not establish the effect in Colorado, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin, the three states we received data for that do not accept ballots after election day.
The Postal Service does not publicly maintain a master list of delivery ZIP codes where it has implemented its logistics changes, called regional transportation optimization or RTO. We compiled a list using filings made to the Postal Regulatory Commission’s online docket, which gives the addresses of individual postal facilities that were eligible for RTO. We considered RTO implemented for any ZIP code served by at least one post office on these lists. If the filings did not list the post office’s delivery ZIP codes, we assumed that the ZIP code listed in the post office’s physical address had undergone RTO. If filings listed multiple implementation dates for a given ZIP code, we used the earliest one.
Because the U.S. Postal Service does not maintain official boundaries for ZIP codes, we used ZIP Code Tabulation Areas from the U.S. Census Bureau, which are generalized areas commonly used to analyze demographics for ZIP codes. A county was considered to have been affected by RTO if a majority of its voting-age citizens lived in ZIP codes where RTO was implemented at the time of the state’s primary. Population data came from the American Community Survey 5-year special tabulation for 2024, the most recent year available. The results of the analysis did not change when accounting for margin of error. Block group data was interpolated to ZIP Code Tabulation Areas. The population was assumed to be evenly distributed.




Graphics by Chris Alcantara and Ken B. Morales. Ruth Talbot and Ellis Simani contributed data reporting.

title: Santa Fe mayor targeted by ‘suspicious hazardous device’
text:
Santa Fe City Hall and surrounding areas were evacuated on Oct. 22, 2026, after a City Hall employee reported a suspicious hazardous device intended for Santa Fe Mayor Michael Garcia. The Santa Fe Police Department is investigating the incident. (Photo by Matthew Mondschein/Source NM)Santa Fe Police evacuated City Hall yesterday after an individual outside City Hall handed a city employee a suspicious package and said it was meant for Mayor Michael Garcia. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The Santa Fe Police Department’s explosive ordinance disposal team responded and SFPD closed nearby buildings and roads throughout the area, interim SFPD Chief of Police Ben Valdez said in a statement. 
At approximately 4 p.m., the EOD unit rendered the suspected device safe and lockdowns were lifted. The investigation remains ongoing. 
“The targeting of an elected official and the disruption of public services at Santa Fe City Hall are reprehensible acts of intimidation that will not be tolerated,” Santa Fe Mayor Michael Garcia said in a statement. “Attempts to intimidate public officials, threaten lives or interfere with the essential functions of local government are attacks on the public’s trust and our democratic institutions.”
The Santa Fe County Clerk’s office, which is also an early voting location, was one of the nearby offices placed on lockdown. Other early voting locations in the county remained open.
Across the country, packages and mail have been sent to election officials ahead of the Nov. 3 general election. Last week, federal authorities intercepted a suspicious package intended for Oregon’s election office. In Arizona and Louisiana, top state election officials evacuated their offices after receiving letters containing white powder. 
Valdez noted it is unknown whether the City Hall incident is related to other suspicious package incidents in Santa Fe that EOD responded to this week: one reported incident in the Railyard area on Sunday and another on Galisteo Street on Thursday morning.
“Santa Fe will not be governed by intimidation,” Garcia said. “Those who seek to threaten our public servants and disrupt our city’s operations will be held accountable.”

name: National
title: 2026 ballot measures are written at a graduate-school reading level, report finds
text:
Voters mark their primary election ballots at Second Presbyterian Church in Little Rock, Arkansas, on March 3, 2026. This year’s statewide ballot measures are written, on average, at a graduate-school reading level, according to a new report. (Photo by John Sykes/Arkansas Advocate)This year’s statewide ballot measures are written, on average, at a graduate-school reading level, according to a new report.
The readability of 2026’s ballot questions — which ask voters to weigh in on issues as varied as abortion, property taxes, voter ID and firearms — varies by state, political data tracking nonprofit Ballotpedia found in its newest Ballot Measure Readability Report.
The report analyzes the level of education voters would need to understand the titles and summaries of the measures put before them. Because ballot measures are often lengthy and full of legal language, states write shorter titles to be published on the ballot for voters to read.
Many of this year’s ballot measures don’t include summaries to supplement the titles. And many voters don’t read beyond a measure’s title before deciding how to vote, Ballotpedia researchers note.
This year, 164 measures have been or will be on the ballot across 40 states. The titles average a reading level requiring 17 years of education, which corresponds to a first-year graduate student. The summaries average a reading level requiring 15 years of education. About 42% of the U.S. adult population ages 25-54 have a bachelor’s degree or higher, according to the most recently available data from the U.S. Census Bureau.
Title readability ranges from a fifth-grade level for an Idaho question asking voters to choose an official state gun to a 48th-grade level for a Colorado constitutional amendment that would establish a right to hunt and fish, Ballotpedia found. No formal education level corresponds to a 48th-grade level, but that rating indicates an extremely advanced language structure.
“The most significant factor driving readability differences isn’t the type or topic of the ballot measure, but which state it’s in,” said Ryan Byrne, managing editor of Ballotpedia’s ballots team, in a statement.
Kentucky, Massachusetts and Tennessee had the lowest average title readability grade level, at 10 years of education, while Colorado had the highest at 33 years, followed by Hawaii at 31 years and Nevada at 26, according to the report.
Research has found voters are more likely to skip ballot questions that have more complex language.
About half of states have enacted laws designed to make ballot measure language easier to read. Earlier this year, Maryland enacted a law requiring ballot questions to be written in plain and clear language. Last year, Arkansas required ballot titles to be written at no more than an eighth-grade level.
But still, the average readability score for state ballot measures since 2017, when Ballotpedia began tracking it, is about 18 years of education, or the equivalent of a second-year graduate student.
This year, Kansas had the longest ballot question title, at 927 words for a constitutional amendment that would have authorized the election of state Supreme Court justices and abolished an existing nominating commission. Voters defeated it in August.
Alaska will have the shortest title, at just five words, for a measure to amend state law to allow only U.S. citizens to vote in elections.
Ballotpedia uses two formulas to calculate readability, which includes looking at the number of syllables, words and sentences in a text.
Readability scores for each of the 164 ballot measures this year can be found in Ballotpedia’s report.
Stateline reporter Anna Claire Vollers can be reached at avollers@stateline.org.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Democratic divisions could hurt El-Sayed, but Trump’s economy may matter more
text:
Abdul El-Sayed, Michigan's Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate, at the Michigan Democratic Party's nominating convention on Aug. 29, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance)With voters still up for grabs in the final weeks of the U.S. Senate race, Abdul El-Sayed and Mike Rogers are campaigning in unlikely places as both candidates seek to chip away at the others’ bases. 
El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee, still faces an uphill battle to unify segments of the party’s base, while Rogers, the Republican nominee, is attempting to extract potential supporters from those very same segments; Democratic Jewish and Black voters, two communities that supported U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Birmingham) in the primary.
But the worsening economy under President Donald Trump could outweigh those efforts in determining voter turnout on Nov. 3.
“I don’t think it matters anymore,” Adrian Hemond, a Democratic consultant and CEO of Grassroots Midwest, told Michigan Advance. “The president ran the economy into a ditch with tariffs and a war of choice in the Middle East, and this administration and Republicans more broadly seem absolutely committed to the bit of replaying the mistakes of the end of the Biden administration. … We have inflation running rampant through the economy, and you have the party in power that’s telling you everything’s fine.”
Republican nominee for U.S. Senate Mike Rogers, right, responds to Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate Abdul El-Sayed, during a televised debate at WOOD-TV, on Thursday, Oct. 8, 2026, in Grand Rapids, Mich. (AP Photo/Paul Sancya, Pool)
Even as economic woes dominate the narrative, El-Sayed’s issues with Jewish voters persist, and Rogers’ associations with Trump may very well deter him in his quest to convert those voters.
Jewish voters only make up 1% of the state’s population, but a big shift in how that community votes might be an equally strong factor as the economy, said Charles Gaba, a Democratic fundraiser and a member of Michigan’s Jewish community.
“What we lack in numbers, we make up for in activism and organization and volunteering and fundraising,” Gaba said.
Meeting voters where they are becomes a big focus for both campaigns
Rogers has been boastful about his efforts to make inroads with Democrats. He created a coalition to court Black and Jewish voters and opened a field office in Detroit, while being supportive of Nonnegotiable Michigan, a group of “rabbis, cantors and synagogue lay leaders” who have demanded that El-Sayed recognize “Jewish sovereignty in Israel,” among other baseline affirmations for the community.
“There is a reason why more Democrats voted against him than voted for him,” Rogers said after a debate hosted by WOOD-TV earlier this month. “They understand that we’re for real, we’re going to help their problems, and actually have solutions to their problems.”
El-Sayed, Rogers trade barbs, accusations during first televised US Senate debate

Rogers’ success on election night could also depend, in part, on his work in the Black community. 
While The Bulwark recently reported that his “Democrats for Rogers” coalition was made up of and primarily funded by Republicans, Hemond said it was apparent that Rogers has been working in Detroit, and he expected Rogers to do better with the city’s voters than he would have otherwise.
However, El-Sayed’s efforts with those communities have been a major plotline throughout the campaign. He spent time over the last few weeks in Detroit, holding rallies, visiting churches and attending events. President Barack Obama is scheduled to rally with him this weekend, while former U.S. Rep. Andy Levin has come in to help him with Jewish voter outreach.
El-Sayed has also spent significant time in West Michigan and up north to sway independent voters and disaffected Republicans fed up with Trump. 
“When you’re getting 1,300 people in Marquette, 500 people in the eastern and western Upper Peninsula, he really has base problems,” El-Sayed said at this week’s WXYZ-TV debate. “He’s going to make a show out of things and needs something to grasp on … but we are actually campaigning.” 
New branding from the U.S. Senate campaign of Republican nominee Mike Rogers, who has unveiled a “Democrats for Rogers” coalition to capture disaffected voters who might have reservations to vote for Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee. Aug. 20, 2026 | Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance
Rogers hoping for strong Black support
Among Rogers supporters in the Black community are Damari Covington-Woods and Beulah Walker.
Covington-Woods, a 25-year-old entrepreneur and bricklayer from Auburn Hills, said he was supporting Rogers because the candidate and his wife were heavily involved in a literacy program, Beyond Basics, that helped him advance in his education. Rogers has touted his personal support for Beyond Basics on the campaign trail and on the debate stage. Covington-Woods, who has appeared in an ad promoting Rogers, said he only met the Republican candidate a year ago, but was impressed with how he carried himself, and how much he listened when he visited Beyond Basics.
“It can’t be overstated, literacy is at a crisis, man. It’s an existential crisis,” Covington-Woods said. “I’ve had solid conversations with Mike. I know what he stands for.”
Damari Covington-Woods (Courtesy of Damari Covington-Woods)
Walker is an activist for access to clean water, both in Flint and in Detroit. She said she was a longtime Democrat and a member of the party’s Black Caucus until she met Rogers a few months ago. Walker said she heard Rogers speak about his housing plans and his rhetoric about Democrats failing Black voters over the last century on things like clean water, poverty and disenfranchisement. 
Walker accused El-Sayed of using the Black community as political capital and invading their spaces as he sought their support in 2018, when he ran for governor, during the 2026 primary and now the general election. She also denounced his work as the health officer and executive director of the Detroit Health Department, associating his decade there with former Mayor Mike Duggan’s initiative early in his first term to shut off water to city residents with unpaid bills. Duggan ended up reversing that effort in 2014, a year before El-Sayed took over the health department. 
Despite tensions, El-Sayed still garnering Black support 
Walker also cited decades-long friction between Middle Eastern and Black communities in southeast Michigan as a reason why she believed some Black voters might reject El-Sayed.
“This is why Black Americans are at this point with Dr. Abdul,” Walker said. “This ain’t just a one-off with the Arabic or Chaldean community and people of color who are not Black. We are talking about decades of disrespect and misuse.”
When Michigan Advance asked whether her comments could be perceived as racist toward Middle Eastern and North African residents in or near Detroit, Walker stood by her remarks.
Beulah Walker (Courtesy of Beulah Walker)
“We’re at the bottom of the caste system economically. So, if anything, the Arabic and Chaldean community is above us when it comes to economics and resources,” Walker said. “The Arabic community has power over us. They own the grocery stores, the liquor stores, and the gas station. They run our core things that we need in life, basic essentials.”
Hemond noted that the tensions between Black and Middle Eastern residents in and around Detroit were real, but had existed well before El-Sayed began his career in politics.
Despite those hangups, some Black voters who supported Stevens in the primary have said they are with El-Sayed, and that they were excited to support him.
“We’re on these doors, so we know exactly what people care about,” said I’Ron Wilson, a member of the UNITE HERE labor union representing hotel and hospital workers. “Healthcare, housing, and cost of living are the top of the list. Black folks are looking for someone with solutions that will actually make their lives better.”
Another El-Sayed ally, Benton Harbor Mayor Marcus Muhammad, has continued to express support on social media.

Black Mayors of Michigan support @AbdulElSayed for United States  Senate. https://t.co/arIiWwHoO7
— Mayor Marcus Muhammad (@marcus4polytics) October 23, 2026

Some Jewish Democrats weigh withholding support from El-Sayed
David Kramer, a Democratic fundraiser and a signatory to the Nonnegotiable Michigan petition, said he still hopes El-Sayed will address their concerns, but feels the prospect has dimmed.
Kramer and former Michigan Democratic Party Chair Lon Johnson co-authored an op-ed in The Detroit News this week urging Jewish Democrats to leave El-Sayed’s section of the ballot blank.
“There is, at least in my experience, a fairly small percentage of Jewish Dems who I talk to who say, ‘I feel so strongly about voting for Democrats with everything at stake,’” Kramer said. “But the majority of people I talk to are either voting for Rogers or leaving it blank.”
David Kramer (Courtesy of David Kramer)
Gaba said some people within his circle, who were loud in their support for El-Sayed, have recently stopped encouraging other Jews to support him — mostly because of his unwillingness to say that Iran was a bigger threat to the U.S. and the world than Israel.
Kramer said many Jews identify as Zionists, and that El-Sayed trying to separate Zionism and Judaism in his political rhetoric has turned them off.
“In my synagogue I go to, when you walk in, there’s an American flag and there’s an Israeli flag,” Kramer said. “There’s a prayer for the state of Israel that you recite during the high holidays. … They’re so intertwined that you can’t separate them out and basically say, ‘Well, I’m supportive of Jews, but not Zionist Jews.’”
A survey earlier this year by the Jewish Federations of North America found that while more than 70% of American Jews felt “emotionally attached” to Israel, only 37% considered themselves to be Zionist.
Kramer was unsure if a movement to withhold support would signal to Democrats that they risk alienating Jewish voters. He did express concern, however, about the message an El-Sayed victory without substantial Jewish support could send to the party.
Progressive Jews, Black voters still showing up for El-Sayed despite defections
Pamela Shifman, president of Democracy Alliance, a group of progressive donors, is publicly urging Democrats to donate to El-Sayed’s campaign. Shifman is Jewish and said she is proud to support him.
Dana Nessel says she’ll vote for Abdul El-Sayed, ending potential Michigan Democratic Party rift

“Abdul shows up. He is willing to engage in conversation, and I think it is really clear that Abdul is getting most Jewish Democrats behind him,” Shifman said. “Dana Nessel, Elissa Slotkin, they’re now campaigning with Abdul. I think they understand the stakes of the election and the existential threat that Mike Rogers poses.”
Gaba began supporting El-Sayed after he secured the nomination, but he was all-in on Stevens after state Sen. Mallory McMorrow (D-Royal Oak) dropped out. Gaba made a commitment to support the nominee and he’ll do so even if he, like Kramer, is not actively encouraging other Jews to support El-Sayed.
“It will have some effect, but I think he’s going to win anyway, if for no other reason that the environment is just so completely toxic for Republicans right now,” Gaba said.
Hemond agreed, and said that the voting bloc issues in play were not going to change the fact that residents were likely to punish Trump and the GOP over the economy.
“I think it’ll be most pronounced with Jewish Democrats, but I think that there are a lot of centrist Democrats that are Abdul skeptical. … A decent number of them are not going to vote for him,” Hemond said. “But it’s always the economy and people’s vibes about the economy closest to them, and that’s all wretched now, including in Detroit and with Black voters, just like all the other voters.”

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: ‘It’s a stressful life’: How energy debt is straining 800K Massachusetts utility customers
text:
NOEMY RODRIGUEZ HAS HAD overdue utility bills stacking up over the last eight years. 
Little has been easy for the single mother in East Boston. While working part-time as an organizer with the local nonprofit GreenRoots, Rodriguez cares for her three children, one of which suffers from epilepsy while the other two navigate attention deficit disorders. That’s left Rodriguez regularly shuffling between her apartment and work, getting her children off to school, and juggling medical appointments.  
When she’s not fending off notices — and paying off some of her utility bill debt just in time — to avoid getting her electricity and heat shut off, that is. 
“When you owe money and are in debt and receiving disconnection notices many times, it’s a stressful life,” Rodriguez, who immigrated to the US nearly 20 years ago from El Salvador, said through a Spanish translator. “It’s either bringing food to the table for your kids or paying your bills.” 
Rodriguez is in much better standing now, after she finally qualified for a low-income discount rate for her energy bills and as of six months ago was enrolled in a payment forgiveness plan with Eversource, her electric provider. But she is one of some 800,000 customers of the six investor-owned utilities in Massachusetts saddled with late or overdue energy payments, known as arrearages. 
Arrearages are seen as one clear indicator of financial distress within a household, particularly for low-income customers. Energy costs, which in Massachusetts and around the country have risen sharply, are one of the top household concerns in the Bay State and have contributed to an affordability crisis that has erupted onto the national political landscape. 
Over time, severe debts can lead the utility company to disconnect that customer’s service for electricity or heat, a last-resort step that poses a health and safety risk. 
A CommonWealth Beacon analysis of filings submitted by the state’s six investor-owned utilities as required by regulators over the course of the last seven years reveals a complicated picture. 
Total arrearages owed by Massachusetts electric and gas customers have roughly doubled between June 2019 and June 2026, the filings show, increasing from around $580 million to $1.12 billion — a 93 percent increase. 
But at the same time, the number of individual customers with arrears has actually fallen over that time. In 2020, around 941,000 customers were overdue on their energy payments. 
This year, around 818,000 customers face arrears — a 13 percent decline that brings the number down below pre-Covid levels. 
The result: The average customer with arrears is far worse off than just a few years ago, according to the filings, which are submitted to the Department of Public Utilities. 
Across the six companies, gas and electric customers with arrears on average owed $815 in 2020.  
Now, it’s $1,366 — a 68 percent increase.  
For customers of certain utilities, the increase has been much larger. For Unitil, the average amount of money owed has ballooned nearly 80 percent. At Eversource, the largest utility in the state, it’s 108 percent. 
Though total arrears continue to grow, the pace of that increase has slowed substantially in recent years. Arrears jumped 21 percent between 2020 and 2021 but rose just 1 percent between June 2025 and June 2026. 
Massachusetts isn’t alone in the rising share of households facing energy insecurity around the country, yet the state, as wealthy as it is, sticks out given its high cost of living and increasing utility bills.  
The percentage of US households facing energy insecurity rose from 27 percent in 2020 to 33 percent in 2024, with nearly one-fourth foregoing or reducing the amount they spend on food or health care to keep the lights on, according to federal data compiled by the National Consumer Law Center. 
“Energy affordability is definitely getting worse,” said Jenifer Bosco, NCLC’s managing director of energy advocacy. “Arrearages are growing. Certainly after Covid, after the disconnection moratoriums ended, people had pretty high amounts of arrears. For some families, that hasn’t really been fully resolved.” 
Massachusetts in particular is headed in the wrong direction.  
Data released by the Bipartisan Policy Center last month shows Massachusetts is the fourth-worst state for low-income customers in terms of energy burden, the share of household income dedicated to energy costs. For these customers, energy burden is so high in Massachusetts that it exceeds what the US Energy Department considers “severe.”  
Average household utility bills in the Bay State are up 38 percent since 2020. And low-income customers consistently owe more money on average here compared to standard-rate customers, though both groups have seen large increases since 2019, NCLC found. 
None of this data captures customers that heat their homes with delivered fuels like oil and propane. Heating oil customers are likely to face unprecedented stress this winter warming their homes, with fuel costs up 75 percent this year compared to last year, according to state data. 
In addition to how expensive basic necessities have become in general, one key driver of the arrearage growth can be traced to the Covid-19 pandemic. 
Arrearages rose sharply between 2020 and 2021 as Massachusetts, along with many other states, implemented temporary bans on utility disconnections for nonpayment.  
Jessica Cain, vice president of customer operations at Eversource, said that 80 percent of customers who receive notice of potential disconnection take action, either by paying their bill, setting up a payment plan, or filing for assistance. The inability to send those notices during the pandemic, she said, coupled with the economic fallout from that time, is a dynamic that’s still playing out.   
“Once people build debt,” Cain said, “it takes a long time to dig out.” 
Massachusetts, in just a matter of days, is deploying a landmark new system meant to help alleviate the state’s energy burden issue.   
State regulators have ordered the utilities to roll out sweeping changes to the discounts afforded to Massachusetts’s lowest income residents. 
Starting on November 1, six new discount tiers for electric and gas bills will be available to residential customers that qualify based on their income status and household size.  
The lowest income customers, earning 100 percent or less than the federal poverty level, will receive discounts of up to 95 percent. That’s more than double the current flat low-income discount rate, which is roughly 42 percent for electric customers and 25 percent for gas customers. 
Though Massachusetts is not the first to establish such a tiered discount system — New Hampshire and Illinois, for example, offer discounts into the 80 percent range — it appears the Bay State’s discounts will be the steepest in the country. 
Alanna Kelly, a spokesperson for the Department of Public Utilities, said in a statement that the new tiered discount rates will help the state’s “most vulnerable customers pay their energy bills” through the deeper savings. 
“Reducing hardship for low-income families through meaningful assistance creates a more equitable energy system, and the DPU will continue to advance energy affordability and protect ratepayers,” she said.  
Ensuring that no household pays more than 4 percent of their household income on energy costs through the new discount rates theoretically lessens the disproportionate pressure on lower income customers.  
But it also means that customers who don’t qualify for the low-income rates could be forced to pay more to subsidize those heavy discounts, including customers that narrowly fall outside the discount window.  
Cain, for instance, estimated that the average Eversource customer not eligible for the new discount rates could see an increase of $5 to $8 per month for gas and $2 per month for electricity.  
One reason Massachusetts’s discount rate is so generous is because the DPU sought to achieve the lower 4 percent energy burden rate. When Connecticut implemented its low-income discount tiers, for instance, it aimed to achieve an energy burden of 6 percent, leading to discounts of up to 50 percent on customers’ utility bills – providing comparatively less assistance to those in financial distress than Massachusetts’s plan but also limiting how much other customers could be saddled with higher bills to pay for the program.
A National Grid van is seen on the side of a street in Brookline. (Jordan Wolman/CommonWealth Beacon)
It’s not that the utilities are necessarily against the new discounts. National Grid in 2025 was the first utility to pilot a tiered system in Massachusetts, though the discount — up to 71 percent for households earning 100 percent or less than the federal poverty level — was less generous. The utility’s program led to some 30,000 more customers being enrolled for low-income discount rates and a drop in the percentage of low-income customers with arrears from 42 percent to 35 percent in one year.  
The two other states in which Eversource operates, New Hampshire and Connecticut, have offered a tiered low-income rate system since 2002 and 2022, respectively. 
Lowering arrearages and reducing energy burden, especially in already stretched low-income households, has benefits for everyone, said Josh Ryor, a principal at the Regulatory Assistance Project who recently left his role as assistant secretary of energy in Massachusetts. 
“The idea is it’s more cost-effective to get the rate to something that customers can actually pay, and actually getting what they can pay from them,” Ryor said. “That will lower everyone’s rates.” 
But it’s the scope of the discounts in Massachusetts that has utilities, regulators, and advocates alike on edge to see how it all plays out. That includes ensuring qualified customers are actually enrolled at the proper rate for which they are eligible. 
And a segment of the population may be in for a surprise: The upper tier of the low-income group will qualify for a roughly 30 percent electric discount, which is less than current flat 42 percent discount. 
The DPU, in its order earlier this year, also instituted a change that exempts customers eligible for the new low-income discount rates from paying into the program themselves, as all ratepayers do for other initiatives like Mass Save. This move, the utilities warned regulators in a joint 2024 filing, “would result in higher bill impacts to non-income eligible customers” and “unfairly increase” those customers’ cost burden. 
“Asking the question of, ‘At what cost is it worth it for some customers to pay for special programs and benefits for others?’ is absolutely critical,” Cain said. 
Outside of the new discounts, struggling Bay Staters have also for the past 20 years been able to enroll in their utility’s arrear management plan (AMP), as Rodriguez of East Boston did, to help them erase debt with monthly payments.  
AMPs are generally considered a helpful tool that both utilities and advocates have supported as a key mechanism that returns customers to good standing and avoids the need for the electric or gas provider to incur costly legal and disconnection expenses. 
Each utility’s AMP is slightly different, but in general, low-income customers with arrears can be placed on a payment plan in which a portion of their debt is forgiven for every new payment made and service will not be shut off so long as those payments are made.  
At National Grid, for instance, AMP enrollment surged from around 16,000 customers in 2019 to more than 80,000 last year, and the utility has forgiven about $30 million in customer debt so far this year. 
Rob Morgan, who receives electricity from Eversource and gas from National Grid, is one of those customers benefiting from AMPs. 
Morgan, a Roxbury resident in his early 30s who lives in an apartment alongside his elderly aunt and cousins, has struggled with overdue energy bills. But Morgan said in an interview that about a month ago he successfully enrolled with Eversource’s arrear management plan and secured the current low-income electric discount rate. 
Jawayne Caesar has met with hundreds of Roxbury residents over the past year who need assistance managing their utility bills. (Jordan Wolman/CommonWealth Beacon)
Jawayne Caesar, an energy navigator at the community organization Reclaim Roxbury, helped review Morgan’s paperwork and coordinate with Eversource to get his utility bills back on track — an important step for him to reach his goal of buying a home next year. 
Caesar said that over the last year alone, as Reclaim Roxbury has incorporated utility bill assistance into its mission, he has met with hundreds of Roxbury residents looking for help managing what has become a major financial pain point in household budgets. 
More and more of those residents are carrying balances upwards of $4,000, he added. 
“I wish it were uncommon for me,” Caesar said. “But the balances are ballooning to the point that it’s untenable. People feel defeated.”

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: UK to open skilled nursing facility at Hamburg campus in Lexington
text:
UK Healthcare's Good Samaritan Hospital in Lexington. UK is opening a new facility at its Hamburg campus. (UK Healthcare)
The University of Kentucky’s healthcare arm will open a skilled nursing facility at their new campus at Hamburg in Lexington, working with Louisville-based Signature HealthCARE. The 105-bed facility will be a halfway point between hospital and home, officials said.
The UK Board of Trustees approved the deal on Friday morning.
“Patients from every corner of Kentucky come to UK HealthCare for the most advanced care available. When they are ready for the next step in their recovery, they deserve a place to go that is connected to the team that cared for them,” said Eric Monday, UK executive vice-president.  
Signature HealthCARE operates 67 skilled nursing care facilities, including more than 30 in Kentucky.
“Leaving the hospital is a major milestone, but many patients still have important work ahead before they can return home,” said Signature HealthCARE President and CEO Joe Steier. “At Signature HealthCARE, our stakeholders help people do that work every day, rebuilding strength, restoring confidence and regaining independence.”
Under the agreement, Beyond Blue Corp., a wholly owned affiliate of UK, will hold 60% ownership of the skilled nursing facility. Commonwealth Regional Skilled Nursing Holdings LLC, an affiliate of Signature HealthCARE, will hold the remaining 40%. 
A separate Signature affiliate, Commonwealth Regional Skilled Nursing Management LLC, will manage the facility’s day-to-day operations. UK HealthCare will provide clinical leadership and medical director services. The facility will purchase services from both Signature and UK affiliates.
UK HealthCare is planning a multi-phase development at its Hamburg property off Winchester Road.

name: Mississippi Today
title: ‘A botch job’: Federal appeals court reverses injunction, reassigns anti-DEI case
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
A federal appeals court decided this week to reverse an injunction preventing the enforcement of a state law banning diversity, equity and inclusion programs in Mississippi public schools and universities. 
The court has also ordered the case be reassigned to a new district judge, after his staff used artificial intelligence to draft an order in the case. 
The U.S. 5th Circuit Court of Appeals’ decision means the law can now be enforced in classrooms across the state. It also resolves a key concern of the plaintiffs: that the law would be interpreted to prohibit discussions of issues related to race, sex and civil rights, said Rob McDuff, one of their attorneys.
“This interpretation by the Court is good news for public school teachers and students throughout the state and signals that they can continue teaching and learning about these subjects as they have for many years,” he said.
Mississippi Attorney General Lynn Fitch’s office defended the law, which was passed during the 2025 legislative session. State attorneys told the court last year that the state government has the right to regulate educational content in public schools. 
But U.S. District Judge Henry T. Wingate sided with the plaintiffs’ attorneys — arguing on behalf of students, parents and educators — that the law was dangerously vague and violated the constitutional right to free speech. 
U.S. District Judge Henry Wingate smiles, Aug. 19, 2022, in Jackson, Miss. (AP Photo/Rogelio V. Solis, File)
As the lawsuit was playing out in court, Wingate came under fire amid revelations that his staff used artificial intelligence to draft an order in the case. The order was riddled with errors — naming defendants and plaintiffs who weren’t parties to the case, misquoting state law and referencing a nonexistent case.
Wingate, who was appointed in 1985 by President Ronald Reagan, initially declined to explain the errors until U.S. Senate Judiciary Committee Chairman Chuck Grassley demanded an explanation. 
The appeals court judges criticized Wingate in the Thursday order vacating his injunction. 
“The proceedings in the district court were a botch job, to say the least,” the order stated. 
In September, Anthony Shults, the state deputy solicitor general, told the three-judge appeals panel that the state has a legal right to regulate the material that public educators teach students. He also said he believed a new judge should take over the case.
McDuff argued that the law’s vagueness would cause chaos, and he told an appellate judge that Wingate’s error was serious, but “it’s not as if AI told Judge Wingate to grant” the injunction.
While the law can now be enforced in public school classrooms and colleges, its scope is fairly narrow as interpreted by the appeals court, McDuff said. 
“In sum, the Act does not apply to students,” the order reads. Other parts of the document say the law names a number of exemptions, including scholarly work, the activities of students and their groups, and creative engagement. 
A footnote says the plaintiffs were wrong to claim that the law would ban the discussion of civil rights history, including the Rev. Dr. Martin Luther King, Jr., the Ku Klux Klan, the 14th Amendment and Juneteenth.
“We’ve got to study the decision more carefully to see how it plays out in the future and go from there,” McDuff said. “But I don’t think this will be much of a problem in the future.”
A new judge will be assigned to the case at a later date.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: University of Northern Iowa President Mark Nook announces 2027 retirement
text:
University of Northern Iowa President Mark Nook announced on Friday his plan to retire at the end of the academic year. (Photo by Brooklyn Draisey/Iowa Capital Dispatch)University of Northern Iowa President Mark Nook has announced his upcoming retirement as the institution celebrates record-breaking fundraising and 150 years in existence.
The Cedar Falls university president, who began his tenure in February 2017, shared with the UNI community Friday morning his intentions to retire at the end of the 2026-2027 academic year with the commitment to stay at UNI until his successor arrives.
Nook said in a news release from the institution that serving UNI and the state has been “one of the greatest privileges” of he and his wife, Cheryl’s, lives.
“In many ways we feel like most of our soon-to-be UNI graduates as they enter their final semester. We are about to leave a place where we have built so many wonderful relationships, a place we love, a place — we call home,” Nook said in the release. “We truly appreciate the care and support the Panther Family has shown us and are proud to be a small part of the UNI legacy of helping our students, alumni, and colleagues enrich lives, communities and the world.”

In the weeks of the fall semester preceding Nook’s retirement announcement, UNI students, staff and faculty celebrated the institution’s 150th anniversary and closed out a fundraising campaign totaling more than $342 million. UNI was also the only state university this year to see higher enrollment of first-year students than in 2025, the total of 1,709 also the highest since Nook’s first year on campus in 2017.
Former board of regents member and UNI Our Tomorrow fundraising campaign co-chair Katie Mulholland said in the release that the UNI community is “indebted to President Nook for helping make a special place even stronger during his tenure.”
Iowa Board of Regents President Robert Cramer said in the release that UNI has evolved its academic offerings to meet workforce needs and has established an “innovative partnership” for placebound students with community colleges.
“The University of Northern Iowa is truly thriving,” Cramer said in the release. “Our state is exceedingly grateful to President Nook and the UNI community for positively impacting so many Iowa families and communities.”
