name: Daily Montanan
title: Commentary: Buy AI is a lot like buying a used truck
text:
A bipartisan U.S. Senate bill would create a panel to advise Congress on artificial intelligence policy. (Photo illustration by Getty Images)Picture three 2024 Ford F-150s, each with about 50,000 miles.
You find the first one on Facebook Marketplace. You meet the seller in a grocery store parking lot, hand over cash and drive off. If the transmission lets go before you hit the interstate, that’s your problem now.
The second one is on a small used lot. The salesman says it passed a 50-point inspection, and you sign paperwork saying it’s sold “as is.” Maybe that inspection was thorough. Maybe it was a guy kicking the tires.
The third one is at a Ford dealership, certified pre-owned, with a warranty and a company on the hook if something goes wrong.
Same truck. Three very different levels of protection. Nobody in Montana needs that explained.
I bring up trucks because of the question I hear most: “Which AI should we use?”
My answer surprises people: “That’s the wrong question.” 
The major AI tools are close in capability. Ask Copilot, Gemini, Claude or ChatGPT the same question and you’ll usually get similar answers, whether you’re on the free version, a personal paid account or the enterprise account the business pays for.
The difference is the contract. The free version is the pickup from the parking lot. You have no protections. The personal paid version trips people up the most. It’s the used lot with the “as is” paperwork. There are signatures on paper, but only slightly more protection than the cash buy. Enterprise contracts can protect you, but they vary. Some protections are automatic; others you negotiate.
Next comes, “What protections do I need? I’m not an AI expert, a lawyer or a software engineer.”
Your vendor should answer four questions: Do you train on my data? Where does my data live, and who can access it? Will you commit in the contract to Montana’s privacy and records laws? And when this relationship ends, how do we get our data back, and will you delete it? 
Those answers belong in the contract, not in a salesman’s word salad.
Many businesses say, “We don’t use AI, so we don’t need a policy.” 
That’s often wrong. A survey of 2,000 U.S. and U.K. workers last November found that 86% used AI for work at least weekly, and 60% said unapproved AI tools were worth the security risk if they helped them work faster or meet deadlines. That’s not malice. It’s people doing their best without guardrails.
Here are four things every Montana employer can do.
First, find out what’s already being used. Not to catch anybody, just to know. You can’t manage what you haven’t found.
Second, decide which tools you’ll allow and how much protection each kind of work needs. A newsletter isn’t the same as medical records.
Third, make the rules plain and teach them. A good AI policy doesn’t scare people off. It guides them. If you haven’t chosen a tool, be clear about what can’t go into personal AI accounts. Once you have one, train people on it. Either way, require human review of anything AI produces before anyone relies on it.
Fourth, have a plan for the day something goes wrong, because sooner or later something will. We plan for equipment breakdowns, hailstorms and data breaches. This belongs on the same list.
Why does this matter? 
Ask Air Canada. 
Its website chatbot told a grieving customer he could apply for a bereavement discount after he traveled. The airline’s own policy said otherwise, and it refused. Before a British Columbia tribunal in 2024, Air Canada argued, in effect, that the chatbot was responsible for its own actions. The tribunal called that “a remarkable submission” and wrote: “It makes no difference whether the information comes from a static page or a chatbot.” The damages were small. The lesson isn’t: The tool doesn’t take the blame. You do.
With the right contract, a policy, trained people and a plan, you’re the buyer at the dealership. Without them, you handed over cash in a parking lot. Every Montanan with a cabin knows a weekend clearing dead timber beats months rebuilding after a fire.
We’re not talking about perfection. The goal is to show that you saw the risk, made reasonable rules, trained your people, and acted when something went wrong. That’s what defensible looks like.
So when someone asks which AI to use, have that conversation. Ask one question back first: What happens if it breaks down on the way home?
Jacob Rebo is a Montana attorney and the founder of Cullis AI, LLC, a Billings firm that helps businesses, law firms and public agencies build practical AI governance programs. He is a former U.S. Army captain who served 14 years on active duty.

name: VTDigger
title: The last Democratic legislator in Rutland County is leaving office. What could that mean for the county’s political future?
text:
(Left to Right) Former Rep. Mary Howard (D-Rutland) and former Sen. Cheryl Hooker (D-Rutland) by Glenn Russell/VTDigger; Independent Rutland County Senate candidate Dave Wolk, courtesy photo; Incumbent Republican candidates Sens. Brian Collamore, David Weeks and Terry Williams by Glenn Russell; Mortimer Proctor, courtesy of the Vermont Historical Society. Background photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger, photo Illustration by Greta Solsaa/VTDigger.

This year, the sole Democrat from Rutland County in the Legislature decided to not seek reelection, leaving an uncertain future for Rutland’s Democratic Party. 
The race for outgoing Democratic Rep. Mary Howard’s Rutland District-6 seat includes Democrat Chris Siliski and Republican Cindy Laskevich.
The Democratic Party couldn’t find anyone to run for all three Senate seats and six out of 16 of the House seats representing parts of the county, said Thomas Fagan, chair of the Rutland County Democrats.
In fact, the three incumbent Republican senators on the ballot — Sens. Brian Collamore, David Weeks and Terry Williams — will also appear as Democrats, having won as write-ins in the August primary. They are facing a challenge from Dave Wolk — who served as a Democratic senator for Rutland County from 1988 to 1992 — who entered the race as an independent, after resigning as Rutland County assistant judge.
While Rutland County has long been majority Republican, voters previously had more options on their ballot and have backed candidates with varying political identities. 
Rutland County voters sent more Republicans than Democrats to the statehouse in the past decade. Republican legislators occupied around two-thirds of the seats, varying slightly year to year. Last session, Republicans occupied all but one of the seats that represent part of Rutland County, some of whom took office as part of a red wave in 2024. 
 The Senate doubled its Republican members, and Republicans captured 18 seats in the House. This came after Gov. Phil Scott put his political weight behind Republican candidates to break the Democratic supermajority in the Legislature. 
Stephanie Jerome — a former state representative who was one of the Rutland County Democrats ousted in the 2024 election cycle — said the Make America Great Again “MAGA” movement influenced the Rutland County electorate in 2024.
“I don’t see it as a permanent red wave. I see it as a temporary red wave instigated by national politics,” Jerome said. 
Steven Thompson, Rutland County Republican Party chair, said he sees Rutland County Republicans’ role as providing a counterweight to the left wing and holding off any supermajority of Democratic voices in the Legislature in what he attributed to Gov. Scott’s goal of “balance.” 
“Our focus in Rutland County is to help get numbers around the rest of the state, maintain what we have here, and then, you know, continue down that path of balance,” Thompson said. 
Political powerhouse
Rutland County has been a historic Republican stronghold with significant sway over state politics. 
“The Republican Party ran Vermont, and Rutland ran the Republican Party,” Vermont historian and Vermont State University Professor Paul Searls said in an interview. 
This was due to industrialist Redfield Proctor, who — along with leading the Vermont Marble Company based in Rutland County into prominence in the 1800s — notably founded what came to be known as the “Proctor Wing” of the Republican Party, Searls said. 
The Proctor family was a dominant political force in the state for nearly a century, with Republican coalitions on the east and west sides of the state taking turns choosing political leaders through the custom of “Mountain Rule,” which aimed to alternate and balance geographic representation in the state.
Mortimer Proctor, Redfield’s grandson, broke the code of Mountain Rule by seeking the lieutenant governor’s office out of turn in 1940, leading to the custom’s death. Ernest Gibson, Jr. defeated Proctor in the 1946 Republican primary, weakening the Republican establishment’s hold.
Following the disruption of the political status quo, Searls said the Republican Party fractured between the “old guard” Proctor wing and the more progressive Aiken-Gibson wing, led by George Aiken and Gibson in the mid-20th century. This set the stage for the rise of the previously marginal Democratic Party across Vermont, including in Rutland County, Searls said. 
The victory of Phillip Hoff, the first Democratic governor in over a century, in 1962 helped bolster Democratic support, particularly in Rutland City, said Cheryl Hooker, who served as a representative and senator in Rutland on and off between 1992 and 2022.
“I think that people felt that it is possible to have Democratic candidates win,” Hooker said.
The pendulum
Rutland County has been dominated by Republican support, but Hooker said that a majority of her colleagues hailing from Rutland City were Democrats during her first term in office. The pendulum swung against many Democratic politicians who supported civil unions legislation in 2000, she said. 
“Everything changed,” Hooker said. “Civil unions caused a huge bifurcation of the population.”
Hooker was one of the few survivors of the red wave during the “Take Back Vermont” movement, she said. 
Hooker won one of the Rutland County Senate seats in 2018, and there was a packed field of candidates across the political spectrum running for office during the following 2020 election cycle. 
Democrats have failed to recapture a seat representing Rutland County in the Senate since Hooker did not seek reelection in 2022.
Voters flipped six House seats to Republican “red” in Rutland County in 2024, after incumbent Democratic candidates were ousted or did not seek reelection in those districts. 
Rutland County voted for Democratic presidential candidate Kamala Harris in the 2024 election, but President Donald Trump won 13 towns and 42% of the vote in the county. 
Robin Chesnut-Tangerman, former representative of the Rutland-Bennington district who served as a Progressive and Democrat, said the Affordable Heat Act, also known as the Clean Heat Standard, was one of the biggest issues that caused political backlash against Democrats in Rutland County during his time in office from 2014 to 2020 and from 2022 to 2024.
Strategy and struggles
It was a hard sell to recruit new Democratic candidates in Rutland County this time around, Fagan said, due to the time and financial resources necessary to run and serve. 
The party focused on recruiting someone to replace the outgoing Democrat in the House, Rep. Mary Howard, given “how important that seat is to hold,” he said.
A full slate of Democratic candidates ran for the three Senate seats and lost against Collamore, Weeks and Williams in 2022 and 2024. Collamore has served as a Rutland County senator for 12 years, and Weeks and Williams have served in the role since 2022.
Voters in Vermont in general are “very hesitant to turn out incumbents,” Rich Clark, a political science professor at Vermont State University, said. 
Candidates in Rutland County have done well when they seize an open seat and rely on “retail politics,” name recognition and community involvement, Clark added.
Weeks said it was “shocking” that Democratic candidates did not run for Senate seats this election cycle. He said winning enough write-in votes to qualify for the Democratic nomination reflects that the three senators are a “good team” and serve Rutland County voters on both sides of the aisle well. The candidates needed 50 or more write-in votes to qualify in the primary, according to Bryan Mills, chief of staff to Vermont’s secretary of state.
Fagan called it “a strategic move” on the part of the Republican senators to accept both party labels in their race against an independent, but the candidates are not endorsed by the Democratic Party.
Rutland County Republican incumbent senators have sought to differentiate themselves from the national political party. Weeks defined himself as a moderate, social liberal who aims to trim and reprioritize state spending. 
“We might be Republicans, but we’re not all drinking the national Republican Kool-Aid,” Weeks said of his political identity.
Collamore said the incumbents are all “Vermont Republicans … trying to find a balance and commonsense in everything,” and mainly focused on lowering taxes for Vermonters so they “keep more of what they have.”
While he too identifies with the moderate moniker, Williams said he is further right compared to his fellow running mates. The three senators typically vote together, but Williams said they have diverged on certain issues. Williams was the sole no vote against an abortion access and protection bill, for instance. 
The Republican candidates in Rutland County campaign as a united force, and it may be to Rutland County Democrats’ detriment that their campaign messages are not in sync, Chesnut-Tangerman said. 
Fagan called Rutland County “reddish purple” politically and said that the Democratic Party in the county has moderate and left-leaning candidates that are open to dialogue, but each candidate has their own platform.
Chairs of both parties in the county said their candidates are focused on affordability and economic development for the region.
For his part, Wolk said he aims to be the first “nonpartisan independent” in the Vermont Senate and seeks to differentiate himself by funding his campaign solely with individual contributions and without political action committee or party money. If elected, Wolk said he could vote based on what he thinks constituents need rather than according to party leadership policy directions as an independent.
Wolk entered the race because he is concerned with the ”loud voices on the left and the right.” 
For her part, Hooker said she has observed that people in the region irked by political labels this election cycle. 
“I think that people also are frustrated as far as parties go,” Hooker said. “People are trying to distance themselves from an affiliation with a particular party and vote more on the values that the candidates have.”

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: District 5 Congressional candidates Molder, Hatcher clash over tariffs in forum
text:
5th Congressional District candidates, from right, Democrat Chaz Molder, Republican Charlie Hatcher, with back to camera, and independent candidate Micheal O'Leary pick questions from a bowl at a Wednesday forum in Spring Hill sponsored by a consortium of chambers of commerce. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)Candidates for Tennessee’s redrawn 5th Congressional district took the stage together Wednesday for what is likely the final time before the Nov. 3 election.
Republican Charlie Hatcher and Democrat Chaz Molder clashed on President Donald Trump’s handling of international tariffs, but agreed on the importance of constituent services and an urgent need to reduce the cost of living.
Independent candidate Micheal O’Leary — an immigrant and Irish pub owner who formerly served as a local official in California — also participated in the forum hosted by the Spring Hill, Maury County and Williamson County chambers of commerce and sponsored by lobbying firm Jigsaw. 
The Democratic and Republican parties are pushing hard to win the race to represent the 5th Congressional district, one of three newly drawn districts that split liberal-leaning Memphis and Shelby County. Tennessee’s Republican supermajority redrew the districts in May in an attempt to stack the odds in Republican candidates’ favor to win all nine of the state’s Congressional seats.
Columbia Mayor Chaz Molder, the Democratic nominee for Tennessee’s 5th Congressional District, walks into Wednesday’s forum with his wife, Elizabeth. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)
On tariffs
Molder, who has served as mayor of Columbia since 2018, said getting rid of tariffs is one of his top priorities to reduce the cost of living.
“They are wrong, and they are at the wrong time,” he said. “It’s causing the cost to go up at a time when people are hurting. We’re using them the wrong way. We’re putting tariffs on our longtime trading allies that are hurting us here at home, and then we’re waiving tariffs on foreign farmers, but are hurting our farmers here in the United States.”
Molder also said that Congress is not heeding its constitutional duty to authorize tariffs, allowing Trump to control tariff decisions.
“I will be a check and balance on tariffs,” Molder said.
Hatcher, a dairy farmer and former Tennessee Agriculture Commissioner, described tariffs as a tool that “can be used effectively, sometimes badly, and the first ones that take the brunt of it are farmers.”



Quotation







We need to support American industries, and we need to support American agriculture so that we can … not have other countries hold us hostage.


– Charlie Hatcher


But Hatcher said that Trump has used tariffs to strike deals with countries that were “taking advantage of us” under former President Joe Biden’s administration. He said effective use of tariffs include putting a tariff on Canadian dairy products coming into the United States and on imported Chinese steel to encourage production within the U.S.
“We need to support American industries, and we need to support American agriculture so that we can … not have other countries hold us hostage,” Hatcher said.
Hatcher said Molder’s statement that Congress is shirking its duty to approve or disapprove tariffs is “talking points.”
When asked if he had a problem with the president announcing tariffs without Congressional approval, Hatcher again said tariffs are a “tool in the toolbox.”
“The international (agriculture) trade is better than it was during the Biden administration by a long shot … tariffs can be very effective,” he said. “I’m not saying they were used effectively every single time, but they’ve been used very effectively in many cases.”





 

Columbia Mayor Chaz Molder, Democratic nominee for the 5th Congressional District, gives the crowd a thumbs up during Wednesday's forum. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)







 

Charlie Hatcher, Republican nominee for Tennessee's 5th Congressional District, with his granddaughter. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)






On the war in Iran
Hatcher and Molder agreed that ending the war in Iran is necessary to reduce the growing cost of everyday goods.
“The war in Iran is causing our diesel and gas prices to rise,” Molder said. “It’s hurting our farmers and it’s hurting our small business owners.”
Hatcher said the quickest fix for rising costs is ending the war, with a caveat.
“That needs to be done as soon as two conditions are met: no nuclear weapons, and they can’t have a stranglehold on the global oil market,” he said.
The long-term fix is to “unleash American energy,” Hatcher continued, borrowing a Trump administration phrase. He said America’s lack of oil refineries is “the biggest reason we don’t have enough diesel right now,” and the country should increase refineries and lean into nuclear energy.
Economists have cited a global lack of refineries as a contributing factor to high fuel prices, but have largely pointed to the war in Iran as the most significant upward pressure on fuel prices.



Quotation







The war in Iran is causing our diesel and gas prices to rise. It’s hurting our farmers and it’s hurting our small business owners.


– Mayor Chaz Molder


On border security and ICE
“When the president’s doing something right, I’ll be the first to say it, but I’ll also have the courage to say when he’s doing something wrong,” Molder said.
One of Trump’s initiatives that he agrees with? Border security.
“I think it’s important that we have secure borders … and I think the border is more secure today than it was before (Trump) got in,” he said.
But Molder also said Immigration and Customs Enforcement, ICE, “is not designed to be law enforcement agents, and that’s not what they should be doing.” He would support a congressional investigation into ICE’s practices, he said.
“They should not be tearing families apart in the darkness of night,” he said. “If you’re here illegally, then there’s no place for you here if you’re committing a dangerous crime, but if you’re here and you’re working and you’re contributing to society, then you shouldn’t be stripped away from your families from a non-trained law enforcement agency.”
Republican nominee Charlie Hatcher: ICE has gone too far in the past but is in a good spot now. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)
When asked if ICE has gone too far under Trump’s second administration, Hatcher said he could see “instances where it did,” naming Minnesota as an example.
“They’ve backed off since,” Hatcher said. “I think we’re in a good spot now.”
Hatcher said he would not support a congressional investigation into ICE.
On the Memphis Safe Task Force
Republicans have repeatedly lauded the dispatch of the multi-agency Memphis Safe Task Force ordered by Trump last September, crediting it with driving down crime statistics. But community members against the task force’s presence point to falling crime numbers that predate the task force, and highlight concerns over due process and ICE agents arresting individuals with no criminal history, separating families in Memphis’ immigrant communities. Members of the task force also fatally shot four Black men earlier this year.
Molder said his first action in office will be contacting the Department of Justice and the Attorney General “to figure out what is going on with the task force in Memphis.”
“We’re seeing violation of constitutional rights, due process rights,” he said. “This is wrong … so that’s going to be the first thing on my agenda when I get to Congress, because the people of Memphis deserve that.”
Hatcher says he’s amenable to Molder’s challenge to debate before 5th District election

When asked when the task force’s work will be considered complete, Hatcher said he would have to review the statistics. 
“I think the local government and the mayor wants that to stay in place for now, doesn’t he? So they can work that out between the local and state and federal officials,” Hatcher said.
On Tuesday night, the Memphis City Council passed a nonbinding resolution calling for the removal of ICE and the Tennessee National Guard from the city.
On debates
While Molder said he still wants to debate Hatcher, who previously said he would be amenable to a District 5 debate, Hatcher said he was satisfied with Wednesday’s forum.
“We’ve got 13 days left, and every minute’s accounted for,” Hatcher said. “We had these three chambers come together, and they … had a really good list of questions. It was a fair environment.”
Molder said he’s hoping Hatcher will “come around” on scheduling a debate.
“At this point, there’s not one on the calendar, and I think that would be a huge disappointment for the people of our district,” Molder said.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Alabama’s SNAP error rate on downward trend, preliminary data shows
text:
A sign advertises that SNAP benefits are accepted at a grocery store in Fargo, North Dakota, on July 7, 2026. Alabama's SNAP error rate is on a downward trend, according to preliminary state data, which could prevent the state from paying a larger penalty in 2027. (Photo by Ceilidh Kern for the North Dakota Monitor)Alabama appears to have reduced the error rate for the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP), officials said Thursday morning, which could reduce a penalty facing the state in 2027.
The One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA), passed last year, introduced a penalty for states with a high error rate in the program. Alabama’s error rate for fiscal year 2025 was 9.52%, which could have cost the state up to $174.3 million, about 10% of the state’s SNAP benefits. 
SNAP Director Brandon Hardin said at a quarterly meeting of the Alabama Department of Human Resources (DHR), which administers the program in the state, that the rate for FY26 is starting to trend down after a bad start due to the 2025 government shutdown.
“It’s a vital program for the nutritional needs of Alabamians. I’ve heard from multiple advocates and grocery store people, this is an economic issue also when you’re talking about what it affects in those areas too,” Hardin said after the meeting. “Ultimately our clients need this thing. It’s up to us at DHR to try to correct those error rates, and the best we can do is to try to move those down where we can have less liability.”
Errors are not a measure of fraud. They can be on the client, the agency, or can be under-issuances or overpayments of benefits. Penalties are tiered based on the error rate.
The unofficial error rate through June is down to 7.89%, according to state data released Thursday morning. The Food and Nutrition Service (FNS), an agency within the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA), will finalize the year’s numbers by next summer, Hardin said. Should the rate stay under 8%, the penalty will be reduced to $87.1 million, about 5% of SNAP benefits.
“I continue to say that it’s unofficial, but this is a significant improvement. This is practically a $90 million savings if we can keep it underneath 8% going forward,” Hardin said. 
Before the passage of the OBBBA, SNAP was fully funded by the federal government.
The changes to the program have pushed over 90,000 Alabamians off SNAP. Hardin said that some of those people could re-enroll in the program if their circumstances change. Most of the disenrollments are attributable to new work requirements enacted by the OBBBA.
As of September, more than 638,000 Alabamians were enrolled in the $1.7 billion program, Hardin said. 
“What passed with the Big Beautiful Bill, with the increase in the able-bodied adult dependents age range and all the exemptions that went away, and the policies that we had to put in place for the payment error rate have contributed to a significant decrease in participation,” Hardin said. 
In an attempt to reduce the error rate penalty, DHR has sought waivers from the federal government. One would have exempted the first three months of FY26 from the error rate penalty, which Hardin said hurts the year’s average.
“We were in a significant hole there because of the government shutdown. We had two months there that were not that great. We’re continuing to work through that piece of it, and I think it looks great,” Hardin said after the meeting. 
A shutdown of the federal government in November left SNAP-recipients without benefits. The average error rate from October to November was 10.95%. The average error rate from January to June was 6.48%.
That waiver was denied, Hardin said.
In 2028, the state’s penalty is based solely on the FY26 error rate, while 2027’s penalty will be the lowest rate between FY25 and FY26. States with error rates below 6% or above 20% will not have to pay penalties. Penalties for states on the high end will have a two-year delayed implementation.
A two-year delayed implementation, regardless of error rate, was a potential solution through the Farm Bill. It has passed the House, but did not receive a vote in the Senate. 
“That’s really the best plan for either this is to get a one or two-year extension,” Hardin said. “Hopefully we have some time in December at the Fed level to address this, but we still don’t have any movement on that, kicking the can down the road kind of thing.”
Commissioner Nancy Buckner said the department would request enough money from the Legislature in the spring to cover the larger penalty because the final error rate will not be determined until after lawmakers adjourn.
“Even though we know what the unofficial rate is, we’re hoping it will hold, but we don’t know for sure that it will hold until the feds give it its stamp of approval, and they’re behind,” Buckner said. 
Budgeting for FY28 will be challenging. Former Finance Director Bill Poole and Legislative Fiscal Officer Kirk Fulford have repeatedly warned state agencies that budgets will need to be conservative.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Stockard on the Stump: Republican lawmaker’s apology on “hanging” seems hollow
text:
Sparta Republican Rep. Paul Sherrell, photographed at the June unveiling of the "Monument to the Unborn" outside the Capitol, recently said in a public forum he would like public hangings to be used in death penalty cases. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)A Tennessee Republican lawmaker is reiterating support for public hangings three years after giving a half-baked apology for calling for a return to “hanging from a tree” as a form of capital punishment.
State Rep. Paul Sherrell of Sparta said in a recent political forum in McMinnville that a “good hanging right here on the public square by the courthouse” could deter crime, the Main Street Journal reported.
Sherrell made the comment during a forum with Democratic challenger Samantha Petit in the Tennessee House District 43 race when she questioned him about his 2023 comments supporting “hanging from a tree” to execute people on death row, according to the report.
Black Caucus wants more than Sherrell pulling street name bill

He backed up the statement by saying Tennessee already can use the electric chair, if necessary, and in the wake of a second botched execution this year, he added that he favors using a firing squad if necessary or bringing back public hangings, the report says.
Asked this week how he squares the apology with his recent call to hang people on the public square, Sherrell deflected the blame to Democrats he claims accused him of using the word “lynching.” He did acknowledge he supports hangings, firing squads and electrocution to put people to death. 
Democratic state Rep. Sam McKenzie, former chairman of the Black Caucus, recalled the incident clearly and said Sherrell’s words brought up images of lynchings of Black men, but he noted no one accused Sherrell of using the word.
The failed execution Sept. 30 of death row inmate Christa Pike is reviving talk about adopting alternative methods for capital punishment. Immediately after the botched execution, Gov. Bill Lee called for an outside investigation and put a hold on executions for the rest of 2026, as he prepares to leave office after two terms in mid-January 2027.



Quotation







It verifies the fact that he was told to (read) that and his heart wasn’t in it, that his heart is still hard as it relates to what hanging from a tree means to a lot of people.


– Rep. Sam McKenzie, former chair, Tennessee Black Caucus of State Legislators


Sherrell was forced to read an apology on the House floor in March 2023 after saying during a Criminal Justice Committee meeting the state should return to “hanging from a tree” to execute death row inmates. He made the comment in support of legislation allowing death row inmates to request electrocution when problems arise with the state’s lethal injection protocol. At the time, the measure was amended to add death by firing squads, but that didn’t come to pass.
The Tennessee Black Caucus of State Legislators wanted Sherrell to be punished, saying his flippant comment revived images of Black Americans being lynched. House Speaker Cameron Sexton declined to remove him from committees, yet the Republican caucus slapped an apology in front of him and told him to read it.
McKenzie called Sherrell’s apology “half-hearted” and said House Republican leaders sat on it for weeks amid the “Tennessee Three” hearing when the House expelled two Black lawmakers but kept one white female lawmaker for their involvement in a floor rally for new gun laws following the Covenant School shooting. 
“It verifies the fact that he was told to (read) that and his heart wasn’t in it, that his heart is still hard as it relates to what hanging from a tree means to a lot of people,” McKenzie said. “It speaks to his insensitivity and the fact that he didn’t mean it. He just flat out didn’t mean it.”
Readers might recall that Sherrell had to go before the Registry of Election Finance four years ago in what is now being called the Great Biscuitgate.
A complaint about Rep. Paul Sherrell was sent to the Tennessee Registry of Election Finance in 2022 over allegations he wrote checks payable to a volunteer fire department to cover ham breakfasts, then asked for most of the money back. The registry declined to take action. (Editorial cartoon: John Cole)
Sherrell, who serves as House Republican floor leader, sounded as if he was crying during a phone interview with the Registry in May 2022, saying “Thank you and praise the Lord” when the Registry board dismissed a complaint against him for allegedly cashing checks to buy country ham biscuits for firefighters at White County volunteer fire halls. According to the sworn complaint, Sherrell would write a check for about $100, buy a biscuit for himself and promise to buy volunteer firefighters biscuits to recognize their service. The problem was that none of the volunteer firefighters ever got one measly biscuit as Sherrell pocketed the money from his campaign account, according to the complaint. 
None of the evidence he presented during the Registry hearing showed how he spent the cash. The board decided against investigating the matter, claiming it was being “weaponized.”
Sherrell did admit he wasn’t perfect and said if he made a mistake he was sorry. When you’re dealing with country ham biscuits, it’s no big deal. But with executions, it’s too late to say you’re sorry if you put the wrong person to death, regardless of the method.
Whaddaya mean, they gave ya da slip?
About 25 years ago, we were sitting in a Miami Beach deli after the family and I spent a day in the sand and surf. We were starving, so I ponied up enough for the cheapest thing on the menu, a $12 hamburger (five total because a nephew was with us), which was a little steep back then. 
Next thing we knew, the deli owner was giving the waiter an earful after a couple sitting near the door ran out on their tab.

SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 
“What happened!?” she screamed. “I don’t know. They gave me da slip,” he answered. “Whaddaya mean they gave ya da slip?” she said. “I don’t know. They gave me da slip,” he said. “How did they give ya da slip?” “I don’t know. They gave me da slip.”
The whole time I was wondering if we’d been warped into a “Seinfeld” episode but also thinking, “I’d like to give ’em da slip.”
Da real slip
Fast-forward a quarter-century and U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn, of all people, tried to give President Donald Trump da slip before reversing course.
Technically, she declined at first to return a “blue slip,” the practice for home-state senators, signaling support for a Trump nominee to a federal judgeship in East Tennessee. The Tennessee Journal reported that Blackburn, who serves on the Senate Judiciary Committee, blocked Trump’s nomination of Signal Mountain attorney Samuel Adkisson, a White House legal advisor, to a U.S. District Court judgeship based in Knoxville.
The Blackburn campaign didn’t respond to questions from the Tennessee Journal, which also reported that Sen. Bill Hagerty backed the nomination. The Blackburn campaign referred questions to her congressional office, which did not respond to the Lookout Thursday.
The Tennessee Bar Association reported Thursday that Blackburn returned the slip, signaling approval.
Adkisson, who holds degrees from Vanderbilt and Yale Law School, is a special assistant to Trump and White House associate counsel. He’s only 33 years old, though, which seems mighty young to be appointed to the bench for life.
And we thought Blackburn agreed with everything Trump did. Wrong. She and Hagerty both voted to certify the Biden election, even though Trump continues to claim it was stolen.
You just never know when …
Former state Rep. Jeremy Durham is resurfacing as a contributing sports editor for the Tristar Daily, a news site published by political activist Steve Gill.
Durham writes about Tennessee Vols football and Major League Baseball, according to the bio at the bottom of his columns, which says he covered sports and worked as a government editor for The Daily Beacon, a student newspaper, while attending the University of Tennessee.
Former state Rep. Jeremy Durham, pictured after his 2022 arrest for or DUI and possession, has a new gig writing about sports for a conservative digital media outlet. (Photo: Metro Nashville Police Department)
It fails to mention that he was expelled from the Tennessee General Assembly in 2016 after an attorney general’s report accused him of sexually harassing 22 women at the legislature, including an intern.
The former state rep from Williamson County also had run-ins with the police in Metro Nashville where he was convicted of DUI and an assortment of charges after a wreck near Lower Broadway. He was arrested again in Florida in January 2024 on DUI charges.
It’s not clear whether he was required to write for Gill as part of any sentence. But the columns, which focus on betting lines on Vols games, aren’t too bad, though we wonder why anyone would put enough stock in Durham’s musings to bet on them.
Maybe, at last, he has found his niche.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Proposed legislation would close ‘voluntary intoxication’ loophole in WV sexual assault law
text:
Del. Kayla Young, D-Kanawha, plans to introduce legislation that would amend state law concerning sexual offenses. (Photo by Perry Bennett/West Virginia Legislative Photography)After a high-profile rape case at Cornell University highlighted what she considers a loophole that fails victims, a West Virginia legislator is joining lawmakers in 15 other states to change laws regarding sexual violence. 
Del. Kayla Young, D-Kanawha, says she’ll introduce a bill during the 2027 legislative session that would amend the definition of “mentally incapacitated,” which is one element of a lack of consent in state code concerning sexual offenses. The new definition would include being incapable of consenting because of voluntarily being under the influence.
Currently, the definition requires that the person is incapacitated because a substance was given or administered to them without their consent. 
Young is one of 21 women lawmakers across the country who are pushing to amend sexual consent laws after a woman at Cornell University alleged in a lawsuit she had been gang raped by seven men after being pressured into snorting ketamine, smoking marijuana and drinking alcohol at a fraternity house in 2024. 
At the time, a local prosecutor declined to bring criminal charges against the men. New York is one of 19 states with rape laws that have “loopholes” for voluntary intoxication. New York governor Kathy Hochul appointed state attorney general Letitia James as a special prosecutor in the case earlier this month. 
The lawmakers are associated with Vote Run Lead, an organization that trains women to run for office.
Young said when the Cornell sexual assault happened, it was apparent through the case’s prosecutor that there’s a legal loophole for people who are sexually assaulted if they’re consuming alcohol or another substance voluntarily. 
“When the Cornell sexual assault occurred, it became very clear through the prosecutor that was originally on that case, that there is a legal loophole for people who are sexually assaulted, that if they were consuming alcohol or any sort of substance voluntarily, like at a party having a drink or something, consent laws don’t really capture that,” Young said. “They only capture involuntary consent.”
 “It’s good that they have involuntary consent,” she said. “But adults sometimes have a drink or something, and that doesn’t mean that that they should not be taken care of when they’re victims of sexual assault.”
In 2024, state lawmakers passed a bill that removed a marital exception from the state’s sexual assault law. Former Gov. Jim Justice signed the bill into law. 
Young said it’s incredibly important that lawmakers address the voluntary intoxication loophole.
“We want to make sure that victims are as protected as possible,” Young said. “And I think that this is an accidental loophole, but it’s something that we can fix. And states have been trying to fix it around the country, and so we just need to get in line with the rest of the states to make sure that intoxicated people are still protected, because it shouldn’t be more difficult for them to pursue criminal charges.”
Young said she does not have any co-sponsors for the proposed bill as of yet, but she’s hoping to work with Republicans.
“I’m hoping it will be bipartisan because it seems like common sense to me,” she said. “And in the past, when I’ve tried to close criminal loopholes, I’ve had bipartisan support. So I’m hopeful I’ll have that again.”
West Virginia’s 2027 legislative session is set to begin Wednesday, Jan. 13, 2027.

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Dispute over Colorado’s congressional seat arose in wake of 1876 election
text:
Guard's Hall at 15th and Curtis streets, one of Denver's top entertainment venues in 1876, is pictured in this photo from the 1870s. (Courtesy of Denver Public Library Special Collections, X-18553)As the weather continued cooling off in October 1876, Denver’s Rocky Mountain News looked ahead to what a headline called “our winter campaign.”



← Oct. 8–14
Oct. 15–28 

This story is part of Colorado at 150.

“Denver promises to be unusually cosmopolitan and lively during the coming winter,” the paper predicted. “Already the town is filling up with strangers, many of them remarkably fine-looking.”
The inaugural state Legislature was set to convene in early November — “many of the more staid and sensible married members are bringing their wives and families with them,” reported the News — while many others who’d been employed in Colorado’s frontier mining camps during the summer months were now returning to the relative comfort of the capital city.
A busy social calendar of “hops,” concerts and other nightly entertainments resumed, many of them hosted by Denver’s vast array of fraternal organizations and secret societies. Surveying the changes in dance fashions, the News observed that “the polka is in high favor again, and the minuet is to be danced at some of the balls and parties this winter.”
“Let our people be hospitable, our business men liberal, and our landlords reasonable — in other words, let our money-getters not kill the goose that lays the golden eggs,” the paper cautioned. “We must make Denver pleasant and attractive if we would derive the utmost benefit from our temporary advantage in these particulars.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The late excitement over the first state elections had now passed, with Denver’s Republican establishment having done enough to avoid disaster against a Democratic Party that made a strong showing in southern Colorado and the mountain mining camps.
Ex-territorial Gov. John Routt had been elected the Centennial State’s first chief executive, and the GOP-controlled Legislature would soon elect its first two U.S. senators, and award its three electoral votes in the 1876 presidential election — a one-time provision in the state constitution that underlined Republicans’ partisan motive for admitting Colorado to the union in the centennial year.
Corruption scandals, silver coins and grasshoppers were the hot topics in Colorado’s 1876 election

But the Oct. 3 election had also set the stage for a controversy that would engulf state politics for the foreseeable future.
Republican James Belford was confirmed as the winner of the race for Colorado’s at-large congressional seat for the remainder of the 44th Congress, but Democrats hoped to get revenge in a second election, scheduled for Nov. 7, for a full term in the 45th Congress, which was set to convene in March 1877.
But now Republicans, flush with victory, said no such election could legally take place. Though the Nov. 7 election had been called by the former Colorado Territory’s Republican-appointed secretary of state, and duly noticed by county officials, the state GOP argued that the authority to hold the election was vested in a state Legislature that hadn’t existed yet. Republicans announced Belford’s withdrawal from the contest and urged the party faithful to “take no part therein whatever.”
“(Democratic candidate Thomas) Patterson and Judge Belford were supported for both the 44th and 45th congresses. … The people elected the one and defeated the other,” state GOP chair J.C. Wilson maintained in the Rocky Mountain News on Oct. 15. “To proceed, then, with an election which has no foundation in law, is not only to impose an unnecessary and heavy burden upon the people, but would also bring the character of our elections into contempt.”
The News, ever the loyal Republican organ, quickly got to work spreading the party line that any result in the Democrats’ favor on Nov. 7 would be a sham.
“As there is no Republican candidate in the field,” the paper wrote on Oct. 22. “Mr. Patterson stands a good chance of being ‘elected.’”



Selected sources

The Rocky Mountain News, Oct. 15 & 22, 1876

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Arkansas amendment would allow local economic development districts
text:
Voters mark their primary election ballots at Second Presbyterian Church in Little Rock, Arkansas, on March 3, 2026. (Photo by John Sykes/Arkansas Advocate)Arkansas voters in November will consider a proposed constitutional amendment that would allow the creation of local economic development districts, a move supporters say will make the state competitive but opponents have derided as unnecessarily growing government.
Issue 3 would permit lawmakers to create programs, loans and grants using public money for the purpose of economic development. 
The Legislature would have the authority to pass laws allowing local governments to create economic development districts where incentives like tax rebates could be negotiated to attract new business to a designated area. 
Supporters of the proposal say it’s needed to make Arkansas more competitive with other states that offer these incentives and spark economic growth in smaller communities. Opponents argue it will grow government and could harm Arkansans who are being asked to approve a program whose rules have yet to be outlined.
Arkansas lawmakers refer three proposed constitutional amendments to 2026 ballot

The proposed constitutional amendment, one of four measures on the Nov. 3 ballot, was referred to voters by the Legislature through a resolution sponsored by Republicans Sen. Jonathan Dismang and Rep. Howard Beaty. Dismang resigned in September to take a job at Arkansas Electric Cooperatives. 
Issue 3 is backed by Arkansans For Strong Communities, a ballot question committee chaired by Randy Zook, president and CEO of the Arkansas State Chamber of Commerce and the Associated Industries of Arkansas. 
The group has raised more than $2.2 million, that majority of which has been spent on advertising, according to an October finance report. The largest donors have been Walmart heirs Jim Walton and his sons, Tom and Stueart, who’ve each donated $125,000.
While there are economic incentives at the state level that have been successful at attracting industrial projects, Issue 3 would give that tool to cities, counties and regions to attract retail developments like shopping centers and grocery stores, Zook said. 
“We have a lot of communities that really, really need that kind of tool, especially in the eastern third of the state where we’ve been losing population and losing retail providers,” he said. 
The proposal faces resistance from some on the right, including Brenda Vassaur Taylor, cofounder of the Conduit for Action and Conduit for Commerce conservative advocacy groups. Vassaur Taylor is also president of Conduit News and treasurer for Truth in Politics Against Issue 3, a ballot question committee that formed last week in opposition to the measure.
Vassaur Taylor said she lived in the Arkansas Delta for 44 years and was repeatedly shown how “government is never the solution.” 
“Government needs to get out of the business of ‘economic development’ and leave that to those who know how to do business in Arkansas,” Taylor said in an email. “Economic development should be encouraged by supporting the businesses already in our state, not by taking their tax dollars to subsidize their competition.”


Let us know what you think...


 

Zook said the amendment would allow a district to use economic incentives, which often look like rebates where a certain percentage of taxes are returned to developers over a specified period of time in exchange for them investing in the area.
The tax status of current businesses located within the economic development district would not change, and incentives would only apply to newly generated taxes resulting from the new business, he said. 
Issue 3 would allow the issuance of bonds to help fund projects, and developers — not cities or counties — would be on the hook for the debt, Zook said.  
The amendment, which would be effective Jan. 1, 2027, allows provisions in the Arkansas constitution that conflict with it to be repealed. The proposed amendment also “supersedes all previous constitutional provisions, amendments, laws or judicial interpretations” that conflict with it.
Vassaur Taylor said her group opposes Issue 3 because it grows government, reduces individual freedoms, benefits a select few with taxpayer dollars, and includes “vague language that will give power over the above-mentioned problems to people yet to be decided.”
“The fact that this vast and vague power grab by a few is asked to be placed in our state constitution is alarming and proves the need for its defeat,” she said. 
Zook said the Arkansas constitution does not currently allow for the creation of economic development districts, so it must be amended to allow the enabling legislation to put specific guidelines in place.
“You have to trust the process,” he said.
The measure is going before voters months after the Legislature set aside up to $300 million from the state’s surplus for incentives aimed at attracting a new manufacturing facility to West Memphis. It also comes as several communities have clashed with local economic development officials over the rapid growth of data centers.
Arkansas Explained: What are the incentives for West Memphis’ possible superproject?

Arkansans have not voted on the creation of economic development districts previously, but they have considered proposed amendments to create other tools intended to attract businesses, according to the Public Policy Center at the University of Arkansas Division of Agriculture. 
In 2000, voters approved Amendment 78, which allowed the creation of Tax Increment Financing — also known as TIF — districts in which the growth of tax revenue from a project could be used to pay off the bond that financed it. 
In 2007, a state Supreme Court ruling prevented TIF districts from using personal and real property tax revenue generated by the minimum 25-mill tax collected for maintaining and operating public schools. A mill is equal to $1 of property tax for each $1,000 of assessed value. 
The court ruled voters were unaware that Amendment 78 would repeal a constitutional amendment approved in 1996 requiring the 25-mill tax to ensure public schools were adequately funded. 
TIF districts still exist, but their popularity declined after the court’s decision reduced the amount of tax revenue that could be used to support them, according to the Public Policy Center. 
Republican Senate President Bart Hester and Democratic state Sen. Clarke Tucker shared their bipartisan support for Issue 3 in a video this week.
Meanwhile, the League of Women of Arkansas, a nonpartisan organization focused on protecting and expanding voting rights, opposes the proposal. 
Executive Director Kristin Foster said the league supports economic development, but has concerns about the amendment’s “broad new taxing and bonding authority” that would be created and decided by the Legislature. 
“Our opposition really is not about the economic development itself, but about granting this breadth of constitutional authority without some clear safeguards and protections for public revenue,” Foster said.  
Dismang filed a bill late in the 2025 legislation session outlining what the economic development district program would look like, but it was never voted on. 
Additional concerns from Issue 3 opponents include giving the government the power to pick which businesses receive advantages, and that finance plans of bonds and ad valorem taxes will lead to the transfer of public funding to private businesses, according to the Public Policy Center.
Using public funds to fund private business through bonds already happens with the state’s economic incentives for industrial developments, Zook said. 
He said Arkansas will continue to be uncompetitive if the measure fails, and he urged voters to approve Issue 3.
“In our view, it’s local choice, local control and no new taxes,” Zook said. 
You can read the proposed constitutional amendment in its entirety here.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Figures, Sewell, Booker rally in Montgomery for 2nd Congressional District race
text:
U.S. Rep. Shomari Figures, D-Mobile, (center) and U.S. Sen. Cory Booker, D-N.J,(right) smile as U.S. Rep Terri Sewell, D-Birmingham (left) addresses the crowd during a rally in Montgomery on October 22, 2026. (Andrea Tinker/Alabama Reflector)U.S. Rep. Shomari Figures, D-Mobile, was joined by U.S. Rep Terri Sewell, D-Birmingham and U.S. Sen. Cory Booker, D-N.J., to rally supporters in Montgomery Thursday in what could be Alabama’s most competitive congressional race next month. 
Speaking to a crowd of at least 250 people, Figures addressed redistricting efforts earlier this year that redrew the boundaries of the 2nd Congressional District, reducing its Black population and making it a more Republican-leaning seat.
“We know what they have done to our district. We know what they have tried to do to our district,” he said. “They have tried to make this district one that we cannot win, where they can predetermine the outcome, where this can be a fixed result that we walk into on Nov. 3.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The move came after the U.S. Supreme Court’s ruling in Louisiana v. Callais, which severely weakened Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, which bans racial discrimination in voting laws.
Figures was elected to Congress in 2024 under boundaries approved by a federal court. His election and Sewell’s re-election that year marked the first time two Black Alabamians served in the U.S. House of Representatives at the same time, in a state that is about 27% Black. 
Figures faces Rep. Rhett Marques, R-Enterprise, in the general election. The Cook Political Report rates Alabama’s 2nd Congressional District as likely Republican, but Figures has managed to outraise Marques, and the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee has bought ads in the race. 
Before Figures walked out, Sewell opened the rally by urging people to vote to combat the actions taken by the Trump administration, such as cuts to healthcare programs, and blamed the president for affordability issues.
“We have an administration that is hellbent on taking us back. We have an administration that made all kinds of promises. Trump promised to lower costs on day one. Are you feeling that?” Sewell asked. “There’s only one person in this race for Congressional District 2 that actually will go in there and fight for you every day, and his name is Shomari.”
Booker, who spoke after Sewell, told the crowd that “a lot of things are beginning to echo with our history back in the 1960s.”
“We are in another moral moment in our country,” he said. “When we have a nation that says all that fight for voting rights, all that fight for fair representation, we’re going to change the rules of the Supreme Court and throw us all the way back to that post-Reconstruction period and try to disenfranchise folks. Well, I’m telling you right now, the people of Alabama have a chance again to say, this is a moral moment, not on my watch.”
Sewell said after the rally, “Montgomery is ground zero in the Civil Rights Movement.”
“If ever there’s a community that understands the importance of fighting back, and the fact of the matter is that they think that we’re going to just not vote, and they’re absolutely wrong,” Sewell said. “And when we vote in the numbers, I know we can, especially if we overperform right here in Montgomery, we will definitely bring back Shomari Figures to Congress.”
Figures also encouraged the audience to vote for Sewell if they live in her district. 
“My race is getting a lot of attention,” he said. “But when my district was redrawn, well, when my district was drawn the first time, that little girl from Selma (Sewell) had to give up part of her district down in (Congressional) District 7, and so when they redrew these districts, her district became a little more competitive too. So let us not forget those of you in District Seven that Congresswoman Terry Sewell still needs you to show up and show out for her, too.”
Sewell will face Republican nominee Ammie Akin next month for Alabama’s 7th Congressional District. According to the Cook Political Report, Sewell’s district is solidly Democratic.
Prior to the rally in Montgomery, Figures spoke at a rally in Dothan with Booker, Democratic gubernatorial nominee Doug Jones and former U.S. Sen. John Tester. Figures also had a campaign event in Enterprise Thursday night.
“We are seeing an excitement around this state that we have not seen in many, many years,” Figures said. “We are seeing an excitement in Montgomery. We are seeing it in Dothan. We are seeing it in Enterprise. We are seeing it in Tuskegee. We are seeing it in Union Springs. We are seeing it in Luverne. We are seeing it everywhere.”
The Alabama Democratic Party is running its largest slate of candidates since 2018, and Democratic-leaning counties saw an increase in voter turnout in the May Primary Election.
The election is Nov. 3.

title: Alabama commission warns 4 law enforcement agencies about crime stats reporting
text:
A close-up of police lights. The Alabama Justice Information Commission Thursday threatened to revoke access to criminal justice database to four local law enforcement agencies for not reporting their crime data. (Getty)The Alabama Justice Information Commission Thursday voted to impose sanctions on four law enforcement agencies who did not appear at a meeting to explain the reasons for not reporting their crime numbers to the AJIC.
The Napier Field and York police departments and the Perry County and Sumter County sheriffs’ offices will have 15 days to report their statistics or risk losing access to state criminal justice databases.
“Agencies have to submit their crime reports to the state,” said Maury Mitchell, the state crime information director for the Alabama Law Enforcement Agency, during the meeting. “In between the last commission meeting and today, there were 74 agencies that were still not compliant with submitting what they should have.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Mitchell told members that warning letters were sent to the 74 agencies after the last regular meeting in July and that 42 had come into compliance. Another 15 agencies were not technically compliant. Of those, 7 received orders to appear before the Commission because they had already not complied for three months.
Four were eventually threatened with sanctions while one continued to have its access revoked.
Napier Field Police Department Chief Charles Duncan said Thursday that he has reported his crime statistics to the commission.
“I talked with him last week, and apparently it is some sort of a computer issue because I have been reporting,” Duncan said of a conversation he had with Mitchell. “I have got a call in to him today to try and figure out what is going on.”
Messages seeking comment were sent to the three other law enforcement agencies on Thursday.
The state could lose out on federal grant money if local agencies do not report their crime numbers.
Law enforcement agencies that are out of compliance could lose access to the National Crime Information Center, a centralized database managed by the FBI. Local law enforcement need commission approval to access the database, which provides data on fugitives, protective orders and gang members, among other subjects. The agencies could also lose access to the Law Enforcement Tactical System, which provides vehicle and driver data and criminal violation information to law enforcement officers when they pull cars over.
During the July meeting, the commission threatened to revoke access to five agencies who had not provided crime data. Since then, the Lowndes County Sheriff’s Office and the Cuba and Fort Deposit police departments have become compliant with the crime reporting requirements, according to the commission.
The Alabama Historic Ironworks Commission has not reported its numbers and continues to be restricted from the databases.
“I felt it was important to get everybody here,” Mitchell said. “As soon as we let one slide, it is just going to seem insignificant what the Commission does.”
The chiefs of the Uniontown and Newville police departments appeared before the commission Thursday to explain the situation.
“I looked back on my forms, and I have January, but I put February,” said Newville Police Department Chief Henry Dazney during Thursday’s meeting. “I have January saved, but I put the wrong date on there, and I put February.”
Uniontown Police Chief Michael Kiser said the work “just didn’t get done.”
“It was a little bit overwhelming, there was a lot of stuff,” he told the Commission. “Being a new chief, I was just a little bit overwhelmed. I am probably going to need a little bit of help to get back into compliance.”
Members allowed both additional time before they would revoke their access.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Commentary: How unfirm a foundation, O counties of West Virginia
text:
The Lincoln Walks at Midnight Statue sits in front of the West Virginia state Capitol building in Charleston, West Virginia. (West Virginia Legislative Photography)West Virginia’s founding math is slowly strangling the most vulnerable parts of the state to death. 
Right after the preamble affirms to “seek diligently to promote, preserve and perpetuate good government in the State of West Virginia for the common welfare, freedom and security of ourselves and our posterity” the Constitution of West Virginia quickly moves from flowery words to hard numbers and legal necessities. Forty-four counties came out of the rebellious Commonwealth of Virginia, six more upon ratification of the constitution in the counties of Berkeley, Hampshire, Hardy, Jefferson, Morgan and Pendleton, plus Mineral and Grant (1866), Lincoln (1867) and Summers (1871) added by acts of Legislature. Once Mingo County was carved out of Logan by the Legislature in 1895, the 55 counties every West Virginia eighth grader gets quizzed on were set. 
The West Virginia Constitution also dictates how each of those counties must be set up. Three-member county commissions, plus prosecuting attorney, sheriff, county clerk, assessor and surveyor. Mandatory offices in all 55 counties. Whether governing the over 80,000 West Virginians in Wood county or the 8,000 in Webster, the foundational government structure is mandated the same. Six offices minimum, times 55 counties, equals West Virginia local government. There have been tweaks, efforts to streamline, while counties have options to change some of the particulars. But the majority of counties still function under the mandate. A mandate based on a 19th century idea of what a county should be, untethered from the reality of minimum viable government based on the reality of population. 
The very words meant to free West Virginia from oppressive rebellion and make it a state are now the pressure points cutting off the future for most mountaineers striving to be free.
Arbitrary structures for declining areas cease to be skeletons to hold up local governance and become cages of fiscal doom when the demographic floor drops out. Without a tax base to support it, local governments cannot function unless heavily subsidized by a state that doesn’t have enough money itself unless heavily subsidized by the federal government. The State of West Virginia’s own conclusion over 20 years ago was blunt: while legally it would have to be voluntary, some consolidation of municipal and county-level government functions — if not the municipal and county governments themselves — was necessary. While an imperfect law with real legal questions, such as  how the state would readjust to a consolidated entity compared to existing, the now codified and legally available Consolidated Local Government Act was on the books. The Act uses legal phrasing like “Certain local governments are at their taxable limits and yet are facing fee increases to remain financially viable” and “The Legislature finds that consolidation of local governments is in the public interest.” 
In the 20 years since, no local government took the state up on it. 
Part of it was the exceptionally high barriers and ballot processes to instigate consolidation, a confusing and tangled web of petitions, reviews, resolutions and charters only the government could conceive as a process of doing something. The need for voluntary consolidation had legal constraints as well as letting the state Legislature write a process that was wholly on someone else’s initiative to implement. Still, in a representative democracy, the government reflects the voters either by omission or commission, and ultimately it is the voters, the people, that would have to make consolidation happen. 
Consolidation is a dirty word in West Virginia after two score and some odd years of school fights that have no end in sight. There is no version of the state telling local folks to “consolidate” that doesn’t come off as having less for yourself. Nomenclature like “right-size” and “cost-efficient” sounds painless, whereas “consolidate” has visceral pain many folks in many communities know first hand. 
Primarily, no move towards consolidation happened for a much more core, human nature reason: the folks with the legal authority to consolidate are also the folks who will lose their own power doing so. Voters have the say, but the commissioners gatekeep the process. Local identity, patronage jobs, parochial weight, the way things are always done, everyone will hate me on Facebook, and dozens of other highly personalized reasons that no amount of math can prevail against paralyzing any movement for change. Thus, not. And didn’t. 
The problems for most of West Virginia’s local governments have only increased since that 2005 change in code. Out West Virginia’s 55 counties, 47 are declining in population, a total loss of 54,832 between reporting periods, more than the population of Charleston. While West Virginia’s decades-long march of school consolidations runs concurrent with politicians, pundits and policy people perpetually talking about “right-sizing” government, the minimally viable local government crisis deepens. But almost all arguments in state and local government eventually boil down to the same thing: a fight over resources, and the county split between the eight haves and the 47 have-nots when it comes to the counties of West Virginia. 
There is an insidious political game at work in the increasing crisis of declining counties. The eight growing counties are continuously highlighted and resourced as success stories. Those counties gained 27,220 in population, increasing the tax base and all the resources that come with it. The 47 declining counties are continuously told to do more with less, do better, and be quiet about it, lest they upset the success narrative of the growing counties. The Legislature can point to West Virginia Code 7A and go “see, we gave you the tools to fix this yourselves” while the local governments are unwilling and unable to take that route while still, and not unjustly, claiming the state isn’t helping them enough. Even imperfect code needs a modicum of political courage and a commensurate amount of give-a-damn to at least try and work. Currently, West Virginia seems to be lacking in both. 
One of the most abused quotes in all of American history is Lincoln’s “a house divided against itself cannot stand.” Lincoln was diagnosing a legal structure that permitted the most grotesque of human abuses in slavery, and yet modern discourse has bastardized it into a watered-down “can’t we just all get along” plea. America was either going to be free or it was not, and remixing scripture with the righteous worry for his country being that wrong about something so fundamental birthed one of Lincoln’s greatest insights and quotable quotes. His own following of such a mandate was uneven, and even Honest Abe as president filtered his principles through political expediency under the justification that war changes things with no precedent for peacetime. 
West Virginia, which has Abe in statuary form eternally contemplating in front of the state Capitol building, isn’t an illustration of a house divided; it is a product of the political and moral next step once the principle was established. Turning division into a better unity so that a free people could self-govern was the genesis of the 35th state, born of blood, battle and some questionable legalities that nevertheless endures as proud history, heritage, and culture. But the inarguable math demands change. 
Consolidation is really a fancy word for together, something West Virginians usually pride themselves on, but painful change has to be acknowledged and accepted to make the required sacrifices worth it to the people. It will be a very hard sell. Whereas school consolidation was done to a community, governmental consolidation has to be pitched and approved as the communities doing it for themselves. It requires courage to change the structure of local government while there is still enough community left to change. But the alternative for many of those communities is a slow decline that only ends in governments in name unable to serve. West Virginia has a long history of generational suffering for far less noble reasons. It can be done. It must be done. Modern mountaineers can never be fully free without a government that gives them a chance today, not arbitrary numbers fixed in the century before last.
