name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Alvarado, Dembo spar over Iran war, data centers and Epstein in central Kentucky debate
text:
Democrat Zach Dembo, left, and Republican Ralph Alvarado, right, debate ahead of the 6th Congressional District election. (Screenshot via Fox56 feed)LEXINGTON, Ky. — The candidates in Kentucky’s close 6th District Congressional race debated each other over rising grocery and gas prices, the war in Iran, data centers and the Epstein files during a televised debate Thursday evening. 
Democrat Zach Dembo and Republican Ralph Alvarado both laid out how they would differ from each other if they are elected in the next couple of weeks and criticized their opponent’s record. Dembo, a former federal prosecutor and Navy veteran, argued he would be an “independent fighter,” regularly casting himself as a moderate Democrat in the race. Alvarado said he would be best positioned to address healthcare and insurance policy as a physician, and attempted to paint his opponent as a “liberal lawyer.” 
As the debate began on Fox56, moderator Andrea Walker asked both candidates to give specific examples of how their families have been affected by rising grocery prices. After saying he would support “an end to this senseless war in Iran,” which was raising prices with the cost of gas and diesel, Dembo said he’s seen a rise in ground beef. 
“Cattle farmers should be able to make a living, but I don’t think the solution is to undercut them by bringing in hundreds of thousands of tons of cheap foreign beef,” Dembo said, referring to a Trump administration plan to import beef to offset prices, after the question was repeated. 
Alvarado said he and his wife grow a lot of food at home, but do buy some beef from local farmers, before then claiming Dembo supported raising taxes. Alvarado was then asked to give an example. 
“My wife does a lot of the shopping for us, so I don’t get to — I mean I’m a physician. Usually, if I go to the Walmart and go down and do some shopping, people will pull me aside, want me to look in their kids’ ears and do examinations, so I don’t do a lot of shopping in person,” he said. 
Walker was joined by reporter Will Kenneally in moderating the debate, which lasted an hour. Afterwards, Dembo came out to speak to reporters. Alvarado did not appear, but his campaign advisor, Tim Murtaugh, spoke instead.
Murtaugh said “that was about the most one-sided debate I’ve ever seen.”
“Ralph Alvarado absolutely plastered Zach Dembo with all of the things that he’s wrong on and all of the things that he’s out of step with Kentucky-6 on,” Murtaugh said. 
Tim Murtaugh, Republican Ralph Alvarado’s campaign adviser, speaks to reporters following a debate between Alvarado and Democrat Zach Dembo. (Kentucky Lantern photo by McKenna Horsley)
Dembo said he plans to spend the remaining days before the election speaking with voters. 
“We’re going to be all over the place,” he said, adding that he will be part of a town hall with End Citizens United on Saturday and “barnstorming” the 16 counties in the district. 
Here’s some of the other answers from the debate: 
War in Iran
Throughout the debate, both candidates spoke about President Donald Trump’s war in Iran, which has become a theme in the upcoming midterm elections nationwide as control of the Strait of Hormuz has been tied to rising gas and diesel prices. 
Asked about suspending the federal gas tax to offset costs for Americans, which Trump temporarily did through an executive order, Dembo said the move “makes sense, but it’s only a Band-Aid.” 
“What we have to do is end this senseless war in Iran. Everyone knows that’s what’s led to these huge spikes in gas and diesel. I have been against this war from the beginning, and let me be clear: a vote for me is a vote to end this endless quagmire in Iran,” Dembo said before adding that the war should be ended “so that we can stop putting my fellow service members in harm’s way with no plan for an exit strategy.” 
Alvarado said he would support ways to lower taxes, including the gas tax, before pivoting to the war. He said Iran has been “at war with us for 47 years, and it’s important that we have no sympathy for the government that’s there,” saying Iran is trying to build a nuclear bomb. 
“We need to make sure that we end the war that’s there. I think it’s time for us to end it,” Alvarado said. “Once it ends, though, however, the gas prices are still going to be high. We need to manufacture more oil refineries that can help refine oil and be able to get gas and diesel prices down lower.”
Data centers and … Epstein? 
Kentucky communities have grappled with allowing or banning data centers leading up to Election Day. The proposals have raised questions about how such centers would affect Kentuckians’ utilities and electric bills and the environment around them. 
Both candidates said they would support federal rate-payer protections. In his answer, Alvarado said people should have local control over if a data center is in their community, before he began questioning a $500,000 donation from Reid Hoffman, the LinkedIn founder who is supportive of building data centers, to a PAC supporting Dembo. Hoffman has been tied to former financier and convicted sex offender Jeffery Epstein. Alvarado didn’t directly name but seemingly referred to former Lexington Mayor and Kentucky Transportation Secretary Jim Gray’s support of Dembo, and his family business, Gray Construction, which has has built data centers. 
In response, Dembo said he has never met Hoffman and cannot speak to PACs as a candidate. Federal law prevents PACs from coordination with campaigns. He later said he was honored to have Gray’s endorsement. 
Asked if he had conversations with Gray about data centers after the debate, Dembo said he only knows Gray through being the mayor of Lexington and overlapping in the Beshear administration. 
“That’s how I’ve known him. That’s how he made the decision to endorse me. I know him as a public servant,” Dembo said of Gray. 
Democrat Zach Dembo speaks to reporters after a Fox56 debate. (Kentucky Lantern photo by McKenna Horsley)
Asked if Alvarado would have voted to release the Epstein files in Congress — an issue that ultimately ignited Trump to primary U.S. Rep. Thomas Massie in the 4th Congressional District this year — Murtaugh said he would have supported the release. 
“So long as the victims and their names are not revealed,” Murtaugh added.
WKYT will livestream a forum next week between Alvarado and Dembo during a Tuesday forum at Estill County High School. 
Election Day is Tuesday, Nov. 3. Early voting in Kentucky begins Thursday, Oct. 29.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Commentary: Like it or not, Kentucky now has a school voucher program
text:
Supporters and opponents of Amendment 2 made their opinions known at the Fancy Farm Picnic, Aug. 3, 2024. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Austin Anthony)Many of us still recall the fight to defeat KY Amendment 2, which would have allowed public funds to go to private schools. Kentuckians overwhelmingly rejected this amendment by a margin of 65% to 35%. This should have sent a clear message to our representatives. 
Yet in February of 2026, the Kentucky legislature passed House Bill 1, which allows the state of Kentucky to participate in a federal school voucher program that was tucked inside the One Big Beautiful Bill. This program provides an “Education Freedom Tax Credit” up to $1,700 per year to people who donate to designated Scholarship Granting Organizations, or SGOs.  
A cursory look at the federal voucher system might show that it’s a “win-win” for Kentucky. No state revenues will be used to fund the program. Public schools will also benefit. What’s not to like? Let’s take a look at the evidence.
One of the touted benefits of the federal voucher program is that public schools can apply for funds to pay for various initiatives that will support their students. The Kentucky Education Foundation has been specifically established as an SGO to administer the dispersion of federal funds in Kentucky. The organization has a regional governing structure and has pledged that all 120 counties will be provided the opportunity to benefit from the program.  All of this looks promising. But there’s more. 
While the information provided by the federal government states that funds can also be used for educational opportunities at public schools, it’s evident that the EFTC is largely aimed at providing school choice. A federal fact sheet states that “[t]he Education Freedom Tax Credit supports national education choice…. In participating states, more families will have access to schools that align with their values and aspirations for their own children.” 
According to the federal register, one of the requirements of an SGO is that it “Spend not less than 90 percent of its income on scholarships for eligible students.”
Presumably, the remaining 10% could go to the SGO. Importantly, federal regulations do not include crucial information clarifying exactly how public school students can benefit from the program. So currently, benefits to public schools remain unclear. 
Further, all families having household incomes up to 300% of the area’s median gross income are eligible for vouchers. Thus, as has been the case historically, most scholarships will go to families who already have sufficient funds to enroll in private schools. It’s worth noting that often scholarships provide only partial payment for private school enrollment, thereby eliminating students whose families cannot afford the additional tuition. 
 
Finally, schools in Kentucky are funded based upon how many students are enrolled. When students leave public schools to attend private institutions, those schools lose money. This can cause overcrowding in public school classrooms and less money for ongoing budget items, like utilities and maintenance. 
Perhaps most problematic is that states cannot enforce additional requirements for SGOs that go beyond the minimal requirements defined in the federal legislation. That is, the authority over which students receive vouchers remains solely in the hands of the SGO, leaving them free to discriminate based on a student’s race, religion, disability, sexual orientation etc. There are currently 531 operating SGOs across the nation; those that focus on nonsectarian, public school, or disabled students make up less than 2 percent.
States are also limited in their ability to oversee the quality of services provided by SGOs and to hold them accountable. Thus, if the SGO is disproportionately providing vouchers only to certain student groups or are allowing them to be spent at low-performing or fraudulent schools, the state has no authority to close the SGO 
It’s estimated the program will cost taxpayers between $26B and $51B annually. And while Congress voted to fund a national voucher program, the House Appropriations Committee has recommended a 10% cut to Title I, which provides funding to lower-income schools. Every county in Kentucky receives Title 1 funds, and some of the poorest counties in Kentucky would have the most to lose. For instance, Harlan County receives $3.1M in Title 1 funds; Bell, $2.6M; McCreary, $2.5M.   So while money is being allocated for a federal voucher program, cuts are being proposed to another critical program that actually helps poorer school districts.
Is the program really a “win-win” for Kentucky’s schools?  As has been found with all voucher systems, it seems that the main winners will be those who already attend private schools, and the organizations that fund them.

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Commentary: Proposed grazing rules would hurt Western cattle ranchers
text:
(Photo by Preston Keres/USDA)A wave of new rules and proposals from the current federal government pose a severe threat to the health of public lands used for grazing livestock.
The federal agencies that manage public lands say they are trying to help American ranchers by bolstering the country’s dwindling cattle herd, which is at record low levels. In actuality, their efforts will neither meaningfully support U.S. beef producers nor lower beef prices for Americans. Instead, they will harm wildlife and undermine sustainable management of public lands, ultimately hurting cattle ranchers as well.
More than 70% of public land managed by the Bureau of Land Management and the U.S. Forest Service in the contiguous United States is available for grazing livestock. That is about 345 million acres, or a land area twice the size of Texas. In Colorado, 7.8 million acres of BLM land can be grazed and at least a million more of National Forest land.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Grazing allotments managed by the BLM and Forest Service are or will be affected by updated grazing rules, by the rescission of  the Biden-era Conservation and Landscape Health rule, by revoking grazing permits for bison, various memorandums of understanding, directives, and plans to guide policy, and more. These changes will primarily impact the western U.S., where federal land is concentrated. The proposed rules are supposed to ease “unnecessary regulatory burdens,” and “promote productive working lands,” yet rules for grazing on public land are already extremely lenient. Ranchers receive 10-year leases for grazing that are often automatically renewed and cost about 20 times less than grazing on private land.
Grazing livestock is one of the leading causes of public land degradation in the West. The BLM has classified at least 37 million acres of land as degraded from overgrazing, including nearly 2.5 million acres in Colorado. Livestock grazing depletes native plant species, allowing invasive plants to proliferate, sometimes with devastating effect. The invasive cheatgrass, for example, fuels more frequent and severe wildfires. Grazing causes erosion, loss of topsoil, and water pollution. In the arid West, cattle use more than their fair share of water. To produce 100 grams of protein, beef requires 1,375 liters of water (to produce the same amount of protein, tofu and pulses use only 93 or 204 liters of water, for comparison). All of these factors make public land less habitable for wildlife like sage-grouse, native trout and elk. Predators like wolves and coyotes are killed to prevent depredation of livestock.
For decades, conservation nonprofits have partnered with ranchers to retire grazing allotments that are particularly important for wildlife or especially degraded, thereby giving the land a chance to regenerate. Now, conservation is not considered a valid, co-equal use of grazing allotments. The BLM is seeking to put livestock back on the 24 million acres of land that have been intentionally vacated. The BLM is also proposing to significantly restrict the public from participating in government decisions about grazing on public land. Land that is, theoretically, owned by the public and managed using taxpayer dollars.
Grazing on public land contributes very little to the supply of beef in the U.S., and doesn’t meaningfully impact beef prices, yet it is highly subsidized. It’s estimated that less than 2% of cattle in the U.S. are grazed on public lands. Ranchers pay a small fee of $1.69 a month per cow (with or without a calf). In 2024, grazing fees generated just under $13 million and the cost of administering the program exceeded $100 million. This discrepancy amounts to a lucrative subsidy for a very small number of cattle ranchers: Two-thirds of public land grazing permits are leased to just 10% of U.S. ranchers. Some of these ranchers are extremely wealthy. The multibillionaire owner of the Denver Nuggets, for example, enjoys subsidized use of public lands that can accommodate 9,000 cows in Nevada.
Some small-scale ranching operations rely on grazing public land to make ends meet, but the Trump administration’s efforts won’t solve the worst challenges plaguing the industry. That’s because perhaps the greatest existential threat to ranchers in the Western U.S. is increasing aridity caused by climate change. Persistent drought reduces the availability of forage on public land and decreases yields of alfalfa and other feed crops — making it more expensive to raise cattle. That, combined with more frequent wildfires, dried up streams and hotter summers harms ranchers that rely on public land far more than public comment or conservation efforts ever have.
The proposed updates to public land grazing are misguided in their attempt to undermine the few meaningful programs in place to manage public grazing allotments sustainably. Ignoring the impact that climate change and drought have on cattle ranching in the West won’t make those issues go away. In fact, as time will tell, the opposite is true. Our treasured public lands will not be able to support livestock indefinitely, and by the time cattle are forced off the land, it may be unfit for wildlife, and the rest of us, too.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: If passed, this bill would strengthen protections for Virginia renters exposed to mold
text:
Mold spore growth along the doorframe to enter an apartment. (Photo by Charlotte Rene Woods/Virginia Mercury)Del. Cia Price, D-Newport News, wants to strengthen tenant protection laws for renters whose living conditions include mold. 
Price pitched a bill to do so in 2025, and it is due to be deliberated again in the upcoming 2027 legislative session. 
The Virginia Residential Landlord and Tenant Act already requires landlords to try to prevent mold formation in their units and promptly remedy it when it is brought to their attention. 
Current state law also mandates  landlords  provide tenants a comparable unit within their property or a hotel room for up to 30 days, but property owners are not required to pay for other expenses that arise after the relocation period. 
Those expenses can include additional transportation costs, lost wages or replacing tenants’ damaged property.
Price’s bill would adjust state law with additional guidance for landlords and tenants when dealing with mold abatement and support residents in recovering losses if they can prove damages.
Prince George resident files lawsuit against apartment management over mold

Price relayed how a constituent had to throw away all of her clothes after discovering  mold in the closet of her newly-constructed apartment, “so obviously it wasn’t something she was doing (that caused the mold),” Price said. 
Personal injury lawyer Jonathan Halperin noted that the past version of the bill may have made it harder for tenants to prove negligence of their landlords. 
While her bill intends to support residents being able to bring legal action against landlords for mold exposure, property damage claims, recoup attorney fees, or to recover medical bills that stem from mold exposure, the current draft would make those awards based on gross or willful negligence. 
Gross or willful negligence would include examples of instances where a landlord ignores mold abatement requests or paints over it rather than professionally having it removed. 
“The way this is written… it basically heightens what the plaintiff needs to prove from simple negligence to gross negligence. Price may not have intended that,” he said. 
Price admits there is still room for improvement.
“The bill that we tried was a big swing and would have really had much far further reaching ramifications in the legal system,” Price explained. “It didn’t have the support it needed to move through both chambers, but we’re going to tailor it more.” 
Further workshopping with her peers, she said, may be able to get it to Gov. Abigail Spanberger’s desk this time.
Halperin suggested Price’s revamped bill could apply ordinary negligence to compensatory damages and attorneys fees, while gross negligence or willful negligence could apply to punitive damages. 
He agreed with Price that Virginia’s mold remediation laws could be stronger and commended her for seeking to change them. 
Price and Halperin noted that mold causation is complex and can occur for a variety of reasons. Halperin pointed to constant humidity and poor ventilation, faulty HVAC units, storm damages, or leaks from neighboring apartments into other units.
“I do understand that … molds can happen when it’s ‘no fault of anyone,’ but at the same time that means that it’s not the fault of the renter either,” Price said.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Commentary: Virginia should do much more to curb PFAS pollution in our waters
text:
More than 100 acres of Chickahominy Tribal lands on the James River in Charles City County, July 31, 2021. (Evan Visconti/ For the Virginia Mercury)
Clean water is not simply a resource. It is the foundation of our health, our culture and our identity.
For the Chickahominy Indian Tribe, Virginia’s rivers, wetlands and landscapes are living connections to our ancestors and to the generations who will come after us. They sustain fish and wildlife, support our traditions and remind us of a responsibility that has endured for centuries: to care for the lands and waters of Tsenacommacah, our ancestral homelands.
That is why the Virginia Department of Environmental Quality should not approve a stormwater permit for Richmond International Airport that allows PFAS pollution to continue without enforceable limits.
DEQ’s proposed permit includes requirements for monitoring and a pollution minimization plan. Those measures are better than doing nothing. But they are not enough.
Monitoring pollution after it occurs does not prevent that pollution from entering Virginia’s waterways. And a plan to minimize pollution without enforceable limits leaves too much to voluntary compliance.
Virginia can and should do better.
PFAS — per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances — are known as “forever chemicals” because they persist in the environment. They can accumulate in water, soil, fish and wildlife, and exposure to certain PFAS has been associated with serious human health concerns. Once these chemicals enter the environment, they can remain there for years and move beyond the place where they were originally released.
That makes PFAS fundamentally different from an ordinary, short-lived pollutant. The consequences of a decision made today can follow a watershed for decades. For the Chickahominy Tribe, that matters deeply.
Our relationship with Virginia’s waters is not new. Rivers, wetlands, fisheries and the natural resources around them have long been part of our communities and our cultural traditions. These places connect us to our ancestors and provide opportunities to pass knowledge and responsibilities from one generation to the next.
When those waters are polluted, the damage is not confined to a technical measurement in a permit or a line on a monitoring report. It can affect the resources our people rely on, the places where traditions are practiced and the ability of future generations to maintain those connections.
That is why protecting water quality is also a matter of honoring the relationship between Tribal Nations and the commonwealth of Virginia.
Our relationship with Virginia is rooted in the Treaty of Middle Plantation, entered into in 1677 between the English Crown and Virginia Indian Tribes following Bacon’s Rebellion.
The treaty affirmed the continued existence of Virginia’s Tribal Nations, acknowledged our relationship with the Crown and recognized our connection to our communities and homelands.
The legal framework surrounding Tribal rights and governmental relationships has evolved since then. But the history remains important. Virginia’s Tribal Nations are not newcomers asking to be heard about what happens to these lands and waters. We are part of Virginia’s history and present, with enduring responsibilities to the places our ancestors called home.
Those responsibilities do not end with a particular parcel of land. Water does not recognize political boundaries. What enters a watershed upstream can affect communities, ecosystems, wildlife and cultural resources downstream — including resources within our ancestral homelands.
That is precisely why the commonwealth should act before contamination becomes a larger problem.
Richmond International Airport has committed to ending the use of PFAS-containing firefighting foam by 2030. That is a positive step, but it is not a substitute for action now.
Decades of PFAS use have already left a legacy of contamination, and ending future use does not make existing contamination disappear.
Nor should Virginians be asked to accept pollution today in exchange for a promise that conditions may improve years from now.
The purpose of environmental regulation is not simply to document harm. It is to prevent harm where we can.
DEQ has an opportunity to do that through this permit.
Enforceable PFAS discharge limits would provide a clear standard and a meaningful mechanism for accountability. They would tell the airport, downstream communities and Tribal Nations that preventing pollution is a requirement, not merely a goal.
They would also establish that Virginia takes seriously its responsibility to protect water resources before contamination spreads and becomes more difficult — and more expensive — to address.
Some may argue that additional requirements are unnecessary because PFAS use will eventually end. But “eventually” is not good enough when we are dealing with chemicals that can persist for decades.
Some may argue that monitoring will give regulators the information they need. It will. But information is not protection by itself.
If we know pollution is occurring, the responsible response should be to stop or reduce it — not simply to keep measuring it.
Virginians deserve more than a paper trail showing that pollution occurred. They deserve clean water. They deserve healthy rivers and wetlands. They deserve healthy fisheries and wildlife. AndTribal Nations deserve to know that the Commonwealth’s environmental decisions recognize the cultural and historical significance of the waters that connect our communities to our ancestral homelands.
The Chickahominy Indian Tribe’s Environmental Office urges DEQ to strengthen the proposed Richmond International Airport stormwater permit by establishing enforceable limits on PFAS discharges.
This is a decision about more than one airport and more than one pollutant. It is a test of whether Virginia is willing to prevent contamination rather than simply document it; whether environmental protections will have the force of law behind them; and whether we are willing to leave future generations cleaner water than we inherited.
For the Chickahominy Tribe, stewardship is not an abstract principle. It is an obligation passed from one generation to the next.
We know that we cannot undo every environmental decision of the past. But we can decide what we do next.
DEQ should choose prevention over pollution, accountability over promises and clean water over another generation of “forever chemicals.” Virginia’s waters are worth protecting. Our ancestral homelands are worth protecting. And the generations who come after us deserve nothing less.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Commentary: Schools are making cuts even though more money is coming in
text:
A sign supporting a referendum for the Elwood Community School Corporation from September 2026. (Photo by Niki Kelly/Indiana Capital Chronicle)Many of you will see a property tax referendum for your local school district on your ballot this year. And you have likely heard lots of concern from superintendents and school boards about cuts to their funding.
I wanted to give you some important context before you make your decisions.
A lot has been made of the changes in Senate Enrolled Act 1, which will lower schools’ property tax revenue by $744 million over a three-year period. Those savings are going mostly to homeowners.
But some lawmakers think there is nuance being lost in the message.
One important caveat is that property tax revenue for schools is still increasing — just not as fast or high as before.
An analysis from the Legislative Service Agency showed that school property tax levies increased 3.2% in 2026 over 2025. That is still a healthy increase, though much lower than the 6.5% and 6.9% in the two years prior. In 2023, the jump was 11.8%.
These increases include all three levers in school property taxes — the operations fund, the debt service fund and special referendums — approved by voters that are outside the state’s property tax caps.
Indiana superintendents say they’re cutting jobs because of property tax reforms

It is that growth rate that Republicans wanted to slow when lawmakers took action in 2025, largely at the urging of Gov. Mike Braun.
But it doesn’t mean that K-12 schools collectively aren’t getting new dollars.
In addition to the property tax revenue funding buses and healthcare and utilities and buildings, the General Assembly also uses state tax revenue to cover the education fund for teachers, textbooks, food and more. And they have added money to that pot consistently every year. This is generally known as K-12 tuition assistance.
That funding has increased 41% since 2016 – a $2.8 billion jump.
“Indiana has continued to increase funding for schools at both the state and local levels. State funding for education has increased every year over the last decade, including a 5% increase in our most recent budget, even as we reduced spending in other areas of government,” said House Ways and Means Chairman Rep. Jeff Thompson. “SEA 1 put reasonable limits on local property tax growth to protect taxpayers. Even with the taxpayer relief in SEA 1, schools are still receiving more local property tax revenue statewide this year than they did last year.”
Terry Spradlin, executive director of the Indiana School Boards Association, acknowledged that schools collectively are still getting new money under the revamped system. But he said that leaves out important context.
Specifically, the changes giving homeowners relief has caused the operations fund to decrease overall in 2026. And debt service increased only $100 million statewide.
The operations fund is important because 76% of that fund goes to transportation, insurance and utilities. As you know from your own household budget, those are areas that are increasing at a much faster pace than inflation.
One example is that the cost of school buses has risen from an average of $90,000 pre-COVID to about $160,000 now.
In personal terms, the situation seems like when you get a 2% raise but your expenses go up 4%.
Spradlin said 196 school districts received less in the operations fund than last year. And even with the 3.2% increase overall in school property taxes, that is below the pace of inflation at 3.7%.
“We need more money to keep up with the cost of doing business,” Spradlin said.
38 Indiana school districts to seek property tax referendums this fall

To cover the losses in operations, many schools are shifting dollars from the education fund. And that means less money there to meet state mandates on teacher pay and benefits. He added that the tuition support increase for public schools this year was just 2%. And many individual districts saw no increase at all due to falling enrollment.
Spradlin noted that Indiana is 38th nationally in per pupil spending, including all types of funding. The national average is more than $16,000 and Indiana is at about $13,000.
That big picture has led to districts cutting transportation, staffing and more. And all of that brings me back to referendums.
Many districts trying to keep pace with inflation have turned to public referendums for additional funding. In fact, 38 of them are on the ballot Nov. 3. That is partially due to the property tax changes enacted and because lawmakers have limited when districts can take these questions to voters to General Election years only.
One of those is Noblesville. The district is asking voters to extend an expiring referendum.
Sen. Scott Baldwin, R-Noblesville — who supported Senate Enrolled Act 1 — posted a letter commending the district for lowering its portion of the property tax rate and making $4 million in cuts.
He said the referendum provides 20% of the districts’ operating funding and cannot be used to build schools or athletic facilities.
Baldwin said that the ballot language is misleading and the Legislature should fix it.
“Every family has its own budget, and I respect that this is a decision each voter must make,” he said. “For me, supporting this referendum comes down to responsible management, results for our kids and the kind of community we want Noblesville to be.”

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: Childcare forum puts NH gubernatorial candidates’ policy differences on display
text:
Gov. Kelly Ayotte and Democratic challenger Cinde Warmington offered their thoughts on addressing childcare affordability and availability during an early care and education forum on Thursday. The election is Nov. 3. (File photos by Maya Mitchell/New Hampshire Bulletin)With Election Day less than two weeks away, incumbent New Hampshire Gov. Kelly Ayotte and Democratic nominee Cinde Warmington on Thursday pitched childcare providers on why they are the best candidate to improve childcare.
During a forum hosted by Early Learning New Hampshire and Save the Children Action Network, candidates were given the opportunity to respond live or by pre-recorded video to questions asked ahead of the event. Warmington attended the meeting and answered questions live. Ayotte did not attend but submitted written responses that were read aloud. More than 90 people from the childcare community attended the virtual event. 
The forum included candidates running for all statewide offices, each fielding questions about how they plan to tackle childcare affordability and availability. 
Warmington, like many other candidates vying for office in the Granite State, focused her responses on lowering costs for working families. 
Cinde Warmington criticized Gov. Kelly Ayotte over the defunding of the childcare workforce grant during the Early Learning NH/Save the Children Action Network forum on Oct. 22, 2026. (Screenshot)
“I’m shocked to learn that two children in childcare is at a cost of over $32,000 a year right now,” Warmington said. “We have so many people that are not in the workforce because they can’t access childcare, and we absolutely have to be focused on this.”
Warmington said that as governor, she would continue to expand the state childcare scholarship, create more home-based childcare programs for rural families and reduce barriers that are making it difficult to open new programs. The former executive councilor also said she would fund the childcare workforce grant, accusing Ayotte of defunding the program. 
“I have visited childcare centers around the state as well, and everyone says their No. 1 priority was to make sure those workforce grants were funded,” Warmington said. “My opponent in the race did defund the program. But it is a critically important program, and we need to make sure that we are funding (it).” 
The unsettled fate of the childcare workforce fund has been an issue since Ayotte took office in January 2025 and proposed her first budget as governor. 
In 2023, the state budget included $15 million from the General Fund for a pilot program to give childcare providers grants to help them recruit and retain employees, thus improving program capacity across the state. The grants helped programs pay for sign-on bonuses, retention incentives and wage increases, credit toward healthcare and paid time off equivalents, training and credentialing costs, and more. 
For the 2025-2026 biennial budget, the Legislature appropriated $15 million in Temporary Assistance for Needy Families dollars rather than state funds amid budget cuts. Before tapping TANF funds for that purpose, the state Department of Health and Human Services had to receive permission from the federal government. That request was denied in October 2025. 
Over the past year, lawmakers have tried to figure out how to fund the program. Multiple bills attempted to amend the budget bill to fund the workforce grant with state dollars, as it was in 2023. State officials later went back to the federal government for clarity on the initial denial, and the Administration for Children and Families denied the request again in January and August. The bills regarding the childcare workforce grant were ultimately either tabled or heavily amended, and the biennium ended without the childcare workforce grant having a clear funding source. 
Feds, DHHS give clear ‘no’ to TANF being used for childcare workforce grants

As a result, programs have not received the money and are not expected to before the year ends. Ayotte has said she supports the workforce grant and would work with lawmakers to get it funded. In her written response to the forum, she announced that the workforce grant was in her budget request for the next biennium and would be funded with state dollars. 
Warmington has previously said she supports increasing childcare for parents who work nontraditional hours, as well as state-funded pre-kindergarten. New Hampshire is among the five states nationwide that do not offer public pre-K. 
Ayotte focused her forum responses on her childcare wins during her first term, specifically signing the tax credit for businesses that invest in childcare bills, and her continued work with childcare stakeholders. 
Ayotte wrote she was proud of her endorsement of a tax credit for businesses that invest to help expand the number of childcare slots available. The bill had bipartisan support and passed the Legislature, and will allow businesses to collect a credit if they help expand childcare programs by 12 or more seats. Ayotte signed the bill into law in July. 
Childcare providers, who are often also business owners, are skeptical that the tax credit will increase the state’s capacity to care for more children due to high startup costs for childcare and limited interest among businesses. Over 97% of New Hampshire businesses employ fewer than 20 people, meaning most may not have enough staff with young children to take advantage of the credit. 
The governor also highlighted a $22 million funding increase for the Child Care Scholarship Program. Since she entered office in January 2025, enrollment in the program has increased, with more than 5,900 children enrolled as of July. 
Ayotte said that if reelected she will “continue finding ways to ease” the burden of high childcare costs, as well as “cut red tape” to build more housing, lower energy costs and “expand opportunities for affordable education and workforce training.” 
“I wake up every day thinking about how we can tackle these challenges, and I certainly don’t have all the answers,” Ayotte wrote. “Advocates and providers like you have played a huge part in what we were able to accomplish on childcare in my first term.” 
While the race for governor has been contentious, there are areas of childcare policy where the two candidates agree. 
Both support continuing investments in the childcare scholarship fund and building up the early education workforce through collaborations with high schools and community colleges.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: White House visits, overseas conferences among Indiana officials’ $132K in travel expenses
authors: Casey Smith, Tom Davies, Niki Kelly
text:
Lt. Gov. Micah Beckwith and his wife attended the White House Christmas party in December. (Photo from official account)Gov. Mike Braun led Indiana’s top officials in reported travel expenses last fiscal year, narrowly outspending Secretary of State Diego Morales even as most of the governor’s travel kept him within Indiana.
Other officials ventured farther. Their schedules included a White House Christmas reception, an Israeli delegation, a nuclear energy conference in South Korea and a Swiss apprenticeship exchange.
The governor, statewide elected officials and top Braun administration appointees listed a combined $132,572 in travel-related expenses in 16 annual reports reviewed by the Indiana Capital Chronicle. The reports cover the fiscal year that ran from July 1, 2025, through June 30, 2026.
Indiana Energy and Natural Resources Secretary Suzanne Jaworowski visits South Korea during a 2026 trip for a nuclear energy conference and economic development meetings. (Photo courtesy American Structurepoint, Inc.)
Braun’s listed expenses totaled $28,014, followed by Morales at $26,563 and Energy and Natural Resources Secretary Suzanne Jaworowski at $25,046.

But the reports vary in how officials list trips and account for expenses, making direct comparisons difficult.

Braun’s report assigned expenses to individual travel days, for example, while Attorney General Todd Rokita listed no state expenses for most of his in-state travel. Morales and Treasurer Daniel Elliott grouped fleet or fuel charges into monthly totals rather than assigning those costs to individual Indiana trips.
Some officials also listed trips paid for by sponsoring organizations without disclosing those amounts. Others reported travel without numeric costs or an explanation of who paid.
A state requires annual reporting on the purpose and location of official travel, expenses incurred and the state fund used to pay for each trip. The requirement followed scrutiny of Morales’ international travel and who paid for it.
The reports filed with the State Budget Agency additionally vary in detail. Some officials identified who they met with and why, while others provided little beyond a general description of a meeting or official event.
Braun stays close to home
Braun traveled extensively around Indiana for speaking engagements, meetings and other events. His office said he twice crossed a state line for an interview while visiting a border county.
His report also lists a February Washington trip described only as being for events and not paid for with taxpayer money. His office said the visit was for a Republican Governors Association meeting and was paid for through his campaign fund.
Morales tops statewide official travel spending

Braun’s expenses for other travel were charged to an Indiana State Police fund, with entries generally identifying the counties visited and describing the purposes as official meetings or events.
Lt. Gov. Micah Beckwith also logged extensive travel around Indiana, along with several out-of-state appearances. His listed expenses totaled $16,355 after reported reimbursements, with about $13,500 associated with in-state travel.
Three visits to D.C. and one to Sarasota, Florida, accounted for about $2,900 in reported expenses after reimbursements.
A December 2025 Washington visit to attend the White House Christmas reception included $1,237.76 in airfare and hotel expenses.
“Susan and I were honored to attend the White House Christmas Reception yesterday in DC,” Beckwith posted on his official X account. “Thank you to @POTUS for the invite and your incredible work this year on the economy, border security, peace deals, and a list too long to mention. Your leadership is truly inspiring!”
Beckwith also attended National Lieutenant Governors Association events in Sarasota and Washington. The organization reimbursed part of those costs.
The Sarasota entries list $2,238.71 in airfare, lodging, per diem and rental car expenses, offset by a $1,905.13 reimbursement. A Washington visit in June for an aerospace event included $938.16 in airfare and lodging, with a $500 reimbursement.
Another capital visit in April, described as being for meetings, included $892.74 in airfare and lodging.
Cabinet travel reaches overseas
Jaworowski accounted for about 62% of the $40,460 in expenses listed by the seven cabinet secretaries.
Her largest expense was $8,283.97 for an April 20-May 1 visit to Seoul and Busan. Her report says she attended a nuclear energy conference and participated in economic development meetings with South Korean officials.
She also listed $2,167.41 for a May visit to New York to meet with a South Korean construction company about economic development opportunities. The report does not name the company.
Other travel included Washington meetings with federal energy and Pentagon officials about nuclear advancement at southern Indiana’s Crane Naval Base, along with an Austin speaking engagement at a small modular reactor conference.
Attorney General Todd Rokita meets with HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. in December 2025. (Photo from official account)
Education Secretary Katie Jenner reported substantially less spending — $5,815.78 — but listed more dated travel-related events than any other cabinet secretary.
Her report contains 83 event entries, including 22 for out-of-state activities. Multiple events sometimes occurred during the same trip or on the same date.
Those out-of-state entries covered 41 distinct calendar dates, including 39 weekdays, according to a Capital Chronicle count of the reported start and end dates. Jaworowski’s 14 out-of-state entries covered the same number of calendar dates and weekdays.
No other cabinet secretary’s report covered more than 12 out-of-state calendar dates. The counts include the start and end dates of travel and do not necessarily represent full days away from the office.
Jenner’s destinations included Washington, Santa Barbara, Denver, New Orleans and Zurich, where she participated in an April exchange focused on the Swiss apprenticeship model and how it could be adapted in Indiana.
Her report lists $70 in state expenses for the Zurich visit. The report notes that outside organizations paid some or all expenses for that trip and several others, but does not say how much they covered.
Her Washington activities included testimony before the U.S. Senate’s education committee, meetings with federal officials and appearances at education policy events.
Transportation and Infrastructure Secretary Matt Ubelhor had the second-highest listed expenses among cabinet secretaries, at $6,952.91. His largest entries were $2,255.52 for a Salt Lake City visit and $1,903.62 for a Denver event.
Commerce Secretary David Adams’ report listed $2,189.25, including $1,327.41 for a Dallas conference. An accompanying letter says the report also includes expenses for a staff member who provided transportation for Adams, with funding from state appropriations and federal funds received through the Department of Workforce Development.
Health and Family Services Secretary Gloria Sachdev listed $456.72, including a $350 virtual conference. Her report also included Washington, San Diego and Boston travel without numeric expenses or an explanation of who paid.
Management and Budget Secretary Lisa Hershman listed 37 travel entries, including a Texas meeting, but supplied no numeric expenses. Business Affairs Secretary Mike Speedy likewise listed no numeric costs for 19 travel entries.
Washington visits and more
Rokita’s report provided little detail about his activities, listing broad regions of Indiana rather than specific destinations for many entries and describing every event’s purpose as official business.
His listed expenses totaled $5,694.54, with about $5,400 associated with 10 out-of-state trips. His dozens of in-state entries included only about $300 in expenses.
State Treasurer Dan Elliott poses in a delegation photo to Israel in December 2025. (Photo from official account)
He traveled to Washington seven times during the year. Two visits listed no state expenses, while the other five totaled nearly $3,400.
Those visits included attending U.S. Supreme Court arguments in two transgender sports cases, a Medicaid fraud event and a Department of Health and Human Services announcement.
“Attended @HHSGov’s announcement today of bold new actions to stop sex-rejecting procedures on children. We are blessed to have an administration in the White House fully committed to the same kind of commonsense values that prevail among everyday Hoosiers in Indiana,” he said on social media.
Rokita also reported two Florida trips totaling about $1,900 without identifying the cities or providing details about their purposes. A Sea Island, Georgia, visit included $60 in expenses.
Morales listed five out-of-state trips with about $8,000 in expenses. Those included National Association of Secretaries of State conferences in Washington and Biloxi, Mississippi, along with another Washington visit for meetings with federal and state representatives.
In July 2025, he traveled to Washington for an election integrity briefing at the White House.
He also visited Phoenix for a securities regulation conference and Providence, Rhode Island, for a corporate records administration conference.
Most of his reported expenses came from travel closer to home. Monthly fleet charges totaled $18,329.49, about 69% of his overall listed expenses.
Elliott reported $6,987.11 in expenses, including about $5,000 in monthly gas card charges for Indiana travel.
His reported out-of-state expenses totaled about $1,900, including visits to Orlando, Washington, D.C., Denver, Salt Lake City and Israel.
The seven-day Israel visit ran Dec. 6-12, 2025, with stops in Jerusalem and Tel Aviv, as part of a delegation with the National Association of State Treasurers and the America-Israel Friendship League.
His report lists $458.59 in expenses for the visit, without establishing the trip’s full cost.
Morales tops statewide official travel spending

Elliott announced $40 million in Israeli bond purchases between November 2023 and May 2024 — a $35 million purchase followed by another $5 million.
His travel report also lists no state expenses for conference or event visits to New Orleans; Dallas; Skokie, Illinois; and New Albany, Ohio.
Comptroller Elise Nieshalla reported the lowest expenses among the six statewide elected officials, at $2,912.39. About $1,600 was associated with in-state travel.
Her report lists four out-of-state conference visits, with the comptroller’s office covering $1,273.29 for a September Washington visit where she was an invited speaker at a Club for Growth event.
The State Financial Officers Foundation paid her expenses for an October conference in Washington and a May conference in Clearwater, Florida, according to her report. The State Policy Network paid her costs for an August 2025 meeting in New Orleans.
Other appointees
Indiana State Police Superintendent Anthony Scott listed $4,716.03, including $3,492.30 for a Denver police leadership meeting.
His total includes $435.53 for two trips taken during fiscal 2026 but paid in fiscal 2027. Another visit, to a Mothers Against Drunk Driving summit in Texas, was described as fully reimbursed by MADD.
Adjutant General Lawrence Muennich’s report listed $869.19 in monthly fuel charges and Indianapolis travel described as daily vehicle usage.
Braun’s chief of staff, Josh Kelley, listed three trips, including an August Washington, D.C. visit. All were described as not paid for with taxpayer money, without identifying the amounts or payers.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: More pressure on cost-burdened Rhode Islanders, more calls for housing
text:
Summer Street Apartments in Providence, a 176-unit development for formerly homeless adults, was highlighted by housing advocates as a sign of progress amid Rhode Island’s ongoing housing affordability crisis. (Courtesy photo from Crossroads Rhode Island)Housing advocates and state and local officials who gathered Thursday in the community room of a new 176-unit Providence apartment building for formerly homeless adults called the development a sign of progress after decades of underinvestment.
The Summer Street Apartments, which opened last year, is also a reminder of how much more housing the state needs to address a crisis.
“Too many residents are struggling to find a home that they can afford,” Melina Lodge, executive director of the Housing Network of Rhode Island, told the crowd gathered for a rally in support of state and city bond measures meant to build more homes.
A new fact book by HousingWorks RI to be released at a breakfast event Friday morning at the Marriott Providence Downtown underscored Lodge’s assessment.
For the third consecutive year, the policy research group based at Roger Williams University found no municipality had a home affordable to a household earning the state’s median homeowner income. For the second straight year, no community had an average two-bedroom apartment affordable to a household earning the median renter income.
“The trends of recent years have not subsided: sale and rental costs have continued to rise and more residents have fallen into the ‘cost burdened’ category,” the executive summary to the 82-page report states. 
About one-third of Rhode Island households — 148,766 in all — spend more than 30% of their income on housing, a common measure of housing affordability, according to the fact book 
For a household earning Rhode Island’s median income of $87,796, 30% of earnings on housing and utilities works out to $2,195 a month, according to HousingWorks RI. The median renter household earns $50,251 a year, the report found.
Driving the affordability gap is the growing divide between Rhode Islanders’ wages and housing costs. Since 2018, wages have risen less than 30%, while housing costs have climbed more than 60%, according to the fact book.
The widening gap between wages and housing costs is part of a broader squeeze on household budgets. A September report from United Way of Rhode Island found that 43% of households were living in poverty or struggling to afford basic necessities such as rent, a finding that echoed an April state housing snapshot.
HousingWorks RI found that 78% of the state’s 20 fastest-growing occupations — including bakers, cooks and welders — don’t pay enough to afford an average two-bedroom apartment. Of those 20 occupations, only financial managers make enough to afford a median-priced home in Rhode Island. Rhode Island’s business climate, which is dominated by small and micro-businesses, routinely ranks as one of the worst in the country.
Kyle Bennett, chief policy and impact officer at United Way of Rhode Island, said larger employers may be able to raise starting pay and pass some of those costs on to consumers. But smaller, family-run businesses have less flexibility to increase wages.
“The majority of employees are technically family members or our neighbors,” Bennett said in an interview. “They don’t necessarily have pay.”
HousingWorks RI Executive Director Brenda Clement also pointed to tariffs on Canadian lumber as one factor driving up home prices.
“Most of a project is wood framing,” she said. “There’s so much in the housing space that we don’t control.”
Rhode Island Housing Secretary Deborah Goddard listens during a rally in support of state and Providence housing bonds at Summer Street Apartments in Providence on Oct. 22, 2026. (Photo by Christopher Shea/Rhode Island Current)
Permits up for multifamily buildings, ADUs
HousingWorks’ report did find some positive trends.
The state issued permits for 3,778 housing units in 2025, up 34% from the previous year. Permits for buildings with at least two units rose 60% to 2,698, while permits for accessory dwelling units — smaller homes built on the same property as an existing house — increased 76% to 287.
But Clement said permits don’t guarantee that homes will get built, or that the finished units will be affordable. That’s where she and other officials said public investment can help. 
Rhode Island voters will decide in November whether to approve a $120 million statewide housing bond.
At least $25 million would go toward housing intended for homeownership, while up to $10 million could support public housing development. Question 2 would fund the construction and preservation of affordable housing through new development, renovations, property purchases and infrastructure improvements. 
Local Question 6 asks Providence voters to authorize a $25 million bond to build affordable multi-family housing through the Providence Housing Trust Fund. 



Quotation







Too many residents are struggling to find a home that they can afford.


– Melina Lodge, executive director of the Housing Network of Rhode Island


Housing Secretary Deborah Goddard told reporters Thursday the bonds would help keep housing development moving in both Providence and the rest of the state.
“We can’t take our foot off the gas at this point,” Goddard said.
Repeated borrowing to fund affordable housing has drawn criticism. The Rhode Island Public Expenditure Council found that, as of April, $52.2 million from the 2024 housing bond had financed 200 rental units, at an average development cost of more than $512,000 per unit.
Goddard pushed back on using the average development cost to judge the bonds, saying the state’s subsidy per unit is much lower. She also argued that some projects deliver benefits beyond housing, such as cleaning up contaminated land and providing onsite services to help residents remain stably housed.
“We are providing the services these people need to stay in their homes and thrive,” Goddard said.

name: National
title: Federal regulators crack down on organ donation groups
text:
The Organ Transplant Service teams at Walter Reed National Military Medical Center started using robotic surgery for kidney transplants in 2018. Nationwide, more than 109,000 people are on waiting lists for organ procurement. (Photo courtesy of Walter Reed National Military Medical Center)Federal regulators are cracking down on the nonprofits responsible for coordinating organ donations, aiming to begin shutting down substandard groups by early next year.
New criteria will score the organizations on donation and transplantation rates and will decertify the bottom tier, meaning their contracts with the federal government will be revoked. Many professional medical groups welcome more stringent evaluations. But the nonprofits strongly oppose aspects of the criteria and have filed lawsuits, warning of potential disruptions in some states or regions.
More than 109,000 people are on waiting lists nationwide for organ procurement, according to federal data as of July. The majority of patients await kidneys. Each day on average, about a dozen patients die waiting for an organ. 
State- and region-based nonprofits known as organ procurement organizations recover organs from deceased donors and work with families and transplant centers to coordinate donations. The procurement organizations have faced heavy scrutiny in recent years, with media reports and research papers highlighting issues such as skipping over some transplant centers and sicker patients, which worsens racial and socioeconomic disparities in organ transplants. 
The feds have shut down at least two groups in the past two years, citing questionable practices and saying that there were cases in which workers ignored signs of consciousness in donors.
Changes have been in the works for years. The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services first announced the new evaluation framework in 2020, in response to an executive order from President Donald Trump. Earlier this year, CMS released proposed revisions to that rule. 
Aiming for better accountability, transparency and oversight of the groups, as well as increasing patient protections and organ recovery, CMS will score the nation’s 55 organ procurement organizations based on their donation and transplantation rates. 
It will rank them into three tiers: Top tier organizations — those calculated in the top 25% of organizations for donation and transplantation rates — would be automatically renewed for another four years. Those that fall in the second tier will have the opportunity to improve and reapply for certification, while those ranking in the bottom tier would be decertified entirely. Other nonprofits will then make bids to the federal government to take over their service areas, according to CMS.
The new evaluation method has stirred debate. Some medical and policy experts say better oversight of the nonprofits is long overdue, while organ procurement organizations say they will face logistical hurdles in coordinating lifesaving organs if some are shut down.
More states try to give patients relief from medical debt

CMS hasn’t yet released which organization’s contracts will be renewed or dropped, but said in March that the process would begin sometime late this year. The current four-year contracts expire in January, but CMS has said it will issue extensions as needed to ensure organ transplants continue. 
CMS did not provide a specific date in response to Stateline’s request for information about when it would release certification decisions. The agency said it “is committed to a process that is transparent, data-driven, and focused on the goal of saving more lives through organ donation.”
But the Association of Organ Procurement Organizations, which represents the nonprofits, says nearly 42% of the 55 organizations could be ranked in the bottom tier, meaning they would face automatic decertification. The association says this may disrupt logistics around organ donation coordination.
Jeff Trageser, the association’s immediate past president, said the organization agrees that underperforming nonprofits should be held accountable. But he noted that many of the groups argue that outcomes such as transplant rates aren’t within their control and shouldn’t be considered in evaluations.
“Decertification needs to be a part of that. There has to be repercussions if there is just no improvement,” Trageser said. “Let’s measure the OPOs on what we actually do, and that is talking to families, advocating for donation, working to get organs allocated effectively to the right patients.”
The American Society of Transplant Surgeons said it supports “long-overdue” changes to how the nonprofits are evaluated and called the feds’ decertification last year of a Miami group a “powerful decision” that will strengthen the system. But it had also raised concerns about using transplant rates to grade the nonprofits.
Dr. Joel Adler, a transplant surgeon and assistant professor of surgery at Dell Medical School at The University of Texas at Austin, said some factors the organizations are responsible for can influence whether a transplant center accepts an organ or not, but that transplant centers’ own acceptance decisions matter too. He also said designing a quality measure for the complex process is difficult, but necessary. 
“At some point, there needed to be quality metrics attached to the whole system, so we can have different ways to measure it and work toward improvement,” Adler said.
Community groups lose HIV-prevention money as feds redirect dollars to states

Nonprofits have brought several lawsuits against CMS — most recently, in August, a nonprofit in Hawaii sued to block the rule, arguing that it would force organ procurement organizations to compete with each other for service areas.
A federal district court in Florida recently upheld the rule in a case brought by organizations serving California, Florida, Georgia, Iowa, Puerto Rico, Texas and Washington state that filed a lawsuit last year. The organizations appealed the ruling.
In some of the legal complaints, the nonprofits called the new evaluation method a competitive “Hunger Games” approach, arguing it would destabilize the nation’s organ donation system.
If a group shuts down, the trust that organizations have spent years building with its local communities could be fractured, particularly in communities of color that may have historic distrust in the medical system, said Dr. J. Thomas Rosenthal, board secretary of OneLegacy, the organ procurement nonprofit that serves Los Angeles and surrounding counties and is a plaintiff in one of the lawsuits. 
“Trust is the key factor in everything that we do,” said Rosenthal, former director of renal transplantation at the University of California, Los Angeles school of medicine.
But Greg Segal, founder and CEO of patient advocacy nonprofit Organize, said he questions the success of community relationships among lower-ranking organizations.
“There’s a lot of fearmongering. If an OPO is tier three, I am not impressed by the strength of the relationships they have built … because if you have done all the things right and built all the right relationships, you are going to have much better outcomes than being a tier three,” he said. “If you’ve been failing and failing and failing, you are not serving patients well.” 
Katie Ross-Driscoll, assistant professor of surgery at Indiana University’s school of medicine, researches disparities in access to care among liver transplant patients.  
“They (organ procurement organizations) serve an absolutely vital role in the system and in the community, and they are what makes the promise of transplantation possible for patients,” said Ross-Driscoll, who is also a researcher at health systems research organization, Regenstrief Institute and statistical editor for Liver Transplantation and Hepatology Communications. “At the same time, I think that objective measures that enable comparability across organizations are what helps us understand how we can do better.”
Stateline reporter Nada Hassanein can be reached at nhassanein@stateline.org.

name: Maine Morning Star
title: Will Maine’s next governor reshape local control in education to improve test scores?
text:
Maine’s test scores remain flat in state assessments and in 2024 were the worst in three decades, according to National Assessment of Educational Progress  data. (Dana DiFilippo | New Jersey Monitor)All three candidates for governor are concerned about Maine students’ declining test scores. But not all of them are willing to change the key policy experts say is holding the state back from widespread academic reform.
Like many other states, Maine has laws enshrining local control, under which a municipality or school district is empowered to make its own rules. But unlike 43 other states, many of which consider themselves “strong local control” states, Maine has not passed any state laws mandating evidence-based learning — curricula and teaching tools backed by rigorous scientific research and data. That’s according to a study by the nonprofit Educate Maine released this year.
The Maine Department of Education last year came up with a more hands-on approach to bolster academic outcomes. But due to the lack of centralized authority, it can’t mandate that districts use these plans developed by expert advisory councils. It also can’t mandate professional development for teachers to be trained in the science of reading, or require districts to adopt the math plan that aims to incorporate the subject more ubiquitously and remove some of the common student fears associated with it.
Instead, districts are left to choose their own curriculum. Four national and Maine education experts told Maine Morning Star that while local control is important because it allows districts the choice to select materials that reflect their students, it can also create disparities when small or rural districts are not held accountable for not choosing learning materials backed by research.
“The more we keep saying ‘local control,’ the more we’re expecting small municipalities to pass muster when they don’t have the resources,” said Amy Johnson, a University of Southern Maine professor and co-director of the Maine Education Policy Research Institute.
“If the state were to screen and say, ‘Here are some curricula that we think are moving in the right direction,’ and then provide resources for those, that certainly should help improve outcomes in the districts that right now either don’t have a curriculum at all … or they’re using a curricula that has not been shown to produce good results,” she added.



Quotation







The more we keep saying ‘local control,’ the more we're expecting small municipalities to pass muster when they don’t have the resources.


– Amy Johnson, co-director of the Maine Education Policy Research Institute


Dan Goldhaber, professor and director of the University of Washington’s Center for Education Data and Research, told Maine Morning Star there are no studies directly tying local control to poor educational outcomes, but there’s some indirect evidence. 
Pointing to changes in the National Assessment of Educational Progress or NAEP (pronounced nape) that tracks students over time across states, Goldhaber said experts have “come to believe that it is states where there have been some state-level mandates, for instance, adopting the science of reading, that have led to changes in student achievement.” 
A vast majority of those states —  led by Mississippi, which experts often cite as the best example of improved statewide outcomes — have passed laws requiring professional development for educators as well as teacher preparation programs that train future educators in evidence-based practices, as well as certain interventions for students not showing progress.
Meanwhile, Maine’s test scores remain flat in state assessments and in 2024 were the worst in three decades, according to NAEP data. 
The lack of a Maine law requiring science of reading instruction may be due to an adherence to local control that goes beyond state statute that puts “control and management of the public schools” in local districts’ hands. 
“Some of the things that I’ve seen that were unable to get passed through the Legislature, it was more about everybody saying, ‘Well, we don’t do that because we’re a local control state,’” Johnson said. “It wasn’t that there was anything preventing them from doing it, it’s more about the shared norm among the policymakers that are sort of their guardrails.” 
For example, in the Sept. 2026 study, Educate Maine found that 46 different reading programs are being used across responding districts (which represent 70% of all Maine schools). The data showed that 18% of responding districts use only science-based reading programs, while 67% use a combination of science-based and other programs. The remaining 15% use only programs that don’t align with the science of reading. 
What districts chose to teach did not necessarily correlate with them being  rural or small, according to Kim Russell from Educate Maine.
“The problem is lack of leadership,” she said. “When you have legislative leaders and a governor that’s fully behind it, then change will happen.”
Asked last year about the commitment to local control, Chloe Teboe, a former spokesperson for the Maine Department of Education, said that in addition to being a requirement of the Maine Constitution, local control “reflects a trust that Maine communities know how to make the best decisions for their students.” 
Maine’s gubernatorial candidates agree on education challenges, but not solutions

“Local control allows communities to elect school boards that support and guide schools to tailor curricula and programs to their local students’ unique needs, while still benefiting from state standards, state-created resources, and statewide accountability systems,” Teboe said.
The Maine Department of Education did not respond to requests for updated comment. 
What the next governor could do
The next governor has the potential to change how much the state helps districts, which are still recovering academically from the impact of the Covid-19 pandemic. Democrat Hannah Pingree, independent Rick Bennett and Republican Bobby Charles have all said this is one of their top priorities. 
Earlier this year, Maine Morning Star asked each candidate their position on local control as it relates to schools.While none of them said they would make substantial changes to weaken local control, they all agreed that the state should play a more prominent role in guiding academic recovery. How exactly they plan to achieve that is still unclear, with Bennett being the only candidate to have released a plan with specific goals for academic achievement.
Pingree said as a former school board member she’s seen firsthand “how important it is for communities to shape schools that reflect their students’ needs.”
“Local control shouldn’t mean every district is on its own to solve big, shared challenges like literacy gaps, teacher shortages, or aging buildings,” she added. “My approach isn’t to mandate reform from Augusta. It’s to collaborate: bringing educators, school boards, and communities to the table, sharing what’s working across the state, finding more opportunities to support schools better working together, and ensuring that our schools have the funding and tools to take action.”
Goldhaber said Pingree’s response is the “most consistent” with the argument made by him and other education researchers “that local control shouldn’t mean that every district’s on their own to solve big shared challenges.”
Pingree, who previously worked under Gov. Janet Mills as director of the Office of Policy, Innovation and the Future, said during the final gubernatorial debate last week that she disagreed with the administration’s approach to educational recovery, which ultimately deferred to individual districts’ authority. “I think we need to go much bigger to ensure that every kid is learning to read and do math at grade level, especially by the third grade,” she said.
“There are schools in Maine who are implementing these programs, but we need to ensure that every school district is making it happen,” she added.
Bennett said he respects Maine’s tradition of local control, “but it works best when the state sets clear expectations, provides strong support, and is transparent about results.” 
“The state still has a responsibility to lead and ensure students are being served well,” he added. 
During the final gubernatorial debate, Bennett cited the lack of Maine districts using science-based reading curriculum, and said, “that is holding our kids back.”
“As governor, I’ll insist that we teach kids scientifically and get them reading before fourth grade.”

Charles said he believes local control should mean that parents have more influence on what their children learn in school. 
“I believe in the concept of local control, but unlike some, I believe that this extends to the most local entity — the parents,” he said. “Control over our education policies should extend beyond the superintendents and school boards to the people who know what is best for students — their family members.”
Goldhaber said Charles is “taking the idea of local control to the extreme” and said his response seemed to indicate support for private school vouchers, which the Trump administration is offering as an alternative to public school. 
During the final debate, Charles said he is supportive of “parallel tracks like private and homeschooling.”
The federal context 
Local control does not mean taking agency away from districts. National education experts including Goldhaber and Vivian Wong, a professor at University of Virginia, told Maine Morning Star a majority of decisions about schools should be made at the local level, but that they need to be supported at the state and federal levels.
But the Trump administration has prioritized downsizing the U.S. Department of Education, eliminating several offices that offer support to states and districts. 
How Trump’s anti-DEI shift unraveled a successful federal investment in Maine schools

“The federal system can really have a strong role in basically supporting the production of high-quality, rigorous studies that districts and states may not be able to conduct on their own,” Wong said.
 “But I think what sort of gets watered down in that Trump push for local control is that for people to be able to make good decisions, they have to be able to see the same facts. Otherwise, it creates disparities between states and localities.”
One of the hardest hit federal offices within the education department was the Institute for Education Sciences, which saw 90% of its staff cut. IES is responsible for administering the NAEP test, functions as the primary education data collection entity and funds education research. Experts including Wong told Maine Morning Star the cuts threaten the ability to figure out how to improve education.
In place of federal education research, the institute now recommends state and localities establish relationships with researchers, and generate their own evidence that guides what to teach.  
“That is a model that works really great for large-scale districts like Chicago Public Schools or Washington, D.C.,” Wong said. “But that type of local control model, or the pairing of local entities with researchers, it’s harder for rural districts or districts that just do not have the same capacity to be able to run basically their own in-house research firm.”
That combined with Maine’s lack of state-level educational benchmarks means districts are responsible not only for finding curriculum but also measuring their own educator effectiveness (which is also a state statute).
“To me, it’s about accountability,” Johnson from University of Southern Maine said.
“I think it’s about policymakers discussing at what point do you intervene when the local community is not able to continue to provide what they might want to provide for their kids?” 
She added, “If a local community doesn’t have the capacity to continue to do what the kids need, then we shouldn’t just look aside and say, “Oh well, I guess that’s local control.’”
