name: Connecticut Mirror
title: CT gets first side-by-side look at Lamont and Fazio in TV debate
text:
Republican Ryan Fazio worked aggressively Thursday night in his first televised debate with Gov. Ned Lamont to reframe the gubernatorial election, urging voters to disregard the daily distractions of a unpopular president and focus on the governor’s responsibility for the high cost of living in Connecticut.
Fazio, 36, a state senator from Greenwich, arrived at the studio of WFSB in Rocky Hill needing to enliven a static campaign that polling indicates has coalesced in favor of the 72-year-old Lamont, a Democrat seeking a third term that would make him Connecticut’s longest-serving governor since statehood.
From his opening statement, Fazio was the aggressor.
“Tonight, all across Connecticut, families are struggling,” Fazio said. “They’re suffering under the weight of the fourth-highest energy bills, the third-highest taxes and the highest unemployment rate in the entire country. Gov. Lamont had eight years to fix it. Instead, he broke his promises and made every single one of those problems worse. He raised your taxes by $3 billion.”
Fazio used the one-minute opening to try to inoculate himself against the certainty of the governor leaning into public opinion that President Donald Trump’s war on Iran and tariffs have had a far bigger impact on inflation than any governor.
“Now tonight, you can expect Gov. Lamont to blame those failures on Washington, D.C.,” Fazio said. “But leadership is about taking accountability. I’ve been willing to criticize the Trump administration when I disagree, just like Democrats in Hartford, and I’ll lead in the exact same way, as an independent voice and a bipartisan leader.”

Gov. Ned Lamont and Republican challenger Ryan Fazio at a debate at WFSB on Thursday, Oct. 22, 2026. Credit: Arnold Gold / Hearst Connecticut Media

Lamont cast his eight-year record against Connecticut’s lost decade after the Great Recession of 2008, the start of a chronic fiscal crisis.
“Connecticut, we’ve been through a lot,” Lamont said. “You know, eight years ago, came into office, inherited $2 billion budget deficits as far as the eye could see. Then we ran into COVID. Now we have Trump’s tariffs and war in Iran driving up the cost for everybody. But I hope you believe that we’ve made progress over the last eight years.”
Fiscal stability and the opportunity he says it brings is Lamont’s central brand.
“Eight balanced budgets in a row,” Lamont said. “We’ve gone from one of the slowest-growing economies in the country to one of the fastest-growing economies. You know what that means? That means jobs and opportunity.”

Gov. Ned Lamont and Republican challenger Ryan Fazio at a debate at WFSB on Thursday, Oct. 22, 2026. Credit: Arnold Gold / Hearst Connecticut Media

Political commercials, including some paid by Lamont and Fazio, bookended the one-hour debate and filled the single commercial break. A second and final debate will be aired live at 7 p.m. Tuesday on WTNH, Channel 8.
The first debate, sponsored by WFSB and CT Insider, came after four days of early voting. As of Wednesday night, 140,830 votes already had been cast by absentee ballot or in early voting that began Monday, the secretary of the state’s office reported Thursday.
Fazio was an assured television presence, finding an easy cadence and command of facts as he looked into the camera and worked to undo Lamont’s assessment that Connecticut has turned a corner on economic stability. Lamont complimented his challenger after the debate — with a significant proviso.

Gov. Ned Lamont and Republican challenger Ryan Fazio at a debate at WFSB on Thursday, Oct. 22, 2026. Credit: Arnold Gold / Hearst Connecticut Media

“I thought it was pretty civil, but his numbers do not add up. He says it with a great deal of authority, but the numbers are going to get us in the exact same mess I inherited back in 2018,” Lamont said. “That’s why the state Senate never could come up with a budget.”
He actually was referring to the Senate GOP minority. Unlike the House GOP minority, Senate Republicans did not offer alternatives to the budget negotiated by Lamont and the Democratic majority.
Viewers could be confused listening to Lamont outline his record cut to the state income tax, worth about $660 million annually, and Fazio insisting it was more than offset by other increases. Fazio’s claim of $3 billion in tax increases is a cumulative figure, not an annual boost.
Once the pluses and minuses are tallied, Connecticut is collecting an average of $412 million more annually over Lamont’s eight years, Fazio says. 
His accounting includes the $500 million collected yearly through a 0.5% tax on payroll that pays for benefits created by the passage in 2019 of a law creating a Paid Family and Medical Leave program, a benefit that taxpayers have accessed since 2022. 
Lamont’s first budget in 2019 also delayed or canceled roughly $650 million in previously approved tax cuts that had not yet taken effect. Most of that suspended relief was headed to hospitals, but retired teachers, property taxpayers without dependents and college graduates with degrees in science, technology, engineering or math also came up short.

Gov. Ned Lamont and Republican challenger Ryan Fazio at a debate at WFSB on Thursday, Oct. 22, 2026. Credit: Arnold Gold / Hearst Connecticut Media

Lamont doesn’t count those as tax hikes. Many Republicans do.
“Maybe he wants to get rid of Paid Family and Medical Leave. If he wants to do that, he ought to say so,” Lamont said after the debate. “We set up an insurance program. It’s incredibly popular. It’s solvent, and if your child gets very sick, you can take some time off, be with your child and still be able to put food on the table. That’s what it’s all about.”
Fazio said he would reduce the payroll tax that he says has produced a surplus for the program.
On Trump’s war against Iran and the resulting jump in gasoline prices, Fazio put himself on the side of consumers, proposing a gas tax holiday — and complimenting Lamont’s anti-war run for the U.S. Senate in 2006.
“I oppose the war in Iran. I’ve said it repeatedly. I’m more of a non-interventionist,” Fazio said. “I actually respected 2006 when Ned Lamont ran for the Senate in opposition to the Iraq war. I think he was right at the time.”
Fazio said the state can afford a gas tax holiday, given that the revenues go to a special transportation fund that is running a surplus. The 25-cents-per-gallon retail tax on regular gasoline and the 49.9 cents-per-gallon levy placed on diesel fuel generate about $42 million and $12 million, respectively, each month.
“Why haven’t you supported a gas tax holiday?” Fazio said, turning the governor.
Lamont, who favored a holiday four years ago, said Fazio is opting for an easy gesture.
“When the price of gasoline goes up $1.75 a gallon, that’s costing our families say $20 a week. I appreciate, ‘Twenty-five cents, we’ll figure out how to pay for it later.’ That’s just the type of political thinking that got this state into trouble,” Lamont said
A question on ICE and Trump’s immigration crackdown prompted Fazio to talk about public safety and border security and pivot to affordability.
“We need common sense. I love legal immigration and our legal immigrants in this state, and we have to support them and make the state affordable for them,” Fazio said.
“You may love them, but ICE is picking them up. ‘You are guilty until proven innocent.’ If you look Hispanic, you are gone,” Lamont said.
The candidates clashed over electric rates in Connecticut, which are among the lowest in New England and highest in the U.S. Fazio has tried to capitalize on text messages published by CT Insider in which the chief executive of Eversource urged the governor to “intervene” in the company’s dispute with Connecticut regulators over $1 billion in unpaid storm costs.
Fazio called the relationship “cozy.” Lamont dismissed Fazio’s claim as “Just no truth to this at all.”
“I do have a relationship with the business leaders of the state. That does not mean I do not hold them accountable,” Lamont said.
In his closing remarks, Fazio made a rare reference to the governor’s age.
“I respect Gov. Lamont’s public service, but he’s had his chance. The first time he ran for office was the year I was born for the office that I currently hold,” Fazio said. “He’s been in politics for decades, and after eight years, Connecticut is more expensive than it’s ever been. We can do better.”
Fazio said later his comment was not about age.
“It’s not about the age. It’s not anything about that. It’s that Gov. Lamont’s been running for office for 36 years, and he’s been in office for eight years. And at a certain point, you have to accomplish what you’re going to accomplish and go back to the farm.”
Lamont, who founded a cable television company geared to university campuses, told reporters he found the comment odd, coming from a man who he says entered politics with a thin resume.

Gov. Ned Lamont and Republican challenger Ryan Fazio at a debate at WFSB on Thursday, Oct. 22, 2026. Credit: Arnold Gold / Hearst Connecticut Media

Fazio has said he was a commodities trader, then became an investment adviser employed by Capital Services, an affiliate of the company his father founded and chairs, MARCorp Financial. He currently has no employment outside the Senate.
“Look where people come from, and that gives you an idea. I think people have a pretty good idea of the business I started,” Lamont said. “I have no idea what experience he brings to politics. All I know is he’s all politics all the time. Figure out what he did in the private sector. I can’t.”
CT Mirror reporter Keith M. Phaneuf contributed to this report.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Kamala Harris says ‘Mississippi matters’ at Columbus rally for Scott Colom
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
COLUMBUS – Former Vice President Kamala Harris campaigned in Mississippi for Scott Colom on Thursday, calling the Democratic Senate nominee a historic candidate whose victory would send a statement that America has begun to reject President Donald Trump and his party.
Harris’ arrival followed a steady stream of campaigning for Colom by Democratic senators and a last-minute large investment from Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, as Democrats grow increasingly hopeful that Colom can pull off an upset over Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in ruby-red Mississippi. 

Speaking to an energized crowd at the Columbus High School gym, where Colom played basketball as a youth, Harris said Mississippi’s increasingly competitive U.S. Senate race is a fight worth waging for Democrats. 
“We’ve got 12 days to make history. And I’ve traveled here because, indeed, Mississippi Matters,” Harris said, referencing Colom’s campaign slogan. “The power is with the people. And the people are with Scott.”
Former Vice President Kamala Harris speaks on behalf of Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Scott Colom at his rally in Columbus, Miss., Thursday, Oct. 22, 2026. (Mississippi Today Photo/Rogelio V. Solis)
Republicans appear to be taking Colom’s challenge seriously. The day before Harris arrived in Mississippi, party leaders announced on Wednesday that President Donald Trump will campaign for Hyde-Smith in the northeastern town of Corinth on Monday.
The crowd at Colom’s rally chanted “Mississippi Matters!” throughout the evening, and cheered, “We want Scott!” as Colom continued to connect the high cost of gasoline and groceries to Hyde-Smith’s approval of Trump’s war with Iran and tariffs. Colom delighted the crowd with his favorite label for his Republican opponent: “Cindy High Prices.”  
“She’s given away our voice, she’s given it away to her MAGA daddy,” Colom said.  
Harris said Trump is leading “the most corrupt administration in American history,” and that Hyde-Smith, a devoted Trump ally, deserves to lose. 
A supporter carries a sign at Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Scott Colom’s rally in Columbus, Miss., Thursday, Oct. 22, 2026. (Mississippi Today Photo/Rogelio V. Solis)
“The junior senator from Mississippi voted in favor of a $1 trillion cut to Medicaid,” Harris said. “It doesn’t have to be this way. We deserve better.” 
Earlier on Thursday, Harris and Colom were at a community health center in Clarksdale for a roundtable discussion about rural healthcare. They were joined by U.S. Rep. Bennie Thompson, the lone Democratic member of Mississippi’s congressional delegation, whose district includes Clarksdale, as well as local doctors, a mother who lost a child as a result of inadequate healthcare access and other local leaders. 
The audience cheers former Vice President Kamala Harris and Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Scott Colom at his rally in Columbus, Miss., Thursday, Oct. 22, 2026. (Mississippi Today Photo/Rogelio V. Solis)Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Scott Colom speaks at his rally in Columbus, Miss., Thursday, Oct. 22, 2026. (Mississippi Today Photo/Rogelio V. Solis)Former Vice President Kamala Harris joins Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Scott Colom at his rally in Columbus, Miss., Thursday, Oct. 22, 2026. (Mississippi Today Photo/Rogelio V. Solis)The audience cheers former Vice President Kamala Harris and Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Scott Colom at his rally in Columbus, Miss., Thursday, Oct. 22, 2026. (Mississippi Today Photo/Rogelio V. Solis)A supporter sits inside the gym at Columbus High School prior to the start of a rally for Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Scott Colom in Columbus, Miss., Thursday, Oct. 22, 2026. (Mississippi Today Photo/Rogelio V. Solis)Volunteer Keisha Gray of Columbus, left, hands out campaign shirts for Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Scott Colom in Columbus, Miss., Thursday, Oct. 22, 2026. (Mississippi Today Photo/Rogelio V. Solis)Janice Richmond of Columbus, right, hands out campaign shirts for Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Scott Colom in Columbus, Miss., Thursday, Oct. 22, 2026. (Mississippi Today Photo/Rogelio V. Solis)Supporters carry signs in support of Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Scott Colom in Columbus, Miss., Thursday, Oct. 22, 2026. (Mississippi Today Photo/Rogelio V. Solis)
Healthcare is an animating issue for voters in Mississippi, a state that has for years struggled with hospital closures and poor health outcomes. Mississippi, one of the nation’s poorest states, hasn’t expanded Medicaid, and many residents struggle to afford care. Throughout his campaign, Colom has hammered Hyde-Smith for voting for Trump’s so-called “One Big Beautiful Bill,” which slashed Medicaid funding. 
“Our junior senator is going to do nothing to fix rural healthcare in Mississippi,” Colom said. “She’s going to do nothing to fix hospitals in Mississippi. She’s made that clear. She’s got no solution. I’m offering solutions.”
Colom promised to work on reversing cuts to Medicaid and Affordable Care Act subsidies. 
Harris said voters in areas such as the Delta have the opportunity to turn their hardships into action by voting for Colom. 
“People are feeling and experiencing pain, and the feeling of being unseen, unheard, alone, hopeless and therefore feeling powerless,” Harris said. “This is a moment where we can understand in this election season with less than two weeks to go, we can turn that pain into purpose.”
Harris’ trip marks her second visit to Mississippi in the past year. She came to Jackson in January for her book tour and spoke before a packed crowd. 
Harris has said in multiple recent interviews that she’s focused on helping Democrats win in November. But she’s not ruled out another presidential campaign after losing the 2024 general election to Trump.
In a statement ahead of the rally, the Senate GOP’s campaign arm said Colom’s embrace of Harris shows he is out of touch with voters in a state Trump won handily 
“Scott Colom is a Chuck Schumer-backed, George Soros-funded, Transgender Defender so out of touch with Mississippi that he is campaigning with Kamala Harris, who lost the state by 22 points,” said NRSC Regional Press Secretary Samantha Cantrell. 
With a little over a week left until the midterm elections, Mississippi has become a surprising battleground state where national party figures are swarming the state to energize their bases. Former U.S. Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg will stump for Colom on the Gulf Coast on Tuesday. Those who have already visited Mississippi for Colom include Sens. Raphael Warnock of Georgia, Lisa Blunt Rochester of Delaware, Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island, Angela Alsobrooks of Maryland and Cory Booker of New Jersey.
Feeling confident about retaking the Senate and House majorities, Democratic leaders have begun to invest in Mississippi, a state that has long been solidly Republican in federal elections. But the state has the highest percentage of Black voters in the nation, a core voting bloc of the Democratic Party. 
If Mississippi, a state which hasn’t voted for a Democratic U.S. senator since 1982, were to elect Colom over Hyde-Smith, it would be an embarrassing rejection of Trump in the Deep South and prove a historic win in the state that hasn’t elected a Black person to a statewide or federal office since Reconstruction. 
Colom on Thursday seemed visibly moved by the possibility of Mississippi, a state that was the epicenter of the Civil Rights Movement and where white supremacists actively worked for decades to disenfranchise Black citizens, potentially electing its first Black statewide official. 
He told the crowd that the state has a chance to write “a new chapter” on Nov. 3 and depart from its past where candidates used divisive and sometimes racist rhetoric to divide voters. 
“So many times throughout history that worked,” Colom said. “But not this time.”

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Engling, Bayh duel over key differences in secretary of state race
text:
Republican candidate Max Engling, left, and Democratic candidate Beau Bayh participate in a secretary of state debate Thursday, Oct. 22, 2026, at Fox59/CBS4 studios in Indianapolis. Courtesy: Grace Smith/IndyStar pool photoDemocrat Beau Bayh and Republican Max Engling agree on one thing: Indiana’s next secretary of state must investigate Diego Morales, the scandal-plagued outgoing incumbent.
But the candidates offered contrasting visions of who should lead such an investigation in the final secretary of state debate Thursday.
Bayh wants to hire Knox County Clerk David Shelton, a private investigator and Republican who previously sought the GOP nomination, to lead an independent audit of the office.
“It’s been a central promise of this campaign that I will conduct an independent audit of this office,” he said.
Morales is accused of spending taxpayer dollars on luxury vehicles and promotional materials, as well as hiring family members and awarding no-bid contracts to donors.
Engling, a late entrant to the race after Morales refused to suspend his campaign, said any investigation should be led by the inspector general to guarantee the “full weight” of the state is behind it.
He described Shelton as a “friend” of Bayh’s who lacks the expertise and authority to compel state officials to cooperate.
“You need to have the person that actually has the authority to compel documents, to look at emails, to investigate dozens of people and make sure what the office has done is proper, or if not, hold it accountable,” he said.
Republican candidate Max Engling speaks Thursday, Oct. 22, 2026, during a secretary of state debate against Democratic candidate Beau Bayh at Fox59/CBS4 studios in Indianapolis. Courtesy: Grace Smith/IndyStar pool photo
Engling and Bayh traded barbs about their residency — neither spent their full lives in Indiana though both claim strong roots to the state — their driving records, campaign contributions, ethics pledges and the debate host’s decision not to invite their opponents.
Libertarian nominee Lauri Shillings and Lincoln Party candidate Greg Ballard did not meet qualifying polling thresholds to participate in Thursday’s debate, hosted by FOX59 and CBS4.
“Max doesn’t want him here,” Bayh said in response to a question about Ballard’s call to make the secretary of state a nonpartisan office, to which Engling asked the moderator to clarify why the other candidates weren’t present.
Bayh quickly added that Engling declined to sign onto a statement supporting their inclusion.
Both candidates pledged to serve the full four-year term if elected secretary of state, rather than resign early to seek higher political office.
And they agreed the office shouldn’t be used toward partisan ends.
Bayh said he would still support candidates and causes he believes in, but wouldn’t let his support affect his decisions in office. Meanwhile, Engling said voters expect elected officials to “link arms” and “move the state forward.”
On voter fraud, Engling reiterated his support for the SAVE America Act to verify the citizenship status of voters, suggesting he would work with state lawmakers to color code state IDs so legal noncitizen residents cannot use the IDs to vote.
“One illegal vote is too many,” he said.
Democratic candidate Beau Bayh speaks Thursday, Oct. 22, 2026, during a secretary of state debate against Republican candidate Max Engling at Fox59/CBS4 studios in Indianapolis. Courtesy: Grace Smith/IndyStar pool photo
Bayh said he would work with county clerks to flag and remove ineligible voters from the voter rolls. He criticized state officials for prosecuting only one of the 21 noncitizen voters they say they identified in a recent review.
“We need to actually hold people accountable when they’re caught,” Bayh said.
Both Engling and Bayh expressed support for Indiana’s voter identification law to secure elections, and agreed the state should extend early voting hours to boost participation.
Ballot initiatives, dark money and campaign contributions
Bayh broke with Engling in his desire to work with lawmakers to bring citizen-led ballot initiatives to Indiana, which he said would result in greater turnout if voters had a direct say in issues like partisan gerrymandering.
“One of the big problems with our politics here is that some of the folks in the Statehouse are too often looking out for the special interests — not the interests of the working people of our state,” Bayh said. “So, I say let’s give the 5 million registered Hoosier voters a more direct say in some of the biggest issues they’re facing.”
Engling said dark money groups are using citizen-initiated referendums in other states to skirt lawmakers, often tricking voters in the process.
“It’s important to trust the voters certainly, but I think it’s also important to use our elected representation in the General Assembly to make law where they’re going through regular order, they’re going through the committee process,” he said.
Personal attacks
Bayh defended his father, former governor and U.S. Sen. Evan Bayh, from attacks by the Engling campaign connecting him to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
“You are running an ad right now about my dad, baselessly linking him to a known pedophile with no evidence,” he said. “He has never met Jeffrey Epstein. He has never talked to Jeffrey Epstein … it’s unfortunate that Max Engling deems it necessary to attack my family. I’m not going to do that.”
Engling said his team is in the process of suing Bayh for defamation for a political advertisement misconstruing decades-old speeding tickets as reckless driving convictions.
“There’s only one person on the stage has been charged with reckless driving, and that’s my opponent, not me,” he said.
Bayh and Engling touted their Hoosier roots, as questions about their time spent out of state continue to circulate.
Engling said he moved from rural Illinois to Indiana as a teenager.
He went to school at Ivy Tech and Indiana University-Purdue University Indianapolis before moving to Washington, D.C. to work in politics, returning to Indiana after more than a decade with his wife and children.
“It’s important to know what it means to be a Hoosier, but also know what it means to serve whether that’s here or in another place,” he said.
Bayh said he is the seventh generation of his family to be born in Indiana. He too moved to Washington, D.C. when his father was elected to the U.S. Senate and spent time overseas when he enlisted in the Marines.
“I didn’t have a say over where we moved,” he said, adding: “My life has taken me many places … I always knew I wanted to get back home.”

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Cooper rallies support one week into North Carolina’s early voting
text:
Roy Cooper speaks to reporters during a "Make Stuff Cost Less" campaign event in Raleigh on Oct. 22, 2026. (Photo: Christine Zhu/NC Newsline)A week into early voting, more than a million North Carolinians have cast their ballots. While the numbers currently swing toward Democrats, Roy Cooper’s campaign isn’t slowing down.
The Democratic former governor spoke to about 150 supporters in downtown Raleigh Thursday night as part of his “Make Stuff Cost Less” campaign blitz across the Tar Heel State. 
Sarah Redd was one of the people in the crowd. The Raleigh behavioral technician said her most important issues are Medicaid and the cost of childcare. 
In her personal life, she’s had to cut back on hobbies and non-essentials, like travel and clothes. At work, many of her clients rely on Medicaid. 
“It’s impacted them a lot, and how many hours we’re able to give them therapy,” Redd said.
Redd voted early in person Monday, one of 1,101,318 North Carolinians who have cast their ballots in the first week of early voting. That’s an increase of 302,540 ballots, or 38%, over the last midterm election in 2022.
Of those numbers, registered Democrats cast 43% of those votes and registered Republicans account for 22.5%. Democrats historically have higher turnout during early voting in North Carolina, while Republicans favor going to the polls on Election Day.
Unaffiliated voters make up the largest share of North Carolina’s electorate — and they’re responsible for 34% of ballots cast so far.
Compared to the 2022 midterm, unaffiliated voters have the largest increase in turnout so far this year. According to an analysis of state voter data by Catawba College political scientist Michael Bitzer, unaffiliated voters were up by 72% over 2022 in the first week of early voting. Democrats were up by 62%. Republican turnout has increased by just 1.7%. 
Democrats outraise opponents in NC’s most contentious congressional races

That looks like good news for Democrats, since polls show unaffiliated voters breaking for Democrats this year, thanks to high inflation and fuel costs, and an unpopular war. But there are still ten more days of early voting for Republicans to catch up. 
Cooper isn’t taking anything for granted. 
“We have to remember that oftentimes, things can change during early voting as we get toward Election Day, so we’ve got to keep working and getting people out to vote,” Cooper told reporters. 
Cooper, a two-term governor and four-term attorney general, is relying on unaffiliated voters to help him defeat GOP candidate Michael Whatley in the contest for North Carolina’s open U.S. Senate seat. 
Democrats, who need a net gain for four seats this fall to gain majority control of the U.S. Senate, view North Carolina as one of their best pickup opportunities this fall. Cooper has led Whatley by double digits in the polls for months. Election forecaster Cook Political Report rates the race as “likely Democrat.”
Whatley, former chair of the Republican National Committee and North Carolina Republican Party, has closely aligned himself with President Donald Trump and said he ran for the seat following Trump’s request. But Trump’s approval ratings in North Carolina have slipped into the mid-30s in recent polls. 
Cooper criticized Whatley for benefitting from corruption and the status quo in Washington. 
“People are very frustrated that their paychecks are not keeping up with the cost of living,” Cooper told reporters. “They’re frustrated that Washington not only is not doing anything about it, they’re making it so much worse with the chaotic tariffs and with this war in Iran.”
Roy Cooper has “DEM GOV” on the back of his shoes, which he said are Democratic blue, at a campaign event on Oct. 22, 2026. (Photo: Christine Zhu/NC Newsline)
The Whatley campaign did not respond to NC Newsline’s request for comment. 
Cooper has centered his campaign around affordability and the economy. For healthcare, he wants to reimplement the Affordable Care Act tax credits and cap annual out-of-pocket costs for prescription drugs. 
That’s one reason Michael Kimsal, a small business owner from Franklin County who attended Thursday’s event, said he’s supporting Cooper. 
Kimsal, who’s self-employed, is responsible for buying his own health insurance. Last year, he said he paid about $650 per month, in part due to extended subsidies under the Affordable Care Act. 
But Congress cut out those premium tax credits at the end of 2025. Now, Kimsal’s health insurance is $1,650 each month. 
“It probably doesn’t seem like much to the insurance companies, but it’s quite a lot for us to absorb,” he said. “It means that that’s $1,000 a month less that’s going to our local community, so eating out less, giving to charities less, going to local events less.”
Kimsal reflected on Cooper’s record as governor of helping to lower costs and increase access to health services through Medicaid expansion.
“We want good change. We want positive change,” Kimsal said. “We need a strong leader like Roy Cooper to go out and deal with people like us.”

name: Daily Montanan
title: Former public defender disciplined in scheme to take a house
text:
The Great Seal of the State of Montana in the Supreme Court (Photo by Eric Seidle/ For the Daily Montanan).The Montana Supreme Court approved discipline against a Missoula lawyer who worked for the Office of Public Defender and tried to take possession of a house without permission of its owner.
The order suspends Scotti Ramberg from the practice of law for five months for dishonest and unethical conduct.
Ramberg worked on staff for the Office of the Public Defender until March 2024 and then worked on contract for the office, after the allegations of wrong-doing had become public.
The public defender’s office did not respond to a request Thursday for her current status, but the order, issued last week, said Ramberg had not been practicing law much of this year.
The order said the state’s Commission on Practice, which recommends discipline for lawyers, expressed concern Ramberg’s conduct “involved a protracted course of self-dealing, conflicts of interest, misrepresentations,” and false statements under oath.
It also said the commission found it “significant that Ramberg has expressed remorse for her conduct.”
The order said Ramberg admitted to violating the Montana Rules of Professional Conduct, and the Commission on Practice recommended the court impose discipline. A separate settlement with the property owner was reached earlier.
Ramberg agreed to the disciplinary sanctions, the order said.
The order stems from complaints the Office of Disciplinary Counsel filed against Ramberg in 2025 based on other legal actions against her.
Those include a misdemeanor theft charge in 2024 and a separate 2023 lawsuit alleging she tried to illegally take a property owner’s house in a complex scheme.
In the 2023 lawsuit, a property owner who lived out of state alleged Ramberg set up a couple of shell companies to illegally record construction liens against his home.
The case was dismissed following a settlement, but a court order found Ramberg, by being unresponsive to the lawsuit, admitted she took possession of the property, changed the locks, and took items from the premises without permission.
At one point, Ramberg claimed she had a contract for the property owner to sell her the house, but the terms were highly advantageous to her, and the evidence didn’t support that claim, according to the complaint by the Office of Disciplinary Counsel.
The order of discipline outlines the related professional conduct violations:

It said Ramberg admitted she broke rules of professional conduct when she communicated with the property owner who filed the lawsuit against her, the order said. It said she knew the property owner was represented by counsel, and the rules prohibit direct communication without consent from the lawyer or a court order.
The order said Ramberg admitted her interactions with the property owner violated rules that prohibit “dishonesty, fraud, deceit or misrepresentation.”
The order also cited the theft of a cellphone, a separate incident. It said Ramberg admitted she committed a criminal act that “reflects adversely” on a lawyer’s honesty and trustworthiness when she “threw her ex-husband’s phone in a courtroom wastepaper basket,” seeing he had left it behind after a hearing, an act resulting in the theft conviction.

Ramberg did not respond to a request for comment left Wednesday.
Lawyer Colin Stephens, who represented Ramberg in the disciplinary case, did not respond to an email Wednesday requesting comment and asking whether Ramberg intended to continue practicing law after the suspension.
The order said Ramberg had not been practicing law for six months prior to the August findings by the Commission on Practice, so the sanctions mean she will not have practiced for nearly a year before she is eligible to seek reinstatement.
The order requires her to obtain a mentor for two years, take a professional responsibility exam and score at least 80%.
It requires her to pay the costs associated with the case and comply with the rules of professional conduct.
The suspension takes effect 30 days after the Oct. 13 order.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Nearly 70,000 residents to get medical debt erased next week
authors: Alison Kuznitz | State House News Service
text:
NEARLY 70,000 LOW- and middle-income Massachusetts residents will see part or all of their medical debt erased starting next week, the Atrius Health Equity Foundation said Thursday.
More than $38 million in debt relief will be distributed to 69,527 people in eastern Mass. through a partnership involving the foundation, the national nonprofit Undue Medical Debt and the Massachusetts Health and Hospital Association. Relief will range from $5 to $86,000, and the latest tranche of support brings the partnership’s medical debt erasure total to nearly $300 million since it started in 2024.
“For too many patients, an unexpected illness or medical emergency can create financial hardship that lasts long after they leave the hospital, ER or doctor’s office,” Undue Medical Debt CEO Allison Sesso said. “Eliminating medical debt gives people a meaningful fresh start and ensures that getting the care they need doesn’t come at the cost of their economic security and mental health.”
Pending regulations from the Department of Public Health would block licensed health care facilities and providers from reporting medical debt to consumer credit agencies. Some debt collectors and health care providers oppose the rules, saying they could undermine the accuracy of credit reports and add financial strain to smaller practices.
Residents next week will begin receiving Undue Medical Debt branded envelopes alerting them to the relief. The foundation says there’s no application for the relief and that “eligible medical debt will automatically be eliminated for those who qualify, no strings attached, with negative credit score marks removed, if relevant.”
The support is provided to individuals whose medical debt is at least 5 percent of their annual income or who earn at or below four times the federal poverty level ($63,840 per person).

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Alaska Lt. Gov. incorrectly put disqualified candidate on the ballot, state judge rules
text:
Early voters line up at the Midtown Mall in Anchorage on Thursday, Oct. 22, 2026. (Yereth Rosen photo/Alaska Beacon)The Alaska Division of Elections and Lt. Gov. Nancy Dahlstrom acted incorrectly when they put disqualified Republican candidate Jose Tagle on the ballot for state House District 22, an Anchorage Superior Court judge said Thursday.
Judge Josie Garton’s decision, published in the late afternoon, means “Tagle’s election may not be certified if he does win a majority of votes in the general election,” she wrote.
Tagle is running against Democratic incumbent Rep. Ted Eischeid, who is heavily favored in the district that went for Democratic Presidential candidate Kamala Harris two years ago.
Garton did not order the division to reprint ballots without Tagle’s name. Absentee and early voting is already taking place, and Tagle may appeal the ruling. A successful appeal could see his candidacy restored.
“The Division’s certification, while erroneous, does not undermine the fundamental fairness of the election,” Garton said.    
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 

The Alaska Division of Elections, Alaska Department of Law and Dahlstrom’s office did not immediately respond to a request for their opinion of the decision.
Tagle did not immediately respond to an email on Thursday afternoon seeking his thoughts.
The head of the Alaska Democratic Party, which filed the lawsuit that challenged Tagle’s candidacy, said she was pleased with the decision.
“Mr. Tagle’s completely blank disclosure left Alaskans in the dark,” said party executive director Jenny-Marie Stryker. “Voters deserve to know the financial interests of our elected officials — that’s the law, and it’s just what’s right.”
New ruling concerns issue that also involved a candidate for governor
Thursday’s ruling comes after a two-month-old dispute that also involved Republican gubernatorial candidate Treg Taylor. 
The Alaska Public Offices Commission, which regulates candidates and campaigns, recommended in late August that Tagle be disqualified as a candidate after submitting a blank financial disclosure form and failing to amend it within a grace period allowed by state law.
It also recommended Taylor be disqualified for filing an incomplete form and failing to amend it before the deadline. Taylor and Tagle submitted amended forms after the deadline.
Dahlstrom initially followed APOC’s recommendation, but days later, she reversed herself and put the two men back on the general election ballot, citing a review from the Department of Law indicating that disclosure forms filed by many other candidates could also have problems.
The Beacon analyzed that review and found many of the problems flagged by the Department were either minor or did not exist at all.
Alaska Democratic Party fought the issue through the summer
The Alaska Democratic Party sued the Division of Elections in July after it permitted Tagle’s candidacy for the state primary election despite his blank financial disclosure form.
It did not challenge Taylor’s candidacy, and subsequent proceedings did not involve him or Dahlstrom’s decision to certify him.
Garton ruled against the party in August, saying that under state law, Tagle had 30 days to fix his blank form, and the party had filed before that grace period was over. In addition, Garton said that the commission, not the Division of Elections, should have the final word on the correctness of financial disclosure forms.
After Dahlstrom certified Tagle despite the APOC recommendation, the Democratic Party filed a new complaint in September and asked Garton to re-examine the issue. She declined to issue an immediate ruling and held oral arguments Oct. 9. 
Procedural problems aren’t an obstacle for APOC decision 
During oral arguments, attorneys from the Department of Law — representing Dahlstrom and the Division of Elections — abandoned the earlier argument that Tagle’s restoration was warranted by the fact that other candidates also had problematic forms.
Instead, they contended that APOC’s disqualification recommendation was not final and that procedural errors — including a notice that failed to state that Tagle could appeal the recommendation — meant that Dahlstrom was not bound by the recommendation.
But writing on Thursday, Garton concluded that based on state laws, regulations and the procedures used by APOC, the commission’s decision was “final and appealable.”
She wrote that while APOC’s statement was officially billed as a recommendation, state law requires the lieutenant governor to follow it.
“While it may be true that APOC’s recommendation ‘did not order anyone to do anything,’ both parties agree, as does the court, that the Lt. Governor has no discretion to disregard a final decision by APOC that Tagle failed to substantially comply with (state law) within the deadline,” Garton wrote.
State attorneys argued that APOC’s recommendation didn’t take effect until 30 days after it was ordered and that procedural problems also left the door open for the lieutenant governor not to follow the recommendation, but Garton disagreed.
“APOC’s decision was effective immediately, and the potential procedural irregularities in APOC’s proceedings did not provide grounds for the lieutenant governor to ignore the clear command of (state law),” she wrote.
Garton said the issues facing Tagle’s nomination “are precisely the circumstances under which the Legislature intended a candidate for public office to forfeit his nomination.”
“By certifying Tagle’s nomination after APOC entered a final decision finding that Tagle failed to substantially comply … within the deadline established by law, the Lieutenant Governor and the Director of the Division of Elections violated (state law).”
Garton concluded that APOC should notify Tagle that he has 30 days to administratively challenge the disqualification decision. He — or state officials — could also appeal Garton’s ruling to the Alaska Supreme Court.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Hinson listens to parents, staff and youth addiction survivors at Iowa recovery facility
text:
U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson, left, visited Ember Recovery in Cambridge, Iowa Oct. 22, 2026. With her is Ember Recovery CEO Andrew Allen and 15 year-old Zoey. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch) CAMBRIDGE — The Republican candidate for Iowa’s open Senate seat, U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson, visited Thursday morning with youth, parents and staff at Ember Recovery Center and talked about promoting addiction education and youth addiction screening. 
Ember Recovery is a residential center offering nature-based and trauma-informed care to Iowa teens dealing with addiction. Staff and a current resident at the facility said they also pride themselves on the work they do to support teens’ relationships with their families to stoke long-term success. 
Zoey, a 15-year old resident of the facility who is identified by first name only for her privacy, said prior to the family sessions run at the facility, she never saw herself being close to her relatives. 
“That’s like my biggest thing now is like my family — that’s my biggest support,” Zoey said. 
Zoey is set to graduate from the program soon, and in addition to helping with her addiction, she said the program has shaped what she wants to do with her life. After high school, Zoey plans to study psychology with the goal of getting into social work. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Her story is similar to Ember’s CEO, Andrew Allen, who entered Ember Recovery, then called YSS Residential Addiction Treatment in Ames, as a teenager dealing with addiction. Allen said he credits the program with “saving his life.” Since the $30 million campus opened in January 2025, Allen said the facility has served more than 300 Iowa youth. 
Speaking to Hinson on a tour of the facility, Allen said, “Part of what we’re trying to do, Ashley, is instead of being known for being number one in the country for binge drinking, we want to be one of the greatest places in the country for young people to recover.”
Dave Muhlbauer, the running mate for Democratic gubernatorial candidate Rob Sand, also toured Ember Recovery in July as a stop along his campaign trail. Muhlbauer defended Sand’s proposals to legalize recreational marijuana — a proposal, Allen said, could lead to more children being exposed to the drug. 
While Ember Recovery is relatively new, Allen said there are already plans for new phases of the facility including trailers for visiting families and a shop where students can learn trades. 
Brian and Mary Lohse helped fund portions of the campus because they said they wished something like Ember Recovery existed when their son was going through addiction treatment. Instead, the Lohses said they had to send their son to Texas and California to get the quality of care now offered at Ember Recovery. 
“We wouldn’t have had to go through that,” Brian Lohse said. “We would have been able to visit him more often. We wouldn’t have had to fly him back three or four times to meet with his probation officer … We had the luxury of being able to do that — most people don’t.” 
Allen said about 75% of Ember Recovery patients rely on Medicaid coverage as they go through the treatment facility. 
Hinson has been criticized for her vote in support of the Republican-led One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which added certain work requirements to Medicaid which the health policy organization KFF estimates will lead to 5.3 million more uninsured Americans by 2034. Allen said the changes to the program from the massive tax bill are not anticipated to impact teens who go to Ember. 
“My whole goal is to make sure people who actually need those benefits can access them,” Hinson said. “… Ensuring that they actually can bill and get paid for the recovery treatment that they’re providing for young people will continue to be a priority for me.” 
Ember Recovery sits on more than 50 acres of rural Iowa land and almost all of the rooms have large windows facing a remnant prairie on the property. 
Jake Rhodes, a lead recovery specialist at the facility, said many of most transformative group sessions happen on the cabin’s four-season porches where residents can feel comfortable opening up to others. 
Rhodes, speaking to Hinson in a roundtable discussion Thursday, said he also sees a lot of need for education around addiction — for youth and adults. While teens are in the recovery program, Ember Recovery hosts a family weekend that teaches parents the warning signs of addiction to help them catch addiction early rather than let it progress. 
“I threw half my 20s away on that lifestyle, and I don’t want to see these kids have to get to that same spot,” Rhodes said. 
Hinson said there could be room for policy that would add more age-appropriate education in schools around addiction. 
Hinson said she recently introduced a bill to improve access to cancer screenings and added that she wonders whether screening youth for addiction would similarly help improve outcomes.
Allen said that currently in Iowa, a teen would have to have three misdemeanor charges before they would get referred to a place like Ember Recovery, even while some children, like Zoey, become addicted to substances as early as 9 years old.
“That – it’s too long,” Allen said. “ … We should be doing screeners on these kids, and not putting them deeper into the system, but giving them resources and tools because there’s 6,000 kids in Iowa that need treatment right now, and some of our programs don’t have wait lists.”

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Denied a campus early voting site, NC A&T students again march to the polls
text:
NC A&T State University students walked 40 minutes from campus to an early voting site on Oct, 22, 2026. (Photo: Lynn Bonner/NC Newsline) 


The “plot twist” sign was one of several NC A&T University students waved as they marched from campus to an early voting site on Oct. 22, 2026. (Photo: Lynn Bonner/NC Newsline)
Several hundred NC A&T State University students filled Greensboro streets Thursday for a 40-minute walk from their campus to an early voting site, partly to do their civic duty and partly as a show of strength.


It was the second Greensboro student voter march this month, following an event last week that drew national attention.
Earlier this year, state and local elections officials denied students’ petitions for an early voting site on campus for this year’s primary and general elections. Students decided to show the power of their numbers with a march to cast their ballots.
Zayveon Davis, a leader of voter engagement at A&T, was one of the students who traveled to Raleigh last January to demonstrate for an early voting site for the primary.
“It’s wonderful that we are able to activate in this way,” he said before the march. “We are the leaders of tomorrow.”
It’s also too bad that they had to do it because elections officials would not agree to locate an early voting site on campus, said Davis, a senior majoring in business management.
The campus had an early voting site for the presidential election in 2024. But the campus didn’t have one in the last midterm election in 2022, so elections officials declined to open one for the 2026 midterm.
Amid protests, NC elections board rejects campus voting sites and Sunday voting in several counties

The massive demonstration of student interest on Thursday should debunk arguments about low student turnout as a reason to deny the campus an early voting location, said senior Shia Rozier.
“I think you can look around and see that we’re more activated than the everyday person is,” she said.
Rozier also traveled to Raleigh earlier this year to support an early voting site on campus.
“Everytime they told us ‘No’ just showed us more and more how, if our votes didn’t matter, they wouldn’t be working this hard and saying “No” so often,” Rozier said.
Thursday was not just about casting ballots for students. It was an event with music, celebrities to cheer them on, and opportunities for photos. When We All Vote sponsored a Party at the Polls on campus.
Students had their pictures taken at a Faces of Change booth. They were able to check their voter registration at another table.


NC A&T students march to the polls
— Lynn Bonner (@lbonner.bsky.social) 2026-10-22T19:40:35.831Z


A&T Chancellor James R. Martin II praised the students. It’s an important time for people who have a sense of responsibility, engagement, and a desire to make a difference in their community, he said.
“I congratulate you for all of what you do to have your voices heard,” the chancellor said. “Today is a showcase for our community and for our nation.”
Marsai Martin, who starred on the TV show Black-ish, is a When We All Vote co-chair. She praised students for their persistence.
“When the path to the ballot box got harder, you guys all found a way forward,” she said. “I know our journey is our resistance. And I know that when this community comes together, it’s how we beat intimidation and fear. And when we show up and vote together, we make it fun and we make our communities impossible to ignore.”
After she voted, Trinity Dobson, a junior, said it wasn’t fair that A&T was denied an early voting site.
The march showed that students won’t be deterred, she said.
“You can’t silence us,” she said. “We’re not just these young, naive kids that don’t have voices or opinions. We’re never going to stop fighting for what we want, because this is our future.”
Early voting continues through Oct. 31.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Once a rarity, Latino candidates are now up and down the ballot in local, state races
text:
Latina connecting at Arepa Zone in College Park include, from left, Colmar Manor Mayor Monica Casañas, Del. Deni Taveras , House Speaker Joseline Peña-Melnyk, Montgomery County register of wills candidate Barbara Ebel and Nicole Rios, a political strategist. (Photo courtesy Joseline-Peña Melnyk)When she entered public life in 1990, Ana Sol Gutierrez was a pioneer, serving two terms on the Montgomery County Board of Education before becoming Maryland’s first Latina state legislator when she was elected to the House of Delegates in 2002.
A native of El Salvador, she came to the U.S. in 1949, the daughter of a founding director of the World Bank and International Monetary Fund. A systems engineer by training, she worked for NASA and was deputy administrator at the Department of Transportation in the Clinton administration. But she also saw the surge of Central Americans coming here to flee war and economic hardship.
“I saw that Latinos were not really represented. I ran with the idea that I wanted to get the Latinos registered and active in politics,” Gutierrez said recently. “I carried applications in my purse, sent [applications] to the kitchen in restaurants, and [left] four or five at the [cash] register.”
That work apparently paid off.
Today, Latinos hold state positions and local office, and work in staff positions throughout state and local government, Gutierrez said. The Maryland Democratic Party said it is following 21 Latino candidates who are running for state and local offices this fall.
Retired State Del. Ana Sol Gutiérrez (D-Montgomery), center, stays active in party politics, voter registration and fielding bilingual calls for the League of Women Voters election hotline. (Photo courtesy Ana Sol Gutiérrez)
“Nine are incumbents, six are new in safe blue seats, two in competitive races, and four in red seats,” said Carter Elliott, a senior adviser for the party. Those candidates “won their primaries for county council positions in Prince George’s, Montgomery, Frederick and Baltimore counties. This also includes multiple Democratic candidates working to flip some council seats blue.”
Afro-Latina House Speaker sets inclusive agenda
Nowhere is the advance of Latinos more evident than in House Speaker Joseline Peña-Melnyk (D-Prince George’s and Anne Arundel), the first Afro-Latino and first immigrant to hold the job.
The groundwork laid by Gutierrez opened the door for Peña-Melnyk, who was elected in 2003 to the College Park City Council, and three years later was voted into the Maryland House. She was unanimously elected speaker last December.
As a child in the Dominican Republic, she was raised by a single mother in a one-room house with a leaky roof. They escaped poverty for a life in the United States, where young Joseline translated documents for her family and others trying to navigate the complex social welfare system.
“When you grow up that way, it gives you perspective on the struggles of life, and it shapes you,” said Peña-Melnyk, who said that life fueled her activism.
Like Gutierrez, when Peña-Melnyk entered political life, few looked or sounded like her. She soon got to work to change that. She and Del. David Fraser-Hidalgo (D-Montgomery) in 2014 co-founded the Maryland Legislative Latino Caucus, which today has 100 members, including eight Latinos and 92 associate members who support its agenda.
Peña-Melnyk says the effort is paying off in legislation that she says lowers energy bills, reins in prescription drug costs, and extends Medicare coverage to undocumented pregnant women — work accomplished with a greater support team.
“Today you have people that are chief of staffs, committee managers, HR directors, working in the governor’s office, in the comptroller’s office, which is so important to have not just Latinos but to have, you know, the workforce reflect the people of Maryland,” she said.
In the run-up to November, she said she has been on a seven-day-a-week campaign across Maryland to get out the vote, and fulfill a promise.
“I told my members that I was going to come to their districts, that I want to get to know all of Maryland,” she said. In late August, she organized a candidate meet-up at Arepa Zone, a Venezuelan restaurant in College Park. Dozens of activists and supporters showed up to celebrate primary victories and listen to what new candidates like 25-year-old Ruben Amaya had to say.
Getting out the youth vote
Born in the United States to Central American immigrants, Amaya’s history in politics began in high school, where he mobilized classmates to fight for gun reform, and to fix infrastructure problems at the school. By his senior year, he was president of the Baltimore County Student Council and in 2022 he ran for the House of Delegates. He finished fourth out of 12 candidates, but garnered political capital in the process.
Ruben Amaya is running for a seat on the Baltimore County Council. (Photo courtesy Robin Stevens Brody)
Amaya is currently the third vice chair of the Maryland Democratic Party and president of the Young Democrats of Maryland, while balancing a day job as an admissions counselor at Stevenson University in Baltimore. In June, he won a crowded primary race for the Baltimore County Council from District 2, and is favored to win in the heavily Democratic district.
“I’m running to be the first Latino to hold elected office in our county’s history. Also, if elected, I’ll be the first Gen Z member to hold elected office as well in Baltimore County,” Amaya said. “I think it’s a big moment, not just for Latinos, but for young people. We’ve been able to inspire a lot of young people to get involved.”
Amaya said his priorities are housing affordability, economic and food security and basic day-to-day county services, applying his known-how of what he learned from his immigrant parents.
“I think that coming to this country with nothing, their mindset was never about what can we do to just reap the benefits. It was about what we can do to contribute back,” he said.
Running for council to be an advocate
For Howard County Council nominee Jessica Nichols, her childhood in rural Texas was “very food insecure.”
“I used to call it ‘peanut butter poor’ because we would often [just] have a jar of peanut butter as the only food in our home,” Nichols said. Her parents fled poverty and violence Central America, she said, and her single mother later moved them east, for better work opportunities.
“That really did inform my service both as a teacher and as board chairperson of Columbia Community Care,” she said of the post-pandemic nonprofit she co-founded to combat food insecurity in Howard County. “Care meant that there was one less little hungry Jessica. That was very impactful to me. It still drives my involvement.”
Nichols, a social studies and resource teacher who was named 2024-25 Howard County Teacher of the Year, has become increasingly engaged in civic life over the last decade. She’s been president of the Columbia Democratic Club, a member of the Democratic Central Committee and the Howard County Education Association, the local teacher’s union.
Barbara Ebel, the Democratic nominee for Montgomery County register of wills, on Primary Election Day in Wheaton with Teresa Ramírez. (Photo courtesy Friends of Barbara Ebel)
When budget cuts threatened county education “was when I realized that the voice that was missing in the room was the voice of educators, because when the educators’ voices are in the room, there’s advocacy for children,” she said of her decision to run. “There’s advocacy for families.”
With no opponent in the Nov. 3 election, Nichols will likely sworn in Dec. 7 as the first African American woman and the first Latina in the post.
A ‘passion … to continue to help people’
Montgomery County register of wills nominee Barbara Ebel said she ran because she decided it was time, after years helping others.
“I found my passion, and it was to continue to help people,” she said at the August gathering in College Park.
Born in Puerto Rico and raised in the Dominican Republic, Ebel parlayed her bilingual skills into a job in 1996 at the Maryland Department of Labor Workforce Development Office as a career counselor, the only Latina hired at the time. Within eight years she was its Montgomery County director, serving along the way as a trainer, business developer and in supervisory positions.
She was elected to the Montgomery County Democratic Central Committee in 2022 and has also served on boards of several nonprofits that advocate for people with disabilities.
Besides the right timing, Ebel decided the job of register of wills would be a good fit. The office administers the legal process of settling a deceased person’s estate, she said. “And, because I went through the process myself, I knew I could really do this job, and, also because I have 26 years of public administration service, have implemented regulations and [am] able to interpret regulations and polices,” she said.
Ebel faces Republican nominee T. Dolores Reyes for the seat, but is favored in Montgomery County, a Democrat stronghold. If elected, she will leave the Labor Department to devote herself full-time to the new position, where she hopes to make the office easier to navigate, easier to understand and welcoming for all county families.
Ebel, who also spoke at the Latino candidate gathering in College Park, said she came away hopeful.
“It was a beautiful synergy to see so many Latinos that really want to do the people’s work. That they are putting themselves out there, running for office to serve the public and make a difference and impact in the community,” she said.
Despite the gains, Peña Melnyk says the fight for equity and representation is ongoing.
“Now more than ever, the immigrant community needs people to speak up for them, to advocate for them, to advocate for human rights. And, we cannot do it alone,” she said. “We need brothers and sisters from different backgrounds. It’s a way to keep us all connected to make sure we make life better for everyone.”
