name: Alaska Beacon
title: Thousands of Alaskans are voting before Election Day. Some ballots won’t be counted until after it.
text:
Demonstrators rally at a No Kings protest in Juneau on Oct. 17, 2026. (Photo by Corinne Smith/Alaska Beacon)Early, in-person voting opened for Alaska’s general election on Monday morning, and as of Wednesday morning, 17,560 Alaskans had already cast their votes.
That includes almost 11,000 people who have voted at early voting sites in the Railbelt, Juneau and Nome, as well as more than 6,000 who had voted absentee by mail, fax or in person. More than 30,000 blank absentee ballots have not yet been returned.
Ahead of the general election, campaigns are urging supporters to vote in advance, and Republicans appear to be taking the advice. More than one in four (26.6%) early votes cast on Monday and Tuesday were from registered Republicans, according to a report from the Alaska Division of Elections.
Registered Democrats made up 19% of early voters during the same period, fewer than one in five. 
During early voting, which takes place in person at select locations, voters’ identity and eligibility are verified on-site, just as it is on Election Day.
With absentee voting, which can take place by mail, a voter’s eligibility and identity is verified after the ballot is submitted. That means absentee votes can be disqualified for technical reasons, such as if the ballot isn’t co-signed by a witness who verifies the voter’s identity, or if it reaches elections officials after a deadline in state law.
Nationally, advance voting — absentee and early voting combined — is happening at a record pace, but here in Alaska, it’s too early to tell whether the state will match that trend.
In other states, more ballots are cast before Election Day than on Election Day itself, but that’s only happened in an Alaska general election once, during the 2020 COVID-19 pandemic emergency.
According to the division’s stated timeline, election night results will include ballots voted at polling places on Election Day and ballots voted at early voting locations from Oct. 19 through Oct. 29.
That means anything voted from Oct. 30 through Nov. 2 won’t be included in the election night total.
The cutoff is for security reasons — it lets the division double-check to make sure someone hasn’t voted both early and on Election Day.
There’s no set timeline for counting absentee ballots. A review board that checks the identities of absentee voters won’t begin working until Oct. 27. 
The board, a multipartisan group of paid, temporary workers, will also look for disqualifying procedural flaws. Already, 81 absentee ballots have been rejected by elections officials. A full count of the reasons for rejection won’t be published until late November or early December.
Whatever ballots the review board manages to check by Election Day will be included in the Election Day total, but many absentee ballots — including some cast before Election Day — won’t be counted until after Election Day. 
Under Alaska law, mailed absentee ballots will be counted if they arrive after Election Day, but only if they were postmarked on or before Election Day and arrive no later than 10 days after Election Day if mailed from within the United States or 15 days after Election Day if  mailed from overseas.
That means election results could change significantly as more ballots are counted after Election Day.
In addition, results from Election Day through Nov. 18 will show only voters’ first choices. In Alaska, voters can rank up to four candidates and a write-in for an office.
If no candidate for an office has more than 50% of the first-choice votes, then a ranked choice tabulation is used to determine the winner.
Because of a policy set by the Alaska Division of Elections in 2022, Alaska doesn’t perform that tabulation until Nov. 18, the deadline for the last absentee ballots to arrive.
Some jurisdictions that use ranked choice voting, such as Portland, Oregon, do multiple tabulations. But others, including Maine and New York City, wait for days after Election Day to do their first tabulation.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: Early voting in North Dakota begins as one group looks to encourage Native voters
text:
Daniela Aki, second from left, and others who joined a Sacred Pipe Resource Center early voting party pose for a photo before going into the Bismarck Event Center on Oct. 22, 2026. (Photo by Jack Dura/North Dakota Monitor)Early in-person voting begins in certain counties throughout North Dakota during the next week, an opportunity one Bismarck-area group is highlighting to encourage Indigenous people to vote.
Staff of the Sacred Pipe Resource Center gathered Thursday with half a dozen voters to all cast their ballots shortly after polls opened for the first day of Burleigh County’s early vote. They donned matching black T-shirts reading “Democracy is Indigenous,” took pictures together and walked inside the Bismarck Event Center to vote.
Voting can be confusing or intimidating and it’s helpful to have support, said Daniela Aki, the center’s director of civic engagement.
“That’s kind of what we want to do is, again, bring down those barriers to voting and say, ‘This isn’t a scary process. We understand it, so come along with us,’” Aki said.
[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: The info you need to cast your ballot.]
Leta Killer, a Mandan, Hidatsa and Arikara Nation citizen, joined them. She said she wants to see change in the world, especially in North Dakota, and supports ballot measures for a $116.5 million Bismarck school bond issue for facility upgrades and free breakfast and lunch for K-12 students statewide.
“We’re all living here together so I would like to see us have a better community, better reaction, better relationships,” Killer said. 
Victoria Fox said the bond referendum motivated her to vote to improve the schools where her 3- and 1-year-old children will one day attend.
“I just thought that it’s only right as a parent to advocate for them,” said Fox, who works as the outreach and development coordinator for the MHA Education Grant Program. 
Sacred Pipe uses its partnerships with other organizations and word of mouth to gather urban Indigenous residents for voting parties, Aki said. 
Sacred Pipe has other initiatives such as civic bingo to talk about candidates and offices and a chaperoned limousine ride for students who have turned 18 to arrive in style to cast their first vote, she said.
“Definitely Sacred Pipe has always kind of encouraged that urban tribal population to get out and vote and to be civically engaged to understand what’s going on in our community and how our voices can help shape those communities,” Aki said.
Voters mark their ballots during the first day of early voting at the Bismarck Event Center on Oct. 22, 2026. (Photo by Jack Dura/North Dakota Monitor)
Identification and address requirements often present a barrier for urban Indigenous voters, many of whom come from different reservations and states, she said. Many of them are transient or might not have an up-to-date ID or a permanent address, or not know they can use a church or shelter as their address, she said. 
Sacred Pipe promoted adding all five tribal IDs in North Dakota into state poll worker training, which Aki said hopefully makes the process easier for Native voters.
Burleigh County Auditor Mark Splonskowski said, “Anybody who comes with a tribal ID, they should be able to be processed, not a problem, and that’s something that we’re happy to make that improvement for.”
Some Native voters might feel nervous or like they don’t belong, Aki said. Voting isn’t an everyday act, she said.
“What I see with urban tribal populations is that if we’re not conditioned to do things like vote, then we don’t vote,” Aki said.
She encouraged people to take advantage of in-person early voting so they can quickly get in and out, rather than risk long lines on Election Day. 
Free school meals debated as a win for families or wrong for North Dakota’s constitution

Stutsman and Ward counties are next for early in-person voting, starting Monday, followed by Cass, Grand Forks and Morton counties on Tuesday and Stark County Oct. 29. Sioux County offers several absentee voting days from Oct. 26-30.
Absentee voting has been available since Sept. 24. Nearly 30,000 North Dakotans had cast their ballots by Thursday afternoon, according to online voting numbers. 
Absentee ballots need to be returned before polls close on Election Day, Nov. 3. Voters can return absentee ballots in person, by mail or county dropbox. Absentee ballots won’t be accepted at the polls on Election Day. Ballots received after Election Day won’t be counted.  
Midterm elections historically have low voter turnout, such as barely 43% in North Dakota in the November 2022 general election. Secretary of State Michael Howe said he’d love to see 100%. 
“The more engagement we can get from every eligible North Dakotan, I think that’s a more representative indication of how the overall electorate feels,” Howe said.

title: Iowa chiropractor fined $1,000 for role in alleged billing scheme
text:
The Iowa Department of Inspections, Appeals and Licensing is responsible for overseeing Iowa's licensing boards. (Photo illustration via Getty Images; logo courtesy of the Iowa Department of Inspections, Appeals and Licensing) State regulators have fined an Iowa chiropractor $1,000 for his role in an alleged scheme to defraud Medicare and other insurers.
The Iowa Board of Chiropractic alleges that in June 2024, Taylor Vanden Wynboom entered into a civil settlement with the federal government “relating to certain billing practices” at his former chiropractic practice, Nova Integrated Health of Ankeny.
The settlement resolved the civil matter with no admission of liability by Wynboom, the board alleges, but resulted in Wynboom agreeing to pay $52,000. The board records do not indicate whether that payment represents a civil penalty or restitution.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The board recently charged Wynboom with failing to notify it within 30 days of any judgments or settlements, and with engaging in unethical conduct or practices that are harmful or detrimental to the public.
Wynboom and the board recently agreed to resolve the disciplinary case with a settlement agreement that calls for Wynboom to pay a $1,000 civil penalty and complete 15 hours of educational training on ethics, plus 15 hours of educational training on the proper billing and coding of patient services.
The Iowa Capital Dispatch was not able to reach Wynboom at his current clinic, the Vero Health Center in West Des Moines.
‘Get paid $$ by insurance and Medicare’
Wynboom was one of several medical providers who in 2020 sued a Florida company called the National Billing Institute. Wynboom and his co-plaintiffs accused the company of “engaging in a widespread scheme to defraud Medicare” while handling their billing for certain services.
According to that lawsuit, a company called Resonant Specific Technologies, or RST, developed a medical device called Sanexas — an electrical stimulation device approved by the FDA for use in treating neuropathy and chronic pain.
The lawsuit asserted that due to “the relative novelty” of the Sanexas device, RST referred medical providers who were its potential customers to the National Billing Institute for assistance in billing Medicare and other insurers for their use of the device on patients. RST’s marketing materials allegedly showed medical providers they could collect as much as $583,000 in annual revenue from using the device, the lawsuit claimed.
In addition, the lawsuit asserted that the National Billing Institute claimed to have developed a proprietary method of billing Medicare for Sanexas treatments that included multivitamin injections.
According to the lawsuit, the institute’s promotional brochures allegedly stated, “GET PAID $$ BY INSURANCE & MEDICARE FOR RST SANEXAS TREATMENTS! … Do you want to drastically increase your revenue while helping your patients ease their chronic pain? Do you want to get reimbursed for your services up to $7,500 from insurance companies?”
Wynboom and his co-plaintiffs alleged the institute “upcoded” their billing for treatments, in part by billing for ingredients not included in the multivitamin injections and by billing for services never delivered.
Later, the lawsuit claims, Wynboom’s Ankeny clinic, Nova Integrated Health, was held liable for more than $100,000 in billings to Blue Cross/Blue Shield.
Court records show the National Billing Institute denied any wrongdoing and in 2022, the claims against the company were dismissed on jurisdictional grounds.
Earlier this year, the Oklahoma attorney general’s office filed a lawsuit against the Neuropathy Treatment Clinic of Tulsa and its owner, James Linn, alleging they ran a multiyear scheme to defraud Medicaid.
The attorney general’s lawsuit claims that Linn and Michael Evans, the founder of the National Billing Institute, “set up a billing scheme that assigned incorrect codes to the Sanexas treatments, such as codes for physical therapy, so that the treatments could be billed to Medicare and commercial insurance.”
Linn and the clinic have denied any wrongdoing. The National Billing Institute is not named as a defendant in the Oklahoma lawsuit.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: U.S. Court of Appeals finds due process violation in ICE incarceration of Iranian refugee in Kansas
text:
A banner showing President Donald Trump hangs on the Department of Justice on Feb. 20, 2026. The U.S. Court of Appeals in the 10th Circuit issued a 2-1 decision regarding fate of an Iranian immigrant who was arrested soon after moving to Kansas in 2025. (Photo by Shauneen Miranda/States Newsroom)TOPEKA — The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 10th Circuit says a federal district court in Kansas misapplied legal standards in an immigration detention case and the federal government violated due-process regulations after incarcerating an Iranian national.
A 2-1 decision Wednesday rejected claims by the administration of President Donald Trump that a six-month detention clock that limited challenges to lawfulness of a detainee’s incarceration could be restarted each time a person was released and detained.
The case involved Kaveh Abedi, who was granted asylum in the United States as a child after his family fled Iran in 1991. He faced removal proceedings in 2002 after a drug possession conviction, but an immigration judge deferred deportation to Iran under the Convention Against Torture. Abedi has complied with terms of his supervised release for more than 20 years, the court’s opinion says.
After moving from California to Kansas in June 2025 with consent of federal officials, Abedi was taken into custody by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. He was informed he could be sent to a third country, the court record says, but he asserted that he wasn’t promptly granted the required informal interview to challenge revocation of his supervised release.
“The government does not dispute Mr. Abedi’s assertion that he has consistently complied with all terms of his order of supervision since he was first released in 2002,” the appellate decision says. “Nor,  does the government dispute that his release was revoked based on the unilateral decision of ICE officials rather than anything he did.”
Abedi filed a habeas corpus petition to contest his detention at the Federal Bureau of Prisons’ Leavenworth prison and to seek an injunction blocking his transfer from Kansas. In October 2025, a U.S. District Court judge in Kansas denied habeas relief and concluded his detention was justified under federal law. The district court said he could file a new habeas petition if detained more than six months.
After eight months in custody, Abedi filed a second habeas petition and a judge allowed his released from immigration detention in February. The federal government sought to dismiss Abedi’s appeal regarding changes in his immigration status because his release from custody made those issues moot.
Court of Appeals Judges Gregory Phillips and Carolyn McHugh, both appointees of President Barack Obama, disagreed with government lawyers on mootness and concluded Abedi could remain at liberty under federal supervision.
Their majority opinion said it was a due process infraction not to conduct a prompt, informal interview with Abedi to challenge the basis of his detention. The judges rejected the Trump administration’s argument that the six-month detention standard could be reset with each re-detention. Instead of resetting, the Court of Appeals said the clock applied to the initial six months after the removal period began and shouldn’t be applied to Abedi’s subsequent stints in detention.
“On the merits, we conclude that the district court committed various legal errors in assessing Mr. Abedi’s claims for relief,” the opinion said.
The U.S. Supreme Court established a six-month period of presumptively reasonable detention in 2001.
U.S. Court of Appeals Judge Allison Eid, appointed by President Donald Trump, offered a dissent to the majority’s opinion.
“Kaveh Abedi has been released from immigration detention,” Eid wrote. “His habeas petition is therefore moot, and no mootness exception applies. Accordingly, I would dismiss this appeal.”

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: SC files more criminal charges involving pregnancy than any other state, report finds
text:
A recent report from national nonprofit Pregnancy Justice found more charges involving pregnancy filed in South Carolina over the past three years than in any other state. (Stock photo/Getty Images)COLUMBIA — South Carolina charged at least 381 women with crimes related to their pregnancy over the past three years, far more than any other state, a national advocacy nonprofit found in a report released this week.
While the report focused on the aftermath of the U.S. Supreme Court’s 2022 ruling on abortion, almost all of the cases documented in South Carolina involved allegations of drug and alcohol abuse during pregnancy, not an abortion, the Pregnancy Justice report found.
The 381 women charged in South Carolina represent more than one-third of the 902 cases researchers found nationwide. Oklahoma ranks second with 222 cases.
The true nationwide total is almost certainly higher, the national advocacy group said. The report is a precursor to a more complete study set for release in 2028, so the numbers will likely continue to rise as researchers discover more cases, said Wendy Bach, who co-led the study.
South Carolina stands out partly because court information was easier to access here, she said.
Substance abuse and abortion laws
U.S. Supreme Court’s June 2022 ruling that the U.S. Constitution does not guarantee a right to an abortion overturned a nearly half-century precedent established by Roe v. Wade and returned the legality of abortions to states to decide, resulting in a hodgepodge of laws nationwide.
In South Carolina, most abortions are illegal after six weeks of pregnancy under a law that took effect with a state Supreme Court ruling in August 2023. In pregnancies due to rape or incest, abortions are legal through the 12th week. Other exceptions to the ban are medical complications that threaten the pregnant woman’s life or anomalies in the fetus so severe they’re unsurvivable after birth.
That law does not allow criminal penalties for women who seek or obtain abortions.
South Carolina’s high number of cases is likely the result of a nearly 30-year-old court ruling, said Bach, who is also a law professor at the University of Tennessee-Knoxville.
In 1997, the South Carolina Supreme Court ruled a fetus counts as a child, allowing prosecutors to charge pregnant women under child abuse laws. The two other states with similar rulings, Oklahoma and Alabama, had the second- and third-highest numbers of cases.
While other states have used those charges as well, the numbers are higher in places with court precedent “because it’s been explicitly blessed by the Supreme Court as a legal theory that you can use to prosecute someone,” said Madalyn Wasilczuk, an associate professor at the University of South Carolina who co-led the study.
“What really strikes me is how normalized these kinds of prosecutions have become in our state,” Wasilczuk said.
Nationwide, most of the charges found by researchers involved women using drugs and alcohol during pregnancy. That was true in South Carolina as well, where 377 of 381 cases involved substance abuse, though some may have involved other charges as well, according to the nonprofit.
Thirteen of the 902 cases documented across the country stem directly from getting or trying to get an abortion. The nonprofit declined to say how many, if any, of those 13 women were South Carolinians, citing concerns about identifying them.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Data questions
The difficulty in tracking down data in other states likely contributed to South Carolina’s lopsided total, Bach said.
In the Palmetto State, researchers were able to get county-by-county breakdowns of charges involving pregnancy. Getting similar data from court systems in other states was much more difficult. Researchers relied instead on news reports and tips from advocates, Bach said.
If direct comparisons were possible, South Carolina would likely still be among the nation’s highest for pregnancy-related charges due to the legal precedent, Bach and Wasilczuk said.
How much the true numbers differ is unclear.
“I think we both believe that there are more cases in South Carolina than in some other states, but also, we know that there are states that we just can’t get data for,” Wasilczuk said.
The data collection methods also left some questions in the report’s findings.
The numbers aren’t comparable to previous studies from the nonprofit because researchers used different methods, which produced different results, Bach said. That means the data can’t show whether the number of cases increased over previous years.
And researchers didn’t track the outcomes of cases, making it impossible to say how many women were actually found guilty of the charges or sent to prison.
Takeaways
The report’s findings point to “an increasing dedication to the idea that the fetus can be the victim of a crime that the pregnant individual commits,” Bach said.
“So, the body of the pregnant person can be a crime scene, and the fetus is the victim of that crime,” she said.
The report found 70 cases nationwide involving the loss of a fetus, whether through an abortion or a miscarriage, Bach said. That seems to be on the rise after the Dobbs decision, likely because of anti-abortion laws, she said.
She was accused of murder after losing her pregnancy. SC woman now tells her story.

“The level of suspicion and criminal investigation of pregnancy loss that is happening across the nation after Dobbs is striking and disturbing,” Bach said.
One prominent case involving a pregnancy loss came out of South Carolina. In 2023, before the state’s abortion ban took effect, a college junior was charged with homicide by child abuse after unexpectedly giving premature birth in the toilet of her apartment.
A grand jury later declined to indict her, clearing her of the charges. The charges came from the woman leaving the baby in the toilet, not the premature birth itself, KFF Health News reported.
When prosecutors charge pregnant women under child abuse laws, they are usually trying to protect children and families, Bach said. But criminal charges might do the opposite, she said.
A pregnant woman struggling with addiction who hears she could lose custody of her baby or get sent to prison probably won’t tell a doctor she needs help, Bach said.
In 360 of South Carolina’s reported 381 cases, court filings suggest evidence came directly from doctors and nurses, who are mandated to report crimes, Bach said. At the same time, though, that could erode trust between a woman who needs help and the doctor who could provide it, she said.
“They know, ‘If I am struggling with substance use disorder and I am pregnant, and I go to my doctor, and I tell them that, these guys are going to hand that information over to the family policing system, and/or to the cops,’” Bach said. “Why would anyone in their right mind seek care?”

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: DOJ is sending election monitors to Utah polls this November
text:
Utah Lt. Gov. Deidre Henderson speaks to reporters at the Utah State Capitol on Oct. 22, 2026. (Alixel Cabrera/Utah News Dispatch)The U.S. Department of Justice is sending election monitors to Utah polls to oversee the Nov. 3 elections, Lt. Gov. Deidre Henderson learned on Wednesday. The move comes amid pressure from the agency as Henderson, Utah’s chief election officer, refuses to release private voter data to the federal government. 
The Department of Justice has sent election monitors to other states before on a smaller scale, usually in response to a civil rights violation. In Utah, the agency sent monitors to supervise elections in San Juan County in 2024. But, Henderson anticipates their presence won’t interfere with the election, and voters may not even notice their presence, she told reporters on Thursday.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“We’re not really sure what to expect, except that they did give us some assurances that I think are good. They won’t be approaching voters. They won’t be wearing any sort of insignia. They have said that they will give us any feedback after the election is over on any challenges or issues that they saw,” Henderson said. “So I think things will be pretty normal. I want to make sure voters are calm and know that things are going to be OK.”
To Utah’s chief election officer’s surprise, the DOJ says it has been investigating her since 2025

Some details about the monitors’ deployment in the state are still unavailable. Henderson said she’s unaware of how many are coming or to which locations they will be sent; however, Salt Lake County has been notified it will receive at least one. Henderson is expecting to learn more about the monitors in a meeting before Election Day.
Henderson is uncertain about why the DOJ is sending the monitors to Utah. While she’s been threatened with criminal prosecution over voters’ data, she said the department is also sending monitors to states that aren’t involved in election litigation.
“I welcome any kind of scrutiny that the administration wants to give to the state of Utah. I am confident in our processes, and you know what? If they uncover some sort of problem, if we’re violating someone’s civil rights in some way, I absolutely want to know about it. We rely on people to tell us when there are problems. We can’t be everywhere in the state,” she said. “So, if any problems are found, we absolutely will be grateful for that information and look into it and correct it if we can.”
Monitors are mandated to only observe and take notes, Jake Bachand, an attorney at the DOJ’s Civil Rights Division said in a letter to the lieutenant governor. They will dress in business casual clothing and won’t be allowed to use any DOJ identifiers. They aren’t allowed to talk to voters inside polling places or to carry firearms.


Let us know what you think...


 

The goal, according to the letter, is to monitor for compliance with federal voting rights laws, including people with disabilities’ access to the ballot box, among other civil rights assurances. 
“I think that they are looking just overall how the elections are being run to make sure everything’s on the up and up,” Henderson said. “You know what? They are in Utah. We have open processes. The public can go watch any of these processes. So, frankly, I welcome that. I welcome people looking and examining. What I don’t welcome is any kind of interference.”  
While Henderson’s office will keep an eye on the deployment, Utah is not planning on following Minnesota’s lead to have state monitors to supervise federal monitors. 
“What we have done is given our county clerks and the public very specific instructions on what to do and how to do it. So we have laws that pertain to any kind of election monitor, and those laws apply to these federal monitors as well,” Henderson said. “So we’re making sure everybody’s aware of what those laws are.” 
Henderson encouraged voters who are worried about going to an in-person polling location to submit their ballots at a drop box ahead of Election Day. 
“I encourage the more people do that, the better. Because honestly, if we have more people voting early and getting those ballots processed early, we’ll have more robust results on election night anyway. So vote early,” she said.

name: VTDigger
title: Bernie Sanders makes rare Vermont campaign appearance, stumping with Amanda Janoo to push universal primary care
text:
U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vermont speaks during an event with democratic gubernatorial candidate Amanda Janoo in Winooski on Thursday, October 22, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
WINOOSKI — Bernie Sanders is a regular sight on the campaign trail — just not much in his home state. On Thursday, though, Vermont’s independent U.S. senator stood alongside Amanda Janoo and voiced support for the gubernatorial candidate’s proposal to offer primary healthcare to everyone in the state, free of charge. 
“I think Amanda’s desire to bring, among other things, universal primary care to the state of Vermont is exactly what we need,” Sanders said in a press conference outside the Community Health Centers of Burlington clinic in Winooski. If she can do it, he added, it would be “an extraordinary achievement.” 
Sanders endorsed Janoo, the Democratic and Progressive parties’ nominee, over Republican Gov. Phil Scott earlier this month. The senator and former Burlington mayor had not endorsed a Scott challenger since backing David Zuckerman in 2020. It’s even rarer, though, for Sanders to make a campaign appearance alongside a state-level candidate for office in Vermont, as he did Thursday. 
None of the previous Scott challengers Sanders has endorsed, of course, have won. That includes Sue Minter in 2016 and Christine Hallquist in 2018. But Sanders told reporters Thursday that Janoo has so far been doing everything right.
“She is a progressive candidate who’s reaching out to working class people and in a variety of ways, I think, fills the agenda of what a strong, progressive governor can do,” he said.
Sanders has devoted much of his time in the leadup to the Nov. 3 election traveling around the country to drum up support for Democratic and progressive candidates. He was in Houston on Tuesday to rally support for Texas Democrats and was in Florida days before with that state’s Democratic U.S. Senate candidate, Angie Nixon.
Next month’s contests will be “the most important midterm election in the history of the United States,” Sanders said Thursday.

READ MORE

Janoo has proposed paying for universal primary care by raising income taxes on the state’s wealthiest residents. She’s cited modeling from the Fair Share for Vermont campaign that found that a 2% tax surcharge on personal income above $250,000 and an 8% surcharge on personal income over $500,000 could raise $344 million in annual state revenue.
Scott, for his part, has expressed skepticism about the viability of a universal primary care system though has not ruled out the idea entirely. The five-term governor has said he favors healthcare policy changes that reduce government regulations, such as an executive order he signed in July allowing insurers to price premiums partially based on age.
Janoo says details of how her plan would work, and exactly what services it would include, would need to be hashed out after she gets into office and has access to the resources of the state government. At Thursday’s press conference, she said that “the nice thing about the program I’m proposing is that it’s very scalable” and that she would be OK starting with piloting just a handful of publicly funded primary care doctors in certain cities and towns.
“We want to make sure that we are doing, like, a proper design with (the state Agency of Human Services), working with the Joint Fiscal Office and also the Legislature, right, to ensure that there’s that appropriate funding in order to ensure its universality,” she said of a primary care program. 
Ultimately, though, Janoo said she sees universal primary care as just a stepping stone to something larger: a full-on publicly funded healthcare system, like Vermont tried to enact in the 2010s only to abandon the effort over concerns it was too costly. Universal healthcare is a goal Janoo shares with Sanders, who made “Medicare for All” a key tenet of his 2016 and 2020 presidential campaigns. 
“It’s about the kind of society we want to live in,” Janoo said Thursday. “Do we want to believe that access to basic healthcare should depend on your income, your employment or your insurance company? Or, do we believe that keeping people healthy is something we all have a stake in — and that we can organize our resources to make it happen?”

name: Delaware
title: Chamber endorsements revive Delaware Way tradition of people over party
text:
With four Democrats and four Republicans receiving support, Delaware’s leading business organization offers a reminder that a candidate’s record and willingness to work across party lines can matter more than political affiliation.
WILMINGTON, Del. — At a time when national politics increasingly encourages voters to choose sides, the Delaware State Chamber of Commerce is offering a reminder of an older First State tradition: Judge the person, not just the party.
The Chamber announced endorsements Thursday, Oct. 22, of eight candidates in the Nov. 3 general election — four Democrats and four Republicans.
The selections reflect a longstanding Delaware political culture in which personal relationships, individual records and a willingness to work together have often mattered more than party loyalty.
Known as the Delaware Way, that tradition has come under increasing pressure as national political divisions influence state and local elections.
But the Chamber’s endorsements suggest that, at least within Delaware’s business community, there remains value in evaluating candidates individually.

In its announcement, the Chamber said the candidates have demonstrated a willingness to engage with employers and consider how government decisions affect jobs, economic growth and Delaware’s competitiveness.
The organization said its endorsement process considers voting records, past engagement with the business community and positions on issues affecting employers and employees.
That approach does not require candidates to agree on every issue. It places greater emphasis on their records and willingness to consider different perspectives.
A reminder of the Delaware Way
Delaware’s small size has historically encouraged a political culture different from the increasingly partisan environment in Washington.
Republicans and Democrats frequently worked together, and voters were often familiar with candidates as neighbors, business owners, community volunteers or local officials.
Former Republican Gov. Mike Castle defended that tradition in 2012, arguing that Delaware’s size made cooperation essential to competing with larger states for jobs and economic opportunities.  Castle described bipartisan cooperation as central to Delaware’s past success.
But that tradition has become more complicated.
Critics argue that the Delaware Way can also protect established political relationships and discourage challenges to those in power. Gov. Matt Meyer campaigned in 2024 as an outsider willing to challenge that political culture.
The Chamber’s endorsements suggest another way of looking at the tradition: Cooperation across party lines does not necessarily mean protecting the political establishment. It can also mean evaluating individual candidates on their willingness to listen, compromise and be accountable for their decisions.
Business interests cross party lines
For Delaware employers, many of the issues facing state government are not easily divided into Republican and Democratic priorities.
Energy costs, taxes, workforce development, education, regulations and government spending affect businesses regardless of their owners’ political affiliations.
The Chamber has consistently advocated policies intended to improve Delaware’s economic competitiveness while working with lawmakers from both parties.
Its bipartisan approach is not new. In 2024, the organization endorsed 14 General Assembly candidates in the general election, including Democrats and Republicans.
This year’s smaller list of eight endorsements suggests a selective approach, although the Chamber has not publicly explained why it endorsed fewer candidates.
The choices also raise questions about what constitutes a business-friendly candidate in a state where Democrats control the governor’s office and both legislative chambers.
For the Chamber, maintaining relationships with members of both parties may be as important as supporting candidates who agree with every position on its legislative agenda.
A different question for voters
The Chamber’s announcement comes as voters begin early voting ahead of the Nov. 3 general election.
Its endorsements are not evidence that Delaware voters are abandoning party loyalty. Nor do they establish that the Delaware Way is returning.
But they provide a timely example of an organization evaluating candidates through a different lens.
Rather than asking only whether a candidate is a Republican or Democrat, the Chamber’s approach focuses attention on other questions: Has the candidate listened to constituents and employers? What does the candidate’s record demonstrate? And is the candidate willing to consider solutions that cross party lines?
In an election season dominated by national political divisions, the endorsements offer a reminder of a tradition that has long shaped Delaware politics.
In a state small enough for voters to know many of their elected officials personally, party labels may tell only part of the story.
Whether more Delaware voters embrace that approach in 2026 remains to be seen.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Manresa Wilds project gets key approval from Norwalk zoning board
text:
A billionaire couple’s ambitious proposal to transform a shuttered power plant overlooking Long Island Sound into a park and event space cleared an important hurdle on Wednesday with the approval of the project’s “master plan” by zoning officials in Norwalk.
The Norwalk Planning and Zoning Commission voted unanimously to approve a special zoning district for the proposed Manresa Wilds development, which covers a 125-acre peninsula that was for decades home to a coal and oil-burning power plant.
The approval clears the way for the project’s developers, Austin and Allison McChord, to continue finalizing their designs for the site within a framework that includes allowances for private events, live music, boat rentals and a restaurant or brewpub. The McChords have committed $410 million to the project, including environmental remediation.
Future phases of the project will require additional approvals from zoning officials, along with more detailed traffic studies, before construction can begin.
“We founded Manresa Island Corp. to take responsibility for this site’s cleanup and create something enduring for Norwalk and the region,” the McChords said in a statement following the vote. “Thousands of people have helped shape Manresa Wilds over the past two years, and we’re grateful to the community and the Commission for the care they’ve brought to this process. This vote brings us one step closer to unlocking a remarkable stretch of Norwalk’s waterfront to the public again.”
While the project was initially hailed as philanthropic endeavor to create park space while preserving the old plant buildings, Manresa Wilds also attracted criticism from neighbors who said it would lead to traffic jams, noise pollution and other disturbances within nearby residential communities. 
More than 200 residents signed a petition urging Norwalk’s P&Z Commission to reject the application for a special zoning district and for the McChords to come back with a more toned-down version of the project.
In order to ease community concerns, the Manresa Wilds team hosted multiple meetings and received more than 4,000 comments on the project’s design, according a press release. The McChords also agreed to drop proposals to allow a hotel on the property, in addition to reducing outdoor lighting and capping parking at 200 spaces available through a reservation system.
Ed Haas, a resident of South Norwalk, said he was among the initial skeptics of the project when it was first proposed. But after meeting with the McChords’ team and encouraging them to incorporate murals and other art installations in the design of the project, Haas said he is now “leaning towards” supporting the project.
“It seemed like they were trying to do too much,” Haas said. “Now that I’ve met with them a couple of times, it seems to be evening out with the community’s input.”
Under the rules approved by Norwalk’s P&Z Commission, Manresa Wilds will be limited to hosting no more than four events each month that draw between 150 and 400 guests. Larger events, with crowds up to 800 people, will be limited to four times a year. On days when multiple events are scheduled, the maximum overall capacity will be capped at 1,000 people.
At one point during Wednesday’s meeting, the commission also debated limiting outings by school groups to Norwalk students, an idea that was rejected by commissioners such as Ana Tabachneck. The commission tabled the idea of exempting school groups more broadly from Manresa Wilds’ event permitting requirements.
“I think this is a gift to all,” Tabachneck said. “We reap a lot of the benefits, we also handle some of the downsides or have to grapple with some of the challenges. But overall this is a benefit to us.”
Jan Schaefer, president of the Manresa Association, a neighborhood group, responded to a request for comment Thursday with a statement saying the commission was “seeming to give great consideration to neighbors’ concerns, and they made modifications to address the issues that were raised about noise, lights, and traffic.”
“The McChords were also sensitive to the impact for neighbors, and they made several changes throughout this process to scale back the scope of the park. While traffic remains a big concern, we hope this will be addressed by the City as they consider applications for the future phases,” Schaefer said.
The first phase of the project — a collection of walking trails, open fields and outdoor classrooms known as the Northern Forest — is already under construction and is expected to open next year. That phase had been approved prior to Wednesday’s meeting under the site’s prior residential zoning designation.
The next phase, which includes the renovation of the old power plant’s turbine hall and administration building, is targeted for completion in 2032.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Commentary: New treasurer, same State Health Plan mistakes
text:
(Stock photo by Wichayada Suwanachun/Getty Images) North Carolina Treasurer Brad Briner says moving many Atrium Health providers and facilities out of network for the State Health Plan is just “behind the scenes bookkeeping,” and that members who choose Atrium can be “held harmless” by Atrium if it chooses to. That overlooks how the tiered plan works. Out-of-network status raises costs for members, and it can raise them for the State Health Plan as well.
I teach economics and personal finance, and I raised this concern with the treasurer’s office months ago. Out-of-network care requires members to meet a deductible before coinsurance begins, which makes that care significantly more expensive for patients. In some cases, an out-of-network visit actually costs the State Health Plan less than the same visit in-network.
One goal of the new tiered plan is to steer members to preferred in-network providers. The new tiers quadruple the out-of-network deductible, strengthening that push. But steering members toward care that costs the plan more undercuts claims that the new system will save a significant amount of money.
Lower member bills are not lower plan costs
Members who want smaller bills can move into the network. For the individual, that is sound advice. For the plan, it works against the stated goal, because the plan carries a much larger share of in-network costs. A quadrupled deductible saves the plan money only if members keep paying out of pocket or skip care. When members do what the policy encourages, changing to an in-network provider, the plan’s costs increase.
Steering benefits providers, not necessarily the plan
Preferred-provider arrangements trade lower negotiated prices for a promise of patient volume. Higher deductibles and removing a system like Atrium are tools for delivering that promise. Providers who gain patients benefit, but it is not clear the plan or taxpayers do. A plan’s first obligation should be to its members and to the taxpayers who help fund it.
Taken together, these concerns point to a basic problem of incentives. A policy that rewards the behavior that costs the plan more, and penalizes the behavior that costs it less, deserves scrutiny.
A familiar pattern
Briner has criticized his predecessor’s approach, which is why the similarities are troubling. In 2019, then-Treasurer Folwell came within weeks of removing most health providers from the network just before open enrollment. Removing a large system like Atrium now raises similar concerns about in-network access, just as members are expected to choose their health plan.
The Clear Pricing Project also relied on steering members toward certain providers. Providers benefited financially, and the plan lost around $150 million annually for several years. When steering incentives are not aligned with the plan’s interests, costs can rise instead of fall.
I do not doubt that the treasurer’s office is trying to manage costs. However, its current approach appears to replicate the same approach that Briner criticized in his predecessor.
Open enrollment has begun, and members like me are choosing coverage without a clear explanation of how continued “steering” through quadrupling out-of-network deductibles and removing providers from the network will save the health plan money. These are matters of arithmetic and incentives, not politics. I hope the treasurer will address them publicly and promptly, while members can still use the answers. State Health Plan members and the taxpayers who help fund their coverage deserve transparency and effective fiscal responsibility.

name: Source New Mexico
title: Course correction needed for New Mexico universal childcare fund, legislative economist says
text:
A legislative economist told lawmakers on Oct. 21, 2026, that New Mexico’s early childcare trust fund, which supports the state’s universal childcare program, will be empty by 2048 without adjustments. (Photo from Mrs. Olga's Daycare in Las Cruces shot in September 2026 by Leah Romero for Source NM)The New Mexico Legislature’s chief economist told lawmakers this week that without adjustments, New Mexico’s early childhood trust fund will be unable to support the state’s new universal childcare program by 2048. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The state created the Early Childhood Education and Care Fund in 2020 with an appropriation of approximately $300 million in order to fund the newly formed Early Childhood Education and Care Department. Since then, the fund has ballooned to $11 billion from deposits of surplus oil and gas tax revenues. 
But two large withdrawals have threatened the fund’s long-term health, Ismael Torres, chief New Mexico legislative finance economist, told lawmakers on the interim Economic and Rural Development and Policy Committee on Wednesday.
During the 2025 legislative session, lawmakers diverted $1.9 billion of deposits meant for the fund in order to support the Medicaid Trust Fund and the Behavioral Health Trust Fund.
Then, earlier this year, Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham signed the state’s universal child care program into law, which included up to $700 million from the fund. That pushed the fund’s payouts above its returns, Torres said, and threatened its long-term sustainability.
By 2031, he added, the fund’s balance will shrink at an “exponential rate” and will be empty — and therefore unable to support the universal childcare program — by 2048.
State Rep. Doreen Gallegos (D-Las Cruces), who co-sponsored the creation of the early childhood trust fund, said that lawmakers “are busy patting ourselves on the back” about being the first state in the nation to offer universal childcare, but “for us to be sitting here…looking for solutions for solvency is not good.”
​Torres said the way to “course correct” is to “find other sources of revenue than the trust fund” to fund universal childcare — such as recurring dollars from the state’s general fund — and to “slow down the withdrawals, which is the primary method by which you can bring the fund back into solvency.” 
The Early Childhood Education and Care Department is “very focused on ensuring the sustainability” of the universal childcare program, Hailey Heinz, ECECD director of policy, research and quality initiatives, told lawmakers. The program, she added, is showing positive results for families in New Mexico.
ECECD’s 2026 Family Engagement and Satisfaction survey shows that 93% of families utilizing New Mexico’s universal childcare policy report a positive impact on their well-being. When asked to describe early child programs’ impact on their families’ lives, survey respondents named direct-cost relief more than any other theme.
Rep. Patricia Roybal Caballero (D-Albuquerque) praised the universal childcare program as a way to “uplift the working poor” and urged lawmakers to be “careful, intentional and implicit” as they approach the next legislative session and work to solve the issue of early childhood fund solvency.
​“The rest of the nation is looking to us for all of our successes and our pitfalls and how we’re addressing them,” Roybal Caballero said.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Flimmaker explores Mississippi’s lack of public defenders in ‘The Dead Zone’
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Mississippi Today Ideas is a platform for thoughtful ideas to be shared about our state’s past, present and future. Opinions expressed in guest essays are the author’s own and do not necessarily represent those of Mississippi Today. You can read more about the section here.   



I first heard William Faulkner’s quote “To understand the world you must first understand a place like Mississippi” from Chris Routh, former Hinds County deputy public defender.
These words were an invitation that would come to resonate far more deeply over the next five years as my husband and I traversed across the state, two parts of a small but mighty filmmaking team behind The Dead Zone, a Sundance-supported feature documentary exploring the presumption of innocence in America. 
As a documentarian, I embed myself in people’s lives, sometimes for years, to intimately understand their lived experiences in pursuit of telling stories that reveal something deeper about the human condition and the systems that shape us. 
Faulkner’s words took on a complicated duality. The state became both a cautionary tale – a place where the failures of our criminal legal system are impossible to ignore – and a source of unexpected hope for what it might take to confront one of the most urgent human rights crises of our time.
When I first embarked on this film back in 2021, America was experiencing a racial reckoning over social injustices and a surge of criminal justice reforms ensued. Progressive prosecutors were elected across the country and public sentiment in favor of bail reform gained momentum.
However, as fears of rising crime skyrocketed, and tensions over constitutional rights exploded, criminal justice reforms started to go in a pendulum swing. Our cultural and political silos made it nearly impossible to collaborate on meaningful solutions.
Nearly 400,000 people were stuck in jail before trial, presumed innocent. This is the equivalent of nearly every Ole Miss homegame football attendee over the course of a season being detained behind bars.
I set out to understand this issue, why the pretrial population had skyrocketed and how our so-called ideals –  like the presumption of innocence, due process, equality under the law – clashed with our lived realities.
I originally set out to explore issues like cash bail, unlawful detention and their relationship to community safety. Yet an old adage in filmmaking is that you might start with an idea of what your film is, but over time the true film will reveal itself to you. And if you end in the same place you started, it probably wasn’t that good of a story in the first place.
After speaking with dozens of legal experts, directly impacted people, advocates and law enforcement officers, I realized I needed to take a systemic approach and document the story from multiple perspectives inside the system –  public defenders, judges, prosecutors and the accused.
One name kept emerging from across our conversations: Public Defender Chris Routh in Jackson. It turned out Mississippi was part of the epicenter of change and hope where I needed to be. The story was revealing itself.
The night before we met Chris, my husband and I sampled beers at Fertile Ground brewery to ease into the filming week in Jackson. The next day we drove to the Hinds County Public Defender’s office downtown. The receptionist buzzed us in, and I immediately noticed the flickering fluorescent lights, magazines from years past scattered across the lobby coffee tables, and a few Christmas decorations still up despite it being May.
But what really caught my eye was a sign on a wall that said: “I hear much of people’s calling out to punish the guilty, but very few are concerned to clear the innocent.” Daniel Defoe.
We sat down and got to know Chris and Chief Public Defender Gail Lowry. Little did they know that this first meeting would inspire a years-long collaboration in the making of this film. We embedded in their office and in Hinds County courtrooms observing quietly and patiently as their undersized but dedicated team took on thousands of cases – from bail hearings to trials – during record turnover.
Over the course of the first year of our filming, their office lost 10 out of 12 lawyers, all of them to higher paying positions that the defender’s office couldn’t match.
Chris and Gail persevered through the storm, working tirelessly to bring in additional funding, attract, train and retain new lawyers all the while managing their own heavy caseloads. A Sisyphean call, but an essential one.
About 80% of defendants in Mississippi require a public defender, yet it’s one of just five states in the country that lack a statewide public defender system.
This is one reason Andre de Gruy, state public defender for Mississippi, has been fighting to address a lack of public defenders, a shortage exacerbated by a myriad of issues like poverty, lack of alternatives to pretrial detention and prosecutorial accountability.
These factors created the perfect storm of people waiting years for their trial in overcrowded jails not convicted of any crime. The gruesome reality of this limbo is that an estimated two people die every day in jail in America awaiting trial.
Unique to Mississippi, the accused oftentimes lack consistent public defenders and could be held with no time limit. This limbo is referred to as the “Dead Zone,” a term used by Jerry Mitchell who reported on this situation.
Attorney Michael Carr, who represented indigent clients in the Delta, also told us that to understand the human toll of the Dead Zone we had to talk to one man in particular: Duane Lake.
Duane Lake stands for a portrait outside the abandoned Coahoma County Jail in Clarksdale, Mississippi on Jan. 10, 2022. He spent six years in jailfor a crime in didn’t commit. The case against him was dismissed. Credit: Rory Doyle/MCIR
Duane grew up in Clarksdale, and was the father of three young children at the time he was arrested for a triple homicide. He went on to spend over six years trapped in a mold and rat-infested jail awaiting trial. His charge carried the threat of the death penalty and legislators had been floating bringing back death by firing squad at one point.
For three of those years, Duane was stuck in legal limbo without a lawyer – the Dead Zone – because there was no one to represent him between his arrest and his indictment. His indictment took three years in part due to how infrequently the grand jury meets and a lack of available defenders.
We met Duane about a year after a jury found him not guilty. He had moved out of state to Kentucky to rebuild his life. Unlike someone who is convicted and later exonerated, Duane was not entitled to any compensation or recourse because he was held pretrial. Not even an apology.
Like Chris, Duane embraced us cautiously but with open arms. We first filmed him making Mississippi soul food delicacies in his new home in Louisville: grits with plenty of butter and a little bit of sugar. Very quickly, Duane let us into his world and opened up to us, letting us document his journey of building a new life while confronting the realities of what he had just lived through and lost.
Filmmakers inhabit a privileged but complex role. Those privileges include seeing the world through new perspectives and getting to witness the lives of others. 
In Jackson, we traveled through elevators at the state public defender’s office gilded with reliefs of Robert E. Lee (the building’s original namesake), through the breezy doors of Hal and Mal’s restaurant, up the carpeted stairs of First Baptist Church for public safety speakouts and through the speakeasy hallway behind Brent’s drugs in Jackson’s Fondren community.
We sampled hot tamales in Cleveland, on the way to the crossroads of Clarksdale and savored the best gumbo we’ve ever had – homemade by Chris himself. We filmed wind turbines whipping in the horizon as cotton rows – an omnipresent reminder of the state’s past – reflected hazy pink sunsets along the Delta highway.
These details may seem ancillary, but they became part of how we came to know Mississippi and, more importantly, how we came to know the people who invited us into their lives.
For us, filmmaking begins with relationships. We believe you have to build trust before you can ask someone to share the most vulnerable parts of their lives. That takes time, honesty, consistency and a willingness to be transparent about who you are, why you’re there, and what you hope to understand. It also means showing up long after the cameras stop rolling.
For us, we couldn’t look away from the injustices we came to witness and the stories we heard from Duane and Chris. We kept coming back and we kept being invited back.
From Chris to Duane and our two additional main participants – Judge Genesis Draper in Houston and Memphis District Attorney Steve Mulroy – this story revealed itself as a powerful, intimate portrait of our country at a crucial inflection point and of the people on the frontlines protecting our justice system against insurmountable odds. Our film asks us all to ponder: Do we still uphold and believe in the core values we claim to? Or is the presumption of innocence dead?
Chris and Duane showed us the importance of keeping on this story, why it matters and the impact it could make. Through all four of our protagonists’ personal journeys, we observed challenges to improving a system that was designed to be broken, but also opportunities for change and above all, the importance of bearing witness.
By cutting through partisan politics and courtroom silos, we hope our film can disarm preconceived notions allowing audiences to embrace a different trajectory forward – one that puts humanity, equality and compassion on a pedestal.
In late 2023, inspired in large part by Duane’s story, Mississippi passed legislation ending the Dead Zone. By law, people who can’t afford a lawyer are now entitled to continuous representation throughout the pretrial process starting from their initial appearance. In theory no longer will a person go without a lawyer between arrest and indictment like Duane.
Mississippi state Public Defender André de Gruy stands in front of his office in Jackson in May 2025. Credit: Imani Khayyam for The Marshall Project
Earlier this year, Gail Lowry fought and received additional funding for the Hinds County public defenders office. Andre de Gruy is working with groups like the Deason Criminal Justice Reform Center to forward new pilot programs across the state to dramatically decrease unnecessary lengthy pretrial detention and provide adequate representation from the start.
Indeed, Faulker was right that Mississippi is a lens through which we can better understand our country, and the world.
When we widen the lens, Mississippi could still be the example for the rest of the country. The cradle of our nation’s most challenging issues could also possess the heart of our greatest solutions. 

Emily Thomas is a documentary filmmaker, cinematographer and founder of Lemon Tree Productions. Her work is rooted in intimately documenting the human experience to illuminate pressing social justice and environmental issues. She recently was the cinematographer on Baby Doe (SXSW ‘25), the associate producer of Bodyguard of Lies (Tribeca ‘25, Paramount+), and director of Last Days at Paradise High (The New Yorker). As a cinematographer, she has worked on films for Netflix, VICE, The New Yorker, PBS and Frontline. Previously, she was a journalist for VICE, Storyful and The Huffington Post, and was an open source investigator at the Human Rights Center. She is a PGA Create alum, a Prison Journalism Project mentor and a graduate of UC Berkeley’s Graduate School of Journalism. She is currently directing the feature documentary, The Dead Zone, and is based in Baltimore.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: CT Education Dept. hires special ed attorney to improve complaint process
text:
The Connecticut State Department of Education announced Wednesday it has hired Kathleen Reiser to fill a newly-created role of dedicated special education attorney.
The department created the position to address longstanding dissatisfaction with the state complaint system, a key tool for parents who feel schools are not meeting their children’s special education needs. Parent attorneys said the state’s findings in those complaints were often legally suspect. In January, the consulting firm WestEd recommended CSDE hire a special education attorney to address the issue.
In a written statement, Education Commissioner Charlene Russell-Tucker said hiring Reiser was part of a broader effort to strengthen the state’s special education systems.
“Kathleen brings extensive experience with special education law, administrative leadership, and dispute resolution that will be invaluable as we continue this important work,” Russell-Tucker said.
The stakes for parents and children in special education can be high. Under the federal Individuals with Disabilities Education Act, all children are entitled to what is known as a free appropriate public education, or FAPE. That standard is meant to ensure schools are meeting every student’s learning needs. If parents in Connecticut feel a school is misbehaving or coming up short, a state complaint is often the most accessible way to force changes.
After parents file a complaint, investigators from CSDE gather information and render a decision on whether school leaders and staff did anything wrong and what, if anything, they needs to change. Critics say that without a lawyer involved, those decisions have often lacked a strong legal foundation, putting the integrity and usefulness of the process at risk.
Andrew Feinstein, a special education attorney and member of Special Education Equity for Kids in Connecticut, pointed to one decision the department issued about seven years ago that has continued to cause “a lot of heartburn.”
The decision “basically says that the email correspondence is not an educational record which has to be disclosed to parents unless it’s independently printed out,” Feinstein said. “It seems to me completely inconsistent with the statute.”
Feinstein said he’s glad CSDE hired Reiser and he hopes she has a positive impact. However, he said he’d like to start seeing major decisions — like the one about email records — elevated to CSDE leadership.
“Those should be done in a conscientious way where the top of the agency knows exactly what’s being said … not just relegated to, you know, fourth, fifth level staff people,” Feinstein said.
According to CSDE’s press release announcing her hiring, Reiser previously practiced at the Law Office of Courtney P. Spencer, LLC, where she represented clients in special education matters. Most recently, she served as director of the Office of Adjudications at the Connecticut Department of Energy and Environmental Protection. 
Feinstein said despite Reiser’s hiring, he remains concerned about complaint enforcement, which he said the WestEd report failed to address.
“The issue we continue to have with written state complaints is that … a violation will be found, and then the same violation occurs in the same district repeatedly,” Feinstein said. “There’s no real follow-up on enforcement of those decisions, and that’s pretty troubling.”

name: Delaware
title: Coons, Katz offer competing visions for Washington at Wilmington Senate forum
text:
Photo taken by Delaware LIVE. Graphics added by on 10/22 using AI.
Federal spending, health care costs and foreign policy highlight differences as Delaware voters begin casting ballots.
By George D. Rotsch, Delaware LIVE News
WILMINGTON, Del. — Democratic U.S. Sen. Chris Coons and Republican challenger Dr. Mike Katz presented different approaches to controlling federal spending, reducing health care costs and addressing America’s foreign policy challenges Thursday during a U.S. Senate candidate forum at the Hotel du Pont.
The hourlong discussion, hosted by the Rotary Club of Wilmington and moderated by Jake Owens of Spotlight Delaware, gave voters an opportunity to compare the candidates as early voting began for the Nov. 3 general election.
Coons emphasized his 16 years in the Senate, bipartisan legislative experience and willingness to challenge President Donald Trump’s policies. He said his campaign is focused on three priorities, in this order: opportunity, security and justice. Coons described opportunity as helping Americans build better lives, security as protecting families and their futures, and justice as addressing political divisions and abuses of power.
Katz, a physician, former state senator and business executive, argued that after 16 years of Coons representing Delaware in Washington, it is time for a change. He characterized the election as a performance review of the incumbent and a job interview for the challenger, calling for new leadership focused on financial responsibility, government efficiency and solutions to longstanding problems.
While both candidates promised to work across party lines, their differences were evident in how they would address some of the nation’s most pressing challenges.
Photo: The Gold Ballroom at the Hotel duPont, the stie of the Candidate Forum on Thursday October 22,2026.
Federal spending and debt
With the national debt approaching $40 trillion, both candidates acknowledged that federal spending and borrowing have become serious problems.
Coons said Republicans and Democrats share responsibility for growing deficits. He advocated increasing taxes on wealthy Americans and highly profitable corporations while providing relief to working families.
Katz argued that Washington cannot continue increasing taxes without addressing the underlying cost of government.
He called for restructuring federal operations, eliminating waste, establishing balanced budgets and developing a plan to reduce the national debt.
Moderator Owens challenged both candidates to identify specific budget decisions they would make, including which constituencies they would be willing to disappoint.
Neither presented a comprehensive deficit-reduction plan identifying specific spending cuts and revenue increases.
Social Security and health care
The candidates also offered different approaches to preserving Social Security and controlling health care costs.
Coons supported raising the income cap subject to Social Security payroll taxes and working through a bipartisan process to consider additional changes necessary to strengthen the program.
Katz said Social Security represents a commitment to Americans who have contributed throughout their working lives. He advocated reviewing how the program operates before considering changes to benefits or retirement requirements.
On health care, Coons defended the Affordable Care Act as a means of expanding access to insurance and preventive treatment.
He argued that improving access to primary care could reduce expensive emergency treatment and improve long-term outcomes.
Katz, drawing on four decades in medicine and health care management, said the system requires more fundamental reform.
He argued that government subsidies and insurance changes primarily determine who pays rising medical bills without adequately addressing why care costs so much.
Katz acknowledged beneficial provisions of the Affordable Care Act, including protections for people with pre-existing conditions, but described the overall law as a failed approach to controlling health care costs.
Neither candidate provided a detailed legislative plan showing how his proposals would reduce costs for Delaware patients and employers.
Tariffs, energy and family expenses
The cost of living was another area of disagreement.
Coons criticized the Trump administration’s broad tariffs, arguing they increase prices for consumers and businesses, particularly those importing construction materials or exporting products to Canada.
He pointed to Delaware industries, including chemicals, agriculture and port operations, as examples of businesses affected by international trade policies.
Katz described tariffs as a legitimate economic tool when used selectively to protect American workers and businesses from unfair foreign competition.
He said tariffs should have clearly defined objectives, measurable results and congressional oversight.
Both recognized the importance of maintaining American competitiveness, but Coons placed greater emphasis on removing trade barriers while Katz focused on targeting unfair trade practices.
Iran war divides candidates
Foreign policy produced some of the forum’s clearest differences.
Coons strongly criticized the administration’s war with Iran, arguing that inadequate planning and insufficient consultation with Congress and American allies contributed to higher gasoline prices and instability in the Middle East.
He called for ending the conflict and restoring shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.
Katz said preventing Iran from obtaining nuclear weapons remains essential to American and international security.
He criticized decades of foreign policy decisions, including the 2015 nuclear agreement supported by Coons, which Katz argued failed to resolve Iran’s long-term nuclear threat.
Both expressed concern about presidential military actions without sufficient congressional involvement, although they emphasized different responsibilities and policy failures.
On Ukraine, Coons strongly defended continued support for the country against Russia’s invasion. Katz criticized failures of American and international leadership but did not outline a detailed alternative strategy for ending the conflict.
Katz questions political process
One of the forum’s more pointed moments came when Katz departed from a question about Ukraine to raise concerns about the conduct of Delaware’s Senate campaign.
He alleged that campaign communications had been hacked, staff members had been threatened and supporters had experienced intimidation.
Katz also criticized the absence of a traditional public debate and what he described as insufficient scrutiny of the incumbent.
The allegations were not substantiated during the forum, and no evidence was presented establishing who might have been responsible.
The campaign has previously criticized Coons for declining other proposed debates, including a student-organized event at the University of Delaware. Thursday’s forum brought both candidates together, although the format did not allow direct exchanges or audience questions.
Bipartisanship and congressional accountability
Despite their disagreements, both candidates supported maintaining the Senate filibuster, which generally requires 60 votes to advance major legislation.
Katz said the rule protects minority-party interests and discourages either party from imposing sweeping changes without broader support.
Coons also defended the filibuster while expressing openness to certain reforms, particularly involving voting rights.
Asked when they would oppose their own parties, Katz pledged to evaluate legislation based on Delaware’s interests rather than party loyalty.
Coons cited examples of bipartisan legislation he had worked on with Republican colleagues, arguing that his record demonstrates an ability to deliver results even when party leaders disagree.
The discussion also touched on artificial intelligence, immigration and U.S. military assistance to Israel.
Both candidates supported responsible AI development, although Katz emphasized innovation and competitiveness while Coons stressed safeguards and the potential impacts of data centers on communities.
On immigration, Katz emphasized stronger border enforcement and legal immigration reform. Coons called for border security combined with greater accountability for federal immigration enforcement and legal pathways for qualifying immigrants.
Different approaches, shared challenges
Throughout the forum, Katz returned to his central argument that longstanding federal problems require changes in management, priorities and accountability.
Coons pointed to his relationships in Congress and legislative experience as reasons he could continue delivering results for Delaware.
Both identified rising costs, federal debt and political division as major concerns. Their disagreement centered largely on whether those problems are better addressed through changes to existing federal policies or more extensive restructuring of government programs.
The forum also left questions about specific spending reductions, long-term Social Security financing and measurable health care savings.
With early voting underway, Delaware voters now have a clearer comparison of the candidates’ priorities — and the decisions each would face in Washington.
