name: Delaware
title: Delaware families face another electric rate hike as power costs continue to climb
text:
Who is responsible for the increases? There is no single cause behind Delaware’s rising electric bills. Several organizations, market conditions and government policies influence what customers ultimately pay. Image created on 10/22 using AI.
Delmarva Power seeks $67.8 million more in annual revenue as regulators weigh grid investments, rising energy costs and what Delaware can do to protect consumers.
By George D. Rotsch, Delaware LIVE
WILMINGTON, Del. — Delaware families already paying substantially more for electricity face another potential increase as state regulators consider Delmarva Power’s request for $67.8 million in additional annual revenue.
The proposal would increase the utility’s distribution base rates by 21.7%, although that does not mean customers’ total electric bills would rise by that percentage.
The request comes after a separate increase in electricity supply costs took effect June 1, adding an estimated $14.64 per month, or about $176 annually, to the average residential customer’s bill.
For households struggling with higher prices for food, insurance, housing and other necessities, the latest rate case raises a broader question: Why does electricity keep getting more expensive, and what can Delaware officials do about it?
Electric bills keep climbing
The cost of electricity has increased substantially in recent years, adding pressure to household budgets.
According to the U.S. Energy Information Administration, Delaware’s average residential electricity price reached 17.15 cents per kilowatt-hour in 2025. Preliminary monthly data show prices climbing further in 2026.
Unlike groceries or gasoline, electricity is difficult for consumers to avoid. Families can reduce consumption, but heating, cooling, refrigeration and other essential household needs place limits on how much they can cut.
The June increase was particularly significant.
Delmarva’s standard electricity supply rate increased approximately 19%, largely because of higher regional power costs. Changes in renewable-energy compliance charges slightly offset the impact, resulting in an estimated 9% increase in the overall bill for a typical residential customer using 811 kilowatt-hours per month.
The pending distribution-rate case represents a separate cost pressure.
Delmarva implemented temporary higher distribution rates July 9 while the Delaware Public Service Commission reviews its request for a permanent increase. The final decision will determine how much additional revenue the utility can collect, with the interim rates subject to adjustment.
Who is responsible for the increases?
There is no single cause behind Delaware’s rising electric bills. Several organizations, market conditions and government policies influence what customers ultimately pay.
The major cost drivers include:

PJM Interconnection — Regional electricity costs: PJM manages the wholesale electricity market serving Delaware, 12 other states and Washington, D.C. Rising demand, limited generation capacity and higher prices for ensuring adequate electricity supplies have contributed significantly to recent increases.
Delmarva Power — Local delivery costs: Delmarva maintains the poles, wires, substations and other equipment delivering electricity to homes and businesses. Its pending rate request would increase revenue collected from customers for distribution services and infrastructure investments.
Delaware Public Service Commission — Rate oversight: The PSC reviews Delmarva’s proposed distribution rates and determines which expenses are reasonable for customers to pay. The commission does not directly control regional wholesale electricity prices.
Delaware lawmakers — Renewable-energy requirements: State law requires utilities to obtain 40% of electricity from renewable sources by 2035, including a 10% solar requirement. Renewable-energy credits and other compliance expenses can add costs, although supporters argue the requirements deliver environmental benefits and reduce long-term exposure to fossil-fuel price volatility.
Regional Greenhouse Gas Initiative — Carbon compliance costs: Delaware participates in this regional emissions-reduction program. Power generators must purchase allowances for certain carbon emissions. Some expenses can be reflected in wholesale electricity prices, while program revenues support energy-efficiency and environmental initiatives.
Growing electricity demand — Pressure on the regional grid: Data centers, economic development and increasing electrification are expected to place additional demands on the power system. Meeting that demand could require more generation, transmission capacity and local infrastructure.

The distinction matters.
Regional wholesale electricity costs have been a major driver of recent increases, but Delaware regulators and lawmakers have greater control over utility distribution spending, renewable-energy requirements and other state policies.
That leaves Delaware officials with an important responsibility: ensuring the costs they can control are necessary, transparent and affordable for the families and businesses paying the bills.
Delaware’s energy policies also carry costs
The debate over electricity affordability increasingly includes questions about the state’s environmental and renewable-energy policies.
Delaware’s Renewable Portfolio Standard requires utilities to obtain an increasing share of electricity from renewable sources, reaching 40% by 2035.
Supporters say the requirements encourage cleaner energy, diversify supplies and reduce dependence on fossil fuels.
Critics question whether the mandates are achieving those goals at the lowest possible cost, particularly as regional electricity prices rise.
The state also participates in the Regional Greenhouse Gas Initiative, which requires participating power generators to purchase carbon-emission allowances.
Revenue from those allowances supports energy and environmental programs, but the compliance costs can also influence electricity prices.
Neither program accounts for the entire increase in household bills, and renewable-energy compliance charges actually decreased slightly during Delmarva’s June supply-rate adjustment.
Still, the programs raise a legitimate policy question: Should Delaware review the cost and timing of its energy mandates as consumers face higher electricity bills?
Does Delaware really need more grid investment?
Delmarva’s distribution-rate request centers on the cost of maintaining and upgrading the electrical system.
The company must maintain infrastructure, respond to outages, replace aging equipment and prepare for future electricity demand.
Additional investments can improve reliability, reduce outages and strengthen the system against severe weather.
But those benefits come at a price.
The question for regulators is not simply whether improvements are needed, but whether the proposed spending is justified, appropriately timed and fairly allocated among customers.
The Public Service Commission has authority to examine the utility’s expenses, investment plans and requested financial returns before approving permanent distribution rates.
That oversight becomes increasingly important when customers are already absorbing higher supply and transmission costs that state regulators have less power to control.
What can Delaware do to lower electric bills?
Although Delaware cannot independently control the regional electricity market, policymakers have several opportunities to address affordability.
Push for PJM reforms. Regional leaders, including Gov. Matt Meyer, have called for changes intended to address rising electricity costs. Increasing available generation, reducing delays for new energy projects and improving market rules could help stabilize prices.
Review renewable-energy compliance costs. Lawmakers could examine whether current requirements are delivering their intended benefits at reasonable costs and whether adjustments to compliance mechanisms or timelines are warranted.
Expand energy-efficiency programs. Weatherization, insulation, efficient appliances and other improvements can help consumers reduce electricity consumption without sacrificing reliability.
Scrutinize utility investments. Regulators can require Delmarva to demonstrate that proposed projects are necessary, cost-effective and beneficial to customers before authorizing additional rate revenue.
Improve transparency. Consumers could benefit from clearer information showing exactly how much they pay for electricity supply, capacity, transmission, distribution and state energy-policy requirements.
Target financial assistance. Existing assistance programs and payment arrangements can provide relief to households with limited incomes, including seniors and residents living on fixed incomes.
Some of those actions could reduce long-term costs. Others would provide more immediate relief without necessarily changing the underlying price of electricity.
The question is affordability
The growing cost of electricity is not the result of one utility decision or one government policy.
It reflects multiple pressures, including regional electricity markets, rising demand, infrastructure investments and state energy requirements.
Some expenses are necessary to maintain a reliable electrical system. Others reflect policy choices that can be examined and adjusted.
The challenge for Delaware’s elected officials and regulators is determining whether the benefits justify the costs and whether enough attention is being paid to the financial impact on consumers.
For families watching their electric bills rise, that question is becoming harder to ignore.
The Public Service Commission is accepting written public comments on Delmarva’s pending rate case through Nov. 4.

Proposed increase: $67.8 million in additional annual revenue, representing 21.7% of existing distribution base rates
Status: Temporary higher rates took effect July 9. The permanent rate request remains under review.
Public comment deadline: Nov. 4, 2026
How to participate: Submit written comments through the state’s DelaFile system at https://delafile.delaware.gov or email psc@delaware.gov. Include Docket No. 25-1555.
Learn more: Delaware Public Service Commission, https://depsc.delaware.gov
Consumer assistance: Residents struggling with electric bills can contact Delmarva Power about payment arrangements or the Delaware Division of the Public Advocate for assistance.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: No clear signs that Legislature will act swiftly on child sexual abuse amendment
text:
AN OVERWHELMING MAJORITY of Massachusetts residents say they believe that the state should eliminate the statute of limitations for reporting child sexual abuse, but Beacon Hill leadership doesn’t seem eager to talk about a bill under negotiation that could do just that. 
Legislative leaders this week have kept their comments general about a provision tacked onto the House’s version of a primary care reform bill that would eliminate the statute of limitations on civil child sexual abuse cases, remove the $20,000 charitable immunity cap, and create a two-year window for survivors to revive expired abuse claims. 
The amendment, adopted with little fanfare in the closing days for formal business this summer, was introduced by Rep. John Lawn, of Watertown, who serves as House chair of the Legislature’s Health Care Financing Committee.  
Lawn, himself a survivor of child sexual abuse, was then left off the six-person conference committee negotiating an agreement between the House and Senate versions of the health care bill, despite serving both as the chief author of the amendment and as his chamber’s point person on the underlying primary care reforms. 
Now, lawmakers are weighing the bill as the state grapples with the latest revelations about sexual abuse in the Catholic Church. Attorney General Andrea Campbell took to the podium on September 30 and announced her office’s investigation into child sexual abuse in three Massachusetts Catholic dioceses. 
More than 270 Catholic clerics in the dioceses of Fall River, Springfield, and Worcester abused nearly 1,000 children for more than half a century, with church leaders shielding predators and concealing allegations, the scathing and long-awaited report found. 
But Campbell said she faced “significant barriers” in bringing charges against any clergy members, since the current Massachusetts statute of limitations allows claims to be within 35 years of a victim turning 18, or when they reach 53 years of age. Advocates note research shows the typical survivor does not first disclose abuse until their 50s. 
Campbell called on lawmakers to update the law, highlighting the efforts by Lawn and Sen. Joan Lovely to craft such legislation. (Lovely has put forward several bills that would eliminate the statute of limitations for these cases.) In response, top Democrats have only spoken vaguely about the proposal and the conference committee discussions. 
A spokesperson for Speaker Ron Mariano’s office noted Wednesday that the amendment is currently in private negotiations and referred to the Speaker’s remarks in late September regarding Lawn’s absence from the committee. With the seriousness of the health care cost crisis, he said, House budget chair Aaron Michlewitz was tapped to lead negotiations.  
“The message I wanted to send was ‘This is extremely important to us. We’ve got our best guy on it,’” Mariano told reporters.  
Lawn did not respond to request for comment Wednesday on the bill or conference committee. In September, Lawn declined to comment about his exclusion when asked by reporters.  
Senate President Karen Spilka did not comment on the amendment specifically, though her office pointed out the Senate approved a similar reform two years ago.  
“The Senate President supports survivors of child sexual assault,” a spokesperson for Spilka’s office said in a statement. “The Senate is on record supporting the elimination of the statute of limitations in civil cases last session. The conferees are currently engaging on this issue to help ensure victims are heard and perpetrators are held to account.” 
Discussion of sexual abuse claims in Massachusetts is often tightly tied to the revelations of widespread abuse by clergy explored in The Boston Globe’s famed Spotlight series that began in 2002. Decades of efforts to widen the window in which survivors can come forward have frequently met forceful public objection from the Catholic Church, warning that a slew of claims from decades past could bring the institution to its knees financially and inhibit its own ability to support survivors. 
Three years ago, the Archdiocese of Boston opposed similar legislation proposed by Lovely, who is a survivor of child sexual abuse. 
“The legislative changes currently proposed and under consideration would jeopardize our ability to continue to [support survivors] and would make it difficult to sustain the many works of mercy the Church is committed to through social justice and support for the neediest,” the Archdiocese said in a 2023 statement. 
The Archdiocese of Boston did not respond to a CommonWealth Beacon inquiry made this week asking if it opposed the current amendment. 
The Catholic League, the nation’s largest Catholic advocacy organization, released a letter to Gov. Maura Healey, Campbell, and bishops on October 2. The group said the letter was because of Campbell’s investigation into the dioceses and called for an investigation into the abuse of students in the public schools.  
“To be fair,” the League wrote, “the investigation must extend back to the days of Prohibition. After all, the probe of the Catholic dioceses extended over a century.”  
The group called for sovereign immunity — which shields some state employees from lawsuits if they were engaged in the normal course of their jobs — to be abolished to clear the way for suits against public school employees.  
Efforts to raise the $20,000 liability cap for charitable organizations must apply to the public sector as well, the League wrote, “otherwise it might be read as religious profiling and therefore subject to a lawsuit.” 
No church or other organization is specifically singled out in the legislative amendment. Campbell described her office’s investigation as part of a long effort to find answers about the scope of sexual abuse in the Catholic Church of Massachusetts.  
“This investigation was not about demonizing a faith or a church,” said Campbell at the press conference, during which she also disclosed that she is a survivor of childhood sexual abuse. “Rather, it was about seeking justice, a value and a promise our faith and the God I serve so deeply reflects.” 
Her abuse, she said, was “not at the hands of the church, but at the hands of a relative.” 
Boston-based group Enough Abuse, the nation’s oldest citizen-based child advocacy organization, released a poll a week after the investigation announcement. The poll of 802 registered voters in Massachusetts was conducted by The MassINC Polling Group, which is owned by CommonWealth Beacon publisher MassINC. 
Almost 60 percent of respondents said they think sexual abuse of children is either very common or somewhat common in the state.  
The poll did not single out clergy. It asked respondents if “organizations such as schools, religious organizations, or youth programs that knowingly enabled sexual abuse to occur and failed to protect children from sexual abuse should be held accountable.” Only 3 percent of respondents disagreed, with 93 percent either strongly or somewhat agreeing. 
The group put the poll in the field weeks before the attorney general’s report was released, with the aim of gauging support for legislation to change state law on child sexual abuse.  
Jetta Bernier, executive director of Enough Abuse, detailed a winding path to the amendment’s inclusion.  
Lovely, Lawn, and Rep. Ken Gordon have consistently filed bills to eliminate the statute of limitations and the charitable cap, as well as create a window for expired claims to be brought forward. This session, Bernier noted, those bills were reported out favorably from the Joint Committee on the Judiciary. 
“We were very pleased that the bills were moving that fast,” she said during a presentation of the poll results. “But as the session began to come to a close at the end of June, I think it appeared that perhaps the bill might be in jeopardy. And so Rep. Lawn introduced an amendment.” 
Pollsters asked about the proposed law to eliminate the time limit for filing civil lawsuits related to child sexual abuse. Respondents overwhelmingly said they would strongly (60 percent) or somewhat (24 percent) support this change, and 79 percent said they would like their state legislators to vote for it. 
At the poll release event, Lovely said the conference committee is “working very hard” on the health care bill, though the subject matter can still make people nervous. 
“I’ve been working for the last almost 14 years in the Senate to talk about this,” she said. “It’s the most uncomfortable subject that you can talk about. People don’t want to talk about it. They shut down and they say, ‘It doesn’t happen in my world,’ when it could have, or has.” 
Chris Lisinski contributed to this report.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Va. Sen. Louise Lucas, six others indicted in federal cannabis corruption case
text:
State Sen. Louise Lucas, D-Portsmouth, faces federal racketeering, marijuana distribution and money laundering conspiracy charges tied to a cannabis business she co-owns.  Prosecutors allege she used her legislative influence to benefit the business.(Photo by Charlotte Rene Woods/Virignia Mercury)State Sen. Louise Lucas of Portsmouth, one of Virginia’s most powerful Democrats, was indicted Thursday on federal racketeering, marijuana distribution and money laundering conspiracy charges, with prosecutors alleging she used her legislative influence to protect and enrich a cannabis business she co-owns.
Lucas, 82, surrendered to authorities, a U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche said during a news conference in Norfolk. Six others were also in custody in connection with the alleged scheme, which prosecutors said involved family members and close associates.
The eight-count indictment accuses the defendants of offenses involving marijuana distribution, money laundering, honest services fraud through bribery, maintaining drug-involved premises, firearms and wire fraud. 
The Justice Department’s release does not specify which defendants face each count.
“This is the circus we always expected it to be, and we will wait for further details to have a more specific response,” Brian Woolfolk, chief counsel for the L. Louise Lucas Legal Defense Fund, told The Associated Press.
The charges against the longtime senator and outspoken critic of President Donald Trump come 12 days before the midterm elections. The investigation predates the Trump administration, but the timing is unusual because federal authorities have typically avoided overt investigative steps involving political figures so close to an election. 
Lucas is not on the ballot this year but has ties to prominent Democrats who are.
Prosecutors allege Lucas directed an organization they called the “Lucas Enterprise,” arranging the acquisition and distribution of at least 100 kilograms of marijuana and supervising the laundering of proceeds.
Marijuana is legal to use recreationally in Virginia but not to sell. Lawmakers passed a legislative framework creating a recreational weed marketplace that is set to launch next summer.  
They also allege she used her position as chair of the Senate Finance and Appropriations Committee to shield the operation from criminal scrutiny and influence legislation benefiting it.
“Our federal prosecutors will continue to be guided by the facts and evidence that led a grand jury to indict Ms. Lucas and her alleged co-conspirators,” Blanche said in a statement.
 Prosecutors outline business dealings

According to the Justice Department, Lucas’ associates included her daughters, Lisa Lucas-Burke and Theresa Lucas-Lamb, and her grandson, Ryan Eichelberger.
Lucas and Lucas-Burke opened The Cannabis Outlet in Portsmouth in 2021. Prosecutors allege Lucas-Lamb and Eichelberger acquired marijuana, supervised its distribution and managed the store for the enterprise.
Carlton Upton Jr., 54, of Chesapeake, was Lucas’ business partner in VA Freedom Life, an umbrella for The CBD Shoppe and The Cannabis Outlet beginning in 2019, according to a press release. 
Upton managed The CBD Shoppe and allegedly worked with Lucas to obtain a recreational marijuana license benefiting the enterprise.
Prosecutors also allege Upton made materially false statements on an April 2020 application for an Economic Injury Disaster Loan for Virginia Freedom Life. The loan was funded for $11,800.
Another allegation centers on a $750,000 payment Lucas allegedly made in August 2022 for full ownership of a business serving as a shell holding company for a co-conspirator’s expected Virginia recreational marijuana license.
Prosecutors allege Lucas failed to reveal that interest on required financial disclosure forms. They say she met with the co-conspirator at her Capitol complex office to receive a partial repayment and discussed the person’s qualification for a marijuana license with officials, including legislators, depending on her receipt of a bribery payment.
Lucas had identified herself as president and CEO of VA Freedom Life on a February 2022 Statement of Economic Interests, according to the release.
The case became public May 6, when federal agents searched Lucas’ Portsmouth legislative office and cannabis businesses. The Justice Department said agents recovered marijuana and firearms at The Cannabis Outlet and The CBD Shoppe.
At the scene, FBI spokeswoman Cassandra Temple told the Mercury: “We are conducting court-authorized law enforcement activity today.” She declined to answer additional questions.
Fox News, which first reported the operation, said staffers were ordered out of Lucas’ office while agents searched. Witnesses saw agents carrying boxes from the building. The network also reported that armed SWAT officers ordered people out of the adjacent Cannabis Outlet and that at least three people were handcuffed.
Lucas arrived after the operation began and told a reporter she did not know what it concerned.
 Lucas has called investigation intimidation

After the May searches, Lucas characterized the federal action as political intimidation, saying it was “about far more than one state senator” and reflected “a clear pattern from this administration.”
In a statement on X at the time, she linked the raid to the redistricting referendum voters approved in April, saying Virginians had voted to “stop Trump’s scheme to manipulate the 2026 midterm elections.” The Supreme Court of Virginia later overturned the referendum. 
“I am not backing down, and I will keep fighting for the people of Portsmouth and the commonwealth of Virginia,” she said. 
Lucas has served in the Senate since 1992 and as president pro tempore since 2020. Her finance committee chairmanship gives her considerable influence over the state budget, taxes and spending.
Earlier this year, she pushed to end or scale back sales and use tax exemptions for data centers, arguing the incentives had become too costly and strained Virginia’s electric grid and infrastructure. Resistance from House Democrats and Gov. Abigail Spanberger contributed to a monthslong intraparty budget impasse.
What the indictment means for Lucas’ role in the Senate and the upcoming legislative session remained unclear as of Thursday morning. 
Senate Majority Leader Scott Surovell, D-Fairfax, urged restraint in responding to the charges against his Democratic colleague. 
“The federal indictment unsealed this week contains serious allegations, and Senator Lucas is entitled to the same presumption of innocence that every American receives,” Surovell said in a statement. 
“She is innocent until proven guilty in a court of law. I will not comment on the evidence in this case, and I urge others to show the same restraint.”
Lucas’ cannabis business had drawn scrutiny years before the federal searches. Lucas co-sponsored legislation legalizing simple marijuana possession in 2021, but that change did not establish a regulated recreational retail marketplace.
A 2022 Mercury investigation found labeling discrepancies and quantities of delta-9 THC that made two tested products from The Cannabis Outlet illegal to sell under Virginia law at the time. 
One cereal bar contained substantially less total THC than its packaging advertised. The reporting examined broader concerns about unregulated cannabis products following legalization of possession. 
This is a breaking news story that will be updated as more information becomes available.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Kansas attorney general candidates question rivals on plea bargain, immigrant crime
text:
Republican Kris Kobach, left, and Democrat Chris Mann tangled in a Topeka television debate bringing together the candidates for Kansas attorney general. In this Oct. 6, 2026, image, Mann and Kobach prepare for their Johnson County debate. (Photo by Tim Carpenter/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — Kansas attorney general candidates Chris Mann and Kris Kobach took advantage of a televised debate to blast each other with prickly questions on holding influential people accountable for criminal conduct and the human cost of lax enforcement of immigration law.
Kobach, the state’s Republican attorney general and a former constitutional law professor, asked Mann during KTWU’s debate Wednesday night to explain criticism of immigration raids in the context of two women killed by men without authority to be in the United States.
Mann, a Democrat and former Lawrence police officer with a law practice focused on victims of drunk driving, queried Kobach about the plea bargain his staff offered disgraced Neosho County Attorney Linus Thuston.
Mann said the attorney general’s office developed a plan to help Thuston avoid jail time if the county prosecutor pleaded guilty to two misdemeanors for misuse of a county credit card and falsification of a document to avoid taxes on a vehicle purchase. Kobach’s staff abandoned the idea of charging Thuston for allegedly extorting about 50 women with demands for nude photos, Mann said.
“The judge on that case had to overrule the deal to give some jail time,” Mann said. “You say you’re tough on crime. Why would you let the powerful go free?”
Kobach, who is seeking election to a second term as attorney general, said he didn’t personally handle the plea bargain. In the 2024 case, Kobach’s staff recommended Thuston avoid jail by paying a $10,000 fine.
“In some instances when you’re brought in to prosecute a case, the evidence that you think is there to put someone behind bars or to impose a very significant penalty isn’t there,” Kobach said. “I didn’t negotiate that deal. My criminal prosecution team did, but they felt that that was the absolute most they could get given the limited facts that they have.”
“We go for the most severe penalty we can in every single case, and I don’t think anyone watching seriously believes that we’d be cutting deals to anyone breaking the law,” Kobach added.
Retired District Judge Merlin Wheeler accepted Thuston’s guilty pleas, but ordered the county prosecutor to pay more than $3,000 and serve 120 days in jail — 60 days for each misdemeanor offense.
A special prosecutor subsequently charged Thuston with felony crimes related to his testimony in a drug case about working with off-the-books confidential informants, including late-night meetings with a woman who sent him nude photos. A jury in August found Thuston guilty of perjury.
“When I’m attorney general, we’ll make sure we go after offenders no matter how powerful they are,” Mann said.
 
Tragic deaths
When it was Kobach’s chance to turn the table, he accused Mann of saying Kansas should strive to keep the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement from conducting raids to arrest and deport people lacking documentation to live in the United States.
The attorney general personalized the issue by touching on the murder in 2005 of Maria Morfin-Rojas in Lenexa and the death in 2007 of Amanda Bixby near Basehor.
Rojas, 30, was stabbed to death by Angel Herrera, who fled the United States and wasn’t arrested until 2023 in El Salvador. Back in Kansas, he was sentenced to 50 years in prison. Bixby, 19, of Tonganoxie, died in a three-vehicle crash caused when Ricardo Flores ran a stop sign. He was initially charged with vehicular homicide, but the case was dismissed.
“They were illegal aliens who killed them. If those aliens had been deported, those people would be alive today and their families would not be grieving,” Kobach told Mann. “Yet, you said, ‘We need to do everything we can to stop ICE deportations in Kansas.’ I’m doing everything I can to help. How would you explain your position to those family members?”
Mann said the attorney general was falsely spreading a claim that he proposed cessation of immigration enforcement activities.
“I never said that to any audience,” Mann said.
Kobach, however, said he had a recording of Mann making the comment.
Mann said violent offenders, whether U.S. citizens or not, should be removed from the streets to make communities safer. He condemned Kobach’s advocacy for a proposed law requiring county sheriffs to sign 287(g) agreements with ICE. The agreements enable local law enforcement to be trained and deputized so they could take on federal immigration duties.
“Many of them don’t have the resources to take on an agreement like that or simply don’t want to,” Mann said. “My opponent has never walked a day in the life, in the shoes, of the men and women who are protecting our communities. I’m going to trust local law enforcement.”
Kobach said the Kansas Bureau of Investigation, which falls under jurisdiction of the attorney general, and 30 Kansas sheriffs had 287(g) deals with ICE to assist with detaining people for possible deportation.
“We’ve also deported a lot of illegal aliens from Kansas,” Kobach said, “and that would probably end if my opponent became attorney general.”
 
Crime statistics
Debate moderator Bob Beatty, a professor at Washburn University, asked the candidates to explain what they would do to address crime in Kansas. He said violent crime in Kansas increased 7.5% despite an overall decline of 5% in the state’s crime rate during 2025.
“Property crimes have been steadily decreasing over the past 18 years,” Mann said. “Aggravated assaults are at a 10-year high and domestic-violence-related homicides are up 65%. While my opponent’s been hanging his ‘mission accomplished’ banner and taken a victory lap, I’ve been on the ground talking to sheriffs and talking to law enforcement leaders throughout the state. They’ve told me they need a better partner in the attorney general’s office.”
Kobach said his work as attorney general was partially responsible for reducing the state’s crime rate to the lowest level in 57 years.
“In the last year only, there was a slight bump upward in violent crime. But property crimes were dropping dramatically. In fact, burglary is now at its lowest point in more than 60 years,” Kobach said.
In advance of the Nov. 3 election, Mann was endorsed by the Kansas State Lodge of the Fraternal Order of Police. It was the first time since 2002 the union representing 4,300 law enforcement officers endorsed a Democratic candidate for attorney general. Kobach said 53 sheriffs endorsed his reelection.
Kobach said it was important to recognize the attorney general’s office led an effort to drive down fentanyl deaths. Fatalities in Kansas caused by people ingesting the powerful drug declined 17%, he said.
“The availability of fentanyl on the streets in Kansas is 120th of what it was when I started in office. Huge accomplishment,” the attorney general said.
Mann said Kansas documented more than 2,000 deaths related to fentanyl and earlier this year Wichita reported 29 fentanyl overdoses in a single weekend.
“The crisis is not over,” he said.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Justices order Lincoln to pay $9,150 to Nebraska AG’s Office after charter fight
text:
The logo for the Office of the Nebraska Attorney General. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — The Nebraska Supreme Court on Wednesday said Lincoln must pay the Attorney General’s Office $9,150 in costs after a court fight about three petitioned charter amendments.
The high court on Sept. 9, in a 5-2 opinion, agreed with Attorney General Mike Hilgers that city officials needed to place three citizen-led city charter amendments from the Good Government Lincoln campaign on the Nov. 3 ballot. City officials argued that the measures qualified for voter review but that they would instead appear on city ballots in May.
Hilgers’ office on Sept. 18 asked justices to require Lincoln to reimburse $19,107. This included the $132 cost to file the original lawsuit and the rest in attorneys’ fees. Three office attorneys estimated they worked on the case for about 61 hours, with pay rates from $300 to $375 per hour.
The seven-member Lincoln City Council. Top row, from left, Sändra Washington, Justin P. Carlson, Tom Beckius and James Michael Bowers. Bottom row, from left, Tom Duden (vice chair), Brodey Weber (chair) and Bennie Shobe. (Photo courtesy of City of Lincoln)
Lincoln City Attorney Yohance Christie objected to the request. Christie said city officials acted “in good faith based on a colorable theory.”
“To award attorney fees would discourage similarly situated public bodies acting in good faith based on a reasonable interpretation of the law on a case of first impression to seek review of their own constitutionally granted rights,” Christie wrote.
Wednesday’s court order states that two judges dissented, but the order does not say who. 
In early September, Justice Stephanie Stacy of Lincoln and Court of Appeals Judge Michael W. Pirtle of Omaha dissented. Pirtle rounded out the seven-member court at the time, as Chief Justice Jeffrey Funke of Nebraska City did not participate in the case.
In a Thursday post on X, Hilgers said Lincoln’s leaders “had every opportunity to follow the clear mandate within the Constitution to put the amendments on the ballot. Yet they refused to do so.”
“Whether it was for political reasons or not, our lawsuit should have never been needed,” Hilgers wrote. “My hope is that this award of fees will help deter them — and others — who may in the future consider ignoring the Constitution.”
A Lincoln spokesperson had no immediate comment on the court’s order Thursday morning.
The general election is Nov. 3.



Lincoln City Charter amendments ballot language
Ballot Question 2: Shall Articles III and IV of the Lincoln City Charter be amended to align city elections with statewide elections beginning in 2028 so that mayoral and district council member elections are held in both 2027 and 2028; and that at-large council members elected in 2025 shall serve until their successors are elected in 2030; and that elected terms of a length different than four years due to this proposal shall count as a four-year term for purposes of term limits?
Ballot Question 3 (City’s Alternative Amendment): Shall Articles III and IV of the Lincoln City Charter be amended to align city elections with statewide elections beginning in 2030 so that mayoral and district council elections are held in both 2027 and 2030; and that at-large council member elections are held in both 2029 and 2032; and that elected terms of a length different than four years due to this provision shall count as a four-year term for purposes of term limits?
Ballot Question 4: Shall Article III, Section 4 of the charter be amended to provide that council members shall not be qualified to hold office for more than two consecutive four-year terms?
Ballot Question 5 (City’s Alternative Amendment): Shall Article III, Section 4 of the charter be amended to provide that council members shall not be qualified to hold office for more than three consecutive four-year terms?
Ballot Question 6: Shall Article III, Section 2 and Article IV, Section 2A of the charter be amended to allow all citizens residing in the three-mile extraterritorial zoning jurisdiction around the city, but not within the city’s corporate limits, to vote in its elections?

name: VTDigger
title: 5 takeaways from Phil Scott and Amanda Janoo’s first debate of the campaign
text:
Vermont’s Republican Gov. Phil Scott and Democratic/Progressive challenger Amanda Janoo talk during their first debate of the 2026 campaign on Wednesday. Screenshot via YouTube/Vermont Public
Vermont’s leading candidates for governor agreed at their first debate of the campaign Wednesday that the state is facing a slew of challenges that make life unaffordable. But Republican Gov. Phil Scott and his Democratic and Progressive challenger, Amanda Janoo, presented at times polar opposite ideas for what to do about it. 
The debate, hosted by Vermont Public, was friendly and did not appear to feature even one tense exchange between the candidates. But with less than two weeks until Election Day, the stakes are high: Recent polls and fundraising data suggest that this year’s race for governor could be the state’s most competitive in a decade.
Here are five takeaways from the hourlong forum.
The same playbook vs. a new one
Gov. Scott knows his greatest hits — and he’s hoping voters remember them, too. At the top of the debate, Scott invoked the major crises Vermont has weathered during his decade-long tenure, including the Covid-19 pandemic and the devastating floods in 2023 and 2024. The governor is banking that goodwill he’s enjoyed from voters across party lines for his leadership during those times will buoy him again this year. 
“We’ve been through a lot together over the last 10 years. And while it hasn’t been easy, we’ve got some tough things done,” he said.
Scott said he has made affordability a campaign issue for years and so voters should trust that it will be top of mind for him again. What needs to change isn’t the state’s governor, he said, but the Legislature’s willingness to work with him more than it has in the past. For Scott’s part, “I’m not changing my style,” he said. 
Janoo, an economist and government consultant who is running her first campaign, is pitching voters on a very different style. “We can’t solve our problems with the same thinking that created them,” she said Wednesday. She said she’s been asking voters across the state, “What do you think the government’s goals are right now? And people have no idea.” 
Janoo wants to restructure the state’s economic system with a focus on redistributing the wealth it already has and improving people’s living conditions “from the bottom up.”

READ MORE

“The standard economic playbook that we’ve been using of just cutting taxes, deregulating industries, gutting and privatizing government services and trying to attract or appease the largest multinationals or big corporations, it’s not leading to the trickle down prosperity, I think, that we have been promised over the last decades,” Janoo said.
Taxes and healthcare dominated
When moderator Mikaela Lefrak asked Scott a question about how Vermont can make itself more attractive to new residents, the governor replied that “we need to do everything we can to reduce the tax burden.” He reiterated that he’ll propose a slate of tax cuts or credits to the Legislature if he gets reelected and said he doesn’t think the state’s tax system needs to be any more progressive than it already is. 
Janoo, on the other hand, said that “we need more government strategic intervention to actually reduce” the cost of basic needs. She pointed to one of her signature proposals: raising taxes on the state’s wealthiest residents to generate revenue for new public services, top among them free primary healthcare for everyone. That would “fundamentally improve affordability,” she said, because healthcare expenses are a major reason it’s so hard for many people and businesses to make ends meet.
“We are at a moment where we can see that our healthcare system is collapsing. And it’s pretty clear at this point, like, a profit-oriented healthcare system is just a bad idea,” she said. “It’s a perverse incentive.”
Scott agreed that healthcare costs are a major issue but was skeptical of the viability of a universal primary care system, instead arguing the state should make less sweeping reforms like building on the executive order he signed earlier this year allowing Vermont insurers to price premiums partially based on age. He questioned why the state would pursue publicly-funded healthcare again after it tried and failed to do so in the 2010s.
“When you promote free healthcare, it’s hard to say no. But, there’s nothing free in this world,” he said.
Some details were left unsaid
To pay for her primary care plan, Janoo has cited modeling from Fair Share for Vermont, a lobbying campaign in Montpelier, which shows that surcharges on personal income over $250,000 could generate between $114 million and $344 million in annual revenue. Pressed by Lefrak about what she would do if that money wasn’t enough to create the system she wants, though, Janoo did not directly answer. She then said the state could start by piloting a program of publicly-funded doctors in just some towns.
At another point, in response to criticism from Scott that the math behind her plan to fund primary care with income taxes “doesn’t seem to work for me,” Janoo said that “the point here is less about, you know, this is the specific pot that we have to use.”
Scott later asked Janoo what salary she would propose paying doctors under a publicly-funded system; Janoo did not give a specific figure and said only in response that, anecdotally, she had heard from existing primary care doctors who would be OK making “the average salary” if they did not also have to deal with the private insurance industry.
Scott, for his part, did not directly answer a question from Lefrak about what his tax package would include. He said it would be geared toward people with lower and middle incomes and that, personally, he does not think social security payments should be taxed.
Trump wasn’t an issue (in this debate)
At the national level, President Donald Trump’s unpopularity, and the extent to which it will impact the outcome of races across the country, has been a major focus. But the president’s name was uttered just once in Wednesday’s debate, and in an unexpected way. 
Asked by Lefrak to name someone from another political party whom she respects, Janoo picked Scott, saying the governor is “just super nice” and that she appreciates how he has not “followed along with a Republican, sort of like Trump, MAGA, fascist regime.” Scott, whom Lefrak directed the question to first, named the former U.S. Sen. Patrick Leahy and the late Vermont state Sen. Dick Mazza.
They disagreed on some other topics, too
Janoo did take aim at Scott in another instance, though. Asked by Lefrak what issue the Legislature spends too much time on, Janoo replied: “school consolidation.” The governor has hinged the last two legislative sessions on his efforts to reform the state’s school funding and governance structure, saying the state needs to centralize decision-making and that some schools will need to consolidate in order to save money. 

READ MORE

Janoo said earlier in the debate that she thinks the state should improve the viability of small schools by locating more community resources at them, including health clinics, services for older adults and food banks. Scott said that his education plan will lower property taxes, which will address the broader affordability crisis, too. 
In response to a question from Lefrak, Scott said he thinks a new “small-scale” nuclear power facility would help reduce energy bills in the state, while Janoo said she does not support any nuclear infrastructure. And, in another set of answers, while Scott reiterated his support for state employees coming into their offices three days a week, Janoo said she would allow them to work remotely as much as they wanted.
Vermont Public’s debate was the first of three televised governor forums in the leadup to the election on Nov. 3. NBC-5 will host a debate Thursday at 8 p.m., while WCAX will host one next Wednesday, Oct. 28 at 7 p.m.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Question 3 would let voters reclaim their voice
text:
HOUSE SPEAKER Ron Mariano says Question 3, which would replace party nomination primaries with a single first round that includes all candidates, is “being targeted by a small group of individuals with a lot of money.” 
“They’re all investment bankers. They want a way to get more Republicans elected, and this is a much better way,” he said, echoing the No on 3 campaign’s claim that “billionaires are paying for this ballot question, which will make it easier for billionaires to buy our elections.”  
The professional politicians of both parties use this argument as a smokescreen because they really don’t want to change the undemocratic, noncompetitive system that keeps them in office for decades without fear of being voted out. 
The No on 3 campaign supports ranked-choice voting as a better alternative to all-party primaries. Left unsaid is the fact that the 2020 ballot question to bring ranked-choice voting to Massachusetts, which was defeated, also received six-figure contributions from wealthy  donors — for precisely the same reason today’s all-party primary has received such funding: because winning a ballot measure that the political establishment opposes requires financial support from anyone with deep pockets. 
The Speaker of the Massachusetts House rivals the governor as the most powerful elected official in the state, yet Speaker Mariano got into the Legislature by winning just 223 more votes than his opponent in a special primary election 35 years ago in the small sliver of the state made up by his Quincy-based district. 
Since then, he has never faced a significant opponent, and in almost all of his 36 elections he was completely unopposed, as is the case again this year. When the previous Speaker retired in 2020, Mariano, the loyal deputy, was rubber-stamped without opposition.  
With his control of committee assignments and the huge annual stipends they bring, the Speaker has unassailable control of members’ votes since he controls their pay. Like most Massachusetts incumbents, Mariano racks up huge donations year after year, building up his war chest, all while running unopposed.  
No wonder he wants things to stay the way they are.  
The premise of the No on Question 3 argument, that competing in both September and November is an unfair burden, treats the general electorate as an inconvenience to be avoided. In Massachusetts, you can count the legislative seats truly contested between Democrats and Republicans on one hand. While voters show up in November for marquee statewide races like governor, the vast majority skip low-turnout September primaries—the contests that actually decide who holds power on Beacon Hill for decades. Question 3 simply demands that lawmakers earn the votes of the entire electorate. 
Today, when challengers dare to take on an entrenched insider, they sometimes come close, only to hit a sudden-death wall: the partisan primary.  
This year, state Sen. Will Brownsberger had an opponent for the first time in 14 years. He drastically outspent his challenger, Daniel Lander, but survived the Democratic primary by only 35 votes.  
Lander would have been a highly competitive candidate in the higher-turnout November election, but he had no path forward. Instead, Brownsberger will now cruise to re-election in the general election, facing only token opposition from an unenrolled candidate. Under Question 3, a challenger doing unexpectedly well in the first round would advance to the general election, earning free media, new money, and volunteer energy. 
Opponents claim that Question 3 could prevent a favored party from having any candidates in the general election, but data from California and Washington show that “lockouts” (where a majority-party coalition is shut out entirely because of vote fragmentation) are rare.  
By contrast, we have the far more common problem of vote splitting in open seat elections. More than 40 percent of open seat elections for the Massachusetts Legislature result in a winner being elected who received a minority of votes in the crucial election. US Rep. Jake Auchincloss came to power via a 9-candidate primary, winning just 22.4 percent of the vote. Similarly, US Rep. Lori Trahan prevailed in a 10-candidate field in 2018 with just 21.7 percent.  
Question 3 addresses this minority winner problem by sending the top two candidates in an all-candidate primary to the higher-turnout election in November, rather than letting a 25 percent primary winner cruise to victory without significant opposition in November, build a war chest, and stay in office for decades.  
What about third parties? They don’t have a chance under the current rules. It was more than 100 years ago, in 1917, that a third-party candidate last won a seat in the Massachusetts Legislature. 
Yet Democratic Party operatives used a specious concern for Libertarian Party and Green Party candidates as a pretense in a challenge they filed that sought to prevent voters from even considering all-party primaries. The Supreme Judicial Court unanimously swatted down this argument aimed at keeping Question 3 off the ballot. The court ruled that the proposed law is a legitimate regulation of elections that treats candidates and parties fairly, referring to its 1908 decision that upheld the identical system used in municipal elections. 
Question 3 would actually benefit third parties by including their endorsement of a candidate on the first-round ballot—unlike the current system, where candidates in the primary can only list public offices held. Under Question 3, an endorsement requires the consent of both the party and the candidate. Third parties could develop a meaningful brand name that would provide voters cues to counteract the domination of the incumbents. 
Although incumbents would still dominate, the best evidence that Question 3 would make them more vulnerable is the steadfast opposition of almost all politicians who would be affected by the changes. 
Question 3 moves the final decision from the elections that most people ignore to the ones that have high participation, fixes the plurality winner problem of open-seat primaries, and empowers small parties by giving them a way to build a meaningful brand.  
Some progressives say that Question 3 is a plot to enable the right wing, while some MAGA supporters claim that it is designed to cement Democratic domination. Neither is true. By  moving the contest to the November election with vastly more participation, all-party primaries will help election outcomes better reflect the wishes of the citizens of each electoral district. After approving Question 3, we could improve the system by approving ranked-choice voting, which would also allow for consolidation of the current two stages into a single, high-turnout general election.  
On November 3, the current system ensures you almost certainly can’t vote out entrenched members of the Legislature or its leadership. But by voting yes on Question 3, voters can finally change the rules of the game and reclaim their voice.  
Paul Schimek is a transportation planner and data analyst based in Arlington. He is writing a book tracing America’s political dysfunction to its unusual regulation of political parties, starting with the 1888 Massachusetts ballot law.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Question 3 would bring California’s primary problems to Massachusetts
text:
QUESTION 3 on the November ballot is a matchup between the grass tops and the grassroots. The “yes” committee has raised $7.7 million (with the largest checks coming from private equity), and the “no” committee, with less than $200,000, is backed by a bipartisan coalition of unions, democracy groups, and working people.  
Much of the debate so far has been about the credible concerns of how healthy it is to have a small group of wealthy individuals bankroll a law that would make our elections look like the chaotic California elections. In fairness, many of Question 3’s mega-donors genuinely believe in this democracy reform, while it’s also true that some of them spent a lot of money trying to defeat the Fair Share Amendment, which funds our schools and transportation. 
Big money aside, less has been written about the merits and the track record of the election system the question would usher in, with all candidates competing in a single primary and the top two finishers advancing to the November final election. Here’s what the top-two election system produces in California and Washington.  
In Washington state’s 2016 race for state treasurer, a majority of primary voters in the five-candidate race picked a Democrat. Three Democrats split nearly 52 percent of the vote in the primary. Two Republicans, with 25 percent and 23 percent of the vote, finished first and second and took both spots on the November ballot. A majority of voters picked a Democrat in the primary yet there were no Democrats on the ballot in November.  
It cuts both ways. In 2022, six Republicans and two Democrats ran in California’s 4th State Senate District. The Republican candidates collectively won nearly 60 percent of the primary vote, but split it six ways, with the top Republican winning 17 percent. The two Democrats got 22 percent and 19 percent and took both spots on the final ballot. In that contest, nearly 60 percent of primary voters picked a Republican, but in November, they had to choose between two Democrats. 
This is the “top-two” system proposed by Question 3 in Massachusetts this year, and we should reject it.  
Supporters claim the top-two system boosts representation. The evidence, and conditions in Massachusetts, suggest otherwise. As chair of the Massachusetts Black and Latino Legislative Caucus, I take the representation argument seriously. Our communities are finally building a bench. More often now, two or three strong candidates of color run for the same open seat.  
Question 3 supporters should welcome that. Yet, under top-two, it’s a risk. In 2012, California’s 31st Congressional District was about 70 percent people of color and more than 40 percent Latino. The leading Democrat vying for the seat, Pete Aguilar, a Mexican-American politician, finished third in the “top-two” primary and was shut out because he split the vote with three other Democrats, while two Republicans finished first and second. In a district Barack Obama won with 57 percent of the vote, no Democrats were on the November ballot because of the top-two system. 
These are just a few examples where “top-two” delivered the opposite of what Question 3 backers claim. Proponents of the California system will say that lockouts like these, where vote splitting shuts a party out of November, are rare. While it’s true that it usually doesn’t happen, it happens enough that the threat of it happening is exactly how money becomes more influential in these races.  
If a party wants to avoid being locked out of November, significant pressure is placed on new candidates with less money and recognition to back out. We just saw this in California, where the state Democratic Party chair asked Democrats who “do not have a viable path” to drop out of the race for governor in order to reduce the real risk of only two Republicans appearing on the ballot in November.  
“Viable path” is often code for money. Gubernatorial candidate Tony Thurmond said party leaders were “essentially telling every candidate of color in the race for governor to drop out.”  
Pushing candidates out may be smart strategy for keeping at least one Democrat on California’s November ballot, but it shows the perverse incentives this system creates. How perverse? In 2022, the Republican leader of the California Senate spent about $50,000 on a mailer promoting a Democrat. The goal was to steer Democratic voters toward one Democrat and away from the other, dropping her below the leading Republican and opening second place for the GOP. We don’t need these perverse incentives in Massachusetts. Running is already hard enough for first-time and working-class candidates. 
Massachusetts wouldn’t be the first state to say no. Voters in Oregon (2014), Arizona (2012) and, in 2024, South Dakota rejected top-two primaries, mostly by about a two-to-one margin. That same year, similar all-party primary measures failed in Colorado, Idaho, Montana, and Nevada. Colorado’s fight looks a lot like ours: Backers led by a former health care CEO raised $19 million, the opposition, largely groups representing working people, raised less than $400,000 and still won via a grassroots effort.  
The promise of a turnout boost doesn’t hold up either. Two studies of top-two (here and here) found no boost in overall turnout. One found that up to 7 percent more voters skip the race when both finalists are from the same party. 
In Massachusetts, the election calendar makes this proposition particularly bad. Far fewer people vote in September. In 2024, 16.6 percent of registered voters cast a primary ballot. In November, about 68 percent voted. If you’re reading an op-ed about primaries, you’re probably a September voter. Thank you for being engaged! It’s true that a small September electorate already picks each party’s nominee. Question 3 wouldn’t fix that. It would give that small electorate a much bigger job: choosing the only two candidates anyone can vote for in November and leaving independents little chance of even making the ballot. Fewer than one in five voters would set the menu for everyone else. 
Finally, supporters say our current system shuts out unenrolled voters. But in Massachusetts, unenrolled voters can already vote in any party’s primary. Ironically, Question 3 would make it much harder for unenrolled and third-party candidates to make the November ballot. Today they can qualify for the November ballot by gathering signatures. Under Question 3, they’d first have to survive the September primary against major-party candidates. That has rarely happened in California and Washington.   
Democracy reform is personal for me. The first time I walked into the State House, I was a 16-year-old youth organizer advocating for our civics education bill with other Gateway City kids. Eight years later, I ran for state rep. and won a challenging primary and general election after fundraising less than $45,000 (California Assembly races can draw as much as $6 million in spending).  
That first session, we renewed our civics push and, thanks to a broad coalition, passed civics education legislation. Democracy is in a fragile spot right now. For too many people, democracy is not delivering, and we have to do better. Many are understandably ready to keep throwing any rock at the system, but we should be wary of big money trying to capitalize on that populist sentiment. The California system threatens to make things worse by further elevating the power of money in our politics and rewarding cynical electioneering.  
If the six- and seven-figure checks behind this campaign aren’t reason enough for concern, look at what the top-two system has produced in California and Washington: vote-splitting lockouts, perverse incentives to game the primary, and pressure on candidates without big money to drop out.  
The lesson is clear: Vote no on Question 3.  
Andy Vargas is a Democratic state representative from Haverhill. He is chair of the Massachusetts Black and Latino Legislative Caucus and co-chair of the Legislature’s Joint Committee on Community Development and Small Business.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: All-party primaries would be a step backwards for Massachusetts
text:
THE ARGUMENT IN support of Question 3 on the Massachusetts ballot is that “all-party primaries”—in which all candidates appear on a single preliminary ballot in September, with the top two vote-getters advancing to the general election in November—will increase electoral competition in Massachusetts and thereby make elected officials more responsive to public opinion.  
As Tanisha Sullivan recently stated in CommonWealth Beacon, “[w]ith inherently more competition, elected officials are better incentivized to listen and deliver.”  
This assumption is not wrong so much as it is misdirected.  
Under the system Question 3 would bring to Massachusetts elections, political parties would no longer play any meaningful role in choosing the candidates who run as members of their parties in either the proposed “all-party” preliminary election or the general election. This would amount to the elimination of Bay State parties’ capacity to act as meaningful intermediary institutions and likely lead to an increase in the already alarming number of wealthy self-funded candidates running for public office, as well as the ability of well-financed special interests to leverage their resources to exert undue influence over both elections and public policymaking. Indeed, the list of Question 3 backers is a who’s who of putative plutocrats and special interest groups. 
While the stated intention behind Question 3 is to “empower” voters, more likely we would see a reduction in the quality of democratic deliberation and, in the long run, turnout declines. Allowing parties to provide voters a meaningful choice between candidates in November connects elections to policy decisions, regardless of how competitive those elections are. 
Question 3 advocates seem to believe that increasing the competitiveness of elections requires voters in the Commonwealth to discount party labels, to “vote the candidate, not the party.” 
While popular with average voters—at least in theory—the truth is that the most meaningful single piece of information about candidates for most voters is their party label. Question 3 would eliminate the ability of Bay State parties to police the use of their party labels by candidates in elections and sever the only meaningful accountability link between candidates/officeholders and party platforms.  
Question 3 would replace the present system with a bit of a free-for-all. Proponents believe competitiveness would somehow guarantee more meaningful choices at the polls for all voters, but it likely would do so only in a narrow way, and only for a narrow slice of the electorate. Proponents of Question 3 are, after all, activists with political and programmatic agendas who want to change the rules of elections to favor their interests.  
Average voters, on the other hand, who we know are disproportionately dependent on the information reflected in party labels, will gain little in real value. Question 3 proponents may be correct that more folks will turn out for a competitive race, but their proposal would sacrifice quality for quantity.  
If enacted, Question 3 would effectively eliminate partisan elections, and voters increasingly will see candidates whose party labels reveal no real commitment to a party’s principles or policy preferences. Elections in which party labels lack real meaning eventually will turn on candidate quality and produce what political scientists call “candidate-centric elections.” It’s notable that, even with meaningful party labels at present, far too much campaign and media focus is on candidates and not ideological and programmatic deliberation and debate. 
Proponents argue that political parties would still endorse candidates in all-party primaries. But the very nature of these races would undermine the value of any candidate’s partisan affiliation. 
Massachusetts political party organizations are already among the weakest in America—both of them. Candidate endorsement and party identification are not substitutes for the utility that partisanship provides to voters. For party labels to provide meaningful cues, there must be a tangible and enforceable accountability relationship between a party and its candidates and officeholders, especially for legislators whose individual outputs must complement collective outputs. This is the only way that partisan affiliation can have any meaning to voters.  
In the long run, the preliminary election in September would produce an unmediated and less meaningful choice for voters, while the November general election would produce personalized food fights between two candidates who would have to rely on policy-lite, candidate-centric campaigns that essentially give voters little they could use to hold the winner accountable for their performance in office. In other words, two non-partisan elections means two expensive races to the rhetorical bottom.  
As a practical matter, Question 3 would complicate the timing and increase the costs of running for office. If its proponents’ objectives include empowering marginalized voices and minor parties, then increasing the costs while reducing the time to organize and campaign seems particularly unwise.  
Supporters rarely mention the extra burden this system would impose on candidates. Instead, they emphasize the fact that this system is already used to elect many local officials in non-partisan local elections. But local elections are inherently different from district-wide contests. The successes and failures of local elected officials are easier for average voters to see and experience first-hand, which is simply not possible in a state legislative, congressional, or statewide race.  
It is worth noting that previous “democratic reforms” to party nomination processes in Massachusetts have done considerable damage to the accountability link between candidates and voters that partisanship promotes. Massachusetts has experienced a rapid decline of party registration since automatic voter registration became the norm. Further weakening the role and influence of political parties will not increase accountability.  
Consider that, if the national Republican Party had had firm control over its presidential nomination process in 2016, Donald Trump’s disastrous presidency could have been averted. Here in Massachusetts, Question 3 would usher in a Wild West of candidate-centric elections that would reward imagery and symbolism but leave voters few benchmarks with which to hold winning candidates accountable for their efforts once in office. 
At the end of the day, if Question 3 passes and is implemented as written, the job of Massachusetts voters will become more difficult and the problem the initiative was intended to mitigate (that is, public policymaking that is insufficiently responsive to the interests of average voters) likely would continue, albeit for different reasons.  
In the case of the Legislature, for example, which Question 3 proponents believe is insufficiently responsive because incumbents “toe the party line” dictated by legislative leaders in exchange for insulation from electoral competition, non-partisan preliminary elections would exchange unresponsiveness due to leadership control of rank-in-file legislators for the gridlock that cripples legislatures full of free agents whose re-elections turn on individual marketing, rather than any commitment to a coherent policy agenda. To the extent Question 3 weakens legislative leadership by enhancing candidate autonomy, we are likely to see increased polarization and culture war posturing, phenomena that, as compared to other parts of the country, Massachusetts has managed to avoid.  
At bottom, if enacted Question 3 likely will undermine the facilitation of accountability provided by partisan elections, a reality long documented by political scientists. The resulting candidate-centric elections, which will turn on the ability of individual candidates to “connect with voters” and not on competing policy preferences or ideological differences, will favor the best campaigners, not the best policymakers and not candidates committed to a coherent agenda or ideological perspective that voters can use to rationally judge winning candidates’ performance once in office.  
Question 3 will, at once, increase the degree of difficulty voters face when trying to distinguish candidates on substantive grounds, while freeing candidates themselves from the tactical inconvenience of clear accountability for meaningful and measurable results if elected.  
Jerold Duquette is a professor of political science at Central Connecticut State University, contributor at MassPoliticsProfs.org, and co-editor of The Politics of Massachusetts Exceptionalism: Reputation Meets Reality. Lawrence Friedman teaches constitutional law at New England Law | Boston and is the co-author of The Massachusetts State Constitution, published by Oxford University Press.

name: California
title: New Medi-Cal limits force hard choices for seniors
text:
Caretaker Lexi Marsh (left) helps Elizabette Guéçamburu eat her lunch in the kitchen of her home outside Patterson on Oct. 16, 2026. Photo by Larry Valenzuela, CalMatters




Some low-income seniors and people with disabilities are being forced to draw down their savings to retain their healthcare coverage under a new Medi-Cal asset limit, writes CalMatters’ Kristen Hwang.
The new limit kicks certain groups off of Medi-Cal if they have more than $21,000 in savings as of July 2027. State lawmakers lowered the cap to help close a $12 billion budget shortfall in a compromise with Gov. Gavin Newsom.
Just two years ago Newsom set a policy that effectively eliminated the asset limit, allowing Medi-Cal recipients to hold on to savings. But when faced with a multibillion-dollar state spending gap, he proposed reinstating a cap at $2,000. The Legislature balked but agreed to lower the limit to $130,000 and then ratchet it down to $21,000 starting next summer.
About 600 people lost Medi-Cal when California imposed the $130,000 limit, according to state data. Senior and disability rights advocates say the cuts unfairly target vulnerable groups. They expect many more to lose Medi-Cal at the $21,000 limit. If the state returned to the initial $2,000 limit, an estimated 62,000 people would have lost Medi-Cal.
Elizabette Guéçamburu, a 44-year-old who has spinal muscular atrophy, requires a power wheelchair and daily caregiving. 
To remain eligible, she’ll likely have to give up financial independence and put some money into a trust controlled by a family member. She also had her family strike her from inheriting any portion of their 100-year-old farm.

Guéçamburu: “I have to surrender our legacy just to have medical security and have the ability to live my life.”

Seen and heard at CA state worker strike


State workers represented by SEIU Local 1000 strike at the state Capitol in Sacramento on Oct. 21, 2026. Photo by Fred Greaves for CalMatters




Thousands of California government workers represented by SEIU Local 1000 walked off the job Wednesday to press Newsom for a better contract than he’s offered, and some of them came dressed to send a message. 
In Sacramento, prison analyst Don Chaddock wore a Santa costume and held a sign reading “Newsom + CalHR = Naughty List.” Chaddock said he is frustrated by the state’s in-office policy, which has him commuting to a suburb south of Sacramento.

Chaddock: “I don’t mind in-person if we’re actually doing something in-person. Right now, I drive to Elk Grove to sit in a cubicle.”

Here’s what CalMatters’ Kate Wolffe and I learned when we talked with striking workers in Sacramento and Oakland.



More cities want to stop data centers


An Amazon Web Services data center under construction in Gilroy on Aug. 31, 2026. Photo by Anna Hoch-Kenney, CalMatters




Local elected officials in California are pumping the brakes on data centers, reports CalMatters’ Katherine Ortiz.
As public concern over their environmental impact and energy usage grows, at least 26 resolutions, moratoriums or bans on data center development across the state have been passed or proposed in the last four months. 
Los Angeles County’s Monterey Park became the first U.S. city to permanently ban data centers in June. Fast forward to October and Oakland’s city council approved a 45-day moratorium on new approvals; San Francisco approved a similar moratorium; leaders in L.A. and Santa Clara counties are considering limitations, too. 

Nicole Ghio, Food & Water Watch’s California director: “This is not a future that I think a lot of people want. I mean, it’s a great future if you’re a tech billionaire. It’s not a great future if you’re a regular American.”

Proponents, meanwhile, argue that developing data centers is a critical national interest.
