name: West Virginia Watch
title: Commentary: West Virginia can’t invest its way out of losing coverage
text:
A hospital “H” sign. (Photo by Sarah Ladd/Kentucky Lantern)West Virginia has been given an extraordinary opportunity to invest in the future of rural health care.
The Rural Health Transformation Program is providing our state nearly $200 million in federal funding for 2026, with additional funding available through 2030. The program promises to expand access, strengthen the healthcare workforce, improve technology and modernize how rural health care is delivered.
Those are worthwhile goals. We should put these dollars to work. We should use them wisely. And we should hold ourselves accountable for making sure they improve the lives of people in every corner of our state.
But there is a fundamental problem with presenting this investment as though it answers West Virginia’s rural health crisis. It doesn’t. West Virginia cannot invest its way out of losing health coverage. The distinction matters.
The Rural Health Transformation Program is a five-year investment designed to change how healthcare is delivered. Medicaid is an ongoing source of health coverage and healthcare financing for hundreds of thousands of West Virginians.
One cannot simply replace the other. The numbers tell the story.
West Virginia received nearly $200 million for the first year of the Rural Health Transformation Program. Over the full five-year program, the federal government will distribute $50 billion nationally.
At the same time, analyses of the federal law’s Medicaid cuts estimate that West Virginia stands to lose more than $5.3 billion in Medicaid funding over the coming decade.
That is not a solution to a funding crisis. It is a fraction of what is being taken away. And we need to be honest about what these new dollars can — and cannot — do.
The Rural Health Transformation Program can support telehealth. It can support remote monitoring, artificial intelligence and other technology-enabled care. It can help recruit and retain healthcare workers and develop new models of delivering care.
All those things have a place in the future of rural healthcare. But AI cannot replace a doctor, telehealth cannot replace a hospital and technology cannot replace health insurance.
A person does not become insured because a new digital platform connects them to a provider. A rural hospital does not become financially stable simply because it has new technology. A community does not maintain access to healthcare when the people who live there can no longer afford to use it.
This is particularly troubling because West Virginia’s rural hospitals were already vulnerable before these Medicaid cuts.
There are hospitals in our state operating on razor-thin margins, some with negative revenue. We have declining patient volumes and persistent workforce shortages. Our hospitals serve an older, sicker and poorer population, and many rely heavily on Medicaid and Medicare, which reimburse providers at rates that can fall below the cost of providing care.
A national analysis published last year identified eight West Virginia hospitals at heightened risk of closure.  The analysis does not predict that these hospitals will close. It demonstrates where the financial pressure could be greatest. West Virginians  deserve to understand the vulnerabilities within their own communities and how policy decisions directly affect them. 
That is the part of this conversation that cannot be solved with a ribbon cutting for a new program.
When a hospital loses Medicaid revenue, it does not simply lose money for innovation. It often means fewer services, fewer providers, more uncompensated care, longer travel distances and, ultimately, the possibility that a hospital that has served a community for generations may no longer be able to keep its doors open.
And not only will there be a massive spike in uncompensated care, but we will see aggressive patient collection efforts that will increase West Virginians’ medical debt and undoubtedly more personal bankruptcies.    
Moreover, beginning Jan. 1, 2027, certain adults ages 19 through 64 enrolled in Medicaid expansion will generally have to complete 80 hours each month of qualifying work, education, training or community service — or meet another exemption — to maintain coverage.
For the people affected, this is not an abstract policy debate. It is another requirement they will have to understand, document and navigate to remain connected to healthcare.
West Virginia has already experienced what happens when administrative requirements become barriers to coverage. During the Medicaid unwinding, people lost coverage because they missed notices, did not understand what information was being requested or could not complete the renewal process on time.
Now we are asking many of the same people to navigate another set of requirements. And when people lose Medicaid, the consequences do not stop with them. They show up in doctors’ offices. They show up in hospitals’ uncompensated-care costs. They show up in pharmacies. They show up when someone delays treatment until a health problem becomes an emergency. And they show up in the financial stability of the very rural health care system we are now being told this new funding will transform.
That is the contradiction we need to confront. You cannot make a healthcare system more sustainable by simultaneously making it harder for people to pay for the care they need.
If we want people to work, they need to be healthy enough to work. If we want people to manage chronic conditions, they need access to a doctor and the medications they need. If we want rural hospitals to remain open, they need patients who have coverage and can pay for the care they receive. If we want mothers and babies to have healthy outcomes, women need access to prenatal and maternity care before a crisis occurs. And if we want West Virginians to live healthier lives, they need health coverage they can count on.
This is not an argument against the Rural Health Transformation Program. It is an argument against pretending that it solves a problem it was never large enough to solve.
West Virginia should take advantage of every dollar available to strengthen rural healthcare. We should invest in our workforce. We should improve transportation. We should use technology where it genuinely improves care. We should expand access to specialists. We should find new ways to bring care closer to people’s homes.
But we also must protect the foundation underneath all those efforts. People need coverage. Providers need patients who can pay. Hospitals need predictable revenue. Those things are connected.
We cannot celebrate an investment in rural health care while ignoring the much larger loss of Medicaid dollars that threatens the stability of that same system.
West Virginia has spent years bringing down our uninsured rate. The Affordable Care Act and Medicaid expansion changed what healthcare access looks like for hundreds of thousands of West Virginians.
That progress matters. And it can disappear much faster than we built it.
So, as we move forward with rural health transformation, let’s measure success by more than dollars awarded, programs launched or technology deployed.
Let’s ask the questions that matter to the people we are trying to serve.
Can they get an appointment? Can they afford to go? Can they get there? Is there a provider close to home? Will their local hospital still be open? Can they afford their prescriptions? And when they need care, will they still have health insurance?
West Virginia has an opportunity to build a stronger rural healthcare system. Let’s seize it. But let’s not confuse an investment with a replacement.
We cannot build a stronger healthcare system by making it harder for West Virginians to remain insured. We need to invest in our hospitals, our providers and our communities. And we need to protect the coverage that allows West Virginians to use them.
We need both.

name: VTDigger
title: Gov. Scott put property taxes and school consolidation center stage. Now Amanda Janoo is rallying opposition.
text:
A sign questioning the property tax rate seen in Jericho on Friday, October 16, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

JERICHO — Henry Listenik Jr. says he’s paying double what he did last year in property taxes. 
The 69-year-old voted for Gov. Phil Scott in 2024, but Listenik said he doesn’t think Scott has followed through on his promises. Now Listenik doesn’t know who to vote for.
The Jericho resident said that his kids, who are parents themselves, are considering moving out of state because they can’t find jobs or keep up with the cost of living. 
“Does our governor hear that?” he said in an interview. 
Vermont’s property taxes are among the highest in the country and have risen more than 40% on average over the past five years. Scott, the five-term Republican, has campaigned on affordability since his first run for governor. And he’s persuaded legislators to use state revenue to buy down property taxes for the past two years. 
Property tax rates are tied directly to education spending under the state’s current school funding system, which allows for little state control over how much local school districts spend. 
Vermont’s system is totally unique because it generally allows local school districts to spend however much they want to educate students, as long as voters approve. Then, they subsequently calculate property tax rates for the average homeowner based on how much the district plans to spend per student. Because districts have this discretion over their own spending, there’s wide variation across the state in how much districts pay to educate each student. 
Scott has pushed for a funding model that would allow the state to dictate school spending, rather than leaving it up to local districts. He reasons that a state-directed model could reign in costs and subsequently lower property taxes. Under his proposed model, districts would receive money from the state based on how many kids are enrolled and how expensive they are to educate. 
A consolidated education system with larger, regional schools would reduce building maintenance and staffing costs, Scott has said. A consolidated model would also improve student outcomes, Scott has argued, because it would help close gaps in resources between schools. 
To his Democratic challenger Amanda Janoo — a political newcomer stoking a competitive race for governor — Scott’s vision for reform is a “a thinly veiled attack on public education,” she said in an interview. 
Janoo offers a platform that challenges Scott’s vision — and she’s rallying Scott’s opposition. Janoo is opposed to school consolidation and said she wants to make small schools sustainable by turning them into community centers of sorts, offering services such as healthcare, afterschool programs and adult school. She wants to lower property taxes for the average homeowner by levying higher taxes on second homes and short term-rentals. 
In a September poll from Vermont Public, 41% of respondents said it was more important to them to keep property taxes as low as possible than it was to keep their local public school. Only 28% said it was more important to keep their local school. 
It was equally important to 29% of respondents to keep property taxes low and preserve their local school. 
An outsized number of polled Republicans — about two-thirds — said it was more important to keep property taxes low, while only a quarter of Democrats in the poll agreed. 
Scott said during a press conference last month that he believes his position on education has made him less popular among voters, responding to two recent polls that showed a decline in his favorability. 
“But I don’t regret anything that we’ve done. I think it’s necessary that we fix the system that we have,” Scott said. 
Vermont spends among the most per-student nationwide, yet most students aren’t meeting grade-level standards, and graduation rates are declining. Its schools see troubling rates of declining enrollment. 
Funding the system
Scott envisions education reform as the key to lowering property tax rates and has called the issue Vermont’s “most critical challenge.” 
Meanwhile, Janoo’s platform vows to address some of the root causes of rising education costs, namely behavioral care for students and staff health insurance. She said she plans to lower healthcare costs in part by creating a system for universal primary care. 
She envisions a tax system in which education funds are less solely dependent on taxing primary residences and include taxing second homes or Airbnbs.
Levying taxes on other forms of property would “discourage the use of housing for that purpose and also generate revenue that can reduce the property tax burden for residential Vermonters,” Janoo said. 
Key to Scott’s vision is transitioning to a state-directed funding model, called a foundation formula, in tandem with school consolidation. 
Most states use a foundation formula model, which allows the state to decide how much it spends to educate each student, with certain added adjustments for kids who are more expensive to educate, such as those from low-income families or English language learners. Scott has said that a foundation formula would help offer more resources to rural schools, and his education secretary has blamed test score disparities on the state’s current funding system. 
“For what we’re paying, we should be number one,” said Scott in a recent campaign video. 
Under current state law, Vermont will transition to a foundation formula model in 2029 so long as districts have the opportunity to consider mergers, and legislators pass laws to decide the specifics of the formula, among other contingencies. 
Sheldon Foley, 42, of Waitsfield, said that he’s now paying $4,000 more in annual taxes than he did five years ago. After growing up in the Warren and Waitsfield area, he said it’s possible he might get priced out of his hometown and be forced to move. 
“I’d be silly not to consider it,” Foley said.
Foley doesn’t have kids, and said he doesn’t know “the nuts and bolts” of the state’s education system. But he thinks the state needs reform to deal with its declining enrollment, he said. 
“I’d hate to see schools close, but this isn’t sustainable,” Foley said. He said he plans to vote for Scott.
As lawmakers continue to debate reform, Scott has gotten them to follow his lead on using state revenue to buy down property taxes. This year, legislators agreed to spend $105 million in state revenue to soften the blow of what was a 12% average projected increase in property taxes. 
Consolidation or keeping schools 
While Scott has supported using property tax buydowns for short-term relief, his push for a consolidated model as a long-term fix has taken center stage in state politics, garnering both fans and skeptics. 
After pushing for forced school district merger legislation this year, Scott ultimately joined lawmakers in backing a process that incentivized voluntary mergers. That process is getting underway this fall. Merger committees are required to submit a final report to the state in September 2027, and any mergers are expected to appear on the ballot on Town Meeting Day in 2028. 
David Schoales of Brattleboro will be voting for Janoo because they disagree with Scott’s vision for consolidated school districts, they said. The retired educator sits on the steering committee for the Rural School Community Alliance, a coalition of educators and parents that want to preserve rural schools. Schoales said they aren’t convinced a consolidated model would save money or lead to better outcomes for students. 
“It doesn’t look at the effect on students, it doesn’t look at the effect on education, and again, it doesn’t save any money,” they said. 
Any costs saved by efficiencies in a consolidated model will be offset by other cost increases such as transportation, Schoales said. When schools in Arkansas consolidated, a 20 year study found the state saw little cost savings, according to The Hechinger Report.
Janoo, who grew up in Strafford attending classes of about a dozen students, said she wants to preserve rural schools because she sees them as pillars of rural communities. 
The state has already witnessed a steady economic decline and a “hollowing out of a lot of our communities,” Janoo said. To close a community’s school is to basically give up on it as a whole, she said. 
Janoo said she supports the community schools model, which focuses on providing resources to meet kids’ basic needs. A handful of schools across Vermont received federal grant funds in 2021 to pilot the model. In some schools, the program involved creating a food shelf for students, and in others it involved driving students to doctors appointments. Although federal funds dried up in 2024, some schools have kept the practice going on their own dime.  
“I just know how important small schools and rural schools are in particular as the center and hub of our communities,” she said.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Commentary: Lincoln-Douglas, they’re not. The sorry scene of today’s political debates.
text:
Charles Booker, right, speaks during a debate with U.S. Rep. Andy Barr at the WKYT studios in  Lexington, Ky., on Monday, Oct. 19, 2026. (Courtesy pool photographer Ryan Hermens)Debates sure aren’t what they used to be.
Do you remember gathering around the TV (how quaint!) to watch two candidates try to politely (how delightfully old-fashioned!) out-argue each other on substantive points of public policy?
It’s not that debates aren’t consequential. Ask former President Joe Biden what a big deal they can be. 
But here in Kentucky, it feels like we have more debates where one person holds forth than actual debates where two candidates argue about issues.
Just this cycle, KET will host three solo debates: Ed Gallrein, GOP nominee for the 4th Congressional District, and two next week with Democrats Drew Williams, running for the 1st District, and Ned Pillersdorf in the 5th District. 
The only real debates so far have been Rep. Andy Barr and Charles Booker battling for Sen. Mitch McConnell’s seat, and the very anticipated matchup between the 6th District candidates Ralph Alvarado and Zach Dembo on Thursday.
Now, the Gallrein conversation happened because of a peculiar set of circumstances. KET, the statewide public television station, has a set of criteria for who gets to be on stage.
Those criteria require each candidate to have raised at least $100,000 by the July filing deadline for the general election. Melissa Strange, the Democratic candidate in the 4th District, had not reached that threshold.
KET spokesman Todd Piccirilli said the same criteria apply for primary and general elections, calling it a “what would be a reasonable minimal threshold of campaign support and viewer interest.” (Piccirilli denied the rules were inspired by Geoff Young, a perennial candidate so unpopular with Democrats that Gov. Andy Beshear disavowed him as a congressional candidate.)
Two points on this: Yes, it’s reasonable to use this as winnowing out of a crowded primary field. And yes, it’s reasonable to expect a viable Congressional candidate of one party in our two-party system to have raised $100,000 by the general election.
In addition, this race has a Libertarian candidate and an independent write-in candidate. 
But I wonder why KET wouldn’t just cancel the debate, since the word implies two people debating ideas. In addition, it sends a bad message about our campaign finance system, and the power of the wealthy on both sides of the aisle to control our political systems.
As Melissa Strange noted in a social media post, Gallrein declined to debate Massie during the Republican primary: “Now he accepts when there will be no one there to challenge him on his unpopular policies, and unconditional support of the president,” she wrote.
It’s not democracy, Strange said. 
Nor is it a debate.
Larger problems
But debates have bigger problems than KET.
The fact is they’re a lot of work and one slight misstep can send viral videos shooting out across the hemisphere.
Tres Watson is a former Republican operative who is now co-host of the Kentucky Politics podcast. He’ll be providing commentary on the 6th District debate on Thursday evening on Fox 56. 
He says campaign experts have realized that in today’s hyperpartisan atmosphere, most voters are unpersuadable, and won’t change their minds based on one debate.
“The partisanship has gotten to a point where they are more likely not to show up to vote than to join your side,” Watson said. “What works best for low propensity votes is fear. It’s cheaper and easier to scare low propensity voters than to persuade undecided voters to vote for you.”
As depressing as that is, it’s also impossible to fact check debates at the speed at which candidates embroider and sometimes erase the truth. They’re too busy coming up with well-rehearsed zingers than providing thoughtful answers to thorny problems.
“If I thought the debates would be substantive, Lincoln-Douglas style debates, then yes, I’d be more enthusiastic, but they’re not,” Watson said. “They say the talking points, they talk over each other, they ignore the questions. There’s this idealized thought we have of debates, but 90% of them, that’s not what they are.”
This is all predictably depressing, another terrible light on our political system. Still, I think debates are one worthy information point in a huge data field. It’s a shame more politicians don’t think so, too.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Kentucky AG says public funding can be used to fund school resource officers at private schools
text:
A child crosses under caution tape at Robb Elementary School on May 25, 2022 in Uvalde, Texas, where 19 students and 2 adults were killed. Dozens of officers from various agencies stood in the hallways for over an hour, reportedly confused about chain of command. (Photo by Brandon Bell/Getty Images)Republican Kentucky Attorney General Russel Coleman says it is constitutional to use public, county funding to fund the placement of school resource officers at private schools, according to a legal opinion published earlier this month. 
Republican Boone County Attorney Jordan Turner had requested the legal opinion as the county fiscal court considered a proposal earlier this year to use county funds to pay for a portion of the costs of placing school resource officers at private schools. The funds would be allocated to the county sheriff’s office, which could then cover a portion of the costs of the school resource officers. 
Christopher Thacker, general counsel for the attorney general, wrote that because private schools had to reimburse the Boone County Sheriff’s Office for the total cost of the time served by school resource officers on campus, not all private schools were utilizing the officers. 
Thacker wrote that using county funds to give to the sheriff’s office that could then use the funding to cover the “out-of-pocket costs” for placing school resource officers at private schools was allowable under the Kentucky Constitution. The reason Thacker cited: because it serves “a public purpose and any benefit to the schools is indirect”. 
“Rather, it is well established that such benefits to a non-public school may be permitted to further a valid public purpose where no direct payments are made to the private schools themselves,” Thacker wrote. “Promoting the greater presence of SROs in all schools within the county unquestionably advances that public purpose.” 
Under the current system, the Boone County Sheriff’s Office requires that private schools reimburse the sheriff’s office the entire cost of the time served by school resource officers, while public schools in Boone County, on average, have reimbursed about 40% of the costs. The fiscal court’s proposal would require public and private schools to reimburse some costs at the same rate. 
The opinion is the latest legal assertion in an ongoing debate over whether public funding should subsidize or pay for non-public schools. 
Earlier this year, the Kentucky Supreme Court struck down a 2022 law passed by the GOP-controlled Kentucky legislature allowing charter schools, arguing it did not meet the requirement in the Kentucky Constitution for lawmakers to “provide for an efficient system of common schools” across the state. Kentucky voters decisively rejected a constitutional amendment in 2024 that would have allowed lawmakers to allocate public funding for private schools. 
Boone County Sheriff’s Office Public Information Officer Philip Ridgell told the Lantern that the county has one of the largest school resource officer programs in the entire state with 36 such officers assigned to various schools. 
“As the need and the want for SROs increases, certainly funding becomes a centerpiece of that with certain private entities, and this question came up earlier this year,” Ridgell said. “This was more of having some foresight and anticipating what could be a question in our growing community.” 
Ridgell said unlike the larger debate over the use of public funding for non-public schools, the discussion surrounding the school resource officer proposal has not been contentious in Boone County because it’s centered on “school safety and staffing.” 
“Some of our public and private schools are neighbors to one another. They’re within less than 100 yards of each other with where they’re built,” Ridgell said. “There’s a lot of those factors to consider, and that’s kind of why I believe that this one isn’t, and shouldn’t be moving forward, rooted in a whole lot of controversy.”

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Elections chief says Virginia is ready for midterms, potential federal interference
text:
Virginia Elections Commissioner Steve Koski in his Richmond office. Koski says state and local officials are prepared to conduct secure Nov. 3 elections and respond to potential disruptions. (Photo by Markus Schmidt/Virginia Mercury)Virginia’s top elections official says voters can have confidence in both the integrity of the Nov. 3 midterms and the results, even if President Donald Trump or his allies challenge Republican losses or attempt to interfere with the election process. 
“I think Virginia voters should be very confident in the level of preparation and experience that their local election officials have in administering elections,” Steve Koski, the state’s new elections commissioner, said in a lengthy interview with The Mercury. 
Appointed by Democratic Gov. Abigail Spanberger after she took office in January, Koski said election officials have prepared for potential disruptions but would not speculate about how the Trump administration might respond if Democrats capture congressional seats now held by Republicans. 
“I cannot speak for any potential actions that anybody else would take. But regardless, I feel prepared, I feel our localities are prepared to run this election well, and we will do so in accordance with the law,” he said. 
Koski also addressed Republican concerns about election integrity, including unsubstantiated allegations of noncitizen voting and ballots being sent to deceased voters. 
Asked whether the Department of Elections had evidence of noncitizens casting ballots, he said: “We have no information at the department to indicate that.” 
 Citizenship checks and disputed removals

Last week, White House spokeswoman Lauren Bias accused Virginia Democrats of “mailing ballots to dead felons” and dismissed Attorney General Jay Jones’ new voter protection unit as a political stunt.  
The accusation followed reports that voting-rights restoration letters had been sent to deceased Virginians as part of Spanberger’s effort to restore rights to people with felony convictions who had finished their time behind bars. 
Spanberger said her administration was investigating the erroneous mailings. 
“The restoration is completely separate from voter registration and requesting absentee ballots,” Koski said, adding that people whose rights are restored must still register, meet eligibility requirements and request an absentee ballot. 
Noncitizens cannot legally vote in Virginia. Registration applicants must attest to their citizenship, and election officials compare voter records with monthly information from the Department of Motor Vehicles to identify potentially ineligible registrations. 
Local registrars review those records individually, providing notice and an opportunity to confirm citizenship, Koski said. 
The procedures became the subject of litigation before the 2024 presidential election, when then-Gov. Glenn Youngkin ordered daily data sharing to identify potentially ineligible voters. 
The U.S. Justice Department and voting rights organizations challenged this effort, arguing it violated federal restrictions on systematic voter removals within 90 days of an election. Youngkin’s administration maintained the reviews were individualized and permitted under state law. 
Voting rights groups warned that eligible citizens could be removed because of outdated DMV records or errors. A federal judge ordered roughly 1,600 registrations restored, but the U.S. Supreme Court stayed that order shortly before Election Day. 
Koski said Virginia now suspends its noncitizen list-maintenance process during the 90-day period. 
The disputed registrations did not establish that those removed had voted illegally. Asked about documented election fraud more generally, Koski described the state’s safeguards but did not provide a number. 
 Preparing for possible federal involvement

On Oct. 15, the Department of Elections and Jones’ office issued a joint bulletin explaining how local officials should respond to federal election monitors, armed agents near polling places or attempts to seize election materials by federal officials. 
The guidance distinguishes among U.S. Justice Department monitors, who generally need local authorization, congressional observers and monitors authorized by federal courts. Local officials are instructed to verify credentials and report disruptive conduct. 
Observers cannot photograph inside polling places, handle sensitive election materials or position themselves where they can see a voter’s marked ballot. Officials may remove those who violate the rules. 
As of last week, no active court order required Virginia localities to admit federal observers under the Voting Rights Act, according to the bulletin. 
If federal agents appear at polling locations, officials should contact attorneys and local law enforcement and, when safe, ask agents to remain outside the 40-foot restricted area. They should document what happens without physically obstructing agents. 
The bulletin also instructs officials to contact counsel immediately if presented with a search warrant, without delaying lawful access, and to record any materials seized. Subpoenas should be reviewed with attorneys.
Koski said his department recently participated in a tabletop exercise with state and federal partners to prepare for security problems. Officials have also worked with local attorneys and law enforcement to clarify responsibilities before Election Day. 
Earlier this month, Jones established a Voter Protection Section to investigate complaints about intimidation, improper registration cancellations, absentee ballot denials and other voting barriers. 
Koski said the attorney general’s office advises his department while exercising separate civil enforcement responsibilities. 
“We certainly will cooperate with their efforts,” he said. 
Asked about federal requests for voter records, Koski cited ongoing litigation and said Virginia had not provided voter information for federal citizenship checks. 
His department also has regional liaisons who help localities resolve problems. Recruiting poll workers remains a challenge, Koski said, encouraging Virginians to volunteer.
 Paper ballots and safeguards against fraud

Virginia’s ballot scanners are not connected to the internet, and must meet state certification standards, Koski emphasized. “Each locality is required to go through rigorous testing for voting equipment prior to the election,” he said. 
Afterward, risk-limiting audits compare hand-counted samples of paper ballots with machine totals. State law requires an audit of at least one randomly selected U.S. House race in congressional election years. 
“It’s important to know that every vote in Virginia has a paper ballot record attached to it, and these all have strict chain-of-custody requirements that are followed,” Koski said. 
Ballots are sealed and stored after elections, with local circuit court clerks responsible for their custody. 
Koski also assured absentee voters following the Trump administration’s attempt to impose new postal requirements before the midterms. 
The rule would have required states to submit voter information to the U.S. Postal Service and meet new ballot-envelope standards, including specialized barcodes. 
On Sept. 15, the U.S. Supreme Court declined to lift a preliminary injunction, leaving the rule blocked for the 2026 election without deciding its legality. 
“Voters should be confident in voting absentee by mail,” Koski said. 
The administration argued the requirements would prevent fraud. But states challenging the rule warned they could prevent eligible voters from casting ballots. Justice Brett Kavanaugh separately cited the lack of time to implement the rule while leaving open whether the Postal Service had authority to adopt it. 
Voters may return absentee ballots to local registrars, designated drop boxes or polling places until 7 p.m. on Election Day. 
Mailed ballots must be postmarked by Nov. 3 and received by noon Friday, Nov. 6. Koski recommended requesting a hand-stamped postmark. The deadline to request an absentee ballot by mail is Friday, Oct. 23. 
Election night results are unofficial, Koski emphasized, “because the local canvas has to happen.” Local electoral boards reconcile precinct records with machine totals, review provisional ballots and count eligible absentee ballots arriving after Election Day. 
The State Board of Elections is scheduled to certify results on Dec. 7. 
Asked about pressure to reject results, Koski said certification is a ministerial duty, meaning officials are legally required to carry it out. Virginia law also provides procedures for recounts and election challenges, including court review. 
“We have secure and transparent processes in place for the handling of ballots, the tabulation of ballots, and voters should be confident about these processes,” Koski said.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Virginia’s 2026 report calls for expanded college access, improved postsecondary planning
text:
Damon Jiggetts, president and CEO of ACCESS College Foundation, and U.S. House Committee on Education and the Workforce Ranking Member Bobby Scott at an October 2026 financial aid workshop in Portsmouth. (Photo by Nathaniel Cline/Virginia Mercury)Virginia is increasingly using statewide postsecondary planning resources to sustain and increase higher education enrollment and expand workforce opportunities, a new report found. 
In 2022, lawmakers directed the Virginia Department of Education and the State Council of Higher Education to conduct annual studies on how the commonwealth maintains and updates statewide postsecondary planning resources for students, families, educators and school divisions.
In the 2026 report, the two agencies recommended that Virginia keep updating scholarships and education-cost guidance to help students and families — including the Dorvals in Chesapeake — compare college, training, military and career pathways.
“This is our first kid, so we’re just trying to make sure that we tick all the boxes off and set her on the right path, and make sure that we’re doing the things that we can do to set her up for success,” said Rebecca Dorval, parent of a Virginia high school senior, at a recent FAFSA application workshop in Portsmouth. 
On Oct. 14, Rebecca and her husband, Jason Dorval, attended an evening financial aid workshop at Churchland High School hosted by the ACCESS College Foundation, which helps make college more affordable and easier to navigate for students. Families and students from Portsmouth, Norfolk and Chesapeake were invited. 
The couple said they are navigating higher education costs for the first time after Jason’s retirement from the Coast Guard in July. He said he and his wife were “lucky” to have no debt from the Coast Guard Academy and to land a good-paying job.
Now, their goal is to give their children similar benefits.
“For both of our kids, to be able to go to college as debt-free as possible is what we’re looking for,” Rebecca said. “We’re just trying to figure out what we can do to make it a little bit easier for them, because everything is more expensive right now, and it’s going to be expensive for them while they’re there, too.” 
ACCESS College Foundation advisors host a financial aid workshop in Portsmouth in October 2026. (Photo by Nathaniel Cline/Virgnia Mercury)
 Findings

The agencies’ report also found that Virginia has a coordinated system for distributing postsecondary planning information, with broad resource coverage, multiple distribution channels and ongoing needs around scholarships and education costs.
The agencies also found that website engagement increased in late summer 2026, with visits rising from 638 in August to 719 in September. Page views also grew from 716 to 821.
In addition, the report detailed challenges students and families face in navigating postsecondary education.
Applying for financial aid is one of the key challenges.
In September 2025, the U.S. Department of Education published a new Free Application for Federal Student Aid, or FAFSA, after a lengthy overhaul. The agency said the changes “simplify” and “modernize” the application process, and it also changed the formulas used to determine aid eligibility.
U.S. House Committee on Education and the Workforce Ranking Member Bobby Scott, a Democrat from Newport News, works with ACCESS to offer financial aid workshops in his district.
“College education is still the primary way for upward social mobility in the United States,” Scott said in a recent interview.
Amid changes to federal aid that limit borrowing, he argued that college affordability means helping students access and afford the education they choose, not simply pressuring colleges to lower prices.
While the event attracted a few people, Damon Jiggetts, president and CEO of ACCESS College Foundation, said the organization’s goal is to help students and parents make informed decisions about postsecondary paths, whether one or a hundred show up.
“We want to make sure that our students and parents are making informed decisions about their post-secondary path,” Jiggetts said.
He said ACCESS advisors start engaging with students as early as 7th grade, helping with the FAFSA application, guiding scholarships and grants to bridge gaps between aid packages and loans and offering internal scholarships to help prevent excessive debt.
 Further recommendations

The agencies’ report advised the state to continue annual updates and interagency coordination, improve scholarship and cost guidance and strengthen access to workforce and postsecondary information.
One policy suggestion called for the state to consider tracking whether students use these resources to complete financial aid applications, select affordable education or training pathways, enroll in postsecondary programs and achieve successful employment outcomes.
State lawmakers will return in January to discuss further education legislation.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Lawmakers pitch reforms for Virginia’s building code update to boost supply, affordability
text:
Apartments under construction in Richmond, Va. on May 15, 2026. (Photo by Charlotte Rene Woods/Virginia Mercury)Every three years, Virginia updates its building code, requirements for new construction that account for safety standards and energy efficiency. 
As the state readies for its next update cycle in 2027, some lawmakers are flagging a series of reforms they argue can help increase housing supply and address affordability issues. 
A 2021 state study found that Virginia had a housing shortage of at least 200,000 units. Virginians most affected by lack of affordable housing are renters, have low incomes and often work in essential occupations, the study also found. 
Lawmakers have since proposed various building code updates and worked to pass numerous housing laws as a remedy. 
Sen. Schuyler VanValkenburg, D-Henrico, and Del. Adele McClure, D-Alexandria, sent a joint letter to leadership of Virginia’s Department of Housing and Community Development on Oct. 21 outlining their latest recommendations. 
They suggested allowing single-stairway buildings in certain multi-unit buildings —  something DHCD’s board has already shown interest in. 
Both legislators said the measure is key to unlocking housing development on vacant or underutilized lots. They hope the new code could allow buildings up to six stories and 24 housing units to only need one stairwell.
The concept, VanValkenburg said, is that narrow lots have less room for additional stairwells that eat into space that could be apartments. Adding more housing stock is one component of addressing access and affordability. 
“When families are struggling to pay their rent or mortgage or being priced out of communities across the Commonwealth, we must reevaluate our approach and find innovative solutions,” VanValkenburg wrote.
But reducing stairwells, fire unions suggest, could also be a safety hazard. 
“Safety is the primary issue, not only for the residents in those buildings, but our firefighters responding to emergencies as well,” Andrew Pantelis, a vice president with the International Association of Fire Fighters, said last May.  
He outlined scenarios where people may be fleeing a building in a panic and trying to exit using the same stairwell emergency responders are entering, creating potentially fatal bottlenecks.
Can one stairwell help solve Virginia’s housing crisis? Lawmakers think so

But research from Pew suggests that may not be as risky as presumed. Fire deaths in New York City’s more than 4,000 single-stair buildings occurred at the same rate as in other residential buildings from 2012 to 2024, the data showed. 
In that time, New York and Seattle recorded a total of four fire-related deaths in such buildings. 
The two cities are among a growing list of localities across the country to have embraced single-stairwell buildings up to six floors. To balance safety concerns, these buildings include square footage limits, unit caps per floor and higher density of sprinklers or placement of smoke detectors. 
“Adopting these reforms in our Building Code will dramatically cut the cost of housing development, without compromising on safety, and add much needed units to our housing stock,” VanValkenberg said.
He and McClure also suggest allowing scissor stairs in buildings that need more than one stairwell. Scissor stairs are two interlocking stairways that wind around each other with a fire-rated wall in between them. 
VanValkenburg said they reduce space that could be residential units while still permitting more than one stairwell in taller buildings. New York City and Chicago currently allow these types of stairs.
They also advise that Virginia revise elevator dimension requirements. Reducing size requirements for shorter buildings can make it more feasible for those buildings to still include elevators, the legislators said. 
Adopting a “missing middle” building code is another suggestion. 
The term applies to smaller multi-family buildings like duplexes, triplexes, quadplexes or townhomes that resemble single-family homes and allow for more density in certain neighborhoods. 
This housing type has been tucked into commercial building codes rather than residential building codes. Cities like Memphis are shifting them to ease certain regulatory requirements. 
In an effort to streamline construction processes and reduce administrative hurdles, McClure and VanValkenburg also propose expanding the use of third-party inspectors. 
Currently, builders can engage licensed inspectors, but fragmented local requirements often make them impractical to operate regionally. Having consistent statewide requirements could ease workflow processes, the lawmakers argue. 
Princeton professor Evan Soltas found that longer permitting timelines raises housing construction costs. McClure and VanValkenburg point to how Georgia, Tennessee and Florida have allowed for third-party licensed inspections. 
DHCD’s board is expected to meet this December to consider proposed regulations, which could be finalized by the middle of next year. 
As McClure serves on the Virginia Housing Commission and VanValkenburg routinely focuses his legislation on the subject, both lawmakers have expressed an eagerness to engage with DHCD in the months ahead. 
“The current code development cycle presents an opportunity to advance meaningful reforms that could lower housing costs and support increased housing production without waiting for another regulatory cycle,” McClure and VanValkenburg wrote in their letter.

name: Maine Morning Star
title: Weighing state’s ambiguous environmental justice standard, judge gives go-ahead to Juniper Ridge
text:
Maulian Bryant, executive director of the Wabanaki Alliance and Penobscot Nation citizen, outside the Penobscot County Judicial Center in Bangor after a July 23, 2026 hearing in the Penobscot Nation's appeal of the Juniper Ridge Landfill expansion's public benefit determination. (Photo by Kaitlyn Budion/Maine Morning Star)With no clear definition from the state for ‘environmental justice,’ a Penobscot County Superior Court justice said he can only consider state lawmakers’ intentions for the standard. And under that narrow interpretation, he has ruled that the state’s initial approval of the Juniper Ridge Landfill expansion will hold, despite concerns raised by neighboring Penobscot Nation. 
The Tribe along with the Conservation Law Foundation appealed the Maine Department of Environmental Protection’s public benefit determination for the second time this year. 
In his order Friday, Justice Bruce Mallonee wrote that the court does not offer an independent evaluation of the determination or its “advisability,” but concluded it does not violate state statute. 
“We have fought pollution, injustice and decades of harm to heal the Penobscot River, a relative that has sustained our people since time immemorial and continues to sustain communities across Maine,” Penobscot Nation Tribal Chief Kirk Francis said in a statement. “We are not asking the state to undo generations of harm overnight. We are asking it not to take us backward. Our cultural survival is tied to the health of the Penobscot River, and there is too much at stake to keep adding to the harms it already carries.”
Juniper Ridge is owned by the state through the Bureau of General Services, which has an operating contract with NEWSME Landfill Operations, a subsidiary of waste management company Casella.
Sharon Huntley, spokesperson for the Maine Department of Administrative and Financial Services, said in a statement that given the significant role that the landfill “serves in waste disposal in Maine and the dire consequences of a stalled process,” the state is relieved that the determination has advanced, allowing the Bureau of General Services to focus on the expansion application.
Jeff Weld, vice president of communications for Casella, said in a statement Wednesday that the company is pleased with the court’s ruling. 
“This decision represents an important step toward ensuring that Maine has the infrastructure and disposal capacity necessary to responsibly manage its solid waste into the future,” Weld said. “We remain committed to working collaboratively with the State of Maine and other stakeholders throughout the remaining permitting process, with a focus on providing safe, reliable and environmentally responsible operations while supporting Maine’s long-term waste management needs.”
The Maine Department of Environmental Protection first issued a positive public benefit determination for the expansion in October 2024, but the Tribe and legal group appealed the decision. 
In January, Mallonee struck down that determination, and in March the department again found that the expansion was in the public interest. The groups returned to court in July, where opponents argued the state has continued to fail to meet environmental justice standards. 
Environmental justice 
In his latest ruling, Mallonee said it “remains a challenge” to determine if the second determination complies with environmental justice, especially because the term is not defined in state law and has not been interpreted by the Maine Supreme Judicial Court. 
And environmental justice, which Mallonee described as an “opaque and difficult subject,” is not a factor in later regulatory approval and any “violation must be identified now, on a limited record.” 
Mallonee noted the department’s “good faith” efforts to apply its expertise to the concept of environmental justice, but said the determination “shows the limits of that expertise.” 
He said that there is no evidence in the record that the location of Juniper Ridge targeted the Penobscot Nation, instead the location was based on convenience, because the landfill was established to serve a nearby paper mill.
But he said the pollution of the Penobscot River has impacted the Penobscot Nation, as the Tribe has lost an important cultural food pathway, a loss that occurs in the larger context of its traditional way of life. 
“No analogy known to the court can compare to the loss this record shows the Penobscot Nation has suffered,” Mallonee said. 
The Penobscot Nation and Conservation Law Foundation argue that the loss is “definitive,” Mallonee said, and the existing damage to the Tribe’s way of life “prohibits imposing any continuing environmental burden on it, or even risking that that burden might be enhanced.”
But he ultimately concluded that he “cannot reasonably read” the environmental justice standards to be as expansive as they would like. 
“Because the statutory terms are (deeply) ambiguous, and the subject matter is beyond the department’s expertise, the court must interpret those terms in accordance with the Legislature’s intention,” Mallonee said. 
And under that narrower interpretation, Mallonee ruled that the determination is consistent with environmental justice standards.
Sludge disposal 
Mallonee noted that the main change from the department’s original determination was the addition of two “notable” license conditions regarding the treatment of sludge, a wastewater treatment byproduct, that has been contaminated with PFAS, or ​​per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances. 
The updated public benefit determination requires Casella to evaluate the availability and capacity of potential future technologies that would reduce the volume of sludge in its annual reports. The department will also establish annual limits on how much sludge, construction debris and oversized bulky waste Juniper Ridge can accept. 
Attorneys for the Penobscot Nation and Conservation Law Foundation previously argued that the department relied too heavily on anticipated sludge-drying facilities that are still in development, instead of existing technology that could be implemented sooner. 
But Mallonee concluded that the change in the second determination was a “substantial and indeed dramatic departure” from the original. And while it doesn’t “minimize sludge disposal to the degree” the groups would prefer, it does fulfill the waste management requirements at this preliminary stage of planning.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Indiana treasurer race draws competing visions for managing state funds
text:
Democrat Coumba Kebe, left, and Republican incumbent Daniel Elliott are competing for Indiana treasurer in a race focused on state investments and financial oversight. (Photos by Casey Smith/Indiana Capital Chronicle)Republican Treasurer Daniel Elliott is touting nearly $1.8 billion in state investment earnings in his bid for a second term, while Democratic challenger Coumba Kebe is calling for greater transparency in how Indiana manages public money.
The Nov. 3 election pits a former software engineer and local government official against a health care executive who says her work with seniors and people with disabilities showed her the consequences of statewide financial decisions.
Both candidates want to expand the office’s work with local communities and help more Hoosiers use its savings programs. But they differ on how to evaluate investment decisions, communicate with taxpayers and use the position to influence broader state policy.
The treasurer serves as Indiana’s chief investment officer, managing more than $16 billion. The job also includes leading the Indiana Bond Bank and Statewide 911 Board, overseeing savings programs and serving as sole trustee of the State Police Pension Trust.
Although the office does not write the state budget or set property tax rates, Elliott and Kebe each emphasized opportunities for the treasurer to influence those decisions — and both candidates promised to work with lawmakers on proposals to strengthen local finances and address the financial pressures facing Hoosier families.
Elliott emphasizes earnings, experience
Elliott, first elected to statewide office in 2022, is asking voters for another four years to continue his investment strategy, strengthen cybersecurity for 911 systems and help local governments finance infrastructure.
His office reported in August that state general fund investments had generated about $1.785 billion during his first term, including about $450.2 million in fiscal year 2026. Elliott argues that earning more from public money reduces pressure to raise taxes.
Indiana Treasurer Daniel Elliott, a Republican, speaks at a religious freedom rally on Thursday, June 11, 2026 in the Indiana Statehouse. (Photo by Leslie Bonilla Muñiz/Indiana Capital Chronicle)
In an interview with the Capital Chronicle, he credited the returns to a combination of available funds, investment flexibility granted by the General Assembly, experienced portfolio managers and favorable market conditions.
Before becoming treasurer, Elliott worked in software engineering and consulting and served on the Morgan County Council. He says that combination of technical experience and local government finance has helped him navigate an office with responsibilities spread across numerous boards and programs.
“I am probably the biggest nerd in the building,” he said. “But if you’re thinking about it, isn’t somebody who’s kind of nerdy who you want as your state treasurer?”
Kebe, a Noblesville resident who founded Scope Consulting, entered the treasurer’s race after losing the Democratic primary for House District 29. She said she began advocating online about Medicaid changes before deciding to run for office, frustrated that elected officials were not listening to concerns from people working in health care.
She’s spent the past decade in the Medicaid and senior care fields, including work managing budgets and operations. That experience, she argues, would bring a different perspective to the state’s financial decisions.
“Government is here to provide to keep people safe and to take care of people, and we can’t continue to make decisions just focused on the numbers,” Kebe said. “We’ve got to focus on people.”
A divide over investment politics
Elliott has made opposition to environmental, social and governance investing — commonly called ESG — a central part of his tenure. He maintains that public investment decisions should focus on financial returns rather than political or social agendas.
“When we’re talking about my role as state treasurer … we’ve got to focus on return, nothing less, nothing more,” he said.
Indiana lawmakers approved restrictions on pension investing in 2023, giving the treasurer a role in identifying investment managers with prohibited ESG commitments.
Elliott placed BlackRock on a watchlist in June 2024. That December, the Indiana Public Retirement System’s board voted to replace the firm for management of a roughly $969 million inflation-linked bond portfolio. BlackRock disputed the allegations. The decision was made by the pension board, on which Elliott serves.
Coumba Kebe, Democrat candidate for Indiana treasurer (Photo courtesy Kebe’s campaign)
Kebe, however, questioned whether that effort served taxpayers’ financial interests and said she wants greater disclosure about the costs and risks of changing investment managers.
“What I would like to see less of in this office is leveraging taxpayer dollars to make political and partisan statements,” she said. “This job is pretty straightforward. You invest taxpayer dollars and you focus on fiscal responsibility and making sure you maximize returns.”
Kebe said the office must follow state law, but she also believes a company’s treatment of workers and management practices can matter to its long-term financial performance.
Elliott, meanwhile, maintains that financial returns should drive the state’s investment choices.
“There’s constantly this give and take, push and pull, and so we’re always adjusting that depending on the market, and that is every single day,” he said.
Kebe’s transparency proposals include more accessible reporting about state holdings, investment performance and fees. She wants to explain that information to Hoosiers through social media, quarterly public reporting, press conferences and community meetings.
“(Hoosiers) want to understand how things impact them, but they don’t necessarily always have the leaders who are willing to meet them on the platforms and where they’re at to explain those things,” she said.
Kebe also wants to use the office to advocate for changes to Medicaid and childcare policy. Those decisions, she noted, affect the workforce and the state’s economic future.
“The things that I want to do will require partnership,” Kebe said. “But I’ve started building those relationships early, even across the aisle.”
Local infrastructure, 911 needs
Both candidates point to local infrastructure as a way the treasurer can help communities facing financial pressure.
Elliott highlighted the Indiana Bond Bank’s new Recovery Advance Program for Infrastructure Damage, or RAPID, which launched Sept. 10 after August storms and floods. He said conversations with local officials helped identify the need for financing while communities wait for disaster assistance.
Under the program, communities can initially borrow up to $1 million at a fixed 2% annual interest rate for cleanup, emergency repairs and other eligible costs. Loans generally run for up to two years and carry a $15,000 participation fee.
Kebe said she wants the Bond Bank to work more proactively with municipalities on infrastructure needs and disaster preparation, including identifying financing options before a crisis. She also wants stronger partnerships with police officers and firefighters as the state makes decisions about its 911 network.
[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: The candidates and tools you need to cast your vote.]
“I intend on bridging that gap and ensuring that we have a better partnership with our police officers and our firefighters when we’re making decisions about the 911 communication system,” she said.
For Elliott, protecting that network from cyberattacks would be a leading priority in a second term. He said smaller and rural communities may lack the staff and funding available to larger counties, making state support especially important.
“911 is critical infrastructure, not just infrastructure like water or roads, but infrastructure that actually saves lives,” Elliott said.
His reelection platform highlights a statewide cybersecurity assessment, dispatcher training and emergency communication services. The incumbent said he wants to build on that work with stronger defenses for local 911 systems and said he’s already discussed the issue with lawmakers ahead of the 2027 budget session.
“Most everyone has good ideas,” he said. “The question is, which ideas can you afford to do? Which ideas can you prioritize?” he said.
Elliott also sees opportunities to help local governments earn more through TrustINdiana, the state’s public investment pool. Better returns and state assistance with cybersecurity costs, he said, could ease pressure elsewhere in local budgets.
Kebe further said the property tax debate needs a fuller accounting of what changes would mean for schools, police, fire departments and other local services. She opposes eliminating the tax without explaining how those services would be funded and wants to work with experts and lawmakers on a sustainable approach.
“There are a lot of professionals in the space that are eager to partner with electeds to talk about what property tax reform could look like without us losing our our incredibly important local programs,” she said. “That’s what I would love to do: partnering with experts who can help us figure out a better, sustainable way of funding some of these programs — and not just talking about eliminating property taxes for the sake of eliminating taxes.”
Reaching more families
Both candidates share an interest in getting more people to use Indiana529 education savings accounts and INvestABLE Indiana accounts for people with disabilities.
Kebe’s plan includes broader outreach, including partnerships with labor unions, to explain that education savings can help families prepare for eligible trade school expenses as well as college. She said the office should do more to meet people in their communities and explain the tools already available to them.
Elliott wants to reach more veterans and other adults who may newly qualify for INvestABLE. A federal eligibility expansion that took effect in January allows people whose disability began before age 46, rather than before age 26, to qualify if they meet the program’s other requirements.
The accounts allow eligible people to save for qualified disability-related expenses while preserving access to public benefits, subject to program rules.
Elliott said his first-term record and experience working with local officials and legislators make him well suited to continue leading the office.
“I have built things across the board,” he said. “What I hope is that they will trust me again for this next time.”
Kebe said she would press for answers about state financial decisions and serve as a fiscal watchdog for taxpayers.
“There’s no allegiance to a party here,” she said. “The allegiance is to the people and reporting back out to them.”

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Black voter turnout higher than normal for Louisiana’s first day of early voting
text:
Black voter turnout was higher than normal on the first day of early voting for the Nov. 3 election in Louisiana. (Photo by Matthew Perschall/Louisiana Illuminator)Black voters made up a larger share of participants on Louisiana’s first day of early voting than they have in almost every other election over the past 18 years, making Democrats cautiously optimistic about the U.S. Senate race.  
Secretary of State data show Black voters comprised 32% of the in-person voters Tuesday, the first of seven days of in-person early voting that will take place over the next week ahead of the Nov. 3 election. 
Since 2008, the only time Black voter participation on the first day of early voting has been higher was for the 2020 presidential election between Donald Trump and Joe Biden, Louisiana pollster and political analyst John Couvillon said, reaching 32.3%.  
Couvillon, who typically works with Republican candidates in Louisiana, said overall participation for the first day of early voting this week was also higher than it has been for most of the past two decades. 
Nearly 115,000 people went to the polls Tuesday, a first-day early voting total exceeded recently only in the 2020 (174,00) and 2024 (177,000) presidential elections.
Other states in the South already several days into their early voting period, such as Georgia and North Carolina, are seeing sustained, elevated Black voter turnout, Couvillon said. This could mean Louisiana will continue to see higher Black voter participation throughout the rest of the election, he said. 

Louisiana and other Southern states are sometimes immune to Democratic waves that take place in other parts of the country, but the party does appear to be making inroads in this election cycle, according to Couvillon, who does polling for clients in several other states. 

“I’m not seeing the Deep South in this partisan island like we saw in 2024,” he said. 
Republican political consultant Roy Fletcher of Baton Rouge said one day of early voting data isn’t enough to determine whether Black voter participation will remain elevated. 

“Give it three days, we will know,” Fletcher said Wednesday. “By Friday, I’ll be ready to opine on it.” SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
Black voters are the backbone of the Democratic Party in Louisiana, and high turnout from the Black community is crucial to any party victory. 

Democrats have struggled to win statewide elections in recent years. Former Gov. John Bel Edwards, who won races in 2015 and 2019, is the only Democrat to win a statewide race in the past decade. 

Yet Democrats said they are seeing more enthusiasm for their U.S. Senate candidate, Jamie Davis, than they have in a statewide race in several years. 

Davis, a farmer and former Tensas Parish police juror, is running against Republican U.S. Rep. Julia Letlow of Baton Rouge, to replace U.S. Sen. Bill Cassidy next year. Cassidy lost to Letlow in the GOP primary election in May, and she defeated Treasurer John Fleming in the June runoff. 
“This notion that Louisiana is a red state is just a notion,” U.S. Rep. Troy Carter, D-New Orleans, said in an interview Wednesday. “Jamie Davis is in play against all odds.” 
LSU political scientist Robert Hogan agreed that Davis is running an unusually strong campaign for a Louisiana Democrat. 
“This is an election cycle that we haven’t had in awhile,” Hogan said. “You’ve got a candidate — and this one happens to be an African American — who is quite popular among Democratic activists.”
Letlow’s campaign said they are still confident she will be the victor in the race.

“Julia is going to win because Louisiana voters want a senator who will lower costs, keep the border secure and put Louisiana first, not one who will hand Chuck Schumer control of the Senate,” her campaign said in a statement. 
Corinne Williams, Davis’ campaign manager, said Democrats still have a lot of work to do in the election. 

“We’re encouraged, but nobody here is counting on anything. We’re running like we’re down,” she said. 
Carter, Hogan and U.S. Rep. Cleo Fields, D-Baton Rouge, also said there are other factors that could drive strong Black voter turnout. Democrats, more broadly, are fed up with Trump and upset about the U.S. Supreme Court ruling that upended the Voting Rights Act in the spring. 

A Louisiana lawsuit challenging the state’s map of U.S. House districts was the catalyst for overturning decades of protections for majority-Black voting districts at all levels of government across the country. In Louisiana, the decision led to the number of majority-Black U.S. House seats dropping from two to one out of six. 
The 6th Congressional District that Fields now represents has been redrawn as a majority white, Republican-leaning seat, which led Fields to decide not to run again. Carter’s 2nd District has remained majority-Black and is the only remaining Democratic-leaning seat in the state. 
In an interview, Fields said he believes Black voters are motivated to go to the polls in Louisiana and other states to express their anger over the gutting of the Voting Rights Act. 

“I often say to people: ‘Don’t make this make you vote less. Make this make you vote more. Now is the time you stand up,’” Fields said.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.

name: National
title: A record number of women are running for state legislatures this year
text:
Members of the Colorado House of Representatives work on the floor during session in May 2022. Colorado has among the nation’s highest rates of women serving in the state legislature. (Pema Baldwin for Colorado Newsline)A record number of women are running for state legislative seats this November, more than two-thirds of whom are Democrats. 
Across the 46 states with legislative seats on the ballot, a total of 3,824 women are running — up from 2022’s previous record of 3,621 women candidates, according to the Center for American Women and Politics at Rutgers University. Women make up 35.5% of all state legislative candidates this cycle.
Currently, women hold about one-third of state legislative seats across the country — a record level of representation but nowhere near parity. 
While some election cycles have seen spikes in the numbers of women running, the long-term trend has been defined by incremental progress, said Debbie Walsh, director of the research center.
“It is a step towards change, but it’s not going to happen in any one cycle,” she said. “Our system is set up in many ways for this kind of slow, steady progress.”
And she noted that Republicans still lag significantly. Of the women nominated this cycle, 68% are Democrats. Currently, about 64% of the women in state legislatures are Democrats.
“If the goal is for there to be gender equity in these legislatures, it’s not going to happen by only electing Democratic women. The Republican Party has to do more,” she said. “For women to be exercising political power, they need to be there on both sides of the aisle.” 
No major gains projected for count of women in Congress after midterms

Across the political spectrum, research shows lower levels of political ambition among women. Women tend to underestimate their own qualifications, are more averse to competition and receive less recruitment and encouragement to run for office. Many women work full-time and are primary caregivers — adding more complexity in the majority of states with part-time legislatures. 
But Republicans face unique challenges: Experts say playing political defense this year, a lack of organizational support for GOP women and a rejection of identity-politics has hampered efforts to recruit conservative women. 
Still, the number of women serving in legislatures has increased nearly 40% over the past decade, according to government relations firm MultiState. But representation varies wildly: Women hold more than half of seats in Colorado, Nevada and New Mexico, but fewer than 15% of seats in West Virginia, South Carolina and Mississippi.
In many ways, this cycle resembles the 2018 elections — when a wave of women ran for state and federal offices during President Donald Trump’s first midterm election. Like that year, the political climate again has soured for Republicans, who could lose control of Congress and hundreds of state legislative seats. 
‘Women are just really sick and tired’
Midterm elections typically favor the party that doesn’t control the White House. And the current focus on affordability offers an extra boost for women candidates, said Republican pollster and consultant Amanda Iovino. 
Polling has shown men tend to think of the economy in terms of income — wages, jobs growth and investment performance, she said. Women, though, have long framed discussions in terms of costs focusing on household budgets and grocery expenses.
“When cost of living is the top issue, and not the economy more broadly, it’s going to favor the people who instinctively talk to the cost side of the equation,” she said. “Of course, you can teach male candidates how to talk that way. I think it just comes a little bit more naturally to the women candidates.”
Former teacher Stefanie Bord, who is running for the Texas state House, said women are able to speak to those issues more credibly than many other politicians.
“Women are sort of like on the front lines of managing their homes and their families, and like the regular everyday life that needs to get done,” she said. “And they see firsthand the problems that happen because of laws that are passed without women involved.”
A Democrat, Bord found her way into politics after volunteering with the gun control group Moms Demand Action. 
She said women have become even more interested in running for office since the Supreme Court’s 2022 reversal of Roe v. Wade that had guaranteed the federal right to abortion. 
“I think women are just really sick and tired,” she said, “especially in Texas, where you know my two daughters have less rights than I had.”
Democrats aim to emulate Republicans in building state power

Bord is running in a predominantly conservative district in the Houston area. She faces Stan Stanart, the previous Harris County Clerk who enjoys support from GOP Gov. Greg Abbott. 
Though it’s an uphill battle, she said the district could flip this cycle. 
Her campaign is being supported by The First Ask, a political action committee working to elect pro-choice Democratic women to statehouses across the country. That group supports first-time candidates by investing early in campaign organization and staffing support.
Executive Director Caroline Welles said she wants to help build lasting political infrastructure to identify and support a pipeline of women running for office every cycle — not just spikes during times of political upheaval. 
She pointed to Nevada, which made history in 2018 by becoming the first state to elect women to a majority of legislative seats. Women have maintained a majority since, now holding about 62% of seats.
“What we’re hoping to do is make this something like a Nevada where women keep winning,” she said. 
She said women are more likely to get legislation passed, compromise with opponents and focus policymaking that benefits families. While her organization is solely focused on the left, she said she welcomes more Republican women running for legislatures, too.
“I wouldn’t see it as a loss if a large number of Republican women were encouraged to run, encouraged to to take up leadership roles. I would see that ultimately as a good thing because I do think they prioritize better legislation than their male counterparts.”
Republicans say they are investing in recruiting women.
Democrats could win majority of governor’s offices for first time in 16 years

In 2021, the Republican State Leadership Committee, which works to elect conservatives to state legislatures, redoubled a longstanding effort to recruit and train women candidates. This year, its Right Leaders Network included a class of 67 women running for legislatures in a dozen states.
Officials with that organization were unavailable for an interview.
Iovino, the Republican pollster, said this year’s tough political climate has likely hampered Republican recruitment efforts.
“If they’re sitting here defending a supermajority, then they’re not necessarily going out and recruiting a new batch of women and minority and veteran candidates,” she said. 
But she believes Republican organizations will redouble efforts to recruit women in upcoming election cycles. 
In 2020, a record number of Republican women ran for Congress and 2022 set a record for Republican women serving in state legislatures.
“I look back to our trends in 2020 and 2022, and look forward to that next batch of women, especially in state legislatures and kind of refilling that pipeline,” Iovino said. 
What women bring to public office
This year, women in Georgia are more politically engaged than during Trump’s first term, said Melita Easters, executive director of Georgia WIN List, a political action committee working to elect pro-choice women to the legislature.
A record 127 women are running for legislative seats in Georgia. The organization has endorsed 76 of those candidates. Plenty of those races are considered long shots, but Easters said getting women onto the legislative ballot can be an accomplishment in its own right — especially in the South, where representation lags other parts of the country. 
“When you have a woman who is running against a Republican incumbent for the first time in a decade, and that Republican hasn’t had a Democrat run against him in more than 10 years, then she attracts some attention,” Easter said. “She attracts some voters who had given up on having a candidate they could vote for, and so that rising tide lifts the rest of the ticket, too.”
Aside from increasing levels of representation, Easters said women bring a different perspective to politics. While many men run to gain power or financial advantage, she pointed to research showing women tend to run with more altruistic motivations focused on public service.
“Women bring a different skill set to holding public office, a skill set that is more collaborative,” she said. “And last but not least, women have generations of experience in cleaning up men’s messes, and the current political landscape is a very messy place.”
Research consistently shows lower political ambition among women. Experts say that means many women only launch a campaign after being specifically recruited.
Georgia state House candidate Michelle Schreiner, a Democrat, walks in the East Cobber Parade earlier this month in Marietta, Georgia. (Photo courtesy of Michelle Schreiner)
“It took three asks for me to raise my hand and say, ‘Okay, I’ll do it,’” said Democrat Michelle Schreiner, who is running for the Georgia House. “I had, frankly, some terms and conditions and that is really needing support early and often.”
Schreiner, a psychologist and researcher, is challenging Republican Rep. Sharon Cooper, who has represented suburban Atlanta in the state House for 29 years. Cooper did not respond to Stateline requests for comment.
To run was “a sobering decision,” Schreiner said. It has meant working on her birthday, missing her daughter’s soccer games and her son’s baseball games.
“It has a real impact on families,” she said. “My decision to run is not merely to challenge the incumbent. My decision to run is fundamentally an act of gratitude and appreciation for my community, and saying I’m willing to step up to do the work if you’re wanting a choice.”
Stateline reporter Kevin Hardy can be reached at khardy@stateline.org.
