name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Wallace tests incumbent Meuser in 9th Congressional District
text:
U.S. Rep. Dan Meuser is running for a fifth term representing Pennsylvania's 9th Congressional District, a GOP stronghold, against challenger Rachel Wallace, a Democrat. (Headshots provided by respective campaigns. Graphic by Emily Previti/The Pennsylvania Capital-Star)Pennsylvania’s deep red 9th Congressional District has elected Republican Rep. Dan Meuser by increasing margins since his first run in 2018.
Meuser’s seat is still considered safe, but he’s facing a strong challenger in Democrat Rachel Wallace.
The 9th Congressional District stretches through the state’s coal region into the northern tier.  It covers all or part of a dozen counties including Schuylkill, where the candidates debated Tuesday night at Penn State-Schuylkill Commonwealth outside Pottsville.
[Voter Guide: 2026 Pennsylvania General Election Voter Guide: The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
Wallace, 38, and Meuser, 62, faced off for the first and only time two weeks before the election and just a few days after the release of third quarter campaign finance reports documenting a strong showing by Wallace.
Meuser has raised $2 million and spent $2 million during this cycle overall – about double Wallace’s reported haul of $1 million and nearly triple her spend of $687,488.
But Wallace raised $378,451 to Meuser’s $219,641 during Q3 and has $389,825 in the bank to his $136,904 cash on hand, the least of any incumbent in Pennsylvania’s congressional delegation. 
Prominent Democrats had taken notice before the recent filing deadline – including Gov. Josh Shapiro, who stumped with her in person this summer amid his own reelection campaign, and James Carville joining for a virtual fundraiser. 
Still, it’s a long shot, say analysts – including Berwood Yost, director of the Center for Opinion Research and the Floyd Institute for Public Policy at Franklin & Marshall College. 
“The fundraising difference is intriguing, but it is pretty well below the kind of resources that are needed to challenge an incumbent in such a district,” Yost said. “There are always surprises in a wave election. But a Meuser loss feels so far from the realm of the possible, given the district.” 
In addition to Meuser’s track record, more than twice as many Republicans are registered to vote in the district as Democrats, state records show. 
“You never know”
Bobby Weaver, a Republican business owner who’s supported Meuser in the past and ran for city council in Pottsville a few years ago, said he went to the debate in part because he finds Wallace’s approach “impressive.” 
“Maybe people are just conditioned to expect Democrats to lose in the county, so therefore they’re not excited,” said Weaver, 32, noting the GOP’s roughly 2:1 voter registration edge. “They haven’t had a candidate to back for years, you know. And she’s treating it like an extremely competitive race. … Crazy things can happen if you treat something seriously.” 
Artist Lance Rautzhan, who runs the project space Cabin Contemporary not far from campus, says he was intrigued that Wallace didn’t mention her campaign right away when she visited the gallery as a patron. 
“She’s going to the right places, and she’s saying the right things and asking the right questions, and listening,” said Rautzhan, an unaffiliated voter who tends to vote for Democrats because they’re typically more supportive of the arts. 
Wallace is also out-raising and -spending challengers in other safe districts – but not the four toss-ups – the 1st, 7th, 8th and 10th – considered flippable to Democrats. 
So, why some momentum for Democrats in the 9th? 
The district is quite safe, “but in this climate you never know,” said Scott Meinke, professor of politics at Bucknell University.
“I don’t think it’s especially likely,” Meinke said. “But if the bottom really drops out for Republicans on Election Day, then I think you would expect a few surprises in some safe Republican seats, and you would look to safe Republican seats with reasonably well-funded challengers first.”
Democratic strategist J.J. Abbott noted the 9th District’s geographic proximity to two tossups – the 7th and 8th. And perhaps, Abbott said, there’s some lingering resentment over the Department of Homeland Security’s plans – since canceled – to convert two warehouses in the district to immigration detention centers. 
The site of the former Big Lots warehouse that Immigration and Customs Enforcement planned to turn into a 7,500-person detention center in Tremont Township, Schuylkill County, on March 12, 2026. (Photograph by Jessica Kourkounis/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)
Some of Meuser’s constituents have criticized him for being inaccessible as public backlash, lawsuits and other opposing maneuvers ensued in the commonwealth and elsewhere. DHS later pivoted; now, both CD9 properties in Upper Bern and Tremont townships are among those on the market, officially. 
Asked Tuesday during a media availability after the debate why he didn’t engage with the public in person when the ICE center was an active concern, Mesuer initially described a meeting organized with a local Indivisible chapter attended by “40 people.”
“They called me a fascist,” he said.
The event happened in December before news broke about the warehouse conversion plans, Meuser said. Some have said rumors about the prospect, as outlandish as it seemed at first, started around that time.
“It was a big surprise. But as soon as it occurred, I engaged immediately … with [former DHS Sec.] Kristi Noem, and then [DHS Sec.] Markwayne Mullin,” he said, noting op-eds he wrote and naming other officials he met with privately. “We were working towards, and we were working towards making it work for the community.” 
Schuylkill County Commissioner Larry Padora at a town hall in Tremont March 13, 2026. (Photograph by Jessica Kourkounis for the Capital-Star)
For a time, Republican County Commissioners in Berks and Schuylkill were updating the public about those discussions at every commissioners meeting. 
Wallace’s campaign focused on the ICE warehouse fallout as a core issue for a while. But it dropped out of her messaging after ICE’s plans changed – even though public backlash partly stemmed from Meuser’s response and tax losses of about $2 million annually, combined, between the two municipalities and their respective schools and county governments. 
Data centers have meanwhile increasingly dominated public protests over development, Abbott noted, and are more universally opposed across the political spectrum in the 9th District and elsewhere.
Meuser pledged Tuesday to fight “like mad” to compensate communities for the tax revenue lost on the warehouse properties until the federal government finds a private buyer.
“There’s no way we’re going to take… this hit,” he said. “We’re going to get that money. I’m determined. I can’t guarantee it, but I’m determined.”
Typical venues for payments in lieu of taxes for federally-owned property are highly specific and don’t apply to the warehouse properties, as the Capital-Star has reported. 
Contentious cadence 
Meuser and Wallace sniped at each other throughout the debate, as they sparred over foreign policy, immigration, healthcare and more. 
Wallace wove critiques of Meuser and accusations against him into her responses throughout. 
Moderator Robert S. Carl Jr., CEO of the Schuylkill Chamber of Commerce, at one point interjected to stress that if Wallace engaged Meuser with an outright question during her response, his answer would count on her time.
“I said what was important to me to say for the topic,” Wallace told reporters later. “I wanted the opportunity to share it with people: This is who I am. This is what I would fight for. And tonight, for me, was also about holding Dan Meuser accountable.”
She was on the offensive from her opening statement, accusing Meuser of insider trading – which he said is “completely false.”
“Any stock that I purchased was well before I got into Congress,” he responded on stage. “And by the way, the S&P, the NASDAQ, and the Dow have increased almost 200% over the last 10 years. And that was the last time I purchased a stock.”
Financial disclosures show he reported stock purchases as recently as June by a dependent child. CNBC and other outlets reported shortly thereafter on members of Congress buying SpaceX stock as the company went public. 
Asked later to clarify, Meuser attributed that particular transaction to his daughter. A financial adviser handles trades on his behalf, he said. 
“I have not directed one stock purchase since I’ve been in office,” he said. “I had my financial consultant, which I didn’t necessarily have to do, sign that I’d have no influence, no direction, no anything. … It’s basically like a blind trust.”
If Meuser had an actual blind trust, however, he wouldn’t be responsible for filing the periodic transaction reports that, for example, documented his daughter and wife’s activity in June.  Blind trusts are rare for members of Congress for several reasons, including costs for setup, servicing and taxes.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: In CT’s 3rd District, DeLauro eyes gavel as Lancia seeks change
text:
This is the third in a series of stories profiling candidates in each congressional district race.

Rosa DeLauro is seeking a historic 19th term in the U.S. House, with the hopes of reclaiming the top spot on an influential committee if Democrats regain control.
Her opponent, Republican Chris Lancia, is looking to defy the odds as he seeks change in Connecticut’s 3rd Congressional District and more broadly in Congress. 
Democrats have had a firm grip on the New Haven-based District since 1983. DeLauro, the longest-serving U.S. House member from Connecticut, is favored to win another two-year term on Nov. 3. But she said she’s starting to see some shifts in the district’s electorate, including in her hometown of New Haven.
“My district is changing. I can feel it,” DeLauro said. “It’s palpable, and there is a move to the right. People in New Haven are not coming out in the numbers that they used to before. The Naugatuck Valley is a much more conservative place.”
At the heart of these political changes, DeLauro says, is the economic anxiety facing constituents and families over how they’ll afford necessities like healthcare and utilities.

U.S. Rep. Rosa DeLauro gives a thumbs up to another speaker during a press conference regarding home heating assistance at the Community Action Agency of New Haven on Tuesday, Oct. 13, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

While affordability is the buzzword of the midterm elections, DeLauro, 83, is quick to give a reminder that she’s not new to the issue. She said she’s been raising alarms about people living paycheck-to-paycheck for years, particularly in her longtime effort to expand the federal child tax credit.
Lancia, 55, is a former Democrat who said he voted for DeLauro years ago. He changed his political affiliation to become an independent and then switched to the Republican Party around the time of the second Obama administration. 
He’s a Coast Guard veteran and former federal law enforcement officer who works as a manager at TNI, a provider of fiber networks. Lancia is a first-time candidate who believes it’s time for a change and a fresh face representing the 3rd District.
“We’re getting hit hard in Connecticut, and my opponent is very out of touch,” Lancia said. “I feel that it’s time we get some new blood down in D.C.”
DeLauro has been around politics her entire life. Both of her parents served as members of the New Haven Board of Aldermen. Before she came to Congress in 1991, DeLauro served as executive director of EMILY’s List, a national group that seeks to elect women to office who support reproductive rights. She also worked as Connecticut Sen. Chris Dodd’s campaign manager and chief of staff.
Since taking office in 1991, DeLauro said campaigns look quite different from when she first got into the game. Social media has transformed both campaigning and legislating, and her X account has had some semi-viral moments. And over the last three decades, she’s seen more polarization and less ticket splitting in elections.

Chris Lancia, a Republican running for election to the U.S. House to represent Connecticut’s 3rd Congressional District, talks with state House District 100 Republican candidate Susan Manke at the Middletown Republican Town Committee Pasta & Politics fundraiser at The Cantina in Middletown on Wednesday, Sept. 30, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

Lancia had a similar upbringing, immersed in local politics. His father was active in Democratic politics in Bridgeport. Lancia said he was used to behind-the-scenes work, and this is his first time moving into a front-facing role.
Like a number of his fellow Republican candidates in Connecticut, Lancia wants term limits with no member of Congress serving more than eight years, saying “politics was never made to be a long-term job.”
“That’s like any job you’re at, when you’re there too long,” he said, “you just become complacent. And at 83, how in touch are you with things?”
Questions around age and long-time political careers have emerged as an undercurrent of this year’s primaries in both parties. In Connecticut, 28-year incumbent John Larson lost a four-way primary to Luke Bronin, who largely premised his campaign on generational change without directly talking about age.
While some members lost primaries to younger challengers and first-time candidates, others survived challenges, including 80-year-old Sen. Ed Markey in Massachusetts.
DeLauro counters that age is not an issue and that what matters is whether a lawmaker is willing to fight on behalf of their constituents and stand up to the Trump administration — at least for Democrats.
“I will fight a Trump administration. I have no fear of doing that,” DeLauro said. “And I think people today do want to see you fight. I don’t think it’s a question of any age.”
“That’s what I hear from people on the street,” she added. “It’s not a particular issue or so forth. Just keep fighting. Keep standing up for us, and that’s what people say to me, and I think I do that.”
This time around, it’s a two-pronged fight for DeLauro: winning another term to the 3rd District and seeking to reclaim the gavel of the House Appropriations Committee — if Democrats can win the majority. She said she doesn’t take either race for granted, though she noted she currently doesn’t have a challenger for the Democrats’ top spot on the committee.

Rep. Rosa DeLauro, D-Conn., holds up a document during Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche’s testimony before the House Appropriations Committee, Tuesday, June 2, 2026 in Washington. Credit: Allison Robbert / AP

The panel crafts spending bills, allocates money and funds the federal government. Her current role as the Democratic ranking member comes during a major strain between the executive and legislative branches regarding federal funding. 
In her quest for the gavel, DeLauro has already started to map out her priorities for next year. She hopes to restore education and job opportunities to help address the higher cost of living and restore her committee’s authority on federal grants. She also envisions handling some oversight by taking a look at where federal dollars are flowing and whether some money “has been transferred illegally.”
“I want to, as I have done in the past, continue to use the appropriations committee as the way to look at how in fact we address this affordability issue, how we put money back into people’s pockets, how we provide the services in all of the areas that have a real effect on their economic security and their lives,” DeLauro said.

Republican candidate Chris Lancia, center, speaks with GOP Lt. Gov. candidate Matthew Corey, right, and GOP House District 100 candidate Susan Manke during the Middletown Republican Town Committee Pasta & Politics fundraiser at The Cantina in Middletown on Wednesday, Sept. 30, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

Lancia and other opponents of DeLauro have questioned her effectiveness on the Appropriations Committee, including when she served at the helm during part of the Biden administration. Lancia noted the post-pandemic inflation that hit during that stretch and argued that she was “rubber stamping the checks” — though he also blamed Republicans for doing the same thing.
“I’d rather focus on the things that are going to help the state of Connecticut,” he said.
DeLauro views her committee work entirely different. All of it benefits Connecticut, she argues, and it also extends to the rest of the country.
“Everything I do is for Connecticut but has national reverberations,” she said.
When she was Appropriations chairwoman between 2021 and 2023, DeLauro said she increased federal funding for the Head Start program, which provides early childhood services that serve low-income children.
She helped revive earmarks — under a new name and with more limitations and accountability. In recent years, when Congress passed annual appropriations bills, Connecticut and other states have received hundreds of millions of dollars in federal funding for local projects requested by members of their state’s delegations. That includes money for local law enforcement, infrastructure projects and nonprofits. (But not all lawmakers participate, and some view it as pork barrel spending for pet projects. The practice of earmarks was banned in 2011 for about a decade.)
For his part, Lancia wants to prevent transgender athletes from playing in women’s sports, expand small business loan options beyond those that help someone start up a business, expand school choice and trade schools, and address military pensions.
Lancia also said he wanted to see larger raises for Social Security benefits — one of the few areas of agreement between the two candidates. He said he wants to see at least a 5% or 6% boost in the next few years to keep up better with the rate of inflation. (DeLauro has co-sponsored a past version of U.S. Rep. John Larson’s legislation that would increase Social Security benefits and bolster its solvency by requiring higher earners to contribute more to payroll taxes.)
He has some differences with the Republican Party and President Donald Trump, but he applauded the president for supporting law enforcement and veterans and closing the southern border.
As a veteran, Lancia wants to see an end to the war in Iran, which has driven up costs like gas prices. He said he wants Congress to reassert itself, since it is the only body that has the authority to declare war. (There have been multiple efforts by Democrats on war powers resolutions to rein in Trump on further military actions, but they have failed to make it through the GOP-controlled Congress.)
“I don’t agree on the constant nonsense of talking so much on TV,” Lancia said about Trump. “I don’t like the idea we’re over in Iran right now, with again no ending.”
Both DeLauro and Lancia avoided primaries in August.

Andrew Rice, an independent write-in candidate for Connecticut’s 3rd Congressional District, participates in a Rally Against ICE outside the Meriden Courthouse on Thursday, Oct. 1, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

At Democrats’ spring nominating convention, Andrew Rice narrowly fell short of the 15% threshold to make the August primary ballot. Rice, a scientist seeking to run to the left of the congresswoman, has raised policy disagreements on Israel’s actions in Gaza and abolishing the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. (DeLauro has pushed back against new funding for ICE without implementing guardrails, but she doesn’t back abolishing the agency because of the need for border protection.)
Rice, who’s gotten involved in community organizing, sought to challenge the convention results and asked for a redo, but his complaint was dismissed by a panel with the state Democratic Party. He’s now running as a write-in candidate for the seat.
“I have no delusions that a write-in campaign has any likelihood of succeeding in the sense of winning the seat away from Rosa DeLauro. But I think it’s important that we still send a message,” Rice said. He said one of those messages is that “voting for Rosa DeLauro, voting for the Republican — the establishment has not given us any genuine change and has not been working for the American people.”
DeLauro continues to hold a significant cash advantage over her opponents.
Given his scant resources, Lancia said his focus has been on meeting voters where they are, especially through door knocking at the homes of all voters, regardless of political affiliation. He said candidates are too focused on fundraising and bemoaned the lack of help from Republicans, statewide and nationally.
But resources are spread thin in both parties. New England’s entire congressional delegation is Democratic, except for U.S. Sen. Susan Collins, a Republican in Maine who’s heavily targeted in her reelection race this year.
“Nobody wants to donate money. They want you to make change, but we have no help from the national party. Trump has not helped us raise money,” Lancia said. “The national Republican Party says that we’re useless, that we can’t do anything.”
“Let us get strong again,” he continued. “How do we get the party back up again if you don’t come in and invest with us?”
No debate or forum appears to be planned for the 3rd District race.
Along with DeLauro and Lancia, Thomas Egan, a lawyer who has run unsuccessfully for mayor and state representative, is also on the ballot as the Independent Party nominee.
In-person early voting began Monday, Oct. 19 and runs through Sunday, Nov. 1. The last day to request an absentee ballot is Nov. 2.

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: New Hampshire sets up digital system to accommodate new Medicaid work requirements
text:
During Wednesday's Executive Council meeting in Pelham, Karen Liot Hill said she's "glad to hear that there's going to be this automated component that hopefully is going to prevent unnecessary losses and people being dropped simply because they didn't submit some piece of paperwork." (Photo by Maya Mitchell/New Hampshire Bulletin)In preparation for incoming Medicaid work requirements, New Hampshire is purchasing technology systems designed to help the state implement the new policy.
Congress has mandated that states like New Hampshire institute work requirements for their expanded Medicaid programs by January. The requirements mean many Medicaid enrollees who aren’t “medically frail” (though some are concerned about how the government will define medical frailty) will be required to work at least 80 hours per month in order to receive health coverage from the program. New Hampshire is currently preparing to implement the requirements.
Now, New Hampshire Employment Security is updating its state-run job matching software to help. The agency’s Job Match System helps connect employers and job candidates. The state hired Florida-based Geographic Solutions Inc. to upgrade the technology system so it can also be used to enroll people in Medicaid, track their work hours and report that information to the Department of Health and Human Services, which runs the state’s Medicaid program.
Employment Security Commissioner Rich Lavers said he expects the vendor to have the system operational before the work requirements go into effect Jan. 1. On Wednesday, the Executive Council approved a contract to pay Geographic Solutions roughly $118,000 to complete the work.
“I’m glad to see this interagency cooperation,” Executive Councilor Karen Liot Hill said, adding: “Certainly there is the risk that people who rely on Medicaid to access healthcare in our state could get cut off the rolls and sometimes due simply to administrative issues. So I’m glad to hear that there’s going to be this automated component that hopefully is going to prevent unnecessary losses and people being dropped simply because they didn’t submit some piece of paperwork, because that can have a really devastating impact on people’s lives.”
The work requirements have, since inception, been widely criticized by Democrats and public health advocates who say they’ll merely kick people off Medicaid who are actually working due to paperwork issues and won’t encourage more people to start working.
In a report Tuesday, the New Hampshire Fiscal Policy Institute estimated 23,000 to 29,000 fewer adults — or potentially about half of the roughly 50,000 expansion population enrollees — could be enrolled in expanded Medicaid by 2028, citing the policy. Although, some have questioned whether it will be that severe. Liot Hill, the council’s only Democrat, said “that number may be on the high side.”
The work requirements also come around the same time as other major changes to Medicaid in both New Hampshire and across the country.
For instance, Congress also instituted cost-sharing for Medicaid enrollees and cuts to other health programs, including the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or SNAP.
On the state level, the New Hampshire Legislature voted last year to start charging some Medicaid recipients premiums. The premium plan has been paused though, while New Hampshire and federal officials sort through questions about whether the plan contradicts federal law.
Congress gave states some latitude on how the requirements are implemented. For example, states choose how to define medical frailty and they choose what evidence enrollees may provide as proof of work. Many experts say the decisions states make here will affect whether the requirements push working people off Medicaid unfairly.
New Hampshire has already made some of these choices. State lawmakers have chosen to require documentary evidence of meeting the work requirements, rather than letting enrollees self-attest to meeting them. Lawmakers also chose to require quarterly compliance checks as opposed to twice-yearly checks required by federal law. On medical frailty, the state plans to require enrollees with disabilities or other qualifying conditions to provide a note from their medical provider verifying that their condition impairs their ability to perform activities of daily living. Still, several other key decisions have yet to be made.
The Fiscal Policy Institute argues that the state’s decisions so far have been more stringent than what is required, which could mean more people lose coverage.
New Hampshire is trying to avoid the mistakes made last time the state implemented Medicaid work requirements. In 2018, New Hampshire enacted a state law requiring Medicaid enrollees to work 100 hours a month. However, about a month after the effective date of the rule, only about 8,000 of the 25,000 people subject to the requirement had complied and documented their work hours. The rest were set to lose coverage until the state reversed course and then-Gov. Chris Sununu paused the requirements. State lawmakers then ditched the plan. Now, however, the orders are coming down from Congress.

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: Emergency funding directed to quash spread of spotted lanternflies in New Hampshire
text:
The $24,620 approved by the Executive Council on Wednesday will fund public education about the invasive insects, among other initiatives. (Getty Images)The New Hampshire Executive Council on Wednesday approved nearly $25,000 in federal funding for “emergency” work targeting invasive spotted lanternflies near the Massachusetts border. 
The flies, which can damage crops, forests and other plants, were first detected in New Hampshire this August in Salem. It is possible the invasive pest, which is already found in Massachusetts, is becoming established in New Hampshire, Department of Agriculture, Markets, and Food Commissioner Shawn Jasper wrote in a letter to Gov. Kelly Ayotte and the Executive Council. 
Adult lanternflies are distinctive, with black polka dots on their external wings and underwings of bright red, black and white. The insects, native to Asia, were first documented in the U.S. in Pennsylvania in 2014. Since then, they have spread to 15 states in the Eastern U.S., including Massachusetts, according to the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service.
Humans brought the flies here and continue to drive their expansion, with cars and trains major factors in helping the invasive insects extend their range, according to the agency. Warming temperatures associated with climate change are also helping the insects spread further and faster.
Spotted lanternflies lay eggs in autumn that hatch in spring and feed on a variety of plants — though they have a preference for the “tree of heaven,” which is also invasive in New Hampshire. The flies’ indiscriminate taste means they could threaten farms, nurseries, vineyards and forests, Jasper wrote in the letter. 
The $24,620 approved by the Executive Council on Wednesday will fund public education about the invasive insects, data gathering about them and the risks they pose in New Hampshire, control measures, “stakeholder coordination” and reporting improvements, according to Jasper.
This August’s detection in Salem could mark an emerging infestation, he wrote. This could lead to spread of the spotted lanternfly in New Hampshire as well as in other northern New England states and Canada, in part because of the proximity of the detections to major transportation corridors, he stated in the letter.
Therefore, the August detection “warrants immediate response,” Jasper wrote.
The New Hampshire Department of Agriculture, Markets, and Food calls for individuals to report sightings of spotted lanternflies on nhbugs.org.

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: Commentary: AI governance — a practical view from a writing classroom
text:
"To counter students using AI to write essays for them, many schools have returned to pencil-and-paper process writing." (Photo by Guido Mieth/Getty Images)Artificial intelligence has upended the writing classroom.
Four years ago, Stephen Marche was bold enough to state that the classic college essay was dead. He was absolutely right at the time. 
AI appeared on the scene as a force most educators were unable to contend with and unable to counter for the sake of academic integrity.  
A disruptor. A beacon of the future. A new modality by which all learning would be reshaped. AI was maybe even going to replace the whole university system as we knew it. 
This all still may be true, but we are now four years down the road — how has the writing classroom responded?
No one is coming to help
It is easy to get swept up in the hype or fear-mongering of AI. I will admit, I have been on both sides of this moment, writing arguments about the doom and gloom of an AI future.
However, as I drafted and advanced these arguments, I failed to see the disturbing reality that was evolving right under my nose as a writing teacher. What is more, I was shocked by how student academic well-being was actively being disregarded in the face of the most disruptive educational innovation since the pencil. 
As more and more of my students turned to AI to escape the productive struggle of writing, I looked for guidance to meet this moment and preserve the intellectual fruits of writing. 
I found many people like myself — long on theoretical concerns and short on practical in-class solutions. 
The AI governance strategies I found were overfit for private sector business development or international government compliance. 
At the federal regulatory level, I observed little, if any, worry about how AI could impact young minds. Washington, D.C., appeared pacified by a “morally binding” pledge from the current AI giants. 
At the state level, New Hampshire has promoted a framework written by the New Hampshire Learning Initiative.
While these frameworks guide districts through AI policy adoption, they offer little practical advice for managing the unprecedented intellectual challenges AI poses in the classroom.
Some New Hampshire schools have adopted these frameworks along with locally developed policies. Others remain strategically ambiguous about their approach to AI in the classroom — waiting for guidance from above to indemnify them against the legal morass AI has created. 
Maybe I was looking in all the wrong places for practical, in-class solutions. After all, answers to my concerns might lie outside of the legal and institutional purview of the places I sought them. 
In that moment, I realized no one was coming to help our most vulnerable minds in their greatest hour of need. The intellectual fruits of writing would be allowed to spoil for an entire generation. 
If I wanted AI governance in the classroom, I had to bring it in myself.
AI governance in the classroom
To counter students using AI to write essays for them, many schools have returned to pencil-and-paper process writing. I have done this myself and find it to be a useful tool.
However, districts will continue to push one-to-one device use, while teachers will continue to be pressured to accelerate curriculum to meet various “data-driven” education mandates.
Consequently, writing assignments will continue to be present on student devices, increasing the likelihood that students will turn to AI to do the work for them. 
Districts need practical AI governance frameworks that account for these realities.
The following are four in-class frameworks I have developed, along with a brief rationale behind each.
Framework 1: Establish an acceptable-use scale
Districts must develop acceptable-use scales that outline the levels of AI assistance permitted for a given assignment. Establishing these expectations in advance provides educators and students with a clear understanding of what is allowed and what is not. It also helps districts navigate the legal and accountability questions surrounding AI transparency. 
Framework 2: Require all digital writing assignments to be completed on school-assigned devices
School-issued devices typically offer native controls that can restrict access to AI applications and websites. While these restrictions can help prevent inappropriate AI use, they also have a significant blind spot that many districts may not fully recognize. On Chromebooks, Gemini cannot be turned off, and the same is true for Copilot on Microsoft devices. Districts cannot assume that issuing a managed device automatically eliminates access to AI.
Framework 3: Require all digital writing assignments to be completed at school during school hours
When school-issued devices operate on school networks, an additional layer of administrative controls can help restrict inappropriate AI access. Requiring students to complete digital writing assignments during school hours also reduces their ability to rely on AI through personal devices on home networks. Just as importantly, completing assignments in class allows educators to observe the writing process as it unfolds, rather than relying solely on a finished product to determine what a student understands and can do independently.
Framework 4: Utilize keystroke recorders to review student writing
Traditional plagiarism detection and AI-detection tools are increasingly unreliable in today’s digital writing environment. Rather than relying on a software-generated probability that a student used AI, educators should consider tools that record the development of a digital document. Reviewing a document’s revision history or keystroke playback can help educators distinguish between writing developed over time and text introduced all at once through copying and pasting.
This approach is not foolproof. Students can use AI-powered humanizers to make text appear as though it was typed naturally. Keystroke recording should therefore be treated as one source of evidence, not definitive proof of misconduct. 
Essays are not dead
I have not implemented these frameworks to catch students cheating. Rather, I have developed them to preserve the productive struggle of writing, a process that is essential to the intellectual growth of young minds.
Generation Z and Generation Alpha have grown up in an information environment that prioritizes instant gratification and offers endless opportunities for intellectual escapism from the friction of reality. School districts must recognize this reality and prevent these learned behaviors from dictating whether the classic essay remains a part of education.
Districts must choose to come to the aid of our most vulnerable minds. Without practical, in-class AI governance frameworks, we risk allowing the classic essay to die. Along with it, we risk losing the intellectual benefits that the struggle of writing provides to young minds.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Opinion: ‘What, me worry?’ Yes, if you’re paying attention to threats surrounding the midterm election.
text:
President Donald Trump speaks during an Oct. 19, 2026, rally at the Heartland Credit Union Arena in Park City, Kansas. (Photo by Sherman Smith/Kansas Reflector)As the November midterm elections draw near, much of the nation seemingly has channeled Mad Magazine’s smiling, redheaded, gap-toothed mascot Alfred E. Neuman and his catchphrase: “What, me worry?” But the nation has plenty to worry about.
Here’s what the current administration has done in the months leading up to November’s white-knuckle vote.
This administration has purged “disloyal” federal workers and pardoned convicted Jan. 6, 2021, rioters who attacked police at the U.S. Capitol. Trump has dumped billions of dollars into beefing up the ranks of heavily armed, masked loyalists now roaming American cities.
His Supreme Court has gutted the Voting Rights Act, which led some formerly Confederate states into racial gerrymanders disguised as partisan gerrymanders. It also has expanded the power of the presidency and weakened our system of checks and balances.
Trump encouraged a mid-decade redistricting push intended to give Republicans an electoral advantage. Redistricting typically occurs every 10 years.
For the first time in more than two decades, the United State has blocked international election observers from monitoring our elections. Amid claims of widespread voter fraud (nearly nonexistent in reality), the president plans to blanket polling places with a network of federal election monitors.
Trump fired the leaders of the U.S. Election Assistance Commission in July, leaving the EAC without any sitting commissioners. A Supreme Court decision expanded the president’s authority to fire members of independent agencies. Commissioners had resisted his push for proof of U.S. citizenship in voter registration. The bipartisan commission certified voting systems, distributed federal election grants and maintained the national mail-in voter form.
He also has continued his claims that voting machines remain vulnerable to manipulation and that his political opponents stole the 2020 election. Fears linger about armed ICE agents appearing in and around polling places. He has until recently discouraged mail-in voting.
This administration has imprisoned people in El Salvador and bombed boats suspected of drug smuggling without due process. 
The president’s party has abdicated its role as a check on the power of the executive branch. 
Trump sent Tulsi Gabbard into a Georgia election office and confiscated ballots. This after calling that state’s election official and asking the man to “find” more than 11,000 votes. Recent national elections have run so close that a campaign only would need to nudge the needle 2 or 3 percentage points to swing the election. 
Despite all this, an eerie silence on what this behavior portends has settled over the nation. Few if any people seem alarmed.  
The president has said unless he wins, the elections are rigged. 
Alfred E. Neuman would not be smiling. He’d be worried. 
Here in Kansas, civic rights organizations have begun ramping up voting integrity efforts in preparation for these threats. 
“We have definitely stepped up our election protection work and have the largest, most robust program we’ve ever had — covering more polling places with more volunteers and prepared for more scenarios,” said Micah Kubic, executive director of the ACLU of Kansas. “We are still recruiting, so I wouldn’t want to commit to numbers yet — but in August, we doubled the size of the program over prior years and anticipate doing the same for November.” 
Boots on the Ground Midwest, a nonpartisan, volunteer-led organization, has a packed calendar of events. The League of Women Voters, also nonpartisan, will send subscribers action alerts as well as provide contact information for elected officials. 
These groups seem to understand the stakes and continue to work to meet the moment.  
But the Rev. Martin Luther King Jr. once said the nation has a two-week memory. It looks worse now.
Everyone should remember former White House aide Cassidy Hutchinson’s congressional testimony. She said that Trump didn’t want metal detectors at his pre-riot rally on Jan. 6, 2021. 
According to Business Insider, Hutchinson said back in 2022 that “the advance team had relayed to him that the mags were free flowing,” referring to metal detectors used by the Secret Service. Apparently, Trump was “concerned about the shot” of the area not being full of people. 
“He was angry that we weren’t letting people through the mags with weapons,” Hutchinson said. “When we were in the offstage tent, I was in the vicinity of a conversation where I overheard the president say something to the effect of, ‘I don’t effing care that they have weapons. They’re not here to hurt me. Take the effing mags away. Let my people in; they can march to the Capitol from here. Let the people in. Take the effing mags away.” 
Does anyone believe that if the Republicans lose big in the midterms that the president would graciously concede? 
Within the past few weeks, Hutchinson has become the focus of a grand jury investigation. The Department of Justice is accusing her of lying to Congress. 
Oh, yeah. Alfred E. Neuman, once considered “The Original Optimist,” would be worried. In actuality, we should be way past worried. 
We should be hoping for the best but preparing for the worst. 
Mark McCormick is a journalist and a nonprofit executive. He’s also the author of four books including “Barry Sanders: Now You See Him” (a New York Times bestseller), “Some Were Paupers. Some Were Kings: Dispatches from Kansas,” and his latest, “Kansas Matters: America’s Social Faultlines.” Through its opinion section, Kansas Reflector works to amplify the voices of people who are affected by public policies or excluded from public debate. name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: Trump rallies support for Republicans in pre-election visit to deeply red Upstate
text:
President Donald Trump arrives for a campaign rally at T. Ed Garrison Arena at Clemson University on Wednesday, Oct. 21, 2026, in Pendleton, South Carolina. (Photo by Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)PENDLETON — President Donald Trump rallied in the Upstate to boost GOP support for U.S. Sen. Darline Graham’s campaign, while discounting polls suggesting the seat her late brother held for almost 24 years could flip blue.
The race between Graham and Democrat Annie Andrews shouldn’t be close, he told thousands of supporters in a county he won by 47 percentage points two years ago.
Trump acknowledged that polls show otherwise by jokingly asking if he was in the right state: “Are you sure this is South Carolina?”
The rally came a day after the nonpartisan Cook Political Report shifted the race from “likely Republican” to “lean Republican,” and Andrews launched a “Republicans for Annie” coalition she said consisted of more than 100 Republicans in South Carolina.

Appointed U.S. Sen. Darline Graham, the GOP nominee for the next six-year term, and her husband Larry Nordone (left) stand with South Carolina’s senior Sen. Tim Scott as they listen to President Donald Trump speak during a campaign rally at T. Ed Garrison Arena at Clemson University on Wednesday, Oct. 21, 2026, in Pendleton, South Carolina. (Photo by Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)

“I’m not a believer in the pollsters. I really am not,” Trump said.
“Nov. 3 is the only pollster that counts,” he said, telling rallygoers “you have to go out and vote for Darline Graham. She’s you. She’s solid.”
But Andrews, he said, is a “radical left lunatic.” He pointed to her F rating from the NRA to mean “she wants to take your guns away.” Andrews, a pediatrician, is a former volunteer for the Moms Demand Action gun safety group and paid adviser for its affiliate, Everytown for Gun Safety.
He also hammered Andrews’ advocacy at the Statehouse opposing legislation barring hormone treatments and puberty blockers for transgender minors. He falsely accused her of supporting “mutilation” of children. And he again referred to her using a slur for transgender people, repeating what he wrote in a social media post earlier this month.
The rally inside Clemson University’s T. Ed Garrison Arena was only a few miles from Graham’s hometown of Central, where she and Lindsey Graham grew up in the back room of a restaurant and pool hall owned by their parents, who died 15 months apart when she was 13. Part of her campaign message is that she can relate to struggling American families.
“This area, and most importantly, its values are ingrained in me: God, family, country,” Graham said on stage. “Those are our values, and I want to take them to a place that’s desperately needed: the United States Senate.”
Other Republicans who took the stage included South Carolina’s now-senior U.S. senator, Tim Scott; U.S. Rep. Sheri Biggs of the 3rd District (where the rally was held); Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, a South Carolina native; and Cody Simpson, the GOP nominee for agriculture commissioner.
Gov. Henry McMaster, who’s leaving office in January, called Graham “one of us.” It was McMaster who appointed her to fulfill her brother’s fourth term, which ends in January. She jumped into the race for the next term with Trump’s encouragement and endorsement.

For more on our 2026 election coverage and information on voting in South Carolina, check out our Voter Guide.

She again thanked him for that.
“Thank you so much for coming to South Carolina. I am so honored to have your endorsement,” she said. “You are one of Lindsey’s dearest friends. You will always be part of the Graham family.”
Graham’s supporters on stage also included a former opponent, U.S. Rep. Russell Fry of the 7th District, who placed third in the special GOP primary in August.
But GOP infighting from that primary continues. Trump rallied in a region of the state won by Graham’s runoff opponent, 5th District Rep. Ralph Norman. He took all 12 counties in the deeply red Upstate, while Graham won the state’s 34 other counties. Graham needs Norman’s Upstate supporters to come out and vote for her.
But some of Norman’s supporters are encouraging Republicans to write his name on the ballot instead of voting for Graham. Norman was not at the rally and made clear during a radio interview earlier Wednesday that he refuses to help her campaign. He’ll still vote for her, since he promised to support the GOP nominee, he said on “The Nashional Briefing with Kelly Nash.”

A protester is escorted out by law enforcement while President Donald Trump spoke at a rally in Pendleton, South Carolina on Wednesday Oct. 21, 2026. (Photo by Katharine Wilson/SC Daily Gazette)

However, he said, “My family is not going to vote for Darline Graham. They’re just not.” He contends the contest wouldn’t be close if he was the nominee.
Biggs alluded to the intra-party spat by urging Republicans to come together and vote for Graham, likening the party to a “big family” that doesn’t always agree.
“Sometimes we even squabble a little bit,” she said. “But when it’s time to vote, we need to stand together, and we need to send Republicans back to Washington to finish the job that President Trump started.”
Trump invited two sports celebrities on stage: championship boxer Evander Holyfield and professional golfer Jacob Bridgeman, a Clemson graduate.
Giving people another reason to vote, Trump reiterated his pledge to give every adult U.S. citizen $5,000. Congress would have to approve that. And that can only happen if Republicans win, he told the audience.
The money will come through tariffs, he said, which Democrats want to stop.
The widely criticized promise is expected to cost more than $1 trillion. Recognizing that people don’t believe the payment will actually happen, Trump pointed to the $1,776 one-time bonus that went to active-duty military last December.
As he did at his Myrtle Beach rally for Graham ahead of the GOP runoff, Trump told attendees to pretend he’s on the ballot.

Gary Hawkins, of Anderson, is attending his first rally with President Donald Trump on Wednesday, Oct. 21, 2026. (Photo by Katharine Wilson/SC Daily Gazette)

But Trump’s backing doesn’t automatically win support for Graham, even among people lining up for the rally.
Gary Hawkins said he was there to see Trump.
“It means a lot that he took the time to come to Upstate South Carolina. This is a red state, red county, and I believe he stands up for the values in our community,” said the 52-year-old from Anderson attending his first Trump rally. “So, I’m here to support that.”
But he’s not sure he’ll vote for Graham.
“She just fell into place because of who her brother is,” Hawkins said.
Others thought Trump’s visit will increase turnout among GOP voters and help Graham win.
“I hope they will. I think they will, partially because President Trump supports her so much,” said Amy Rozelle, a speech pathologist from Spartanburg.

Amy Rozelle, of Spartanburg, heads toward the line for the rally headlined by President Donald Trump in Pendleton on Wednesday, Oct. 21, 2026. (Photo by Katharine Wilson/SC Daily Gazette)

Jennifer Lewis, also from Spartanburg, said she’s been a Trump supporter for years, “and it is amazing for him to be in our neighborhood.”
She was going to vote for the GOP nominees anyway, she said, adding “I also trust Trump’s recommendations as well.”
Gabriel Brey, who came from North Augusta with his 8-month-old daughter, said he wasn’t going to miss out on the “pep rally for adults.” He noted the rareness of a presidential visit in South Carolina ahead of a general election.
“It’s not historically a battleground state,” he said. “We wanted our baby to see a president for the first time.”
Ahead of Trump’s visit, Andrews’ campaign put out a statement welcoming him to the state.
“I hope he hears directly from the families, farmers, and workers who are paying more every month for groceries, gas, diesel, and health care, with the war in Iran driving prices even higher,” she said in the statement.
She also accused Graham of not having the “backbone” to stand up to Trump.
“Sen. Graham must do more than play politics — she needs to fight for South Carolina,” she said. “She’s asking President Trump to help her win an election, but she needs to ask him to end this war and lower costs for the families she represents.”
On Iran, Trump praised last year’s Operation Midnight Hammer and said “we’re close” to ending the war that began Feb. 28 with joint U.S. and Israeli air strikes.
Trump’s roughly 90-minute speech was briefly interrupted several times by protesters who yelled out, but they were quickly escorted outside.
The president praised officers’ speed: “Your law enforcement is fantastic! Man, they are so fast!” he said.
President Donald Trump rallies in Pendleton, South Carolina, to support Sen. Darline Graham’s campaign on Wednesday, Oct. 21, 2026. (Photo by Katharine Wilson/SC Daily Gazette)

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Fewer Georgians are planning to vote by mail, with one day left to request an absentee ballot
text:
Georgians turned in a record number of absentee ballots during the 2020 election cycle. This year, the number of absentee ballot requests has noticeably decreased. Jill Nolin/Georgia Recorder (file photo)Peach State residents who want to vote by mail in the midterm elections have one last day to file their absentee ballot request, and so far, Georgia is seeing less demand for that form of voting.
Mail-in voting is still an option for this year’s midterms. Here’s what voters should know.

About 154,000 absentee ballots have been requested as of Wednesday evening, according to data from the secretary of state’s office. Of the roughly 153,000 ballots that have already been sent out to voters, more than 62,000 have been returned and accepted. Georgia voters have until Friday to submit their absentee ballot requests to their county election office.
During the last midterm elections in 2022, nearly 286,000 voters requested an absentee ballot. This year that number is noticeably lower, despite the fact that overall voter turnout has hit record levels, exceeding 2022 numbers by over 12% as of Tuesday.
Bartow County election director Joseph Kirk, who is also the past president of the Georgia Association of Voter Registration and Election Officials, urged voters who might need to vote absentee to be proactive about filing their requests.
“If anybody might need one, go ahead and request it,” Kirk said. “After that Friday, I can’t accept any other applications for any reason.”
But voters who mark the wrong candidate, change their mind about voting absentee or are worried that their ballot might not arrive in time to be counted still have the opportunity to vote in person, according to Georgia Elections Director Blake Evans. Election workers at the polls can cancel an absentee ballot at a voter’s request and issue them an in-person one.
Early voting is underway in Georgia. Here’s where you can cast a ballot in your county.

So far, about 94% of Georgia voters have chosen to cast a ballot in person at one of their county’s early voting sites. Voters can also cast their ballot on Election Day at their assigned polling place. But for many residents — including older voters, voters with disabilities, military and overseas voters and college students — absentee voting may be the most convenient choice, or the only one available.
Georgia is a no-excuse absentee voting state, meaning anyone can vote by mail without needing to provide a reason. However, they must fill out an application from the secretary of state’s office in order to receive their absentee ballot. Ballots must be delivered by 7 p.m. on Election Day in order to be counted.
To request an absentee ballot, voters can complete a paper form or an electronic application found on the secretary of state’s website. The application must be printed out and signed, then voters can mail, fax, email or drop it off in person at their county registrar’s office. A full list of county election offices can also be found at the secretary of state’s website.

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: High-profile sex abuse case brings test for new Ohio anti-grooming law
text:
Getty ImagesThe arrest of a former executive at a Catholic charity organization in Columbus stands as a high-profile test of a new anti-grooming law passed just last year by Ohio lawmakers.
Scott Hartman faces a number of different charges related to allegations of sexual conduct with a minor, and one of the charges, misdemeanor grooming, didn’t exist before April 2025. Hartman has pleaded not guilty to all charges.
Hartman, 49, was arrested by the Franklin County Sheriff’s Office’s Internet Crimes Against Children Task Force Oct. 1, for “online sexual abuse of a minor,” according to a release from the office earlier this month.
According to the sheriff’s office, an investigation began in April of this year after a “teenage victim reported to school counselors that she had engaged in an online relationship with Hartman that included text messages and video calls involving video sex acts and the exchange of nude images and videos.”
The activities went on for six months before they were discovered, the sheriff’s office said, alleging Hartman attempted to meet the teenager for sex and “convinced the victim to delete any evidence and attempted to hide the fact that she was a minor.”
“Due to the nature of their conversations, one or more of his alleged social media accounts were shut down and reported to the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children,” the sheriff’s office said in a statement.
Hartman was listed as a senior vice president and chief development officer for The Catholic Foundation.
The foundation’s president and CEO, Loren Brown, said Hartman had been fired and the foundation was cooperating with law enforcement.
“What Scott Hartman did is a violation of trust and stands in direct opposition to our mission and our Catholic faith,” Brown said in a statement.
Hartman was indicted on Oct. 13, charged with pandering sexually oriented matter involving a minor and other related felony offenses, along with tampering with evidence, and a misdemeanor grooming charge.
The grooming charge was part of a bill enacted in April 2025 to update sex offense statutes in the state of Ohio. Other provisions were updates to civil actions related to misconduct alleged to have happened years, even decades ago.
Former Ohio state Sen. Bill Seitz, a Republican from Cincinnati, co-sponsored Ohio House Bill 322, which came about partly because of Ohioans who wanted more consequences for those who fail to report alleged sexual abuse, and those who have groomed victims before committing any sexual acts. But it was a balancing act to make sure those attempting to help children didn’t see unintended consequences.
“The trick, obviously, is to differentiate between the casual, sympathetic arm around the shoulder for somebody who’s facing an adverse childhood experience — which is perfectly legal — and something that shows elements of a pattern going well beyond that,” Seitz told the Capital Journal.
It was that pattern and proving intent in the pattern that gave the bill appeal, he said.
The grooming statute under which Hartman is charged states that no person older than 18 years old can “engage in a pattern of conduct” with anyone younger than 16 years old and four years younger than the adult when “the pattern of conduct would cause a reasonable adult person to believe that the person is communicating with a minor” for the purposes of sexual activity or preparing a minor to engage in sexual activity, according to the law.
The charge is a misdemeanor, a low-level offense which typically does not carry a significant prison sentence, unless charged alongside felonies.
While Seitz didn’t comment on Hartman’s case specifically, he said having the law in place will help not only be able to charge offenders in current cases, but allow more civil action and deter more serious crimes.
“I do not think there will be a huge influx of cases, just because it will be somewhat difficult to prove, but (supporters of the bill) wanted something on the books that would enable this kind of conduct to be nipped in the bud before it became far more serious,” Seitz said.
Also included in the legislation was a longer statute of limitations for charging those required to report any information about potential sex abuse crimes who fail to do so.
H.B. 322 moved the statute of limitations from two year to four, something mothers who talked with Seitz about bringing up the bill wanted to see. The group was advocating for more punishment particularly for priests accused of abuse.
“That was a concern that these mothers had, too, that by the time they found out that some of the priests were acting badly, the time for any possible prosecution of others who might have known of the priests’ malevolent activity were off the hook because the statute of limitations had expired,” Seitz said.
A third component of the law that was important to Seitz was updating a law from the mid-2000s, giving individuals the right to use civil action in cases where statutes of limitation had expired.
In the law, if a court finds in a civil proceeding that there is enough evidence to prove an individual is a child sex offender, Seitz said the individual would be placed on a sex offender list.
While he doesn’t think the law passed last year will lead to an overabundance of legal cases, he believes times have changed enough to make the laws enough to target abuses that he hopes are becoming “a thing of the past.”
“I think people were very, very relaxed in their attitudes back in the 50s and 60s, and even into the 70s,” Seitz said. “But now, all of these organizations have adopted pretty stringent requirements for training and for making sure that they’re not letting the wrong kind of people around the kids.”
In Hartman’s case, a bond was set at $750,000, and he remains incarcerated as the court case continues.

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Ohio labor market weakens in September
text:
Crews work on a construction site. (Photo by Dan Koeck, States Newsroom.)Ohio’s job market took a double hit in September, with unemployment rising and labor force participation falling, analysts report.
The number of jobs in some sectors appears to be falling in the face of rising prices and interest rates. Meanwhile, people are leaving the labor force as the state ages, working-age immigrants are deported and wages fall relative to inflation.
The Ohio Department of Job and Family Services last week reported that the state’s employers shed 5,000 jobs last month, according to Policy Matters Ohio. Unemployment rose from 3.3% in August to 3.4%, and inflation rose from 3.4% to 3.7%.
Meanwhile, participation in the labor force continued a decline that started in June of 2025. By September, Ohio’s participation rate stood at 61.2% compared to 61.8% nationally, according to the Buckeye Institute.
The reasons for falling workforce participation can be complex.
The measure doesn’t consider people who have aged out of the workforce, only those who are of working age and able-bodied, but not looking for a job. Those people are not counted in the unemployment rate.
Policy Matters reported that Ohio’s working-age population grew by 4,000 in September, yet labor force participation fell.
Before employers began pulling back in recent weeks, more jobs seemed to be available. President Donald Trump’s mass deportations appeared to remove many of the 2 million foreign-born men who left the country over the past two years, and 80% of whom were employed.
However, many of their jobs were in sectors such as construction and agriculture that native-born workers can be reluctant to fill.
In any case, the nonpartisan National Bureau of Economic Research in April found that large deportations hurt the labor force. Perhaps ironically, the study showed that they lead to drops in employment among native-born male workers.
Income inequality may also play a role.
Americans were already trapped in a post-pandemic affordability crisis when Trump began his second administration. Then he slapped high tariffs on most of the world and started a war with Iran, making it worse.
In a written statement Buckeye Institute Vice President of Policy Rea S. Hederman Jr. said inflation is making man Ohio workers poorer.
“While private-sector hiring was revised up from the August jobs report, September’s job losses kept private-sector employment flat over the past two months,” he said. “Ohio’s workers are struggling as inflation-adjusted wages have fallen over the last year.”
Ironically, people can become so financially stressed that they can’t afford to work. Things such as child care, transportation and even clothing can make it not financially worthwhile to take a poorly paid job.
Molly Bryden, a researcher at Policy Matters Ohio, said lawmakers need to take such workers into account as they try to address an economy that has so many struggling.
“Combined with inflation and lackluster growth, this should be an early-warning signal to lawmakers,” Bryden said in a written statement. “Federal and state lawmakers must re-prioritize and focus on worker supports to draw people back to the labor force, expand pathways to quality jobs with family-sustaining wages, and restore affordability through shared prosperity — rather than pushing ‘pro-business’ policies that leave working families behind.”

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Commentary: Ohio lawmakers cut state share of public school funding from 47% in 1999 to a projected 32% in 2027
text:
School students. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/States Newsroom)When Ohioans cast their midterm ballots over the next two weeks, many will be asked to vote for or against proposals for local tax levies, which includes more than 130 statewide school issues to fund what the legislature won’t in public education. 
Local property taxes are already the largest source of funding for most public schools across Ohio. Residential property owners are tapped out and plenty tired of schools coming to them hat in hand. But when district levies fail cash-strapped schools do without. Without staff. Without services. Without programs to enrich learning. 
Multiple public school districts have been forced to lay off teachers, cut courses and extracurriculars. Classroom size has swelled to capacity. Teachers are overburdened. 
Students get less than the optimum instruction they deserve. Educating the next generation of Ohioans should be the top priority of state leaders. 
Yet Ohio has repeatedly scaled back its investment in the public school system that educates nearly 90% of the state’s K-12 students. 
For almost 30 years the Republican-run legislature has shirked its constitutional duty to fund a “thorough and efficient system” of public schools and shifted the load of paying for local districts on to homeowners. 
The state share of public school funding has fallen from a high of 47% in 1999 down to an estimated 35% in 2026 and 32.2% for 2027.
Ohio ranks near the bottom nationally (around 45th) in state K-12 revenue. Statehouse Republicans appear determined to put public schools out of business.
In the current state budget, legislators scrapped the final phase of a six-year, bipartisan school financing formula that was designed to more accurately reflect the genuine cost of educating students and the financial capacity of each community to support its schools. 
The Fair School Funding Plan (FSFP) marked a significant step toward correcting the decades-old disparity in school funding that was heavily dependent on local taxes. 
But for the 2021 funding plan to be successful in fixing the long-broken, unconstitutional funding model for Ohio’s public schools it had to be sustained by future budget-writing lawmakers. It was not. 
The biennial budget for 2026-2027, passed by Republican majorities in the General Assembly and signed by Republican Gov. Mike DeWine, effectively abandoned and underfunded the FSFP by about $2.75 billion (compared to what the plan mandated) and provided just 5.7% of the state-level funding increase schools required based on the actual cost-based formula. 
Republican Ohio House Speaker Matt Huffman, who has done more to privatize public education in Ohio than anyone, called the proposal to fully fund the last two years of the Fair School Funding Plan a “fantasy” and claimed the state couldn’t afford it.
Ohio again spent more than a billion dollars on private school vouchers during latest fiscal year

Too expensive, scoffed Huffman while simultaneously funneling massive amounts of public money — over $1 billion annually — into private, primarily Christian schools. 
The state-paid tuition checks (with no strings attached) are called vouchers. 
Unlike state funding for public schools, that comes with oversight and accountability of tax dollars spent, there is zero accounting for Huffman’s private school boondoggle that finances religious institutions at the cost of local schools most Ohio kids attend. 
In the 2026 fiscal year alone, the total amount of public funds spent on Ohio’s five private school voucher programs was $1.173 billion. 
Almost half of that money, $532.8 million, went to the Education Choice Expansion vouchers that Huffman made universally available to every affluent family in the state (regardless of income) whose children attend private schools. 
Last week an Ohio appellate court concluded the EdChoice voucher program violated the clear language of the state constitution by effectively setting up a “competing system of uncommon schools that is not subject to the same obligations imposed on Ohio’s system of common schools.” 
The Ohio 10th District Court of Appeals ruling, which affirmed a lower court’s decision in 2025, noted that participating non-public schools on the public dole receive taxpayer funding in a manner that operates at the “detriment of Ohio’s public schools, and, consequently, the children who depend on those public schools for instruction, support, and opportunities that shape their future.” 
State Republicans shrugged off the expected ruling confident it will be overturned by the Republican-majority on the Ohio Supreme Court.
Meanwhile, Huffman & Co happily handed Ohio property owners an even heavier public school funding burden this election cycle — with a slew of school levy issues on the ballot to counteract the legislature’s latest round of reduced state-level contributions to K-12 education — while adding more than a billion in taxpayer subsidies to the tab to bankroll diocesan schools. 
Ohio’s 600-plus public school districts in the state can twist in a perpetual panic over funding shortfalls, negative cash balances, or severe deficits. 
Private school lobbyists got their voucher hooks in the general revenue fund and, with powerful GOP backing, they’re not letting go. But Ohio voters may want a say in the matter especially as they’re filling out ballots over the next two weeks that promise bigger tax bills to keep their public schools afloat. 
They may draw the line at subsidizing a “competing system” of parish schools when they’re already paying the lion’s share of one district’s operating budget. 
Why not find out definitively what Ohioans think about funding Huffman’s exploding universal private school vouchers program — twice ruled unconstitutional — with an up or down statewide vote? Seems fair.
Colorado, Kentucky and Nebraska did in 2024, and voters rejected the creation or expansion of private school vouchers in all three states. 
Ohioans are paying billions to prop up private schools while their public schools go wanting. The issue belongs on a ballot for Ohio voters to decide themselves.

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Enough is enough in Ohio on polluting data center gas power plants
text:
A server room in a data center. (Photo by Getty Images)Today, on Thursday, Oct. 22, at 6 p.m. at the New Albany High School, the Ohio Power Siting Board will hold a public hearing for the PowerConneX New Albany 3 Energy Center, the third major gas combustion plant to power an EdgeConneX data center in the New Albany International Business Park.
If approved, PowerConneX 3 will become the seventh gas plant to power a data center in the New Albany business park. Together these seven gas plants total 1936 MW – roughly equivalent to the electricity demand of over 1.3 million homes.
These seven gas plants have the potential to emit 11.9 million tons of greenhouse gas pollution, 766 tons of fine particulate matter, and hundreds of tons each of other harmful pollutants such as nitrous oxides, carbon monoxide, sulfur dioxide, volatile organic compounds, and hazardous air pollutants each year – all next to populated areas of New Albany and Licking County. 
Serious health effects
Particularly harmful to human health is the fine particulate matter – less than 2.5 micrometers or 1/30th the width of a human hair. 
This pollutant is breathed deep into the lungs, enters the bloodstream, and causes inflammation throughout the body. 
Extensive scientific evidence shows that long-term exposure to fine particulate matter is associated with heart disease, stroke, respiratory illness, asthma, and premature death. 
A 2026 study of a 135 MW gas plant powering a data center in Virginia found that it could result in $53 million to $99 million in annual health-related damages due to missed work, missed school, hospitalizations, and 3.4 to 6.5 additional deaths per year in the impacted region. 
The study was conducted by a Harvard-affiliated health scientist. 
The seven gas plants approved and proposed in New Albany have a combined power output 14 times larger than the gas plant studied in Virginia.
Most vulnerable are children whose lungs are still developing. Almost 13,300 children live within a five-mile radius of the business park where these seven gas plants will be operated.
Inefficient technology
One reason these gas plants powering data centers are so polluting is they are not using the best available technology. Most utility grade gas plants use combined cycle turbines, which generate electricity from the combusted gas in two different turbines. 
The gas plants in New Albany are using less efficient technology. This includes simple cycle turbines, which generate electricity in only a single stage, with the polluting exhaust and waste heat expelled out of a short stack at 800 degrees.
Even worse, the PowerConneX 3 gas plant will use 30 reciprocating internal combustion engines – like a gas car engine, only longer than a full-sized school bus and about as tall as a two-story house. Because this equipment is less efficient, it uses more gas to generate the same amount of electricity, resulting in more pollution.
Data centers are installing this more polluting equipment because it’s faster to procure and construct. But more pollution means accelerated climate change due to greenhouse gas emissions and worsened air quality due to pollutants like particulate matter.
That is not acceptable. According to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, July 2026 was the warmest month on record for the contiguous United States. This past July, the Columbus area set a record for the worst-ever air quality index since the Mid-Ohio Regional Planning Commission began keeping records in 1999.
Accelerated process
Another issue is the Ohio Power Siting Board’s process for approving the gas plants powering data centers. Five plants in the New Albany business park have already been approved – three through the accelerated application process that included no public notice, no public hearing, and automatic approval – not even a formal vote by board members. 
For the two gas plants approved through the standard application process, the siting board held public hearings as required. But these two hearings, held in August and October of last year, each had only two to three individuals offer testimony. All such individuals were either oil and gas industry representatives or representatives from unions whose members would financially benefit from these projects.
While the first few gas plants in New Albany were approved quietly, word is now getting out, and area residents have had enough. More than 50 people packed a New Albany meeting room on October 6 for the most recent public hearing on the 500 MW NEO Power Generation Facility, the fourth gas plant planned to power Meta’s Prometheus data center, and the sixth gas plant proposed for the New Albany business park.
Five representatives from the oil and gas industry and unions spoke in favor of NEO, while 20 people passionately voiced their opposition to the project. The opposition included a few environmental advocates from other parts of the state, but the vast majority were residents of New Albany and surrounding communities. 
While data centers say they are creating jobs and contributing to our communities, no amount of economic benefits can outweigh the cost to the environment and the public’s health that will result from a massive build-out of inefficient, subpar natural gas technology. 
One need not be against data centers, AI, or natural gas power to oppose these gas plants. Rather, this is simply too much, too fast, and too polluting.
