name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: House Democrats say GOP discord dashed hope for a skill games bill this year
text:
Pennsylvania Skill Games in a Delaware County convenience store. (Photo by Peter Hall/Capital-Star)A deal between state lawmakers to legalize and tax skill games is dead, leaders in the Democratic-controlled House said Wednesday.
House Appropriations Committee Chairman Jordan Harris (D-Philadelphia) said Senate Republicans were unable to muster votes needed to pass a skill games bill in the upper chamber, dashing hope for an agreement before the end of the legislative session next month. 
“I think it’s the worst kept secret in this building that over the last couple days we’ve been negotiating, trying to get skill games done,” Harris told the Capital-Star. “But at this juncture, the Senate Republicans have created a problem and have killed the solution, and therefore I don’t see that happening.”
A spokesperson for House Majority Leader Matt Bradford (D-Montgomery) confirmed negotiations with the Senate had ended but declined further comment. Senate Majority Leader Joe Pittman (R-Indiana) did not respond to a request for comment.
After Wednesday, only two session days for each chamber remain on the calendar in November. The General Assembly’s next session begins in January.
State lawmakers have been working over the last four years to pass a regulatory and taxing scheme for skill games. The effort intensified this summer after the state Supreme Court declared in June that the slot machine-like games are gambling devices required to be licensed by the state Gaming Control Board.
Before the ruling, skill games occupied a legal gray area created by lower courts that found the devices are distinct from casino slot machines because they give players a chance to win back their bets by completing puzzles and memory games. In the past decade, they became common in taverns, restaurants and private clubs, where owners said they depended on the extra money the machines brought in.
Recognizing the upheaval its decision would cause as an estimated 70,000 machines became contraband, the Supreme Court delayed enforcement of its ruling for four months. That Oct. 14 deadline prompted eleventh hour efforts to extend the deadline and find common ground between lawmakers who differed on details of a regulatory scheme.
Harris said he would not discuss the details of the proposed legislation, but debate has centered on how much skill game hosts, operators and distributors would be taxed, whether the Gaming Control Board would have regulatory authority, and how the additional revenue would be used.
“We’re still here if the Senate wants to run a bill out of the Senate, send it over,” adding that the House has bills that are already most of the way through the legislative process that can be amended to include skill game oversight.
Gov. Josh Shapiro proposed a 52% tax rate — comparable to casinos — as part of his 2026-2027 budget proposal. His office estimated it would eventually generate $2 billion in revenue for the state’s general fund. Shapiro said earlier this month in a debate against state Treasurer Stacy Garrity, the Republican nominee for governor, that he would use a core portion of the money for mass transit. 
Sen. Camera Bartolotta (R-Washington) told the Capital-Star last week that she and other rural senators opposed sending the lion’s share of the money to Philadelphia, where it is needed to offset a funding shortfall for the Southeastern Pennsylvania Transportation Authority (SEPTA).
Gaming industry sources said there was “still lots of disagreement” about competing proposals, including one to provide a portion of the revenue to the commonwealth’s ailing horse racing industry, which the state’s original gaming law was intended to support. Another point of discord centered around how licenses would be distributed and whether the games would be limited to establishments with liquor licenses.
Among the lawmakers pushing for an extension of the Supreme Court’s stay was Sen. Gene Yaw, whose district includes Miele Manufacturing, which produces physical skill game devices. He disagreed with House Democrats’ assertion that leaders had agreed on a bill to put up for a vote but conceded no action could be taken in the remaining days of the session. 
“Quite frankly, it’s too late to do anything now,” he said. 
While Senate leaders had endorsed a proposal to tax skill games at 35%, Yaw offered a competing proposal at 16%. Then as the deadline approached, Yaw and Sen. Anthony Williams (D-Philadelphia) proposed replacing the tax structure with a monthly $500 per-machine fee that would generate $300 million annually.
Senate Bill 1079 also would have addressed pop-up casinos, or store fronts that serve as skill game parlors with no other associated business, Yaw said.
He noted that the commonwealth’s skill game industry, which includes not only distributors like Georgia-based Pace-O-Matic, but also amusement companies that operate the machines and the establishments that host them, employs about 40,000 people. Yaw said some operators in his district and elsewhere have laid off dozens of workers since the ruling took effect. 
“My goal was to protect the jobs,” he said. “So where that income went, as long as it wasn’t starting some new pie-in-the-sky program, I would have gone along with it.”

name: VTDigger
title: State panel sanctions ex-Rutland officer for violations of anti-bias policing and other policies
text:
The Rutland City Police Department seen on Thursday, September 10, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

The Vermont Criminal Justice Council disciplined a second officer who worked for the Rutland  Police Department for violating the Vermont Fair and Impartial Policing Policy.
The council, which oversees police officer conduct in the state, voted Tuesday to issue a written warning to Nicholas Fontana for improperly seeking identification of people in a vehicle at a traffic stop and turning off the audio recording of his body-worn camera during the encounter.
“It’s my understanding from public records that he’s not presently working as a police officer in Vermont,” Christopher Perkett, the council’s associate general counsel, told the panel prior to the vote.
Fontana did not take part in the meeting Tuesday where the vote was taken, and he could not be reached for comment. Rutland City Police Chief Matthew Prouty also could not be reached Wednesday for comment. 
The council approved the written warning sanction for Fontana with no debate during the public meeting. 
Every law enforcement agency in the state must either adopt the state’s model Fair and Impartial Policing Policy or a stricter local one of their own. 
In this case, the violation was of the Rutland policy which says: “Absent reasonable suspicion of unlawful activity, Rutland City Police Department employees shall not require that passengers in motor vehicles provide identification or other documents. If requesting such documents, Rutland City Police Department employees will state that passengers are not required to provide them.”
The policy places restrictions on local, county and state law enforcement when it comes to immigration enforcement activities.
Fontana’s matter had initially been set for a contested hearing last month. However, the parties reached a stipulated agreement to resolve the matter, with the council voting to approve it Tuesday.
According to the stipulated agreement, Fontana is required to present the document imposing the written warning to any law enforcement agency in “any location or jurisdiction” where he may seek employment as a law enforcement officer.

READ MORE

The case against Fontana stemmed from his role in a traffic stop in 2025 when he worked as a Rutland City police officer, according to council documents. Fontana, the documents stated, had arrived at the scene of the traffic stop that was conducted by fellow Rutland City police officer, Tyler Tavares. 
During the traffic stop, the council documents stated, Fontana “intentionally muted” his body-worn camera during a period where he “interacted” with people in the vehicle, a violation of the body-worn camera policy..
At one point in the traffic stop, the documents added, Fontana asked for identification from the passengers in the vehicle and did not tell them they were not required to provide that information to him.
Earlier this year, VTDigger reported that the Vermont Criminal Justice Council issued a written warning to Tavares — also as part of a stipulated agreement — for violating the policy by contacting federal authorities to get immigration details about people in the traffic stop.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  State panel sanctions ex-Rutland officer for violations of anti-bias policing and other policies.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: DeSantis’ congressional map was designed to flip 4 seats to the GOP — Will it?
text:
CD-22 Democratic candidate Pia Dandiya (photo from Pia Dandiya campaign).Among the four seats Florida Republicans are supposed to flip from the Democrats this year following their mid-cycle redistricting is Florida’s 22nd Congressional District in South Florida.
The Palm Beach County district has been held for 14 years by Democrat Lois Frankel.
Its geographic bounds have shifted west. It now covers inland Palm Beach and the Broward County areas of Wellington and Parkland. It then moves further west to gather all of rural Hendry County and then into southern Collier County.
From a partisan perspective, it shifted from a district that voted for Kamala Harris in 2024 by more than five points to one that supported Donald Trump by more than 10 points.
As in other races in Florida, the new map set off a game of congressional musical chairs. Frankel dropped out of the race and ran instead in Congressional District 23. Democrat Pia Dandiya, 39, dropped her challenge to Republican Brian Mast in Congressional District 21 to run in the new CD 22.
She easily won the Democratic primary in August and now takes on 57-year-old Naples businessman Casey Askar, who defeated six other Republicans in his primary, winning 31% of the vote.
The new map sent to legislative leaders from Gov. Ron DeSantis’ office in May showed CD 22 flipping from blue to red, but that’s not guaranteed by any means in this political environment. The Cook Political Report recently shifted it to a “toss-up” election.
Dandiya is a 39-year-old Palm Beach native and daughter of Indian immigrants. A Harvard graduate with a B.A. in government, she is a former high school teacher and principal who later went to work for Apple.
Like many candidates from both parties this year, she’s running hard on an anti-corruption platform.
“If there’s one thing principals believe in, it’s celebrating progress but also holding people accountable. And I think that it’s time, as key measures to earn back the trust of voters across the country in government, to say we are standing strong against corruption — whether it’s banning congressional stock trading, whether it’s banning prediction market betting by members of Congress, ending Citizens United, and so much more,” she told the Phoenix last week.
After founding and serving for five years as principal at Democracy Prep Public School in Harlem, Dandiya spent a year working under both the Trump and Biden administrations as a White House fellow. She then worked for more than three years as a manager in the Strategic Initiatives Group for Apple. That’s been a point of contention for Republicans, who say she served as a lobbyist for the company.
Dandiya said she was leading public-sector initiatives, finding ways to use technology to better achieve outcomes in education and healthcare.
“These are ways that we can help our society be more connected and effective in reaching communities from so many different walks of life, and anyone at Apple who had even a single conversation with an elected or a state leader had to technically register as a lobbyist,” she said. “That job was very distinct from the full time corporate lobbyist that Apple does hire at the state and national level.”
CD 22 GOP candidate Casey Askar (from his Facebook page).
Casey Askar
Dandiya’s GOP opponent, Casey Askar, was born in Iraq and immigrated to the United States with his family when he was a child. He has said that they were Christians escaping religious persecution.
Askar responded to a request by the Phoenix for an interview by asking us to send him some questions, which we did. He did not reply upon receiving them, so we turned to publicly available information.
At 18, he signed up to serve in the U.S. Marines. He’s now a restaurant franchise owner with a net worth of $176 million, as calculated by Quiver Quantitative based on previous disclosures. This is his second bid for office. He ran in the 2020 Republican primary race in Florida’s 19th District, finishing third in a race won by Byron Donalds.
Askar is in synch with Dandiya in calling to ban members of Congress from trading stocks, but otherwise there are few similarities between the two candidates.
He says the Affordable Care Act needs to go and be replaced “with a vehicle that works for all Americans.”
In June, he said he wants to rename the Alligator Alley portion of I-75 the “President Donald J. Trump Interstate.” The president responded in September by endorsing Askar. However, on his website under endorsements, Askar lists eight individuals and CPAC but not the president.
In a recent interview with Newsmax, he said he was running “against a socialist.”
“A Harlem school teacher-principal that runs on a DEI-agenda, where the Democratic Party falls in the far-left. Transgender, LGBTQ,” he added.
He boasted about his abilities as a job creator, saying his company, Asker Brands, has employed thousands of people across the country and in South Florida, and that Democrats can’t run on a pro-business agenda.
“They have no substance. They just speak in non-sequitur, all hyperbole, vapid, no-nothings, just against our country. Hating our country. Hating our sovereignty and they’re socialists, communists. So, the message is very clear and we’re getting that to the voters.
Dandiya insists, “Unequivocally, I am not a socialist.”
She adds that she’d rather define herself by what she believes in, which is that she wants to be “a fixer, not a fear-monger.”
Money
There has been a lot of outside spending in this race.
Dandiya is getting a boost from a media campaign by the Everytown for Gun Safety Victory Fund and the House Majority PAC. The two Democratic PACS announced last week that they were spending $10 million to elect Moms Demand Action volunteers in CD 22 and seven other Democratic congressional races.
A Super PAC tied to President Donald Trump has spent more than $3.76 million against Dandiya, according to midtermmoney.com.
Republicans have about a 8-point voter registration lead in the district, but Democratic data analyst Matt Isbell notes that it contains a large block of moderate voters. On the same day the district backed Trump in 2024 by more than 10 points, data analyst Matt Isbell notes that it voted for Amendment 4, the ballot measure that would have enshrined abortion rights in Florida, by a 20-point margin.
In addition to CD-22, Democratic incumbents Jared Moskowitz, Kathy Castor, and Darren Soto all saw their seats redrawn to make it more difficult to win re-election next month.
Moskowitz moved to the CD 25 race, which the Cook Political Report now says leans Democratic. The Congressional Leadership Fund, the top Republican House super PAC, decided this week to cancel $6 million in planned television spending in the market, PunchBowl News reported Tuesday.
Cook lists Castor’s CD 14 seat as a “toss-up.”
Soto’s CD 9 seat in Central Florida was the most radically redrawn of any of the state’s 28 congressional districts, going from a 3.5-plus seat for Harris in 2024 to one that would have voted for Trump by nearly 18 points. That district remains “Likely Republican,” according to the Cook Report.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Senator facing theft investigation says he will resign if reelected, citing ‘changes in my judgment’
text:
Sen. Ron Alting speaks in committee on Wednesday, March 26, 2025. (Leslie Bonilla Muñiz/Indiana Capital Chronicle)Weeks after allegations of shoplifting broke, Republican state Sen. Ron Alting announced he will resign his Senate seat after 28 years if voters reelect him.
“Over the past several weeks, I have been undergoing extensive medical evaluation for concerning changes in my judgment, behavior and cognitive functioning. That evaluation has included specialists in neurology, geriatrics and mental health, as well as an MRI and other testing. That work is continuing as my doctors seek a definitive diagnosis,” he wrote in a lengthy Facebook post.
“During this time, I did things that were wrong and completely out of character for me. I take responsibility for my actions. I am deeply sorry for the hurt and disappointment I have caused my family, friends, colleagues, constituents and the store employees involved. After many difficult conversations with my family, my doctors and people I have trusted for many years, I have concluded that I need to bring my time in public office to an end and devote my attention to my health and my family.
“I have informed Senate President Pro Tem Rod Bray of my decision to resign from the Indiana Senate.”
(Screenshot from X)
A special prosecutor is weighing multiple Wal-Mart theft cases involving Alting in his Lafayette-area district. A new allegation just this week involves a Florida Wal-Mart.
Alting, 70, is on the ballot for reelection against Democrat Natasha Baker, though he took a step back from campaigning earlier this month.
“Because voting in this year’s election is already underway, my name will remain on the ballot. If I am elected, my successor will ultimately be chosen through the Republican Party’s vacancy process,” Alting wrote. “I have great confidence that this process will produce an outstanding leader who will serve Senate District 22 and its people well.”
The move could be a way to salvage Republican control of the seat as Baker has gained momentum in recent weeks.
Alting was first elected to the Indiana Senate in 1998 after serving on the Lafayette City Council for three years. He currently represents all of Carroll County and portions of Tippecanoe County and is the most senior member of the Indiana Senate.
He has been chair of the Senate Committee on Public Policy since 2011. In this position, he has presided over legislation including alcohol regulations and gaming matters.












Republican colleague Sen. Spencer Deery thanked Alting for his years of service to Tippecanoe County and the Indiana General Assembly.
“I know how much he loved serving his constituents in the Indiana Senate and that this must have been a difficult decision for him,” he said in a social media post. “But it was the right decision, and I applaud him for having the courage to make it. He will be in my prayers as he works with his doctors and navigates this transition.”












Alting is a widower and resides in Lafayette. He was born and raised in Lafayette. He graduated from Lafayette Jefferson High School and was inducted into the school’s hall of fame in 2001. Alting was also a part of the 1974 Lafayette Jefferson High School state finals basketball team.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: Advocates make case against measure to raise constitutional amendment threshold
text:
Voters participate in the general election Nov. 5, 2024, at Northview Church in south Fargo. Voters this November will decide a ballot measure that would require 60% approval for future constitutional measures. (Photo by Dan Koeck/For the North Dakota Monitor)A coalition of North Dakota-based advocacy groups has formed to oppose Measure 1, which asks voters whether constitutional amendments need at least 60% of the vote to pass.
The coalition hosted an event in Fargo on Tuesday to make their case against the measure, which they said changes a fundamental aspect of North Dakota’s political system.
“A minority vote would be able to overrule the will and the vote of the majority,” said Amy Jacobson, executive director of Prairie Action North Dakota. 
Talking to event attendees, including a group of University of North Dakota students, Jacobson said the measure would also take a longtime check on government out of the hands of North Dakotans.
“Measure 1 would, in our opinion, effectively eliminate that path for the voters and people of North Dakota,” she said.
Amy Jacobson, executive director of Prairie Action North Dakota, speaks to a group of University of North Dakota students about Measure 1 during an event at Railyard Offices in Fargo Oct. 20, 2026. (Ceilidh Kern/For the North Dakota Monitor)
During a debate about the measure on the Plain Talk podcast on Monday, proponent James Kerian, a Grafton businessman, said the majority of amendments voters have approved over the last 20 years — such as measures creating the Legacy Fund or passing term limits — have received 60% or greater support. 
“This is not some impossible-to-reach threshold that good ideas will not be able to clear,” Kerian said on the podcast.
Proponents of Measure 1, which was placed on the ballot by the Legislature, argue it should be harder to change the state constitution.
Jacobson is also a sponsor of Measure 2 to provide free school meals to K-12 students, which supporters brought after lawmakers rejected similar proposals.
Jacobson said that in her experience, measures aren’t put on the ballot “on a whim,” but rather come after years of unsuccessful attempts to work with the Legislature. She said the process is far from simple.
“It’s a very laborious process in order to come up with a policy and organize people in the campaign,” she told the group.
60% threshold for changing North Dakota’s constitution debated as a protection or a barrier

The American Cancer Society Cancer Action Network of North Dakota is another member of the coalition opposing Measure 1. The organization argues the measure would make it harder to advance public health protections.
Jessica Gilbertson, the network’s government relations director for the Dakotas, told the Monitor that while the organization isn’t working on public health-related ballot questions, recent developments in South Dakota show the importance of keeping that pathway open.
Advocates spent seven sessions trying to get Medicaid expansion through the South Dakota Legislature, Gilbertson said, before they decided to put the issue on the ballot instead.
“I feel like that’s a really good example of how many times people asked before they were able to get healthcare for 30,000 more people in South Dakota,” Gilbertson said.
That measure passed in South Dakota with 56.2% of the vote. 
“So if we were to have something like that come up in North Dakota that we really thought was important, that we brought back session after session after session and weren’t getting anywhere, this is the option,” said Gilbertson, who lives in Bismarck.
South Dakotans will also vote this election cycle on whether to raise the approval threshold for constitutional amendments to 60%. Gilbertson said her organization has been working to oppose both states’ measures.
Other members of the coalition are labor unions North Dakota AFL-CIO and North Dakota United, the League of Women Voters of North Dakota and North Dakota Watchdog Network.
[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: The info you need to cast your ballot.]
Protect the North Dakota Constitution, which opposes Measure 1, has raised at least $1.75 million in monetary donations, nearly all of that from Washington, D.C.-based Fairness Project, according to online campaign finance reporting. 
North Dakota House Speaker Robin Weisz, R-Hurdsfield, the chief sponsor of the bill that became Measure 1, last month pointed to the funding from the out-of-state interest group as a reason to support a 60% vote threshold to protect the interests of North Dakotans.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Illegal voting charge filed against noncitizen in Vigo County
text:
A volunteer holds a stack of clipboards with blank voter registration application forms — featuring a highlighted citizenship question, among others — after a judicial naturalization ceremony at the federal courthouse in downtown Indianapolis on Thursday, July 3, 2025. (Photo by Leslie Bonilla Muñiz/Indiana Capital Chronicle)Criminal charges have been filed against a Terre Haute man, alleging that he voted illegally in Indiana elections as a noncitizen.
The Vigo County charges announced Tuesday against Francisco Romero, 41, include one felony count each of submitting a fraudulent voter registration and perjury and three counts of casting illegal ballots in the 2022, 2023 and 2024 general elections.
The charges come 13 months after Secretary of State Diego Morales announced his office had identified a noncitizen in Vigo County who had completed voter registration with the Bureau of Motor Vehicles in 2018 and voted in six elections since then.
Attorney General Todd Rokita and Vigo County Prosecutor Terry Modesitt announced the charges that Rokita said represented the first prosecution in the state of a noncitizen for illegal voting.
Court documents filed by prosecutors say Romero was born in Mexico, has been in Indiana since 2006 and has remained in the U.S. under the the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals program. 
The DACA program, created by the Obama administration in 2012, is intended to help people brought into the country without legal documentation as children. 
Romero told investigators that he simply signed the voter registration forms given to him at the Bureau of Motor Vehicles branch in 2018 and 2023 and did not fill them out himself.
“He said that he did not know the box was checked saying he was a U.S. citizen,” the investigator’s affidavit said. “He claims that on both occasions, he advised the BMV employees that he is not a U.S. citizen.”
Romero was released on bond Tuesday from the Vigo County Jail, according to online court records. No defense attorney was listed for him and the Capital Chronicle couldn’t immediately determine a telephone number to contact him for comment.
The investigator’s affidavit cites BMV branch workers as having no memory of interactions with Romero, but saying that their procedure is to review the voter registration form twice with customers before they sign it.
The charges against Romero are each Level 6 felonies carrying potential sentences of six months to 2-½ years in prison.
Rokita and Morales announced last year that a federal agency review found 21 noncitizens had cast ballots in recent Indiana elections, along with 165 noncitizens who registered to vote in the state.
There are 4.7 million registered voters in Indiana.
“Voting by illegal aliens and other noncitizens is unacceptable, and anyone who commits that act must face consequences,” Rokita said in a Tuesday statement. “Two years ago, I started a process to verify the citizenship status of registered voters in Indiana and was successful in obtaining that data from the federal government. Now, we are acting on that information and it’s certainly not the end of our enforcement.”

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Campaign finance group seeks investigation into Roger Marshall’s alleged ethics violations
text:
U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall prepares to speak to a group of Kansas business leaders on Aug. 27, 2026, in Olathe. (Photo by Anna Kaminski/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — A national campaign finance watchdog group requested the U.S. Senate Ethics Committee investigate U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall of Kansas for using taxpayer funds to travel to political events and staff who work for both his office and campaign. 
End Citizens United, a PAC that supports campaign finance guardrails, compiled allegations from the past six years examining Marshall’s travel, his office staff’s expenses and communications and the absence of paid campaign staff in federal campaign finance reports.
The 22-page letter details trips Marshall took to New Orleans, where he attended the Sugar Bowl, to New York City for television appearances that coincided with boosts in fundraising, and a pattern of arranging at least one official meeting for trips to Dallas, Chicago and Philadelphia so that taxpayer dollars could fund the trips.
Across two trips to New York City in 2023 and 2025 where the only publicly identifiable official events were live appearances on Fox News, the organization found Marshall and his office staff spent a combined $23,000 in office funds for travel and per diem while the campaign took almost $120,000 from New York-area donors. 
The use of office funds for political travel and evidence of Marshall’s staff conducting campaign work without receiving campaign salaries provide the basis for the letter’s allegations, which Tiffany Muller, president of End Citizens United, said are among “the most egregious examples of government waste, fraud and abuse of taxpayer dollars.”
She urged the committee to investigate Marshall immediately. 
“While Kansans are working hard to make ends meet, Roger Marshall seems to think public office comes with an unlimited expense account courtesy of the American taxpayer,” Muller said. “The sheer arrogance of thinking he can simply declare a personal or campaign activity as official business to justify sticking taxpayers with the bill is astounding.”
The letter repeatedly relied on a joint investigation from Kansas Reflector and MS NOW, which obtained audio, video, photos, calendar items and screenshots of more than 200 text messages involving Marshall and his staff from 2020, when he first ran for Senate. Legal and ethics experts said the records appear to show Marshall and his top aide repeatedly crossed the line in terms of using congressional staff and government resources for a campaign.
Kansas Reflector and MS NOW also reviewed campaign finance reports, expenses and financial disclosures, and talked to multiple former staffers who recounted instances where the taxpayer-funded Senate office functioned more as an arm of the campaign.
In one instance revealed in the investigation and referenced in the letter, Marshall, then a U.S. representative, called a mandatory all-staff meeting in which he discussed campaign strategy. Following the call, staff documented in text messages their concern that Marshall violated Senate ethics rules.
​​The Senate Ethics Manual dictates it is “inappropriate to use any official resources to conduct campaign or political activities,” and Senate appropriations are for official representational and legislative duties.
Brent Robertson, Marshall’s chief of staff who is named numerous times in the letter’s allegations, told Kansas Reflector and MS NOW that the campaign does have paid staff. He said they are paid through an affiliated PAC that funds Marshall’s campaign. 
Payton Fuller, a spokesperson for Marshall’s office and campaign who appears in the letter, did not respond to Kansas Reflector’s request for comment for this story.
The letter detailed the senator’s itinerary for the late 2022, early 2023 trip to New Orleans where Marshall attended the Sugar Bowl that featured Kansas State University’s football team. It showed Marshall traveled from Washington, D.C., to Sarasota, Florida, where Marshall had a vacation home, to New Orleans and back to Sarasota before traveling to four cities in Kansas before returning to Washington.
“Put simply, taxpayers sent the Senator from Washington to Sarasota, Florida — to the location of his beachfront vacation home and the reported destination of at least 14 taxpayer-funded trips between 2021 and 2024 — then to New Orleans, then back to Sarasota, before he ever set foot in Kansas,” the letter said.
Campaign finance records also showed two disbursements dated Jan. 3, 2023, to New Orleans restaurants: $245.43 to Tujague’s and $421.21 to Justine.
The letter said it was unclear whether the $4,000 trip to New Orleans served any official purpose.
“It would be highly unusual for Senator Marshall to engage in any official activity during the holiday period, and the record contains no evidence of any official activity in New Orleans,” the letter said.
In a September 2025 trip to New York City, the itineraries for Marshall, Robertson and Fuller totaled $12,516.15, according to the letter. 
“And every one of them appears to have billed taxpayers per diem above the federal government’s standard rates — the Senator’s alone topped $1,000 a night — in a city where the maximum General lodging and meal rates were $342 and $92, respectively,” the letter said.
That trip also coincided with an influx in campaign contributions from the New York area, the letter said. The organization found 35 contributions, totaling $69,900, from 34 donors in the New York City area dated Sept. 10 through Sept. 16. Marshall was there from Sept. 11 to Sept. 14.
As Marshall has campaigned in a close race with his Democratic challenger, the Rev. Adam Hamilton, the letter said a pattern of questionable financial practices has continued. In federal campaign finance reports that encompass activity through Sept. 30, Marshall’s campaign, joint fundraising committee and leadership PAC have not reported salary or payroll payments, the letter said.
In the most recent filing, federal election records show Marshall’s campaign paid roughly $3,500 to Abbi Enders for campaign consulting and reimbursement on Sept. 3. Enders is also an assistant press secretary in Marshall’s Senate office.
“It is not plausible that a campaign spending at this scale has no staff,” the letter said.
Hamilton’s campaign spokesperson, Glynnis Harvey, said Marshall “is an example of Washington corruption at its worst.”
She said the details that continue to emerge about Marshall’s office are “deeply concerning” and “clearly warrant a deep and thorough ethics investigation.”
Hamilton previously called for an ethics investigation into Marshall’s use of taxpayer dollars.
Sherman Smith contributed to this story.

name: VTDigger
title: Vermont Conversation: ‘We can’t solve our problems with the same thinking that created them.’ Amanda Janoo would ‘lead a different way.’
text:
Candidate for governor Amanda Janoo speaks during a Democratic Party unity rally in Burlington on Wednesday, August 12, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
The Vermont Conversation with David Goodman is a VTDigger podcast that features in-depth interviews on local and national issues. Listen and subscribe for free on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, YouTube or wherever you get podcasts.
Who is Amanda Janoo? And how is this political novice polling closely with Vermont Gov. Phil Scott, now running for his sixth term?
“The conventional political wisdom would say I shouldn’t have a chance,” Janoo told me. “But I don’t think that these are conventional times.”
With two weeks to go before Election Day, we invited Amanda Janoo, the Democratic/Progressive candidate for governor, and Gov. Scott, a Republican, for separate interviews on The Vermont Conversation. Gov. Scott’s campaign declined. Janoo was eager to talk. 
Amanda Janoo grew up in South Strafford, and then attended Macalester College in St. Paul, Minnesota, where she earned a degree in political science. She went on to study at Cambridge University in the UK, where she earned a master of philosophy in development economics. For the past six years she has worked as an economics and policy lead for the UK-based Wellbeing Economy Alliance, which advocates for an economy that centers quality of life over economic growth.
Janoo’s only electoral experience in Vermont was being elected justice of the peace. But in March, she announced her candidacy for governor, and five months later she won a close primary against Aly Richards, a former aide to Gov. Peter Shumlin and CEO of the childcare advocacy group, Let’s Grow Kids.
Janoo’s signature policy is a state-backed program of free universal primary and preventive care. She estimates the program would cost over $300 million that would be paid for by a 2 percent tax on Vermonters with individual incomes over $250,000, and up to 8 percent on incomes over $500,000.
Critics have called Janoo’s plans “magical thinking” and cited Shumlin’s attempt to implement single payer health insurance a decade ago that he abandoned when confronted with its high cost. Janoo acknowledged that a full analysis by state fiscal and health officials would be needed.
Still, she argued that Vermont must confront the role of insurance and fee-for-service medicine in rising costs. “A profit-oriented healthcare system is a terrible idea,” she said. “We’ve got to move towards universal healthcare.”
Janoo would address Vermont’s housing crisis by taxing luxury second homes and private equity–owned housing, which she calls “extractive.” She has also called to ban AI data centers, invest in community schools, and support local food initiatives.
Janoo contrasts her approach to crisis leadership with Gov. Scott. She praised him as “a really nice man” who cares about Vermont and supported the state through Covid-19, but said his approach relies on an outdated economic playbook.
“We can’t solve our problems with the same thinking that created them,” she said.
Scott was widely praised for his leadership during the pandemic. Dr. Anthony Fauci, the country’s leading infectious disease expert, hailed Vermont’s response to Covid-19 as “a model for the country.”

READ MORE

With artificial intelligence, climate change, fiscal strain and democratic instability converging, Janoo said Vermont should seek to shape events rather than simply endure them.
“If it’s not Vermont, who’s going to do it?” she said. “There are a lot of opportunities for us to not just keep reacting to crises, but actually to proactively lead a different way.”
Janoo argued that the foundation for that shift already exists in the state’s libraries, granges, festivals, mutual aid and local initiatives. The role of government, she said, should be to “nurture, uplift and support” ideas already working in Vermont communities.
“This isn’t some utopian mission,” she said. “It’s already happening.”
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont Conversation: ‘We can’t solve our problems with the same thinking that created them.’ Amanda Janoo would ‘lead a different way.’.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Education Sec. Linda McMahon blames DEI for CT student not learning to read
text:
In a speech Tuesday extolling the second Trump administration’s education agenda, U.S. Secretary of Education Linda McMahon reflected on a news story she’d learned of a few months before she was sworn in.
The story was about a girl who had recently graduated from a Connecticut high school.
“She graduated with honors, earned a scholarship, and was starting college,” McMahon said. “But this same young woman — very, very bold young woman — decided to sue her local education board, alleging that she could not read or write.”
Those details sketch an almost perfect outline of the experiences of Aleysha Ortiz, who graduated from Hartford Public Schools in 2024 without knowing how to read. She sued the district not long after. The Connecticut Mirror profiled Ortiz in September of that year, and the story drew nationwide attention.
[RELATED: This Hartford Public High School grad can’t read. Here’s how it happened.]
McMahon offered her thoughts on what went wrong.
“This young lady’s school district has a budget of over $400 million. During her time there, the district employed about 1,800 non-teaching staff, such as a chief of talent and DEI,” McMahon said.
“The Biden administration devoted competitive grant funds to her district … to sponsor professional development surrounding diversity, equity and inclusion,” she added.
It all led to McMahon’s main point. The Trump administration has “taken billions away from DEI classroom initiatives and bureaucrat-centric projects and reinvested those dollars to supercharge the fundamentals: the ability to read well, write clearly, understand mathematics, and to think critically,” she said.
But Connecticut education leaders have a different diagnosis for what went wrong in Ortiz’s case. 
Hartford’s budget is large, as are the needs the district must address. A state review recently found the district is facing a deficit of tens of millions of dollars, a problem many link to the lack of taxable property in the city. There was broad bipartisan support among lawmakers this year for increasing state funding to public schools to help mitigate the problem.
Hartford Public Schools Superintendent Andraé Townsel has spoken frequently about his district’s fiscal plight in the past. For this story, however, the district declined to comment due to Ortiz’s lawsuit, which is ongoing. So did the chairperson of Hartford’s board of education, Shontá Browdy.
Former Hartford Association of Teachers President Carol Gale was not so hesitant.
“That’s crazy,” Gale said after listening to McMahon’s take.
As president of the teachers union, Gale said, she was often critical of how many directors Hartford had on staff. But “even if you got rid of some of the excess directors … it wasn’t going to make up for the millions of deficits that the city is facing constantly,” she said.
Nor did she think there was any merit to the idea that DEI efforts had contributed to Ortiz not learning to read. She recalled the DEI-related executive McMahon mentioned but said the position only existed for a couple of years before being cut.
Hartford Mayor Arunan Arulampalam also took issue with McMahon’s comments.
“Instead of supporting the hard work happening in our classrooms every day, federal leaders are traveling the country and blaming the challenges of Hartford Public Schools on the diversity of our students — this is why the federal government is failing public schools in America,” Arulampalam said in a statement.
Luke Bronin, who was mayor of Hartford when Ortiz attended the city’s schools and is now running for Congress, expressed a similar sentiment.
“Linda McMahon is actively undermining public education, and she couldn’t care less about kids with special education needs. She’s literally dismantled the Department of Education and handed responsibility for special education to RFK Jr. — who has no business dealing with our health, let alone kids’ education,” Bronin said in a statement.
Connecticut State Department of Education spokesperson Matt Cerrone said Gov. Ned Lamont and the General Assembly have made “significant investments” in literacy instruction in recent years.
“Through initiatives such as the Science of Reading Masterclass, high-quality instructional materials, professional learning, and literacy coaching, we are providing educators across Connecticut with the tools, resources, and support they need to meet the needs of their students,” Cerrone said in a statement.
Gale, the former union leader, pointed to the expansion of school choice programming as partially responsible for funding shortfalls. “I am convinced that the rise of magnet schools has spread out the dollars way thinner,” she said.
Students who leave Hartford for choice programs — Capitol Region Education Council (CREC) schools, for example — take a portion of sorely-needed state funding with them, district leaders have said. Hartford hired a firm this spring to recruit students back from CREC but faced pushback for potentially violating the landmark civil rights case Sheff v. O’Neill in the process.
School choice also happens to be a major part of the Trump administration’s education agenda, albeit in a slightly different flavor. A signature piece of that effort is the Federal Scholarship Tax Credit, which uses federal dollars to support scholarships for a range of purposes from private school tuition to third-party tutoring. Lamont has not yet said whether he will opt Connecticut in.
McMahon made it clear in her speech Tuesday that expanding school choice is very much the point.
“Whatever a parent decides for their child, our country now affirms what should have always been evident: That that choice belongs to you,” McMahon said.
The current president of the Hartford Federation of Teachers, Corey Moses, criticized the tax credit as an effort to privatize schooling in America.
“Instead of exploiting a student that our system failed, the secretary should join us in advocating for the resources needed to ensure every student can grow, achieve and prosper throughout their lives,” he added.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Rutgers does not need state OK to add new degree programs, judges say
text:
Two judges sided with Rutgers University in its fight for autonomy over new academic degrees, rejecting New Jersey's claim that the state can veto new programs. (Courtesy of Rutgers University)Rutgers University has sole authority over its academics and does not need the state’s approval to add new degree programs, as New Jersey higher education officials have long insisted, a state appellate panel ruled Wednesday.
The decision comes five years after state lawmakers expanded academic oversight of colleges and universities by giving the state Office of the Secretary of Higher Education veto power over new majors.
The office’s New Jersey Presidents Council had long been tasked with reviewing and commenting on proposed academic programs, but legislators in 2021 empowered state higher education officials to nix them if the council determines they would duplicate existing programs, require significant state funding, be unsupported by market demand, or fall short of “sufficient academic quality.” The members of the council, which was created by state law in 1994, are presidents and administrators of public and private universities and colleges.
But lawyers for Rutgers had argued that a string of laws dating back to the early 1900s that regulate higher education in New Jersey contained some exemptions for schools that existed before the late 1800s. Rutgers, now New Jersey’s flagship university with more than 69,000 students enrolled and over 27,000 faculty and staff, was founded in 1766.
So Rutgers challenged the new regulations soon after they went into effect in March 2022, saying they infringed on its autonomy and that state laws pardoned Rutgers from the new approval requirement.
Superior Court Judges Lisa A. Firko and Stanley L. Bergman Jr. agreed, reversing the Office of the Secretary of Higher Education’s administrative determinations in 2023 and 2024 that Rutgers had to comply with the 2021 changes.
“The State minimizes this expansion of its authority,” the judges wrote. “But, it is a significant difference for Rutgers.”
The appellate judges conceded that lawmakers began expanding state regulation over colleges and universities’ academic degrees in 1912 and repeatedly tweaked the regulations in multiple later laws. But those laws typically excused universities established 25 years or more before the 1912 law, which was 1887, the judges said.
And 70 years ago, New Jersey legislators passed the 1956 Rutgers Act specifically to prevent the state from exercising unlimited regulatory power over Rutgers, including by passing new statutes and regulations foisting new obligations on the school, the judges wrote.
That law also created Rutgers’ board of governors — a board that, by design, gives the state input over Rutgers academics, the judges added.
“The State was granted the authority to appoint the majority of the Board’s voting members (through appointment by the Governor, with the advice and consent of the Senate), and the Commissioner of Education was designated a non-voting member of the Board of Governors,” the judges wrote. “Thus, the Board of Governors serves as the oversight with respect to Rutgers’s academics and degree programs.”
Firko and Bergman also cited the Higher Education Restructuring Act of 1994 as a clear effort by legislators to restore autonomy to colleges and universities. That law gave colleges’ boards of trustees final authority over their institutions’ management, including program and degree offerings, they wrote.
“The Act was clearly intended to free public colleges and universities from the Department of Higher Education’s control over their operational decisions. Nothing in the Act’s history suggests that it was intended to impair Rutgers’s autonomy,” the judges wrote.
The judges said they also found no evidence the state has ever rejected any new programs Rutgers has proposed.
Dory Devlin, a Rutgers spokeswoman, didn’t have details Wednesday on how many and which programs the university has added or discontinued in recent years. But she said the school is “pleased” with Wednesday’s ruling.
“Today’s ruling preserves the University’s academic freedom to design and implement programs of its own choosing, consistent with its charter as codified under state law,” Devlin said.
Spokespeople for the state Attorney General’s Office and the Office of the Secretary of Higher Education did not respond to requests for comment.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Revealed: The money behind the last-minute fringe candidate ad blitz in Alaska’s U.S. Senate primary
text:
A super PAC listing this Wasilla office space as its address boosted a Green Party and fringe Democratic Party candidate in Alaska's U.S. Senate race. (Amy Bushatz/Mat-Su Sentinel)A left-leaning dark money organization and a GOP fund were among the groups behind the last-minute blitz of cash into Alaska’s U.S. Senate primary in August, when super PACs flooded the state with ads for fringe candidates on both the left and right, according to new filings with federal campaign finance regulators.
The ads were part of apparent efforts to boost lesser known candidates onto the four-person general election ballot who would dilute support for the mainstream candidates opposed by the groups.
At the time, the super PACs — Fair Deal Alaska and Right for Alaska — disclosed spending millions of dollars on mailers, phone calls and digital ads to boost Alaska U.S. Senate candidates like Richard Grayson, who lives in Arizona and said he was running “for fun,” and conservatives Gerald Heikes and Earl Southworth, who have reported no fundraising.
But federal law allowed the vast majority of the groups’ donor information to remain secret until after ballots were counted, which one critic describes as a major loophole.
“It’s outrageous that super PACs, which must, by law, disclose their funders, are able to game transparency rules in so many ways,” Michael Beckel, the director of money in politics reform at Issue One, a Washington, D.C. advocacy group, said in an email. “No super PAC should be able to avoid disclosing its donors until after voters have already made their choices at the ballot box.”
The policy issue, Beckel added, is a “bipartisan problem, and neither party has clean hands.”
“The sad reality today is that both Republicans and Democrats are pumping massive amounts of money into opaque groups,” he said, “leaving voters in the dark about which ultra-wealthy megadonors and special interests are trying to buy access and influence through large political contributions.”
The Aug. 18 primary resulted in Democrat Mary Peltola advancing to the general election along with incumbent Republican U.S. Sen. Daniel S. Sullivan and two other GOP candidates who could end up pulling votes from him: Heikes, and Petersburg teacher Daniel J. Sullivan.
Leading up to the primary, GOP-aligned Fair Deal Alaska spent more than $800,000 on mailers and phone calls to boost multiple fringe left-leaning candidates who, had they advanced to the general election, could have pulled votes from Peltola.
Fair Deal Alaska listed its address as a suite in a Wasilla office building that offers “virtual office and mail services,” and at the time, its officials did not respond to requests for comment about its ad campaign.

Graphic by Claude; data checked by the Anchorage Press.
Only this week did the group say where its money came from: $650,000 from Senate Leadership Fund — the main GOP group supporting U.S. Senate candidates across the country, which in turn has drawn much of its cash in recent months from Elon Musk.
Another $100,000 for Fair Deal Alaska came from Last Frontier PAC, a group supporting incumbent Sen. Sullivan that’s funded by wealthy conservative donors. The last $100,000 came from First Principles Digital, a super PAC that says it backs “pro-crypto” candidates.
Last Frontier PAC, Senate Leadership Fund and First Principles Digital did not respond to requests for comment on their contributions to Fair Deal Alaska.
The Democratic-aligned Right for Alaska, meanwhile, spent nearly three times more. Much of its $2.35 million went toward boosting fringe Republican and other conservative candidates in apparent efforts to put candidates on the general election ballot who could pull votes from Sen. Sullivan.

Democrat-aligned Right for Alaska created this website boosting retired Petersburg teacher Daniel J. Sullivan, who Republicans accuse of trying to dupe supporters of incumbent GOP U.S. Sen. Daniel S. Sullivan. (Screenshot)
Because of the late timing of most of its contributions, Right for Alaska had to disclose only the donor behind a single $100,000 contribution, a retired Massachusetts doctor. The group’s officials did not respond to requests for comment at the time.
New filings made in September show that the rest of Right for Alaska’s money came from two groups. Roughly $1 million came from Sixteen Thirty Fund, described by Politico as “the left’s preeminent dark money hub,” which put more than $300 million into liberal causes and elections in 2024.
Sixteen Thirty Fund is a 501(c)(4) “social welfare” nonprofit, meaning that it does not have to disclose its donors. The fund did not respond to a request for comment sent Thursday.
The rest of Right for Alaska’s fundraising, another $1.3 million, came from what the group identified as an Alexandria, Virginia-based contributor called “Liberty Force Action Fund.”
There’s no evidence of that group’s existence online — Google returns no results for a query of its specific name — though its Alexandria post office box was once used by a Texas-based company called Liberty for All Inc.
The same political operative behind Right for Alaska, Thomas Datwyler, is also affiliated with another apparently Democrat-aligned super PAC, Alaska Values, that this week disclosed more than $1 million in spending to oppose the incumbent Sullivan and boost Heikes, the Republican U.S. Senate candidate who’s reported no fundraising.
New Facebook ads from Alaska Values feature a man attacking Sullivan for supporting for “the largest debt increase in history,” and urging viewers to vote only for Heikes on their ranked choice general election ballots. The group has not yet disclosed any of its donors.
Beckel, the campaign finance reform advocate, said that proposed federal legislation already exists that would force groups like Right for Alaska, Fair Deal Alaska and Alaska Values to disclose information about “large, last-minute campaign contributions.”
The Stopping Hidden Interests and Non-Disclosure in Elections Act, or SHINE Act, was introduced earlier this year by Democratic Rep. Jason Crow of Colorado. It remains stuck in committee.

title: US Supreme Court allows gender-affirming care for trans people in federal prisons
text: WASHINGTON — The U.S. Supreme Court Wednesday denied the Trump administration's emergency request to implement a rule that would terminate gender-affirming care for transgender people incarcerated in federal prisons. It means a lower court order that blocked the policy from going into effect will remain in place for now, and gender-affirming healthcare for transgender inmates will continue. “This is a critical ruling for our clients and all transgender people in Bureau of Prisons custody,” Li Nowlin-Sohl, senior staff attorney with the ACLU’s LGBTQ & HIV Project, said in a statement. “The denial of medically necessary health care, including gender-affirming health care, to people in prison is a violation of their fundamental constitutional rights.”  The order did not give an explanation. But conservative Justices Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas noted that they would have sided with the Trump administration’s request to stop treatments by lifting a lower court's injunction. The block has been in place since June 2025 by the District Court for the District of Columbia.The suit stems from President Donald Trump’s executive order that prevented the Bureau of Prisons from providing gender-affirming care to transgender inmates.In response, the American Civil Liberties Union sued, representing roughly 1,000 transgender inmates who have been diagnosed with gender dysphoria, which is treated with gender-affirming care such as hormone therapy and other care. The class action lawsuit was filed first by two transgender men and one transgender woman at federal prisons in Florida, Minnesota and New Jersey.The suit argued that the policy violated the Eighth Amendment protections against cruel and unusual punishment. In a brief to the Supreme Court, the Trump administration argued that it rejects recommendations from the World Professional Association for Transgender Health, previously followed by the Bureau of Prisons. The Department of Justice contended the recommendations “did not reflect the latest scientific information,” and that the prior policy “raised security and prison-administration concerns that outweighed whatever limited benefits they had.”

title: The 2024 gun law has saved lives. A yes vote on Question 9 will keep it in place.
text:
MASSACHUSETTS HAS THE lowest rate of gun deaths in the continental United States, a statistic that is cause for celebration and one that we earned through our commonsense firearm safety laws. Study after study proves that our laws save lives and are designed to keep firearms out of the hands of those who cannot safely possess them. 
We know that if we walk back our gun laws, the number of firearm-related deaths in our state will increase. That is why we are concerned by radical interests that are trying to reverse the policies that have made us the safest state in the nation. Those groups have put a question on this November’s ballot—Question 9—that would repeal the landmark 2024 law that has kept Massachusetts at the forefront of gun safety. A “yes” vote would uphold the lifesaving law; a “no” vote would repeal it. 
As the architects of that gun safety law, we worked closely with all stakeholders – from police chiefs and district attorneys to gun owners and community violence prevention organizations – to identify trends in gun crimes and gun violence. We then used their input to craft a law that provided public safety officials with the tools they need to respond to the increases in illegal firearm trafficking and to make us all safer without infringing on the rights of lawful gun owners. 
Put simply, the law focuses on the root causes of gun violence to make all Massachusetts communities safer – and it is working.
Before the law’s passage, bad actors sold “ghost gun” kits that allowed the purchasers to build untraceable firearms and then flood our streets with them. Because of old legal definitions, our law enforcement professionals were essentially powerless to seize these firearms before they hit our streets, resulting in a growing number of shootings and other crimes across the Commonwealth involving ghost guns. 
The old laws also did not account for new technology in firearm modifications, like so-called “Glock switches,” that converted traditional guns into automatic weapons capable of spraying dozens of bullets in a matter of seconds.  
Massachusetts law enforcement officers were well-aware of these problems and eager to respond to them—but they lacked the authority they needed to get ghost guns and Glock switches off the streets. The 2024 gun safety provided that authority, and we are all safer as a result. 
The law includes dozens of additional provisions that promote community safety, and we will highlight a few that are representative of our commonsense approach to reducing gun violence. 
The law says that if you are too drunk to drive, you are too drunk to hunt or carry a firearm.  
It aligns our laws on harassment prevention orders with our domestic violence restraining order laws, allowing a court to require a defendant to temporarily surrender their firearms after a hearing.  
The law allows our gun licensing authorities to review police reports detailing an applicant’s involuntary mental health hospitalization if one exists. 
And it makes crystal clear that a copycat or duplicate of an illegal assault-style firearm remains illegal. 
Despite the rhetoric you will hear from those who wish to remove these safety measures, the 2024 gun safety law does not infringe on lawful firearm ownership. If anything, it streamlined and made clearer the rights and expectations of an applicant. The numbers bear this out. Last year, the first full year after the new law took effect, Massachusetts gun licensing authorities issued seventeen percent more licenses to applicants that the year before. 
Under the 2024 law, Massachusetts residents who are eligible for gun licenses have no problem getting them. The law, as it should, makes it more difficult for criminals and those who pose a risk to themselves or others to legally possess firearms. We think this is, well, commonsense. 
While we find it regrettable that the lifesaving 2024 gun law is facing a referendum sponsored by Second Amendment absolutists, we also recognize that Question 9 is an opportunity for all of us to affirm that we deserve safe streets and that we deserve laws that keep guns out of the hands of those who cannot safely handle them.  
This November, we will be voting “yes” on Question 9 to keep Massachusetts safe for all of our residents. 
Cynthia Creem, a Democrat from Newton, is the Senate majority leader. Michael Day, a Democrat from Stoneham, is House chair of the Joint Committee on the Judiciary.
