name: VTDigger
title: Picture future you: How young teens can explore their potential at VSAC’s career and STEM fairs
text:
Think back to middle school. Maybe you hadn’t thought much about life beyond high school, or maybe you hadn’t spent much time outside of your community or home state. What if someone encouraged you to think bigger and more broadly about your possibilities? What if you could find a way to reach out of your comfort zone and into your curiosities? 
That’s the experience LaKysha Patnode had when she was a student, and exactly what she’s hoping to pay forward for other Vermont kids when she spends a day at VSAC’s Career and STEM Fair.
LaKysha Patnode and her colleague, Ryan Gillen of Champlain College, at their booth at the career fair.
LaKysha says she didn’t know what she wanted to do and she definitely wasn’t thinking about college when she was at Colchester Middle School and the Center for Technology in Essex. But her experience with VSAC’s GEAR UP college and career readiness program, and her VSAC outreach counselor (who, in LaKysha’s words, “believed in me 100% at a time in my life when I didn’t know what I wanted to do or how to get there”) encouraged her to explore and try. 
With help, LaKysha went to Champlain College, graduated with a bachelor’s degree in computer networking and cybersecurity, and went on to get her master’s degree, also from Champlain, in information security operations. 
Now, LaKysha is an information assurance advisor at nuHarbor in Burlington. In plain terms, that means she works in cybersecurity, on data security and privacy. When she presented at VSAC’s Career and STEM Fair in Lyndon earlier this month, LaKysha was excited to see so many students engaged in her session, where she provided hands-on demonstrations about cybersecurity hygiene and how to protect their privacy when, for example, they download a new app to their phone. “Most kids don’t think about checking the permissions associated with that,” she said. “Does every app need access to your microphone, camera, and all your contacts? No!” 
LaKysha says it’s meaningful to her to have the opportunity to help broaden horizons for the next generation. “I feel like my journey is a testament to what can happen when people see potential in you at a young age,” she added. “Because of VSAC’s GEAR UP, I was thinking bigger about my own possibilities. Then, Champlain and nuHarbor’s partnership is why and how I ended up here. All along the way, I was encouraged to make connections and reach out of my comfort zone. Opportunities like these career fairs really help. Even if the students don’t realize it, these are the building blocks for how you move forward professionally.” 
A day of hands-on experimentation nudges students along
Courtney Skar is a school counselor at Montgomery Elementary School, which serves children through 8th grade. She says that participating in the fair helps her students relate things they are learning at school to real life examples and picture themselves as adults. Everything at the event is a conversation-starter, helping kids think about the connection between their interests, the skills they notice about themselves, and potential future careers. 
“I had to pull students away from the hands-on parts,” she laughed. “There were robotics and coding opportunities, where kids could steer robots, medical exhibits where students were able to wear a team vest and go through a scenario, a LEGO racetrack where they could understand the dynamics that made cars go faster or slower, and a science area where they were building cells and talking about how things work. At this point in the year, we’ve started some conversations about their future that get them thinking, but the career fair is a real catalyst that escalates ideas and reinforces where they can go and what they can do.” 
Courtney, like LaKysha, benefited from VSAC’s support when she was in school. As a participant in VSAC’s Talent Search for first-generation students motivated to attend postsecondary education, Courtney leaned on the support the program provided to navigate the college search process and to visualize her own career. “That experience is what led me to work in schools, and it’s such a neat experience to help realize those connections for the next generation,” she said. 
“When your students come back feeling a little more like they can see themselves as their future adult selves, that’s a win,” she added. 
Self-designed bikes propel students to think about engineering careers
A little over a week later, VSAC hosted nearly 400 students on the Castleton campus of Vermont State University for a fair of similar format in the Rutland area. 
James Holden is an engineering instructor at Stafford Technical Center. He brought four students with him to the event to showcase their mechanical engineering projects, which are unusually engineered bicycles. 
Each Stafford student succeeded in creating their own design and translating it into a machine shop project and then a final product. The students were motivated to finish their projects for the fair and excited to showcase them there. 
About 170 middle schoolers donned helmets and rode the bikes, which ranged from one with caster wheels to encourage rotation and drift, one with hand pedals and feet steering, and one with handlebars similar to a zero-turn mower and a treadle pedal. These unique engineering creations were a hit at the event, with middle schoolers able to ride them and learn about why they were engineered the way they are. They were also able to see Stafford students—not much older than they are—take pride in their projects. 
“Not everyone feels successful in every subject or in every learning environment,” James said. “When we show the STEM fair attendees that we can offer learning in a different way and with projects kids can really see themselves in, they start to see how they succeed.”
All told, nearly 1,200 students from 27 middle schools across Vermont explored STEM identities and future career pathways at two Career and STEM fairs, in the Northeast Kingdom and Rutland. VSAC’s Career and STEM Fairs are held annually and produced in partnership with Vermont State University, Careers CLiC, the Vermont Department of Labor, and the J. Warren and Lois McClure Foundation, as well as the many local employers and organizations who gave their time to engage and inspire students. 
Looking ahead, VSAC will host a virtual career panel for middle school students across the state in November. If the Career and STEM Fairs are any indication, Vermont’s extraordinary students will bring curiosity, energy, and enthusiasm from start to finish!

The Vermont Student Assistance Corp. was created by the Vermont Legislature in 1965 as a public nonprofit agency. We advocate for Vermont students and their families to ensure that they have the tools they need to achieve their education and training goals. We create opportunities for all Vermont students, but particularly for those—of any age—who believe that the doors to education are closed to them. Growing families save for education with VT529, Vermont’s official 529 savings program. To help Vermonters plan and pay for college or job training, our counselors work with students in nearly every Vermont middle school and high school, and are also available to work with adults. name: California
title: Big California state worker strike set to begin today
text:
A tablet at the counter of the Department of Motor Vehicles in Fresno on Oct. 2, 2026. Photo by Larry Valenzuela for CalMatters




Perhaps today is not the best day to go to the DMV.
California state workers are planning a one-day strike today in multiple cities including Sacramento, San Francisco and Los Angeles. They’re protesting what they say are unfair labor practices by Gov. Gavin Newsom’s administration. The work stoppage could affect services at the DMV, unemployment offices and other departments. 
SEIU Local 1000 represents about 100,000 workers employed in dozens of agencies across the state. They’re accountants, government analysts, nurses, IT workers, custodians and more.
The union has been negotiating a new labor agreement since its contract expired on June 30, and is demanding better pay, more affordable healthcare coverage and more flexibility to work from home. 
CalHR, the state agency that handles state labor negotiations, said it “remains focused on achieving a fair and responsible agreement and continues to be available at the bargaining table.”
With as many as 95,000 union members eligible to strike, you may experience some delays in government services. DMV offices might close early, according to a department spokesperson. State parks could be affected, too, though rangers are not represented by Local 1000. Hearst Castle in San Luis Obispo County, for example, adjusted its tour schedule to accommodate people who already have reservations.
This may not be ideal from a customer service standpoint, but union president Anica Walls urges Californians “to give our employees some grace.”
The union is taking a risk with the strike, noted former state Senate President pro Tem Don Perata. He supports labor and wants the union to get a good deal. 

Perata: “Somebody ought to pay attention to them. The strike costs those people a lot more than anyone else.”

Read more.
More on the labor fight: Local 1000 was once in Newsom’s corner, kicking in $1 million to help him fight a recall campaign. CalMatters’ Adam Ashton has more on what led to today’s strike, including the wage cuts that Newsom demanded to get out of a budget jam. 



Join CalMatters, AAJA Sac, ABC 10 and The Sacramento Observer for a free VotingMatters event today in Sacramento. The event enables attendees to learn and discuss the upcoming election and focuses on the ballot propositions and insurance commissioner race. Register here to attend in person.
Other Stories You Should Know


Taxing the rich, but not just billionaires


Students at an eighth-grade science class at Lawson Middle School in Cupertino on Aug. 26, 2025. Photo by Florence Middleton for CalMatters




The billionaire tax may be drawing the most attention on the ballot, but another tax-the-rich proposal will face voters in November too, reports CalMatters’ Carolyn Jones.
Proposition 3 would permanently extend an income tax on the wealthy to fund schools, healthcare and other state services. Voters first approved the tax in 2012, when it was first touted as a temporary measure, and then renewed it again in 2016. Now, supporters are asking voters to make it permanent before it expires in 2031.
The tax generates between $5 billion and $15 billion a year. In flush years, it makes up about 15% of the state’s overall K-12 education budget. If it doesn’t pass, school districts will be forced to lay off up to 50,000 teachers, according to the California Teachers Association.
But at 13.3%, California already has the highest personal income tax rate of any state. The Howard Jarvis Taxpayer Association, an anti-tax advocacy group, questioned whether schools need more money given their declining enrollment.

Susan Shelley, the association’s vice president: “We have fewer and fewer students. Does this mean we need fewer teachers? Maybe it does.”

Read more.



Where lives depend on levees


A repaired section of the levee near Isleton on the Sacramento River on April 1, 2025. Photo by Miguel Gutierrez Jr., CalMatters




A state audit has found that California water officials aren’t doing enough to make sure levees in the Central Valley are adequately maintained to protect against flooding. But water managers argue that stepping in to oversee more than a thousand miles of levees and flood control structures isn’t so simple, writes CalMatters’ Rachel Becker. 
The audit warns that nearly a third of agencies maintaining flood control levees on the tributaries of the Sacramento and San Joaquin rivers have been carrying out “unacceptable routine maintenance.” It also said the state’s Department of Water Resources has not taken over levee maintenance when local agencies fail to do so, despite it being required under state law.
But state water managers said it would take at least $165 million more per year than they or local agencies currently spend to fully address the issue. The department also told the auditor that levee risk depends on the threat, the levee’s performance, and what it protects — not just its maintenance.
Read more.



And lastly: Tell us your car crash story


Loren Chow holds a photo of his wife, Jenny, who died in a 2022 semitruck collision, at the home they shared in Los Altos on Aug. 19, 2026. Photo by Anna Hoch-Kenney, CalMatters




This week, we brought you the latest installment in License to Kill, a series investigating the staggering rise of deaths on California’s roads. 
Our reporters are now hard at work on their next story, and they could use your help. 
If you have a story about someone being killed or badly hurt by a driver who wasn’t prosecuted, we want to hear from you.

CalMatters columnist Dan Walters: The federal government’s crackdown on voting by noncitizens aims to bolster President Donald Trump’s unproven claims of widespread voter fraud rather than combating serious crime.
The state’s mandate forcing a California school district to leave a Nevada high school athletic program because of Nevada’s exclusion of transgender athletes is loaded with logistical challenges, writes Xavier Jimenez, who helps manage a ski shop and lives in Truckee.
